en: A Concise Commentary on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle One; Treatise Text, Part One and Two.
Compiled by Ji.
I pay homage to the Honored One, the Great Awakened One of devas and humans, whose merit and wisdom are both perfectly complete.
To the unsurpassed and most wondrous Dharma of the words and meanings of the *Anuttara*, To the noble Saṃgha who receive and study it with right wisdom,

Because it is uninterrupted,
it is called "continuity.
As for "concomitant":
Because the seeds always function in conjunction with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Regarding their establishment:
they are established based on these nine stages in relation to the eighth consciousness.
The seeds that proceed in continuity together establish four characteristics.
It does not depend on active manifestation for three reasons: first,
because it is a single continuity.
Second, because they are the causes of all phenomena;
third, because they are not separate from consciousness.
If one speaks of seeds:
He then spoke of the various consciousnesses; another interpretation says:
within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), all seeds [are contained].
The four characteristics are established upon the dharmas that proceed in continuity; that is to say,
they are based upon all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
The four characteristics are established because all conditioned phenomena— whether contaminated or uncontaminated—
if they arise, necessarily function together with their seeds.
This is a general explanation of the meaning of the four characteristics based on both the manifest and the seeds;
it states that "change" occurs immediately after "arising."
This has two meanings.
First, it causes [beings] to develop revulsion;
that is, to reveal that the very nature of arising is subject to transformation and is thus not to be cherished.
If one were to speak of "abiding" immediately [after arising],
it would give rise to much attachment and delight because of the production of abiding; furthermore,
[the sūtra] intends to show that the various characteristics have no distinct time of activity.
This is precisely the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).
Its name differs from those of the preceding and succeeding [characteristics].
Since this is so, that which follows and continues [the arising] is named "abiding" (*sthiti*).
Because it is subsequently designated as "cessation" due to its non-abiding,
this differs from other schools regarding the two types of distinct natures.
The first refers to the difference between preceding and succeeding moments within the same category of phenomena;
the latter refers to the difference between preceding and succeeding moments across different categories of phenomena.
This [text] speaks only of arising.
It arises by the power of conditions;
the others are established based upon this,
without depending on further causes for their formation.
Therefore, it is said that [the categories] are established separately by means of concise terminology and distinct states.
The *Khyāpana-kārikā* states:
"Because they are contrary to the causes of arising."
If there were no causes for abiding or cessation,
it would entail the fallacy of being naturally abiding and eternal;
therefore, one should know that [cessation] occurs spontaneously.
This is as explained in the fifty-second [chapter] and in the second chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* regarding the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*).
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the designation of the names;
second, the general presentation of the essential nature of the four conditions.
Third, furthermore, from the passage beginning "by way of seeds," the mind is specifically indicated to demonstrate the four conditions,
as explained at length in the seventh chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. As for the substance of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*):
He said: "It refers to conditioned phenomena directly producing their own results;
first, actual manifestation."
Regarding the two types of seeds:
as for why only "seeds" are mentioned here,
that assembly stated:
There are those who claim that only the seed is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*);
they do so based on emphasizing what is prominent,
rather than stating it exhaustively according to the principle.
The Noble One taught that the evolving consciousnesses and the ālayavijñāna serve as mutual causes and conditions for one another. As for the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya),
it refers to the eight manifest consciousnesses.
Together with those mental factors,
the preceding aggregate equally opens the way for the subsequent one,
causing it to arise with certainty.
In the fourth fascicle of that [text], this passage states:
"If this consciousness is immediately followed by the arising of that consciousness," this is a general statement with a specific intended meaning.
The meaning is not contradictory. Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), he says:
"It refers to any phenomenon (*dharma*) that..."
This carries its own characteristic;
it may be associated with the mind,
or that which is contemplated or relied upon.
This essence is twofold:
first, the direct;
second, the indirect.
This general explanation is likewise not contradictory. Regarding the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), he says:
This means that if there is a phenomenon possessing a superior power or efficacy that can either accord with or oppose other phenomena;
as he himself stated in his commentary:
Although the first three conditions are also sovereign conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
the present fourth [condition] excludes those and takes up the remainder.
In order to clarify the specific distinctions among the various conditions,
it is now stated here: "That is to say,
with the exception of the seed, it refers to the remaining bases and their auxiliary companions."
Regarding the "other basis," this refers to the exclusion of the equal-and-immediate basis; therefore,
it is not explicitly stated that the objective sphere [is the basis].
Furthermore, because it is known that [the mind] excludes its objects of perception (*ālambana*),
the four conditions are manifested based solely on the mind; thus,
mental factors (*caitta*) are not stated to be the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Regarding the sixth [category], the enumeration of the "wholesome and so forth," only three types of wholesome are established because those that lack ultimate meaning are said to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
"Wholesome pertaining to the portion of merit" refers to wholesome states conducive to saṃsāra;
"wholesome pertaining to the portions of liberation and penetration" refers to those conducive to liberation and the stages of penetration.
As stated in the *Abhidharmapitaka* (Dharma-skandha-pāda),
the thirteenth chapter, and its *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*: "The right efforts that are wholesome" refers to the four right endeavors (*samyak-prahāṇa*).
It is also called "right abandonment" (*samyakprahāṇa*),
because it excels all evils and because its essential nature is preeminent.
Because it is not wrong effort, it is called right exertion (*samyakpradhāna*).
"Immeasurable wholesomeness" refers to the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*). "Wholesomeness with a basis" refers to...
There is that which relies on seeking;
seeking the good within the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*). As for the good that is without reliance, it is that which does not rely on seeking.
Aspiring for nirvāṇa is wholesome.
Furthermore, giving material things is called wholesome with a basis;
rejoicing without material things is called wholesome without a basis.
Wholesome states that possess signs are called "wholesome with a basis.
All signless wholesome states are called "wholesome without a basis.
The essence of cultivated wisdom is called "fundamental wholesomeness," while the five aggregates associated with it are called "concomitant wholesomeness."
Because they cultivate the category of wisdom,
or because they consist of both the fundamental and the preparatory paths of action,
they are called "fundamental and preparatory virtues."
Because the two are combined into a single category within the section on karmic paths (*karmapatha*),
it speaks only of the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*) and not that of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).
This is because the remaining wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) apply according to their respective correspondences.
Regarding the eight types of rebirth through merit:
first is the minor regional king of the desire realm;
second is his minister.
Including the six heavens of the desire realm (ṣaḍ-kāmadhātu-deva), there are eight;
this differs from ancient interpretations,
which exclude the ministers and instead include the wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
The wheel-turning kings constitute nine;
the immovable wholesome constitutes ten—
namely, the wholesome of the form and formless realms.
And as for "thoroughly understanding phenomena," this refers to the knowledge of causes.
Regarding the statement that among the arts (śilpa) they serve only for amusement and the like,
other sources explain that in reality they pertain to all three natures (trividha-svabhāva).
Now, we shall merely exclude the defiled [states],
because their characteristics are difficult to discern;
that is to say, they arise from playfulness, pleasure-seeking, greed, restlessness, and so forth.
Because it is not for the sake of discerning the practice of livelihood,
this defiled craft of play and amusement is,
in its essential nature, actually indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Discernment is wholesome,
because it arises from the discernment of a wholesome mind, wisdom, and so forth.
As for the term "wisdom-eye":
In reality, it is not form (*rūpa*), because its category is the same as that of the eye;
this is what is stated here.
It is not one of the five [aggregates].
The wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus) subsumes the five types of wisdom; among these,
the wisdom of the Buddhas constitutes the present wisdom-eye,
for wisdom is its essential nature.
They come for the sake of convenience; among them,
those with blinking eyes immediately blink their eyes,
while those like the eyes of humans have no blinking.
The eyes do not blink;
they are like the eyes of a cicada or similar insects.
As for the "eye as a basis," this refers to the original physical eye.
Based on this, one gives rise to the eye of transformation,
which is called the "eye of the locus."
Alternatively, because it supports the sense-faculty and is the locus of the eye, and because worldly convention calls it "the eye," we likewise establish this name as a conventional designation.
As for "the ear that scrutinizes with precision": [it is so called because]...
Nor is it form; its essence consists of the wisdom of hearing and so forth,
because it is spoken of in terms of the ear.
I have come for the sake of the literary flow, wishing to manifest that both the eye and the ear possess superior functions. Regarding "those with ears that hear loftily":

this refers to those who, with their ears, hear the wholesome Dharma, the supreme Dharma, and the meaningful Dharma. Regarding "those whose ears do not hear loftily": [this refers to those who do not hear these].

"Listening to unwholesome dharmas, inferior dharmas, and meaningless dharmas with the ear"— the phrase "pervading all within the body and following after all the faculties" clarifies the sense that the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) is omnipresent within the [other] four faculties.
Regarding "falling into the conceptualization of designations":
"designation" refers to names and expressions.
To have one's cognitive object consist of names and expressions is called "falling into designation."
Among the eleven types, "internal and external" refers to the distinction between one's own body and the bodies of others.
Regarding the seven stations of consciousness:
The Abhidharmakośa, chapter eight, states:
"Those with different bodies and different perceptions;
those with different bodies and identical perception."
Reversing this, there is one [station] consisting of the perception of the body,
and thirteen consisting of the formless [perceptions];
thus, there are seven stations of consciousness.
The others are not subject to destruction.
First, there are material sentient beings who differ in body and differ in perception.
For example, among humans, the gods of the desire realm, and those in the first dhyāna—
excluding the time at the beginning of a kalpa—
their bodies are diverse while their perceptions are one.
It is like the Brahmakāyika devas at the beginning of a kalpa;
their three bodies are one thought, yet they appear as distinct,
just as in the second dhyāna.
One enters the joy of the fundamental [dhyāna] by wearying of the equanimity of the preparatory stage;
one enters the joy of the fundamental [dhyāna] by wearying of the equanimity of the preparatory stage.
There are four bodies and one perception.
As in the third dhyāna,
the first dhyāna is called "unity of perception" because its perceptions are defiled;
the second dhyāna is called "diversity of perception" because its two wholesome perceptions are distinct.
The three meditative absorptions (dhyānas) are designated as "one" by virtue of their maturation and perception;
this is because they are moved by wholesome joy.
The remaining three are the three lower formless attainments (ārūpya).
In other places where consciousness is destroyed,
they are not called "abodes of consciousness.
As for "designation-contact" (adhivacana-saṃsparśa):
The sixth is the contact associated with speech,
because it can give rise to speech and because it can take speech as its object.
It increases in both the spheres of sound and mental phenomena (*dharmas*);

because it increases through contact, it is called "contact with designations" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*). Contact with resistance (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*) is the contact associated with the five consciousnesses.
Because the faculties possess resistance, they pertain to those who indulge in sensual craving;
this refers to the desire realm. Those characterized by renunciation pertain to the form and formless realms as well as the untainted; these possess the flavor of attachment.
That which is with outflows is said to be "tasting of craving";
that which is without outflows is said to be "worldly";
and that which is conceptualized is said to be "supramundane."
This refers to the absence of conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*). Regarding the nine abodes of sentient beings (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*),
the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
It should be understood that, including the Peak of Existence and the non-percipient beings,
these constitute the nine abodes of sentient beings.
The others are not places where one does not dwell with pleasure;
these are the seven stations of consciousness and the first existence (bhavāgra).
Together with the Heaven of No-Perception (Āsaṃjñika),
these are called the nine abodes of sentient beings.
The remaining evil destinies and so forth are not abodes of sentient beings.
Because one does not delight in dwelling [therein].
This is explained at length as stated there.
Regarding the increase of form (*rūpa-vṛddhi*).
That which relies on a material substrate is light that possesses a substance;
that which does not rely on a material substrate is light that is devoid of a substance.

Alternatively, light that is attached to a physical basis is called "dependent," while light that is remote from a physical basis is called "independent. Regarding "light that is correct or incorrect":

this refers to the light of the sun and moon during their phases of waxing and waning, and so forth. As for "accumulated matter" (*rūpa-saṃcita*): [it refers to matter formed by the aggregation of atoms].
Regarding the various shapes and forms, among the nine types [of derived matter], internal and external are not mentioned.
Even if one's own or another's body were considered an external base (*bāhyāyatana*),
it would certainly be stated separately from the sense faculties (*indriya*).
In fact, similar sounds possess only two natures.
Those that are unwholesome or obscured receive those names because they are produced by the corresponding volition (*cetanā*).
The *Xianyang lun* states:
"That which manifests conventionally applies to both good and evil;
its substantial reality is not so."
The same applies to the preceding form realm.
Regarding sound,
"if one transgresses or emerges" means:
Having committed an offense, one returns to purity. As for "the words of the Sage":
they are called "Sage" (ārya) because they accord with reality; they are "Sage" because they are correct.
Regarding "turuṣka" among incenses:
this is what was formerly called "douloubo" incense.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "As for the *kukkuḷa* incense,
[the amount] called *sukṣmāñjali* is about the size of a sesame seed."
Red dyes such as vermilion and the like are not found in this land.
This is the "Great Fragrance.
Regarding the three pungent aromatics (*trikaṭu*):
in the Western Regions, these generally consist of the three items—sesame, *pippalī*, and ginger.
Form them into pills and eat them;
this will cause one’s food to be digested. Regarding "finger-scent" (*aṅgulī-gandha*) and the like:
they are so named because their shape resembles a finger.
Regarding the taste of healing:
it refers to the taste that cures and eliminates illness among the five types of tangible objects.
Because mosquitoes and gadflies constitute two [separate categories],
among the six [types of external contact], that which is co-nascent is the fourth;
this is because it exists simultaneously with the body within the internal physical frame.
That which is to be remedied consists of the defilements and so forth;
that which remedies them is the antidote.
That is to say, water and so forth;
the meaning of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is like that of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra), and so on.
Regarding the three types within the dharma-realm— namely,
those with form and those without form, as well as the conditioned and the unconditioned—
the conditioned consists of two kinds.
That is to say, there are those with form and those without form,
together with the unconditioned, making three;
or alternatively, there is one category consisting of those with form.
Second, those without form;
third, those both with and without form—
namely, the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Regarding the increase of the four [factors],
the term "only" refers to provisional matter (*prajñapti-rūpa*) and does not denote substantial matter;
this includes non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), restraint (*saṃvara*), and so forth.
All schools agree that form is conventional;
here, we speak of it as conventional and omit the real for brevity.
As for those phenomena included among the non-conceptualized, which are neither form nor unconditioned, they are subsumed under both the conventional and the non-conventional.
Based on their characteristics, it is taught that suchness is real,
while all others are merely conventional designations.
This includes the wholesome, the indeterminate, and the unconditioned.
Furthermore, according to their characteristics,
true thusness and so forth are wholesome,
while emptiness and so forth are indeterminate.
Among the ten augmentations:
first, mental attention;
second, sensation.
Third, perception;
fourth, volition;
fifth, contact.
Sixth, space;
seventh, cessation through deliberation;
eighth, cessation not through deliberation.
Ninth, true suchness.
Tenth, there are three phrases;
the first phrase is the unconditioned of immovability.
The latter two phrases refer to the unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*) of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*).
It is not [the cessation of] feeling, because that which is "perception" (*saṃjñā*) is what is intended here;
this is stated according to what is predominant.
Therefore, there is nothing remaining;
alternatively, the "first" [category] excludes feeling, perception, and volition,
leaving the remaining mental factors.
Because it arises simultaneously with the mind,
the fifth [category] is dissociated;
form is omitted and not mentioned here.
Or it may touch [the object] at the very beginning,
because it arises simultaneously with the mind;
this is stated according to what is predominant.
The concluding statement— that there are six hundred and sixty distinctions among the dharmas of the six internal and external bases—
is based on the twelve bases,
each being increased tenfold.
Each one contains fifty-five types;
these amount to six hundred and sixty.
This constitutes the method for increasing the number as required.
In reality, this is not so;
among the increases of the five faculties,
none involve an increase of ten.
There are eleven [bases],
of which five have already been accounted for;
the sense base of mind extends to the twelfth.
There is no increase of ten;
thirteen remain at the end.
When added to this increased number, eighteen remain.
How much more so when one does not take into account the eighty-seven dharmas subsumed within the dharma-dhātu?
From this, it should be understood that [the calculation] is based solely upon the twelve āyatanas.
Each increases up to ten, making a total grand number.
Regarding the explanation of names:
"eye" (cakṣus) is called *cakṣu* in Sanskrit.
"Chopping" (zhao) means proceeding;
"grass" (chu) means exhaustion.
This refers to being able to proceed toward and exhaustively perceive objects.
Because one sees all forms through the exhaustion of formations,
it is called "the exhaustion of formations.
Now, as for what is called "the eye":
Regarding the meaning of the term "body" (*kāya*),
it is appropriate; as for "ear," in Sanskrit it is *śrotra*,
which here means "that which is able to hear."

This is what I have heard; the term "hearing" (wen) refers to the sense organ because its essential nature corresponds to that meaning. As for the tongue, it is precisely the tongue-faculty (jihvendriya), for it is capable of eliminating hunger and thirst.
That which is the basis for the faculty of speech is conventionally designated as the "tongue."
Therefore, it is designated by that name.
As for the reckoning of "what belongs to me" (*mama*) and "I and what belongs to me": regarding "what belongs to me," it is as follows.
Whatever exists externally to the self,
and even that which is "I" or "mine," refers to what is reckoned as the preceding moment of self.
The "self" of the subsequent thought-moment is precisely the "self" of the preceding thought-moment;
it is the very self that belongs to the subsequent thought-moment.
The meaning of "sentient beings" and so forth is explained in full in the Saṃgītiparyāya-vibhaṅga.
As for the secondary summary verse (uddāna):
The preceding section clarified various meanings;
since these are all specific distinctions within the mental stage (*manobhūmi*), this verse reiterates them to define their essential nature and manifest their meaning.
Because this refers to the essential nature (*tattva*) of those stages,
only the six types of skillfulness are mentioned;
however, the *Madhyāntavibhāga* explains ten types of skillfulness in general.
In the lower section of the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*,
the skillfulnesses of the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] are explained;
this corresponds to the "Chapter on Accomplishing Skillfulness" in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
The various skillful means taught are all intended to dismantle attachments; therefore,
their enumerations differ.
As explained extensively therein,
regarding the matter of origination— namely, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and dependently arisen phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna*)—
the Abhidharma states:
The cause is termed "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda), while the result is termed "dependently arisen" (pratītyasamutpanna).
Regarding the distinction of phenomena, it refers to the immeasurable realms.
These are the five immeasurables:
namely, the realm of worlds, the realm of sentient beings, the realm of phenomena, the realm of those to be disciplined,
and the realm of the means for disciplining them.
The following shall be explained in due course.
The subsequent *uddāna* consists of ten sections:
first, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-kalāpa*).
2. Chapter on Correspondence; 3.
The Three Times; 4.
The Four Characteristics.
Five conditions;
six natures;
seventy-two places of increased enumeration.
8. Explaining the names of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
9. Skillfulness (*kauśalya*).
10. The eight assemblies of persons (*pudgala*).
It is taught according to what is predominant;
in the fourth fascicle, within the objects of the nine stages,
they are divided into four.
The preceding two stages clarify the substance of the object;
these three stages, beginning with "with vitarka and vicāra," constitute the characteristics of the object.
This is called the purpose [of the investigation]: because there are differences in terms of inferiority and superiority, and coarseness and subtlety.
"Seeking" (vitarka) refers to searching.
Vicāra means investigation;
it refers to the examination [of an object]. Thinking (cetanā) and wisdom (prajñā) that push toward a coarse [object] are called vitarka, while those that examine a subtle [object] are called vicāra.
They do not coexist in a single moment,
because they differ in their degree of coarseness and subtlety.
Now, [this is determined] based on the presence or absence of those dharmas.
These two establish the three stages;
this is called the explanation of the names. Regarding the explanation of the essence of the stages (*bhūmi*), there are three masters.
The initial explanation states:
"These three stages are established based on the correspondence between the two preceding and succeeding [moments]."
Regarding the "mindless ground":
since the first two stages are said to be the "mind-ground," it is known that the various phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) belonging to the lower stages [are included therein].
All are termed the stage without vitarka and without vicāra. The second master says:
"These three are established based on the two types of detachment from desire.
Within this fascicle:
Since it is called the stage without applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ*) precisely because it is free from the defilement of applied and sustained thought,
we know that those defilements must exist according to their respective conditions.
These are named the first and second stages. The third master says:
"These three are all established in terms of realms and stages;
this fascicle speaks of the desire realm."
Furthermore, both the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and the birth (*upapatti*) of the first dhyāna are termed the "stage with vitarka and vicāra" (*savitarkā savicārā bhūmiḥ*). Thus,
it is known that these are established solely in dependence upon the realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*).
The refutations of the previous masters are all shown to be incorrect.
Now, I shall explain that text exactly as it was stated.
Within this stage:
The main text is divided into three parts:
first, the question;
second, the brief answer.
Regarding the subsequent section, "How are the designations of the elements established?
(kathaṃ dhātuprajñaptivyavasthānam), this is a detailed explanation of the preceding heading.
Within this, there are five parts; specifically, within the designation of the elements (dhātuprajñapti), it is divided into three sections.
First the question,
next the answer in eight sections,
and finally the detailed explanation of each.
The first section, "Establishment by Enumeration," is divided into two parts.
First, the distinction between those who fall within the realms and those who do not;
second, the passage beginning with "Among these, the desire realm... and so forth.
A separate explanation of the three stages:
"to fall" (patita) means "to abide" (sthita).
It is "falling.

It falls because it is subsumed within the realm (*dhātu*). That which is not included in the realm of falling refers to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the cessation of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*) free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
A general explanation of the three vehicles:
"Skillful means" refers to the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), because it is the cause for proceeding toward cessation. As for "the cessation of the view of a personal identity" (*satkāyanirodha*):
The extinction of the deceptive body refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) refers to suchness (*tathatā*).
Its nature is free from conceptual discrimination because its essence is untainted; it is understood only by the Mahāyāna,
or [is taught] as a skillful means.
All emanation bodies [arise] because they benefit sentient beings through the skillful means of the three wheels.
As for the cessation of the transitory collection (*satkāya-nirodha*):
The so-called "Dharmakāya" refers to the manifestation through the extinction of the deceptive body. The "realm of non-outflows free from conceptual proliferation" refers to the Saṃbhogakāya.
The five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) are free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
"If it is meditative absorption" means attaining that absorption in a higher or lower stage;
"if it is birth" means being born in that stage.
Regarding "without vitarka and with only vicāra": although a certain sentient being, by cultivating this [state], attains the status of Mahābrahmā,
they share the same level of meditative absorption (dhyāna) and are bound to the same plane (bhūmi).
There are no separate categories;
one must first subdue discursive thought and craving, being free from the defilement of such thoughts,
before that concentration can be attained.
It is like when one cultivates the contemplation of impurity in the desire realm;
although one has not yet categorized and subdued the underlying defilements, they are nonetheless suppressed.
One must first temporarily subdue craving before being able to enter meditative contemplation;
this case is exactly the same.
Therefore, he is specifically designated as Mahābrahmā.
At the beginning of the kalpa,
the Ābhāsvara Heaven was already present in this intermediate space.
Because it is a karma of fixed maturation, one attains rebirth in a lower realm;

initially as Mahābrahmā, this is not a case of being born in the second dhyāna and then receiving the retribution of rebirth in a lower realm. In this context, because of the principle of being free from vitarka and vicāra, it is designated as the "ground without vitarka and vicāra," and so forth.
The second master in the *Śāstra* cites this as proof:
"One who has not yet abandoned the defilement of vitarka and vicāra..."
The provisional designations for all phenomena in the desire realm and the first dhyāna are called the stage with vitarka and vicāra.
The provisional designations for all phenomena in the intermediate dhyāna—
Having already abandoned the defilement of vitarka but not yet having abandoned the defilement of vicāra,
it is called the stage of "without vitarka and with only vicāra."
Regarding all dharmas from the two meditative attainments upward that are designated as conventional,
since they are all already free from defilement,

In the fifth fascicle, the upper section distinguishes the bliss of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while the lower section distinguishes the first dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the phrase "experiencing the joy and bliss born of seclusion" and so forth:

This means it is produced from this;

The physical well-being of that basis is called pleasure (*sukha*);
this very joy and pleasure arises from seclusion.
Regarding the statement, "The first dhyāna is called the joy and bliss born of seclusion; the second dhyāna experiences the joy and bliss born of concentration":
"concentration" refers to one whose basis has been transformed, with the mind abiding in a single object.

"Joy and bliss" are as described before.

The two types of joy and bliss arise for the first time from meditative concentration;

Furthermore, it is free from fault; as for that which experiences the bliss of the purity of equanimity and mindfulness in the fourth dhyāna,

The nature [of sensation] is not that of pleasant feeling, as explained at length in that [text].

third, there are calamities and misfortunes;

Fifth, they are unable to sever the great suffering of future lives;
amidst burning afflictions,
they are like those afflicted with scabies.
Just as when one suffers from scabies, a sense of pleasure arises;
though it is actually suffering,
one falsely conceives the notion of pleasure.
Worldly pleasures are likewise thus:
when one has leprosy and is being bored by maggots,

Furthermore, there are ten types.

the fourth [section] mentions "other wisdom-lives," which refers to the heterodox wisdom-lives of non-Buddhists.

this explains the distinctions mentioned previously.
This is not a separate category.
The lack of discernment in equanimity is delusion (*moha*).

second, the distinction between joy and sorrow;

First, the demonic army of the True Dharma refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth;

The *Sutra of Bequeathed Teachings* states:
"Restraining the body and eating at the proper time, one maintains a pure livelihood.
Regarding the phrase "those who indulge in various desires" and so forth below,
it follows the respective order.

as for the statement that pleasant feeling is suffering because it is subject to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*): [it means that] because it is subject to transformation, it is suffering.
Because it gives rise to suffering at the time of its destruction, and because the sensation of suffering is itself suffering,
"suffering" (duḥkha) refers to that which is already suffering by its very nature;
when this further encounters the suffering of conditions, it is called "the suffering of suffering" (duḥkhaduḥkhatā).

Alternatively, it is called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) because it is the suffering of being oppressed; it is called suffering because the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*) is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
"Conditioned existence" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the flux of the outflows (*sāsrava*);
its nature is inherently unstable, and thus it is called suffering.
The *Śataka-śāstra-vṛtti* states regarding its own school’s position:
"When merit is extinguished, suffering arises;
the 'retribution of merit' refers precisely to the cessation of pleasant sensation."
An external objection states:
Since sin and merit are mutually contradictory,
pleasure ought to arise at the time when sin is produced.
Answer: Happiness arises at the time when merit ceases, because merit and demerit are mutually exclusive;
it is precisely this that causes happiness to arise at the time when demerit occurs.
Furthermore, suffering should arise when merit is extinguished,
because merit and demerit are mutually contradictory; likewise,
pleasure should arise when demerit is extinguished.
Since the time when merit arises is pleasant,
the arising of demerit produces suffering;
because of this suffering, it is difficult to equate it with pleasure.
Regarding the differences in their characteristics:
the suffering of suffering exists only in the desire realm,
while the suffering of change pervades both the desire and form realms.

As for the five hindrances:
The eighty-ninth discourse states that these five hindrances are established in opposition to five positions:
first, the position of the householder.
Because one is swept away and submerged by the objects of desire, thereby contravening the holy teachings,
the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) is established;
secondly, because one is incapable of receiving the instructions and admonitions of those who share the Dharma.
It contravenes the sublime Dharma,
establishes the hindrance of ill-will,
and is thirdly contrary to śamatha.
The hindrance of sloth-and-torpor is established as being contrary to *vipaśyanā*; the hindrance of restlessness-and-regret is established [as being contrary to *śamatha*].

The fifth is the establishment of the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*), which consists of a lack of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the noble teachings, the analytical determination (*viniścaya*) of treatises, and investigative wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyāna-prajñā*).

Because they give rise to evil most powerfully, they exist only within these three; thus, they are the three outflows (*āsrava*).
The Abhidharma treatises state that the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) is established based on its flowing outward toward external objects.
The outflow based on the internal door is established as "with-outflows" (sāsrava);
the outflow based on those two doors of support is likewise established.
The establishment of the outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava) is intended by that treatise to reveal all afflictions (kleśa) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Excluding ignorance, all afflictions of the desire realm are called the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
Excluding ignorance, all afflictions of the form and formless realms are called the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*).
Ignorance within the three realms is called the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Now, regarding the ten afflictions for each of the four truths in the desire realm,

In the realms of form and formlessness, there are five doors;

Sixty-four explanations state that this includes all afflictions of the desire realm,

This includes all afflictions of the form and formless realms,

All ignorance is termed the "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyā-āsrava*),

The other two outflows are established based on the remaining afflictions that depend upon it.
Because the upper and lower [realms] differ,

Why is it called "having its fruit in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmaphala*) in this context?
Because herein one commits a crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*),

This is called "to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
That which arises subsequently, leading to rebirth in the Avīci hell and so forth, is called "to be experienced in the next life" (*upapadyavedanīya*);
these are not mutually contradictory. [Next,] regarding karma to be experienced in the present life:
If they do not experience the collective fruit,

Answer: It is by means of the preparatory action that one experiences distinct results in the present; it is by means of the fundamental action [that one experiences them in the future].

therefore, regarding the intrinsic nature of the precepts, only bodily and verbal actions are mentioned, while mental action is not.

Because one receives the Bodhisattva precepts, they pervade the three karmas; as for their basis pervading both sentient and non-sentient objects,
this applies to both natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) and prohibitory precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*) according to what is appropriate.

this refers to the four immeasurables.

regarding the "basis," this refers to the sentient beings of the three realms who serve as the objects of focus (*ālambana*), categorized collectively into three types.

Impartiality that causes one to leave behind ill repute is "equanimity" (*upekṣā*).

there are two interpretations.

Below the third dhyāna, there is the experience of distinct retributive results.

Within the context of karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*) and so forth, both this [treatise] and the Abhidharma state that there are three types.
The name is derived from its initial state;
in the present, it consists solely of individual retribution (vipāka),
while the remainder comprises both collective and individual types.
It was previously stated that there are two types,
namely the determinate and the indeterminate.
In the sixtieth fascicle, it is stated that there are four types of karma.
1. Determination by fruition;
2. Determination by time-period;
3. Determination by both.
Fourth, both are indeterminate.
The *Xiányáng shèngjiào lǎoshì jīng* (19) states that there are five types of karma:
first, that which is determined to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-niyata*).
Second, the determination of receiving [the result] in the next life;
third, the determination of receiving [the result] in a subsequent life;
fourth, the determination of receiving the retribution.
Fifth is the determination of the action itself.
This does not depend on time but concerns the retribution;
therefore, there are only two types: those that are determinate and those that are indeterminate.
If one discusses time and retribution together,
there are only three types of karma,
as it does not exceed these.
Regarding the relative conjunctions and disjunctions of time, there are four;
distinct times are not mentioned here because they are treated collectively.
It is said that there are five types [of karma] based solely on their determination by time, result, and action,
because indeterminate karma is excluded.
Although the phrasing differs, there is no contradiction in the underlying meaning,
as the intended referents are distinct.
Regarding the statement "if they are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth," it refers to those engaged in study.
This refers to all ordinary beings who,
after having generated the roots of goodness conducive to liberation by resolving upon the three vehicles,
are all designated as "learners" (śaikṣa).
The training (śaikṣa) encompasses both the tainted (sāsrava) and the untainted (anāsrava);

the state beyond training (aśaikṣa) is likewise. As for that which is neither training nor beyond training (naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa), it refers to all karmas during the stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) prior to the arousal of the thought of enlightenment.
Among the sixty-six [types of persons],
only the noble ones are described as being "in training" (śaikṣa),
because they have realized a superior attainment.
This is discussed in terms of the synthesis of their bases;
furthermore, the wholesome states acquired at birth by those in training (*śaikṣa*) are also termed "of training."
Otherwise, it would not be so;
for it would not accord with those [teachings] regarding karma that is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and so forth.
The statement that only unwholesome karma leading to the miserable realms is abandoned through insight refers to projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*).
If full-completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*) is included as well, it pertains to all five destinies.
Therefore, the treatise states, etc.;
the fifty-third [fascicle] says:
"The course leading to the evil destinies."
Only afflictions arising from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) are capable of initiating [karma].
Among the three evil destinies, both the projecting and completing karmas arise from conceptual discrimination;
therefore, this is stated with particular emphasis.
The distinct evil karma experienced among non-humans is not abandoned by the Path of Seeing;
nor is that which is innate [karma] such as to cause rebirth in the evil destinies.
Although the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and others are also abandoned by the Path of Seeing, [they do not function in this manner].
It is not a severance through detachment from bonds;
therefore, it is not mentioned here,
or else it is included by the word "etcetera."
As explained in the commentary on the eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and in the fourth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa*,
having already clarified the ten types of activity through the three gates above:
Among the four types of karma— black-black and so forth—
that which is called non-meritorious karma is black-black;
this refers to the general karma for the three evil destinies as well as the specific unwholesome karma for the five destinies.
That which is immovable karma is called "white-white," referring to the wholesome karma—
both general and specific— of the form and formless realms.
Those various meritorious karmas are called "black-white" or "black-and-white" karma.
This refers to the collective karma of humans and devas in the desire realm,
as well as the specific wholesome karma conducive to the five destinies.
Because the wholesome is the adversary of the unwholesome, it is called "black-and-white karma" (karma that is both black and white).
Because black karma has not yet been abandoned,
his meritorious karma receives this name;
even if black karma were already abandoned.
Because they belong to these respective categories,
they are also called "black-and-white karma.
These three types are explained in the Abhidharma treatises.
Both cause and effect receive this name;
it is called "black-black" because its cause is defiled.
Because its fruit is not to be craved;
it is a white cause of white [results],
because it is non-defiled.
Because its fruit is desirable;
because it is black-and-white with black-and-white causes,
as it is mixed with evil and good.
Because the fruit of unwholesome karma is intermingled with the fruit of merit,
the fruit of meritorious karma in the desire realm is necessarily termed "black-and-white" because it is mixed with the non-meritorious;
whereas the fruit of non-meritorious karma itself is not mixed with merit, and is therefore [termed] "black."
It is not termed "white-black" or "black-white" karma.
According to the Abhidharma, the eighth [chapter] and the sixty-sixth [treatise] state that black-black karma is the same as this. As for that white-white karma:
This refers to wholesome karma of the three realms.
Black-and-white karma refers to mixed karma of the desire realm.
A single moment of karma does not encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
however, based on intention (*āśaya*) and by way of application (*prayoga*),
these are combined and designated as a single "mixed karma" (*miśrakarma*).
This refers to karma that is black by way of its underlying intention (*āśaya*) but white by way of its application (*prayoga*),
such as when one cultivates various virtues with a deceitful mind.
There may be karma that is white by way of intention (*āśaya*) but black by way of application (*prayoga*),
such as when one instructs a disciple to engage in evil physical or verbal conduct.
These black and white karmas encompass both wholesome and unwholesome natures.
This treatise, based on the three types of karma— meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable—
clarifies the "black-black" and other categories of karma.
That treatise explains "black-black" and other types of karma based on the distinction between pure and mixed good and evil; therefore,
there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, regarding the sixty-six [dharmas] and the Abhidharma,
these are based on the gate of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha-mukha*); herein, however, we rely on the gate of conventional reasoning (*anuvṛtti-naya-mukha*).
The *Abhidharmakośa*, chapter sixteen, states:
"Unwholesome [karma], form [karma], wholesome karma of the desire realm, and that which can exhaust them—
the untainted (anāsrava)— should be known as black, white, both, and neither, respectively."
If it were said that this treatise conforms to their school's tenets,
then white-white karma would have to be exclusively wholesome karma of the form realm; however,
such is not the case according to reason.
Therefore, as stated previously:
regarding the statement that "karma which is neither black nor white and has no ripening result can exhaust all karmas," it is called "non-black" because it is non-defiled.
It is called "non-white" because it is not a contaminated wholesome state;
it is called "karma without ripening" because it does not bring about the fruit of non-obscured neutral [states].
Because it is able to sever the three preceding types of karma,
it is called "that which can exhaust all karma.
In the Abhidharma, this is described as non-black-and-non-white karma without maturation (*avipāka*), which is capable of exhausting all karma.
He says that "non-black" refers to being free from afflictions (*kleśa*),
and "white" refers to being exclusively pure.
This is to distinguish it from tainted white wholesome karma, which is contrary to the nature of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
It is called "without maturation" (avipāka).
This indicates that not all untainted (anāsrava) phenomena are this karma;
rather, it is said to be that which can exhaust all karma.
Regarding the antidote that abandons the first three types of karma,
the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains its nature as follows:
"The four dharmakṣāntis and the eight [moments] of uninterrupted path associated with the abandonment of desire."
The twelve types of outflow-free volition exhaust only purely black karma;
the ninth uninterrupted-path volition of the four dhyānas of detachment exhausts both mixed and purely black karma; and [the same] four [volitions] cause purely white karma to be exhausted.
If one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it should be stated in verse:
"Ten [types of action] in the desire realm are sequential; the first nine are purely black karma, while the last one is both black and mixed;
the [first] eight of the higher realms are purely white and sever [the black]."
Only by abandoning the desires of the desire realm, Relying on the first dhyāna, one transcends to the third;
One [type] is entirely black, and one is mixed; By abandoning the upper [desires], all are severed.
From the first, one transcends to the fourth; In total, there are ten types of unwholesome [paths].
The first nine [moments] sever only the black; the thirteenth severs both.
The Bodhisattva’s path of seeing consists only of volition. The diamond-like samādhi and the three [subsequent moments] likewise sever these;
this is called the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*). According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is capable of severing karma.
If suppressed by means of preparatory application, all [defilements] are increased; the path of seeing is excluded.
According to the text of this fascicle, within the path of seeing of the two vehicles:
The first uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*),
as well as the first eight uninterrupted thoughts (*cetanā*) of the gradual abandonment of desire,
exhaust only black-black karma.
The ninth path of immediate succession exhausts both purely black karma and mixed karma.
It is distinct from the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments.
The ninth path of uninterrupted realization exhausts only white-and-white karma;
this is stated with reference to those who attain the fruit through gradual progression.
If, relying on the initial *anāgamya* or the first *dhyāna*, one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and attains the third fruit:

in that single path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), one abandons both purely black and mixed [karmas]. This applies if one has already previously abandoned the defilements of the higher stages.
Based on the four dhyānas, one attains the third fruit [of the path].
First, there is the uninterrupted volition that abandons purely black and mixed karma,
as appropriate for each case.
Regarding white karma: if one proceeds from the first fruit to the fourth fruit,
the eight preceding courses of immediate volition (ānantarya-cetanā) are exclusively free from black-black karma.
The ninth thought-moment of immediate succession is conjoined with the abandonment of all three types of karma;
however, if a bodhisattva possesses a single thought-moment of immediate succession upon the path of seeing,
they abandon only black-and-black karma.
By means of the single thought-moment of uninterrupted concentration that is like a diamond (*vajropama-samādhi*), the three types of karma are simultaneously severed;
all paths of unwholesome karma are cut off as soon as they arise,
and all wholesome karma is liberated from the bonds of its conditions.
Because it is exhausted when the defilements of one's own stage are completely abandoned,
it is only at the ninth moment of uninterrupted thought (*ānantarya-cetanā*) that one is said to have exhausted white karma.
What has been explained above concerns the abandonment of the seeds of outflowing karma through volition.
As for the suppression of active manifestations, this occurs exclusively on the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga),
as there is no uncontaminated preparatory stage (anāsrava-prayoga) [prior to it].
The remaining paths of cultivation,
together with the path of preparation,
are able to suppress the active manifestations [of the afflictions].
In this context, only the various untainted (anāsrava) karmas are discussed,
because they serve as the antidotes for abandoning the aforementioned three types of karma.
This refers to the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) of the two vehicles.
Although there is also the abandonment [of afflictions],
as well as the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva,
which are abandoned by their respective remedies.
Because none of these are karma,
they are not mentioned.
Therefore, the Abhidharma states:
Non-black-and-non-white karma refers to all untainted (anāsrava) karma within the preparatory stages (prayoga-mārga) and the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga).
Because these are the remedies for severing those various karmas,
and because they are established based on excellence,
one does not take up other paths of further progress and so forth.
All [these] depend on distinct practices,
and furthermore, they do not entirely suppress all categories of karma;
therefore, they are not mentioned.
The four types of karma mentioned above, as appropriate to each case,
differ in being either defiled or pure; nevertheless,
they all have volition (*cetanā*) as their essential nature.
If one follows the Abhidharma, the verse should be stated as follows:
Successively, ten [types of] volition arise from desire; Nine abandon what is purely black, and [the tenth] abandons the mixed.
The latter one [of the faculties] abandons three together; the upper eight abandon only their own [respective defilements].
If one attains the third fruit by leaping over, only one [faculty] abandons three [defilements].
From the first stage up to the state of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa), the first eight are the vision of the Bodhisattva.
Only by exhausting the purely black and the mixed [karma] are all three types severed by the vajra-like [samādhi];
this is said to be the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*). As for the remedial factors that can sever karma:
if it is suppressed through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), everything except that which is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) is included.
Only the preparatory [path] and the uninterrupted [path] can suppress and exhaust [the afflictions],
while the preceding paths of superior progress and liberation lack this superior function; therefore, apart from these,
it is explained that they constitute "separation from bondage" rather than having the sense of non-arising and so forth.
According to the Abhidharma,
the first three types of karma result in the fruits being attained by the two vehicles in succession;
in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is one thought-moment of uninterrupted intention (*anantarya-cetanā*).
Furthermore, the eight preceding uninterrupted thoughts (*ānantarya-cetanā*) in the gradual abandonment of desire [are of mixed nature],
because they abandon both purely black and mixed karma.
The ninth uninterrupted thought, however, [is exclusively white].
Excluding karma that is purely black, mixed, or entirely white;
excluding the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments;
and excluding the volition of the ninth path of immediate succession.
Only the white-and-white karma is excluded;

this is stated based on attaining the fruit through gradual progression. If one enters the path of seeing by leaping over the four dhyānas and attains the third fruit, then even a single uninterrupted volition excludes three types [of karma].
If one leaps from the first fruit to take up the fourth fruit, [the same applies].
The eight volitions of the uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga) preceding [the first bhūmi],
as well as the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing (darśana-mārga),
abandon only purely black and mixed karma.
The ninth uninterrupted volition,
as well as the Bodhisattva’s diamond-like concentration,
are both free from the three types of action.
This explains the severance of seeds;
as for the suppression of active manifestations,
this applies to all stages except for the Path of Seeing.
In all other stages, the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) is added; the remaining meanings are the same as before.
If one speaks of the abandonment of bonds and so forth, [the same applies].
The meaning is also not fixed;
it should be reflected upon according to reason.
Among the five types of karma:
There are two successive [explanations],
which together comprise three interpretations.
One meaning states:
The wholesome and unwholesome karma of non-Buddhists is called "crooked," because it obstructs the straight path of the Buddha-dharma.
Second, this very crookedness is called "defiled."
Because it defiles the True Dharma;
because it defiles the body and mind—this very crookedness and filth is called turbidity;
and because it is the dregs of evil dharmas.
Because they defile both body and mind,
they all pertain to all wholesome and unwholesome karmas;
therefore, this treatise says:
That is to say, crooked karma (*kuṭila-karman*) is also called defiled karma (*kliṣṭa-karman*);
and this same crooked-defiled karma is also called turbid karma (*kaṣāya-karman*). Regarding these two meanings:
"crooked karma" is as previously explained.
Regarding those who engage in defiled actions:
this refers to ordinary worldlings within the internal Dharma of the Buddha’s teaching.
Ignorance, greed, hatred, pride, and the view of a self-identity are collectively termed "perverted views.
The grasping at views and the grasping at precepts and observances are termed "abiding in one's own grasping at views."
"Wrong view" refers to false certainty;
"doubt" refers to indecisive cognition.
These are applied as appropriate to each case.
Either it is associated,
or it serves as a proximate cause,
or it serves as a remote cause.
The three types of karma— wholesome and unwholesome— that are thus produced are called "defiled karma" (*saṃkliṣṭa-karma*),
because they defile the True Dharma and are profoundly foul and evil.
These are the ordinary worldlings within;
they are undetermined regarding both the false and the correct gateways.
Preceded by doubt, they are called those whose cognition is characterized by hesitation.
All wholesome and unwholesome [actions] are called turbid karma,
because they arise from doubt and are extremely defiled,
and because they are residual evil karma.
Among the aforementioned impurities,
doubt arises from wrong concentration (*mithyāsamādhi*);
this [impurity] arises from non-concentration (*aniyata*), and thus it constitutes a distinction.
This is because it does not obstruct the true path of the Buddha-dharma, and one can still enter it.
It is not said that internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) also possess crooked karma. The third meaning states:
these three types of karma all arise from non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Misguided conduct arising from wrong understanding is called "crookedness.
This very crooked karma obstructs the arising of conditioned merits and is therefore called "corrupt."
They are called "turbidities" because they obstruct the realization of unconditioned merit;

all of them pertain to the three types of karma—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral. In the eighth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are two successive expositions that explain the aforementioned three types of karma.
The initial passage states:
"The three karmas that obstruct the Eightfold Path are called 'crookedness' (*vaṅka*).
That which defiles the mental continuum and gives rise to obstructive karma is called 'filth' (*doṣa*)."
If it arises based on the inverted views of non-Buddhists (tīrthika), it is called "turbid.
Only this turbid karma is said to be "arisen by non-Buddhists";
it is not stated who gives rise to the former two.
Therefore, we know that this principle applies universally to both the internal and external [realms] from which [phenomena] arise.
Since it does not specifically distinguish between natures,
it is clear that it encompasses both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Nevertheless, there is no fault in this further explanation. He further explains:
"The view of extremes, wrong view, and the view of a self-identity follow their respective order."
The various karmas thus produced are termed crookedness, corruption, and turbidity.
By this same principle, these too arise solely from non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
These three types of karma follow those afflictions.
The distinct meanings arising from the internal and external paths are explained separately;
they do not have fixed, independent essences.
Although their meanings differ, they are nonetheless not mutually contradictory.
Unlike the Hīnayāna teaching that crooked, defiled, and turbid karma arises from deceit (*māyā*),
hatred (*dveṣa*), and greed (*lobha*), within this [Mahāyāna] doctrine these are condensed into three categories:
first, the three types of karma produced by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are termed "crooked" (*vaṅka*).
Furthermore, there are three categories of ordinary beings within the internal dharma:
first, those fixed in error who give rise to defiled karma;
second, those not fixed [in either destiny] who give rise to turbid karma.
Third, the pure karma arising from right concentration:
all the superior karmas, whether with outflows or without outflows, belonging to all noble ones (ārya),
are called the karma of the Sage (muni-karma).
"Muni" has the meaning of "silence.
This is called "tranquility," because one realizes the principle of tranquility.
If one relies on the stage of the wisdom derived from hearing at a lower level,
all bodily and vocal actions as well as the mind present within the bodies of all noble ones constitute the essence of the three types of pure action.
The mind is mental action (*manas-karman*);
this is different from that [which follows].
That [text] speaks of the bodily *mauna*-action of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Only the untainted [karma] is taken;
tainted karma is termed "threefold pure karma," as this distinction is not made in relation to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Now, because this [discussion] distinguishes between ordinary beings and noble ones, as well as between internal and external paths,
pure karma exists only among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
As for all three types of karma within the bodies of noble ones (*ārya*), [they are not considered pure].
All are termed the deeds of a Muni.
Because they are observed in relation to different [contexts], there is no contradiction. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"The bodily and vocal actions of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are themselves the mind."
The three *muni*s and the three purities should be understood as being none other than the three types of sublime conduct (*sucarita*).
Regarding the ninth category, the faults of karma:
the offense incurred in the present life refers to one who, like a self-harming person,
initiates the preparatory effort for killing.
The karmic retribution for the act of killing has not yet been completed;
though one is currently harmed by another,
it is not certain that one will experience [the full result] in the future.
Because the heavy karma has not yet been completed;
it is also like when an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) first commits acts such as killing and is then immediately killed by another.
Subsequently, they may enter the state of sainthood and no longer incur further offenses;
or, they may transfer future retribution to experience it in the present life so that they do not undergo it again later,
as was the case with Aṅgulimāla and others.
It is also called "an offense pertaining to the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmika-āpatti*).
This refers to the same [consequence] as previously mentioned, because it can cause self-harm;
thus it says, "as for example," while one is undergoing the mental and physical distress and suffering produced by that [offense].
Regarding the "six kinds of faults," these refer to the first six among the seven types of defects of this karma;
since [the karma] cannot be accomplished, [these faults arise].
In vain one accumulates sorrow and suffering;
in vain one applies skillful means.
Since the task is not accomplished, those who cannot discern this will find nothing to their satisfaction.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of faults and afflictions:
violating the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera,
and the grief and suffering arising from those violations.
Because they are offenses committed from the very beginning, only ten are mentioned;
this is because one cannot receive full ordination [if these are present].
As for the four types of unwholesome courses of action:
These are the first four branches among the five precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*):
the three bodily and one vocal courses of action (*karmapatha*) which are natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*),
while drinking alcohol is a prohibitory precept (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*).
Therefore, this is explained separately.
*Cchandika* is a name for a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
This has no corresponding translation;
therefore, the Sanskrit original is retained.
Regarding the third [category], the defilement of birth (*jāti-saṃkleśa*), there are two [parts].
First, four types are indicated;
subsequently, they are explained individually.
Regarding the thirty-six locations of the desire realm:

The eight cold and eight hot hells, etc., are as explained previously in the fourth fascicle of the treatise. The eighteen abodes of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are likewise. Regarding the fifty-eight births, there are thirty-six in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
There are eighteen [realms] in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and four in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
As for those born from the overcoming of black [karma]:
The evil karma of one's lineage is called "black";
it is called "victorious" because its power is strong, or because it is the extreme among the black, thus it is called "black-victorious. As for the *caṇḍāla*:
A butcher; *bukkasā* (also spelled *pukkasa*) refers to a family that removes filth and waste.
As for those who are elders or families of great wealth and status:
Not of the kṣatriya or other castes,
but possessing superior skills and being upright and worthy of respect, such is called a householder’s family; not black, not white, they are those of superior birth.
These refer to the vaiśyas and so forth.
There are five types of birth with indeterminate [status]:
first, the mutual indeterminacy between oneself and others.
Second, the uncertainty of suffering and pleasure;
third, the uncertainty of location;
fourth, the uncertainty of other bodies.
The five similes establish [the reason] as inconclusive.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "I observe that upon the great earth not even a small space can be found," the intended meaning is that within the great earth there is no small space whatsoever.
From beginningless time,
you have undergone immeasurable births and deaths in this very place.
This clearly indicates that from time immemorial,
in every single location within the great earth,
one has undergone immeasurable births and deaths.
Reading the flow of the text at length, its meaning and principle are also profound.
Furthermore, it says: "I observe that among sentient beings in the world, it is not easy to find anyone who, throughout the long night of saṃsāra, has not been your mother, father, or the like."
"Unchanging" means difficult;
it is difficult for sentient beings to attain.
It does not mean that they are not your mother or father;
rather, it means that all have at one time been your parents and so forth.
It means that they have previously acted as parents to one another.
These are the distinctions between the two.
The *ācārya* is the preceptor (*upādhyāya*); the *kalyāṇamitra* is the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
"Upādhyāya" refers to the preceptor (upādhyāya) and the teacher (ācārya).
"The mountain of broad and expansive flanks" refers to...
Formerly called Mount Vipula,
its shape is like the flank of an asura.
Fourth, there are four types of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) within the cycle of birth and transmigration.

First, the single essence;
