Regarding the "Essence" (*tattva*) that subsumes all sutras:
it generally clarifies the essence of the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—the cyclic flow and cessation of causes and effects through the stages of the three periods of time;
it does not specifically manifest the individual distinct essences of each of the twelve links of dependent origination.
The gate of differentiation regarding the individual entities of each shall be explained extensively;
in that section of the text,
the individual entities will be fully revealed.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the presentation of the three characteristics;
second, the detailed explanation of each.
To summarize this later:
as for the three characteristics,
the first is that [the middle limit] arises from the prior limit.
Second, they arise from the middle limit toward the subsequent limit.
Third, from the middle limit, they either proceed toward cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) or proceed toward the ultimate purification.
The first two are called the process of flow (pravṛtti),
and the last one is cessation (nivṛtti).
Flow refers to the process of birth in accordance with conditions.
Cessation follows the order of extinction.
The past is called the prior limit;
the present is called the middle limit.
The future is called the "subsequent limit.
Within the present,
if one does not feel revulsion or opposition, [it is the subsequent limit].
One then proceeds toward saṃsāra;
if one feels revulsion toward it,
one then proceeds toward purification.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that the ten causes and two fruits necessarily do not belong to the same temporal period;
the present treatise relies upon this principle.
Therefore, dependent origination is distinguished across two lifetimes.
Furthermore, it is said therein that the first seven [links] exist within the causal state.
Craving, grasping, and becoming may be either different or the same;
[they may be counted as] two, three, or seven [factors].
Each is fixed as belonging to the same time period.
This thus reveals the dependent origination of the three time periods.
Here, however, we merely refute the Small Vehicle’s (Hīnayāna) assertion that dependent origination is fixed within the three time periods.
Based on these two periods, it is shown that [the number] is not fixed at only this;
there are seven in the past and three in the present.
The two future [karmas] are so called because they are karmas that bring about maturation as subsequent retribution (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*).
Within the detailed explanation, there are two parts.
The first [section] clarifies the first [of the three],
and the latter [section] clarifies the latter two.
Within the first [section], there are further three parts.
First, birth from a womb is explained;
next, the other three types of birth are explained;
finally, the places of birth resulting from the three types of karma are elucidated.
The beginning and middle further consist of three parts:
first, the question;
second, the answer.
Regarding the three fetters: "ignorance regarding the prior limit" refers to the failure to understand the two types of suffering—the conventional and the ultimate—pertaining to the prior limit.
From this arise two delusions; as for "conventional suffering":
That is to say, the three miserable realms and all worldly conventions are known as suffering; as for ultimate suffering:
This refers to humans and devas;
for those of superior wisdom know this to be suffering,
as stated in the seventh chapter of the Abhidharma.
Delusion regarding the suffering of the conventional world is called ignorance of maturation (*vipāka-moha*);
it gives rise to non-meritorious formations (*apuṇya-saṃskāra*).
Delusion regarding the suffering of ultimate reality is called ignorance of the true meaning (*tattvārtha-moha*).
They give rise to meritorious and immovable formations;
because they are largely deluded regarding the prior limit and manifest two types of maturation,
it is said that these deluded ones do not understand the prior limit.
In reality, this ignorance also deludes one regarding the future limit (*aparānta*);

however, because it mostly deludes one regarding present causes, it is not mentioned here in brief. It is for this reason that consciousness, following karma, continues to flow without interruption until the end of life.
Among the five kinds of consciousness, the [mental] consciousness is supreme;
consciousness is the master of retribution,
and all are not separate from consciousness.
This is a general designation for "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); alternatively, it is called "consciousness" alone because it refers to that which is first produced.

Although these seeds of consciousness and so forth have already been perfumed by the habitual tendencies of names and words (*nāma-vyañjana-vāsanā*), their specific place of rebirth was previously unknown.
Gathered by karma,
the fruits will arise within the two realms of good and evil destinies;
because consciousness evolves in accordance with its causes, it is called "consciousness following karma."
Once it has been perfumed,
it continues without interruption until the end of the previous life,
serving as the cause for the subsequent consciousness in the present.
When about to produce its fruit in the present world,
it cannot arise of itself as an evil;
rather, it arises within the preceding body by depending on the moisture and assistance of past internal and external craving that has become manifest.
The aggregate of feeling has two types.
First, the feeling of maturation,
which arises conditioned by the internal body.
Second is the feeling of objective experience (*viṣayavedanā*),
which arises conditioned by external objects;
it is because of these two types of feeling [that this occurs].
It gives rise to internal and external craving,
which serves as the moisture for [rebirth]. Previously, it was stated that "following karma" refers to consciousness,
which subsumes the five types beginning with consciousness.
Now, both internal and external craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are subsumed under "grasping" (*upādāna*). Alternatively, internal craving is termed "craving," while external craving is termed "grasping.
This meaning clarifies that the six factors—beginning with the formations moistened [by craving]—are designated as "existence in the prior limit" (*pūrvānta-bhava*).

In the present life, the resultant consciousness evolves accordingly, and the remaining factors such as name-and-form arise in succession. Thus, the resultant consciousness continues in a stream together with name-and-form, up until old age and so forth.
If categorized according to developmental stages:
during the first seven days it is called *vijñāna* (consciousness),
and during the next seven weeks it is called *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form).
Now, the narrowness and breadth of the various stages from beginning to end are explained.
Since it is taught that they are mutually dependent and subsume the six sense bases and so forth,
it speaks only of these two [stages] up to old age.
It is not otherwise, nor is there anything else.
Furthermore, within the present factors of birth and old age,
that which is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) is dependent upon consciousness and form (nāmarūpa).
Because the characteristics of the fruit have manifested, its name is spoken;
it is not that the factors such as form exist in the present state among the ninety-three [dharmas].
Consciousness is the support;
it has been explained as having the function of maturation.
Now, however, it is explained as that which depends [upon the support].

Regarding the statement that the karma of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and its maturation fruit are distinguished as collective and individual maturations due to the distinction between the support and the supported: it is because [consciousness] necessarily evolves in dependence upon the six bases.

That is to say, the six sense faculties subsumed within name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Therefore, when the Sūtra states that "name-and-form conditions consciousness," this refers to the Bodhisattva’s reverse contemplation of suffering and its origin,
wherein consciousness and name-and-form serve as mutual conditions for one another.
Having completed the observation of the truths and finished seeing them as mutual conditions,
one observes suffering and its origin until reaching consciousness and then stops.
As explained extensively in the ninety-three [sections],

that which serves as the support for the six consciousnesses according to their respective requirements does not refer merely to the manifest consciousness produced from the seeds of the five types of consciousness.
That is exclusively the eighth;
therefore, it is stated in the ninety-third [verse] and below that the name is established based on the totality of all continuities.
The "six groups of consciousness" are taught because the meaning clearly indicates that, in general, the consciousness of a single lifetime is being described; thus,
it is said that "name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness."
It is sustained by consciousness;
consciousness is its support;
and consciousness conditions name-and-form.
They take that as their support,
or they observe it as their object. If,
among the multitudes of sentient beings possessing form— namely, those born through transformation in the desire and form realms— their sense faculties are definitively complete upon birth.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that although those born through transformation who possess form have all five sense faculties at the initial stage of taking birth,
[they do not yet exercise their functions].
Yet they are not yet functional,
because at that time they are not yet designated as the "limb of the six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
This refers to those first born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Although the mental faculty (manas-indriya) certainly exists,
it is not yet distinct and thus is not designated as the sense base of mind (mana-āyatana);
this is what is intended here.

For those beings of miraculous birth, at the moment of initial birth, that which is called the "limb of consciousness" (vijñāna-anga) subsequently gives rise to the five sense faculties and the mind-base (manāyatana) as appropriate.
That which has not yet become clear is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Next, the six sense faculties are clarified as the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Finally, because the factors of contact (*sparśa*) and sensation (*vedanā*) gradually grow, they arise.
Although the faculties are determined and complete, they differ from those previously mentioned;
likewise, the five factors beginning with consciousness also have a sequential order. Question: In the lower realms, there exists manifest matter that can serve as the support for consciousness.
There is no form, nor is there manifest form;
consciousness relies upon non-material seeds.
Answer: Lower-level consciousness takes manifest form as its object.
The name-consciousness (nāma-vijñāna) takes form (rūpa) as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and relies upon it; the seeds of form take consciousness as their object-condition.
Thus, it is said that consciousness relies upon the seeds of form.
Furthermore, regarding those born into the human or celestial realms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) by virtue of meritorious karma (*puṇyakarman*):
these three cases all refer to the attainment of results through projecting karma (*ākṣepakakarman*),
specifically karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīyakarman*).

Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives consists solely of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*); only when this includes both projecting and completing karma (*paripūrakakarman*) is it designated as the member of "formative action" (*saṃskāra*).
The arising of this ignorance is termed the member of "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
The intensification of this craving is termed the "link of craving-and-grasping" (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*).
That which is accumulated through this karma is termed the five [links] beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*).
When these six [links] have evolved, they are then termed the "link of existence" (*bhava*).
This "existence" (bhava) which brings about birth is called the limb of "birth-and-aging" (jātijarāmaraṇa);
it reveals all karma currently being experienced and specifically assists future karma.
None of these are factors of conduct (*saṃskāra-aṅga*).
Otherwise, meritorious karma would give rise to rebirth in all five destinies;
this was stated earlier in this fascicle.
Wholesome karma refers to that which brings about the maturation of rebirth in the happy realms of the desire realm,
as well as being conducive to the maturation of the five destinies.
This meaning is explained in detail as set forth in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. By means of this,
that karma is produced by both the agent and the object.
The accumulation of subject and object;
the moistening of subject and object;
the production of subject and object.
None of these are subsumed within the twelve links of dependent origination.
The explanation of the latter two gates is further divided into two parts;
first, there are two questions.
This will be explained separately later.
First, the explanation of how [the present] arises from the intermediate state (madhyānta) toward the future state (aparānta) is divided into two parts.
First, the explanation:
To conclude: those who experience the results of two kinds of prior karma— namely, first,
internal maturation results (*vipākaphala*), and second,
external dominant results (*adhipatiphala*)— or those who hear what is not the true Dharma.
This refers to the present life, or to that which was previously habituated in past lives;
both of these are delusions arising from conceptual construction.
One initiates karma through delusion regarding the internal manifestation of one's own self and the future existence;
one moistens rebirth through delusion regarding external objects.
Since one is thus deluded regarding the internal fruit manifest in the present, [the cycle continues].
Because one does not subsequently know suffering as it truly is, and due to this newly performed karma, this consciousness is called "consciousness following karma" (karmānuvartin-vijñāna);
that is to say, because the seeds of consciousness follow after karma.
Consciousness arises by virtue of formations;
it arises through the process of gathering and accumulating,
rather than arising from the discernment of its own essence.
By virtue of being a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
if the first member of the consciousness-link refers exclusively to the eighth consciousness,
it is explained as applying generally to all consciousnesses throughout the duration of a single lifetime.
It pervades the six groups of consciousness;
it connects with name-and-form from the prior limit and is able to serve as the basis for the six consciousnesses.
It is likewise so:
the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is that which draws forth the fruit,
while name-and-form (nāmarūpa) follows as its seed.
Name-and-form follows as the seed for the six sense bases;
the six sense bases serve as the basis for contact to follow as its seed;
and contact serves as the producer for feeling to follow as its seed.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
"These five, beginning with consciousness, are called the 'projected' (ākṣepya),
because ignorance and formative forces are the projectors."
Both that which is projected and that which projects are equally the projecting cause.
Because they produce birth, aging,
and death through a remote causal force,
they are all termed "projecting causes" (ākṣepa-hetu).
The five factors, beginning with consciousness,
arise through causes and conditions as birth, aging, and death.
In the ninety-third [verse] and herein, it is stated that "alone" refers to the drawing cause (*ākṣepahetu*).
The treatise says: "Because by this, consciousness is drawn forth."
This continues until the body for one lifetime is received.
Ignorance and formations are not included among the projecting causes (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
Regarding the distinction between the projector and the projected, various teachings differ.
The *Cheng weishi lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra) states:
"The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is exclusively that which is induced;
this is because the seeds of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) are designated as the 'link of consciousness' (*vijñānāṅga*)."
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that consciousness (*vijñāna*) alone is capable of projecting [rebirth],
because the seeds of karma within consciousness are designated as the "consciousness link" (*vijñānāṅga*),
and the seeds of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) are subsumed under the category of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that the consciousness link (*vijñāna-aṅga*) encompasses both the projecting and the projected;
for both the seeds of karma and the seeds of consciousness are termed "consciousness.
Consciousness is the support for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Because they are not subsumed under name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*),
the meaning is made clear: craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are termed the "producers," while the factors of birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are termed the "produced."
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that although the five types of consciousness and so forth are simultaneously produced through the impregnation of karma,
they are nonetheless distinct.
However, because they differ in terms of primary and secondary, general and specific, superior and inferior, cause and effect, and their respective characteristics,
the various sacred teachings employ conventional designations of "prior" and "subsequent.
Alternatively, these are based on the states of future manifestation.
Because there is a sequential order,
it is said that there is a before and an after;
for this reason, one should also reconcile the various preceding and succeeding passages.

For this reason, these consciousnesses and so forth are also said to be "active" (*samudācāra*), because at the time of the cause, there is certainly no sense of being active. Due to this craving, some give rise to the seeking of desire (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*), which is the desire to be born in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*);
others give rise to the seeking of existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*).
Seeking birth in the realms of form and formlessness—
these two constitute the aggregate; that is,
craving is the first and the four types of clinging are the latter.
Because two types of seeking arise first, two types of grasping subsequently emerge separately.
These are subsumed under the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) of subsequent existence;

that is, the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is established by both the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the karmic condition (*karma-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The member of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) alone is designated as "birth" (*jāti*).
The members of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are not included within the causes of birth;
this is the teaching of the Abhidharma and the Vijñaptimātra.
Because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) possess the capacity to produce the fruit that is about to arise,
they are collectively designated as "the productive [factors]," which is not contradictory. However, the Abhidharma states that at the time of the cause,
there are both the "projecting" (*ākṣepaka*) and the "projected" (*ākṣipta*).
This means that at the time of the fruit, there exist that which produces and that which is produced;
what is not yet matured is called the cause.
It is not the case that cause and effect do not exist.
That which has already matured is called the fruit;
it is not the case that there is no cause for the fruit.

These definitions are distinct according to their respective meanings and are not mutually contradictory. Question: Both the "projecting cause" (ākṣepa-hetu) and the "projected cause" (ākṣipta-hetu) are projecting causes.
The producer and the produced are both subsumed under the simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Having understood that future suffering has its cause in present accumulation, [one contemplates it].
The present accumulation also has the consciousness arising from prior accumulations as its limit;

It is not because present ignorance exists that it is said that with the cessation of ignorance, the six sense bases and so forth cease;

It arises following ignorance;

That which can depend upon them—such as feeling and so forth—all likewise cease accordingly. "Constantly experiencing disjunction from fetters" means that one experiences feelings that are not bound by fetters;
all tainted feelings (*sāsrava-vedanā*) are increased by the binding of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, untainted feeling (*anāsravavedanā*) is called "feeling of dissociation" (*visaṃyogavedanā*);
it is not necessarily the case that all [such feelings] are untainted feeling. Regarding the phrase "the holy life has been established": [it refers to one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship].
The knowledge of the truth of cessation fulfills the truth of the path, leading to ultimate nirvana.

The Abhidharma-śāstra states:
Regarding the arising of consciousness:

visual consciousness arises, and so forth.
Regarding the maturation of external crops:

and the sprout as the condition for the stalk, and so forth.

That is to say, with the predominant power of the collective karma of all sentient beings as the condition,

This refers to the fact that sentient beings in the three realms continue to exist by taking the four nutriments as conditions; and that,
through the predominant power of their own performed karma, they obtain the desirable or undesirable fruits according to that karma.
This means that with wholesome and unwholesome conduct as conditions,
one proceeds to good and evil realms.
As for "power":
That is to say, taking internal realization as the condition,
one brings forth the most excellent qualities such as the supernormal powers;
this is what is meant by "purification."
This refers to taking the wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) as a condition,
proceeding in succession until one attains the fruit of arhatship and so forth.
(From the lower fascicle of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*).

Within the third section, the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there are two parts.

The Abhidharma-śāstra states:
"First, the meaning of being devoid of sentient beings is that there is no inherent self."
This refutes the Vaiśeṣikas, the Vātsīputrīyas,
and others who hold that the self is the agent,
because it is distinct from those sentient beings.
Regarding the second meaning of impermanence:
because it is not eternal,
this refutes the Sāṃkhya doctrine that the *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is permanent.
It is the basis of all phenomena;
because it conditions the formation of things,
it manifests impermanence.
It also refutes the Mahāsāṃghika and Saṃmitīya schools and others who claim that the twelvefold dependent origination is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma.
Third, regarding the meaning of "abiding for a moment":
Because at the time of arising, [a phenomenon] has already passed and does not abide for even a moment,
the Abhidharma treatises also establish the meaning of *kṣaṇa* (moment).
This refutes the Saṃmitīya school’s [position regarding] matter (*rūpa*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and so forth.
The four characteristics of a single lifetime of all dependently originated phenomena are not momentary.
Regarding the four meanings of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*): it is so called because it arises based upon various conditions.
This refutes the non-Buddhist school of Naturalism (Svabhāvavāda),
which holds that phenomena exist spontaneously and are not produced by dependent causes.
Therefore, it is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Fifth, regarding the meaning of being devoid of functional activity:
because the activity of the various conditions is empty.
This refutes the Sarvāstivāda position that there exists a real,
functional activity which serves as the causal condition for the arising of entities.
Now, it is shown that functional capacity (śakti) is devoid of causal operation (kāritra).
Regarding the meaning of the uninterrupted continuity of cause and effect:
the causal moment perishes.
The fruit arises at the very moment [of the cause],
because their temporal divisions and so forth are identical; thus,
there is a continuity between cause and fruit.
This refutes the non-Buddhist extremists who hold the view of annihilationism regarding the lack of continuity between cause and effect,
and it also negates the Sautrāntika masters' position that there is no ripening of causes and effects across past and future lives.
Nevertheless, they do not exist simultaneously,
because cause and effect are discontinuous.
Regarding the seventh point, the meaning of the transformation according to the similarity between cause and effect:
Because [things] do not arise from everything out of everything,
cause and effect are similar;

To calculate that one is reborn in the heavens after taking the slaughter of sheep and the like as the cause would mean that various wholesome fruits have unwholesome things as their causes; thus,
cause and effect would not correspond.
This now demonstrates that a virtuous cause yields a virtuous maturation;
the same applies to an unwholesome cause.
Thus, cause and effect are similar.
Regarding the meaning of "one's own karma as one's own action":
because the fruit is not experienced within other continuums,
one experiences the fruit of one's own karma by oneself.
This refutes the view that there is no cause and effect and that [suffering] does not arise from karma;
it also refutes the proponents of nihilistic views who maintain the position that others create the actions while the self receives the fruit.
This refers to the theories of various proponents of non-homogeneous causes (*vaiṣamya-hetu*),
which have been extensively explained in both the *Abhidharma-śāstra* and the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*;

that which is its opposite is called ignorance.
Through reflection, one investigates and analyzes.

That which is to be remedied is called "non-insight."
Therefore, it is said that these three types are taught because of the distinctions among their respective objects of treatment;
and because of the distinctions among their own natures as weak, medium, and superior,
they are called "darkness," "delusion," and "the darkness of ignorance."
In this context, it is explained that all forms of non-cognition serve as constituent factors;

One takes only those [defilements] capable of producing karma that correctly brings about good or evil in future lives.

Second, the ground of abiding in desire-attachment;

The five stages of the abiding ground of ignorance consist of the four preceding afflictive obstructions and the single final cognitive obstruction.
That sutra itself states:

The ninth chapter on Consciousness-Only agrees with the scriptural exposition.
Among the four types of afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*),

The Abhidharma treatises state that there are two types of ignorance (*avidyā*) that initiate karma.
1. Delusion regarding the true nature of reality, which gives rise to meritorious and immovable formations;
2. Delusion regarding maturation.
They give rise to non-meritorious formations.
Both of these are abandoned solely by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This is stated in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
Because the noble learners (*śaikṣa*) have eternally abandoned the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*),
they do not create new karma.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states:

that which assists it is not fixed."
Therefore, we select only that ignorance belonging to the stage of abiding in one place (*ekadeśasthāyī bhūmi*) which is associated with views.
This, moreover, is threefold:
first, that which produces only collective karma (*saṃgrāhaka-karma*).
The second [type of ignorance] gives rise exclusively to individual karma;
the third gives rise to both types of karma.
Here, we take the ignorance associated with the first and the last types of karma.
Therefore, it is said that only those [mental factors] capable of initiating karma that truly brings about good or evil results in future lives are taken here.
Furthermore, there are four such types:

Second, the unique [afflictions];
third, the envelopments;
fourth, the latent dispositions.
All are capable of initiating karma—
whether they be followers of external paths or internal paths, ordinary beings, those who are heedless or those who are not— heedless or not,

The karmas initiated by the four types of ignorance are each distinct,
as extensively analyzed in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*. Herein,
it is stated that "formations" (*saṃskāra*) pertain to body, speech, and mind.
Its intrinsic nature consists solely of the seeds of the manifestation of the wholesome and unwholesome,
as well as provisional matter and volition;

That which is thus produced is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*).

He said: "The intensification of craving is called 'clinging' (upādāna).

In the stage of moistening karma, the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) increases preeminently;

Only through repeated watering can the sprout of existence (*bhava*) arise.
Furthermore, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are distinguished as two separate factors based on their initial and subsequent stages;
although all afflictions are subsumed within the factor of grasping,
it is craving that is predominant in its capacity to moisten and intensify them.
This is called the increase of craving;
therefore, these two passages do not contradict one another.
[They refer to] the two links of craving and grasping.
Both manifest [craving] and its seeds are capable of providing moisture; thus,
craving serves as the causal condition for grasping.
Within the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*),
the first section explains the three existences (*tribhava*),
while the latter clarifies the seven existences (*saptabhava*).
In the desire realm, there are ten types of existence (*bhava*).
First is prior-time existence (*pūrvakālabhava*),
which exists from the moment after birth until the moment before death.
Between these two, there is that which is called "prior existence" (pūrvakālabhava) and "karmic existence" (karmabhava),
namely the link of volitional formations (saṃskāra).
Because it is moistened by craving and grasping,
that which can produce future fruit is called karmic existence (*karma-bhava*).
Third is the existence at death (*cyuti-bhava*).
At the very last moment of actual death,
there are four intermediate states:
the moment of death, and the moments of birth following that moment of death.
The interval between the two preceding destinies is called the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
There are five types of existence (*bhava*);
the first moment of birth within a destiny is the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*).
The existence of the other five destinies constitutes the general category,
while the preceding five constitute the specific categories.
The first five [elements] are broad and pervasive;
the latter five are narrow in substance.
Karma exists within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

One type of karma can be called "existence" (bhava),
while all others are merely "possessions" (parigraha);

From the moment one enters the intermediate state until one reaches the fundamental state of existence,

all [stages] are subsumed under the "birth" member (*jāti-aṅga*).

Therefore, the intermediate state (antarābhava) is included within the "existence-in-between" (antarā-bhava). There are six types of existence in the form realm (rūpadhātu), as the four miserable destinies (durgati) are excluded.
There are five types of existence in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Furthermore, because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is excluded,
this present link of existence (*bhavāṅga*) consists solely of the link of karma;
for it is said to be the appropriation by afflictions (*kleśa*) of previously performed formations (*saṃskāra*).
The *Cheng weishi lun* states:
"Craving and grasping, acting together as moisture,
are able to draw forth the seeds of karma."
And the causes that are projected are also termed "existence" (bhava),
because both are capable of bringing about the immediate presence of the fruit of future existence.
His intention is to say that the five factors, beginning with volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*),
are called the limb of existence (*bhavāṅga*) when they proceed, moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*).
Its essence consists solely of seeds,
because it is that which is moistened and because it is that which produces fruit.

Now, this general statement that "the ten [categories] are called 'existence' (bhava)" means that existence (bhava) consists of the combination of the capacity to exist (bhava) and that which exists (bhāva).
This is a general explanation of the meaning of existence.
It is not only that one understands the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*);

It exists within the intermediate state of the transition to rebirth,
because it occurs between two destinations;

In the past, there was existence at death and existence at birth;
these are the existences of the five destinies,
which are established separately.
Therefore, it is not established within the branch of birth (*jāti*).
First, the ten phrases are explained individually.
The subsequent section provides a summary of the meaning.
The first four lines describe the two modes of birth from womb and egg;
the next line describes the two modes of birth from moisture and transformation. Regarding "the body parts arising instantaneously":
This refers to the simultaneous arising of the limbs.
In the case of those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), the sense faculties arise all at once;
that is, the limbs such as hands and feet likewise arise simultaneously.
Moisture-born beings are not like this;
that is to say, their sense organs arise gradually,
while their limbs and members appear all at once.
This does not contradict the previous fascicle’s explanation that the sense faculties arise gradually for those born from a womb, an egg, or moisture.
The following five phrases apply to the acquisition of the aggregates (skandha-prāpti) across all four modes of birth.
This refers to the arising of the substance of the aggregates (*skandha*), the acquisition of the elements (*dhātu*). That is to say:
the seeds of the aggregates, the causal conditions of the aggregates, the manifestation and accomplishment of the aggregates, and the accomplishment of the seeds of the elements.
Regarding the attainment of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), both the manifest and the seeds [are involved].
The remaining three conditions are established.
Within the summary of the meaning, there are six points: intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The two phrases "gathering birth" (*saṃgraha-janman*) and "manifestation" (*abhinirvṛtti*) refer to the stage of the place of birth (*janma-sthāna*).

The two phrases concerning the acquisition of elements (*dhātu*) and the acquisition of bases (*āyatana*) refer to the support for what is projected [by karma].
The single phrase concerning the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) refers to co-nascent support.
This includes the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
The meaning of the single phrase can now be understood.

The latter explains death.

first, the individual explanation of seventeen phrases.
The subsequent summary of the meaning consists of ten phrases.
The first six phrases each subsume one [of the preceding] points.
The seventh concerns the deterioration of deportment.
This comprises five phrases,
namely from the seventh phrase to the eleventh phrase.
The eighth phrase is comprised of the transformation and decay of the formless faculties;
the tenth and thirteenth phrases [are likewise];

The fourteenth and fifteenth phrases subsume the point that the tenth stage has already passed and the lifespan is nearing its end.
The sixteenth and seventeenth phrases subsume the two types of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) at death.
First, the eleven phrases are explained individually;

"If one dies" subsumes the first two phrases.
Because it is the very essence of dying; if it is the nature of death, it subsumes the third and fourth phrases:
the factor that is understood and the factor that is not understood.

The tenth item, "the activity of the Māra of Death," refers to the actual entity of death itself;

This is also subsumed under the distinctions of death;

It is also said that these two factors of birth and death are subsumed within the state after death;
their nature consists of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), as appropriate to each case.
Because it manifests as suffering,

alternatively, this may include both the seeds and the manifest.
The *Cheng weishi lun* states:

All are comprised within the sense bases (*āyatana*).

The disintegration of the body and the end of life are termed "death" (*maraṇa*).

This treatise provides three interpretations.
Regarding the first "furthermore" section,
as for the statement that "due to wrong conduct, the mind becomes inverted," one interpretation holds that this refers to the five factors beginning with consciousness.
Furthermore, the five factors of the cause are explained based on the five stages of the present arising of birth, aging, and death in the future limit;
they are not explained based on the five factors while they are still in the causal stage.
Therefore, it is established as *vijñapti-mātra*.
Because their distinct characteristics are difficult to know during the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*),

If one follows this meaning,
that which is the inversion of mind refers to the consciousness that accords with karma.
Present volition is called "formations" (*saṃskāra*);
the sowing of karma is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*),
because it is said that the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) continues through rebirth.

This refers to the members of contact (sparśa) and feeling (vedanā).

The four subsequent links are established as the branches of birth, old age, and death belonging to the past life.

whereas this refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Therefore, there are only four factors;
through present feeling, craving arises,
whereby the afflictions increase and moisten the karma for future existence.
Up until the future existence where there is birth, aging, and death,
it is only said that [ignorance] moistens karma, not that it initiates it; however,
based on the prior limit (pūrvānta), one should understand that it does initiate karma.
This is merely a shadowy indication:
in the past, it was said that [ignorance] initiates karma but does not moisten it;
in the present, it is said that it moistens karma but does not initiate it.
Regarding the future, one speaks of birth, old age, and death,
but not of name-and-form and so forth;
regarding the present, one speaks of name-and-form and so forth.
It does not speak of birth, aging,
and death because they are known through the illumination of two lamps and two torches;
it seeks to demonstrate that the three time-periods of cause and effect are uninterrupted.

this is the gateway for the initiation of karma and the projection of rebirth. Regarding external objects as conditions:

this is the gateway for the moistening of rebirth and the arising of its fruit. As for those who give rise to delusions such as the grasping at a self: [this is the gateway for the arising of afflictions].
That which is associated with delusion, or that which arises because of it, is "unshared" (asādhāraṇa) delusion.
That which follows such karma and frequently gives rise to discursive thoughts refers to the manifesting consciousness;
it means that karma acts as an auxiliary companion to the consciousness.
The seeds of consciousness;
because the seeds perfumed by karma act as their auxiliary companions.
The various categories such as name-and-form and so forth are all termed "consciousness"; therefore,
they are able to induce the three types of suffering in the future.
The suffering of the initial arising of one faculty refers to the initial arising of the two faculties of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and mind (manas).
The suffering of the perfection of two faculties [refers to the completion of the male and female faculties].
That is to say, the six sense bases;
and the suffering of experiencing objects,
which is contact.
That is to say, when combined with names and phrases, there are two kinds of productive capacities.
In principle, there should actually be two fruits: consciousness and sensation.
Consciousness is designated as the seed.
Therefore, it does not exist within the fruit.
Regarding the designation of "external feeling" and "internal feeling," it does not exist within the fruit,
because craving necessarily arises only by depending upon feeling.
Regarding sensation (*vedanā*): it is said that while it does not exist in the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), it exists in the subsequent limit (*aparānta*).
This is because contact (*sparśa*) in the prior limit is said to result in sensation in the subsequent limit.
Although each has its own distinct basis, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises conditioned by contact, with sensation as its support.
"Craving (tṛṣṇā) gives rise extensively to pursuit;
below that is grasping (upādāna). By way of the door of activity":
"door" refers to the means [by which it functions].
This refers to activities such as those of kings who perform purificatory rites;
"the gateway of gain" refers to sitting, reclining, plowing fields, and so forth.
These two arise from external objects of desire and are termed the "quest for desire. Alternatively, it may be by way of the gateway of ascetic observances (*śīla-vrata*).
This refers to the precepts and observances based on wrong aspirations, or those arising from the gateways to liberation;
that is, the grasping at views.
Through the first two gateways, one initiates the pursuit of external desires.

From the gate of *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (adherence to precepts and observances), there arises the seeking of one's own body, because one seeks a body that will yield the fruit of happiness in the future.
From the gate of *mithyāvimokṣa* (false liberation), there arises the seeking of false liberation. Regarding this, there is one interpretation.
The gateway of activity refers to the desire for gain;
the gateway of material benefit.
This refers to the grasping at views;
for the sake of gain and honor,
one clings to their own views as superior.
The gate of precepts and observances refers to the grasping at precepts and observances.
The gate of liberation refers to...
This refers to the clinging to the doctrine of self (ātmavādopādāna).
Because it is based on [the four] truths and because one dwells [in them],
one clings to the intrinsic nature of a self as being liberation.
Consequently, these four types of clinging give rise to three kinds of seeking:
first, the seeking of sensual desires, because one seeks after the five objects of desire in abundance.
Second is seeking within one's own body;
this is "seeking that which exists," because it seeks the self-substance.
The threefold quest for false liberation is itself the quest for a false holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Because one seeks false liberation, when this quest arises, it causes the previously arisen afflictions and karmic actions of the four types of clinging (*upādāna*) to arise as well.
That is to say, karma is a link of existence;
ignorance serves as the condition for initiating karma,
causing future fruit to arise.
Ignorance is not a limb of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
For the third time, there are three [points].

In the previous two sections,
the dependent origination of defilement and purification was explained;
now, this is taught solely for those seeking purification, specifically for those who delight in worldly purity.
They do not delight in the supramundane;
because they delight in the realms of humans and gods, it is called "pure.
Nevertheless, due to ignorance, they also create non-meritorious karma. Or, there is that which is induced by the arising of remorse.

they regret non-meritorious actions; or,
out of delusion, they do not understand the causes for such regret.
Regarding these three karmas: "the mental continuum abiding as induced by joy" means that it abides as a continuum of seeds perfumed by a joyful state of mind;
this is precisely the *vijñāna* link.
With this as the cause:
for those lacking merit, it is a lower action;
for those possessing merit, it is a middling action.
Due to the superior karma of those who are immovable,
that which is capable of producing the seeds for the results of the three types of suffering in their future place of birth is called the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"Manifest activity" refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth;
it does not mention feeling (*vedanā*) and the rest, as the meaning follows from the previous explanation. "Delighting in sense objects" means:

attachment to objects constitutes existence.

aging, and death of the future limit.

Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, it is said: "It is because the Blessed One taught that for those who have attained liberation through wisdom, the fetters are severed first. This means that because the Blessed One taught that for those who have attained liberation through wisdom, the fetters are severed first, he taught that the fetters are severed prior to the cessation of ignorance.
