Before entering the state of a noble one,
during the initial stage of the equipment (sambhāra-avasthā),
one first contemplates in accordance with the sequential order.
Within the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*),
one contemplates in reverse order,
giving rise to forty-four knowledges (*jñāna*), seventy-seven knowledges, and so forth.
Because they are abandoned in accordance with the sequence of entering the path of seeing and so forth,
it is said that "with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease," and so on;
this occurs based upon the body of liberation belonging to one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
In the present life, with name-and-form as the precursor and feeling as the seeds for the latter four branches,
they cannot serve as the cause to produce the fruits of birth, aging, and death in a future existence; this explains that the causes of suffering cannot [by themselves] produce [the result].
The following clarifies that suffering does not arise because feeling has ceased:
when one who is liberated encounters present objects,
craving and its latent tendencies— that is, the factors of craving and grasping— do not arise.
Because they are forever uprooted by the power of the noble path so that they do not arise again,
this is called the permanent cessation of the origin of afflictions (*kleśa-samudaya-satya*) which serves as their moisture;
since this cause is permanently ceased, [the result follows].
The seeds of name-and-form and so forth previously cited as causes will not produce their effects;
this is called the cessation of the remaining members.
The intent of this statement is to clarify that.
The seeds of name-and-form existing in the present do not produce future fruits,
because one has previously contemplated the Truth of Suffering.
With the cessation of name-and-form as the primary factor,
by what is this cessation brought about?
It is brought about by the cessation of craving, grasping, and so forth, which are comprised within the truth of origination and have the power to moisten [existence].
The seeds of name-and-form and so forth will not produce fruit;
these seeds of name-and-form and so forth are the causes and conditions for birth, aging, and death in future lives.
Because they are direct causes and conditions,
it is said that these [factors] cease first;
ignorance and the others are indirect.
Subsequently, because one begins to investigate the cause that provides moisture [for rebirth], one does not state that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the primary factor to be extinguished.
Thus, having attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one contemplates: "Due to the absence of what is there the absence of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)? and so forth.
The remaining sequential cessations should be understood accordingly.
Seventh, regarding the etymological explanation:
within the explanation of the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
There are five kinds.
Regarding the explanation of the name based on its syllables:
it arises by virtue of the bondage of afflictions as a condition.
Because the various realms of existence arise again and again,
it is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).
This is based on the word *pratītya* and the word *samutpāda*.
Explaining the term "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda), it is therefore called "relying on letters. Regarding the explanation based on the meaning of "momentariness" (kṣaṇika):

this distinguishes [the position] from the Mahāsāṃghikas, the Mahīśāsakas, and others who hold that dependent origination is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and it also refutes the Saṃmitīyas' doctrine of the four characteristics (lakṣaṇa) occurring over the duration of a single lifetime. As for the phrase "the various conditions have passed away yet are not abandoned," etc.:
If considered according to their stages,
the first ten members serve as conditions,
while the final two members constitute the arising.
The preceding members possess the four conditions, such as the causal condition;
although they perish moment by moment and enter the past,
their seeds remain within the body and are not abandoned.
Therefore, it arises based on its own subsequent effects;
alternatively, each preceding member of the twelve links serves as a condition for each subsequent member to arise.
This is what is meant by "because this exists, that exists."
"Because this arises, that arises" reveals the meaning of dependent origination as being without an agent (*nirīha*).
"Not otherwise" means that the resultant phenomena exist solely by virtue of the existence of conditions.
It is not the case that a condition possessing a real, functional activity can produce an effect;
nor, because there is no producing factor as a cause,
can even a slight amount of produced phenomenon be established.
The two types—non-action (anabhisaṃskāra) and impermanence (anityatā)—act as conditions;
neither other functional activities nor the two types of non-arising act as causes.
Therefore, it is said that "it is not others."

This distinguishes [the term] from those such as Īśvara who possess real causal activity, and from those who reckon the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as being able to serve as the condition for dependent origination;
thus it explains its name. This is the fourth explanation.

It is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) because it repeatedly encounters conditions and the sequence of conditions arises again and again. Regarding that which "arises in equal continuity after having awakened to the nature of conditions in past lives":
this refers to the time when one first realizes *bodhi*.
Having awakened to dependent origination,
one subsequently gives rise to speech equally for the sake of sentient beings;
because it is taught [in this way], it is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).
Self-benefit is termed the "condition," while benefiting others is termed the "arising";
this refers to the meaning of the Wheel of Dharma being proclaimed through successive transmission.
The eighth section, on the meaning of the four conditions, has two parts:
first, the four conditions;
second, the two causes.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"In relation to one another, the various members [of dependent origination] certainly possess the nature of predominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*)."
The existence or non-existence of the remaining three conditions is not fixed;
in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*,
based on their definitive existence, it is stated that there is only one [condition].
That is to say, it refers to the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*): namely,
craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in relation to grasping (*upādāna*),
and existence (*bhava*) in relation to birth (*jāti*).
There is the sense of being a causal condition (*nidāna*).
If it is said that the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the seed of karma,
then volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) also act as a causal condition for consciousness.
The other members [of dependent origination], when viewed in relation to one another, lack the sense of being "conditioned by cause.
As for the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* stating that ignorance is "conditioned by cause" in relation to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*),
this is said with reference to the karmic latencies (*vāsanā*) of actions at the time of ignorance.
Because it is associated with ignorance (*avidyā*), it is metaphorically designated as "ignorance";
in reality, however, it is a seed of formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
This is consistent with the text of this passage.
Regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that the various members [of dependent origination] lack the condition of direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) when viewed in relation to one another,
this is based on the teaching that craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are solely karma.
To clarify this distinction, it says:
Ignorance in relation to volitional formations;
craving in relation to grasping;
and birth in relation to aging and death.
There are the conditions of immediate contiguity (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and object (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This refers to the relationship between the formless [aggregates] and the formless factors,
as well as the relationship between existence (*bhava*) and birth (*jāti*).
Feeling is related to craving by way of the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), but not by way of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This refers to the relationship between the members consisting of form and those consisting of the formless.
Regarding the mutual relationship between the remaining factors, both are absent;
this text provides a general statement,
while that text provides a specific explanation.
It should be explained as follows: regarding "form in relation to form," this refers to the form within name-and-form (nāmarūpa) in relation to the five bases (āyatana),
and to karma in relation to the arising of form.
Form arises in relation to form; aging and death arise in relation to form.
The formless arises in relation to the possessed of form;
ignorance arises in relation to formative forces.
There are five points regarding reputation:
the arising of the formless is superior to the aging and death of the realm of form.
In this context, non-karmic existence is not mentioned.
Therefore, it is not explained [here]. In this context, for the time being, the exposition of dependent origination is presented according to its immediate sequence, without confusion.
When these are compared with one another,
their functioning as conditions is indeterminate;
those who are wise should reflect upon this according to reason.
Regarding the question, "For what reason is it said that dependent origination is established based on the nature of cause and effect? and so forth:
the intent of this question is that the cause (hetu) encompasses all four conditions (pratyaya).
What is meant by "without causes and conditions"?
The intended meaning of the answer here is that,
among the ten types of causes:
Inducing, drawing forth,
and giving rise.
Within the categories of distinct determination, commonality of function,
and non-contradiction.
Although there are causes and conditions,
there exists a distinct cause for their specific determination,
from which a separate nature arises.
Co-existent causes do not contradict one another;
their substance extends to remote factors, though these are not discussed here in detail. As for their functions: they induce, project, and bring about [arising].
In seeking the names and explaining their meanings,
there must be causes and conditions; however,
this is based solely on the mutual observation of their manifest activities.
It is called the "inducing cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*),
because it is explained as referring to the karmic latencies (*vāsanā*) within the states of formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*), whether moistened or not yet moistened.
It is a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The seed of craving is not obstructed with respect to grasping,
and the seed of birth is the cause for the production of aging and death.
There is the sense of having a causal basis;
furthermore, this does not exclude the five factors, beginning with consciousness, during the stage prior to moistening,
in relation to birth, aging, and death.
It acts as the cause of attraction (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
Having moistened the five factors within existence (*bhava*), such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth, it relates [to them] in terms of birth,
aging, and death (*jāti-jarā-maraṇa*).
It serves as the cause for arising;
it possesses the sense of being a causal condition because the objects of expectation differ.
Nor is there any contradiction;
among the two causes— arising and projecting—
the factors from consciousness up to those branches subsumed within the stages of birth and old age and death [are included].
Regarding "that which draws forth the cause for birth":
this refers to the linking of rebirth through the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna*),
wherein the projector (*ākṣepaka*) and the projected (*ākṣipta*) occur simultaneously.

Yet, because they differ in terms of the time periods for producing their results— one being distant from the result and the other being simultaneous— they are both called "projecting causes" (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
This is because their capacity to produce the result is distinct across two different lifetimes.
That which is proximate and capable of producing [an effect] alone is called the "productive cause" (*janana-hetu*).
As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
"That which is proximate to and directly produces a fruit is termed the productive cause."
The cause that projects a remaining fruit at a distance is called the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
All the various categories explained here are as described in that commentary.
[This concludes the discussion on] the three natures and the ten causes.
As stated in the *Śubhāṣitasamuccaya*,
this explanation concerns defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and thus does not contradict other [teachings].
This is discussed in the ninth section on the analysis of conditions (*pratyaya*).
This is analyzed by means of twenty-seven sections.
First, the analysis through questions and answers regarding each individual member.
Regarding "ignorance has two questions and answers" and "is impelled by the power of karma and afflictions that give rise to birth and defilement," etc.:
That is to say, the defilement of birth arises from the defilement of karma;
the defilement of karma arises from the defilement of afflictions.
Therefore, it is said that [karma] is produced by what has been perfumed by those [afflictions]. The substance of karma refers to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Its primary cause has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its substance.
Although all afflictions are causes of karma, [ignorance is specified here as the primary one].
Ignorance alone possesses eleven superior characteristics;
therefore, it is specifically discussed in terms of its object and so forth.
As explained at length in the sūtras,
the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Ignorance is not said to have a cause."
The birth-link would have a beginning;
old age and death would not be said to be the fruit.
Birth and death would thus have an end.
From afflictions arise afflictions and karma;
from karma arises the objective entity;
and from the objective entity arise the factors of existence (bhavāṅgas) consisting of entities and afflictions.
Because the principle is solely this,
the twelve links [of dependent origination] constitute the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra.
Regarding the formations (saṃskāra), there are three questions and answers.

First, regarding the statement that "due to not understanding the causes of conventional suffering as dependent origination, one performs non-meritorious actions (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*) and so forth," the characteristics of the suffering of the three miserable realms (*durgati*) are easy to recognize.
This is called conventional suffering;
it is the suffering of the realms of humans and devas,
which is subtle, hidden, and difficult to discern.
That which is known by noble wisdom is called ultimate suffering (*paramārtha-duḥkha*).
Alternatively, some commentators explain that among the eight types of suffering:
According to the Abhidharma treatises, the first seven types of suffering are called conventional suffering (*saṃvṛti-duḥkha*),
while the eighth type of suffering is called ultimate suffering (*paramārtha-duḥkha*). If this interpretation is adopted, then since the eighth—
suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*)— pervades all five destinies (*gati*).
One should also give rise to meritorious and immovable karma while being deluded only regarding the miserable destinies;
since the first seven types of suffering pertain to both humans and devas,
one should also create non-meritorious karma while being deluded only regarding the happy destinies.

The three types of suffering—the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)—pervade all five destinies;
for this reason, it is known that the previous explanation is correct. These are the conventional and ultimate sufferings.
This conventional and ultimate suffering is explained according to the distinction between the coarse and the subtle, and the ease or difficulty of being known;
it is explained according to the general characteristics of the objects of engagement for both ordinary beings and noble ones.
Nor is there any contradiction; the proximate motivating cause for meritorious and immovable karma is exclusively wholesome volition (*cetanā*),
whereas the remote motivating cause is initiated by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because one is deluded regarding the future fruit, ignorance is said to be the condition;
furthermore, even for non-meritorious karma,
ignorance serves as its proximate cause.
Because they are deluded regarding their future results.
To answer the question of why this section speaks generally of the conditions for meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable karma:
the three unwholesome roots give rise exclusively to non-meritorious karma.
The unwholesome root of delusion (moha-akuśalamūla) pervades both the meritorious (puṇya) and the immovable (āniñjya) [karmas];
therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that there exists a lower-grade ignorance capable of giving rise to higher-grade actions.

If that were not the case, then the higher meditative absorption (dhyāna) arising when one first subdues the defilements of a lower stage would not constitute the factor of "volitional formation" (saṃskāra).

Because ignorance has not yet arisen in that stage, the unwholesome root of delusion (*moha-akuśalamūla*) universally gives rise to the three types of karma. Question: The arousal of karma involves both the auxiliary and the primary;
why do you speak only of the primary while omitting the auxiliary factors?
The existence that gives rise to moisture has both primary and auxiliary [causes].
When it is said that there is no dharma that is primary without an auxiliary, the answer is: a single cause does not depend on many.
It is said that the primary practice alone cannot bring about awakening;
its auxiliary conditions must necessarily rely upon cultivation.
Therefore, both the primary and the auxiliary are presented together. As for the statement, "based on the conditions that give rise to all practices," it means:
It is not merely because they are said to have bodily and vocal conduct as their conditions that volition (*cetanā*) is not said to be the condition for body and speech; rather,
it is said [that they arise] based on the conditions of wholesome or defiled volitions that have been produced.
Therefore, it is said that ignorance is the condition;
it is not said that indeterminate formations are the condition,
because the two types of formation— those of body and speech— are exclusively indeterminate.
It is because it is taught that ignorance gives rise to the various formations (*saṃskāra*);
because it is proximate in its ability to give rise to the three types of wholesome and defiled actions of body, speech, and mind;
and because consciousness (*vijñāna*) can serve as the cause for their new arising, and so forth.
Consciousness enters the womb as the cause for new birth,
because the general retribution can serve as the condition for the specific retribution;
or alternatively, the seed of consciousness serves as the direct cause for name-and-form.
Because it causes [the embryo] to be newly born,
this explains the meaning of the initial linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
This should be understood by analogy with the subsequent entry of consciousness into the womb.
The previous explanation is superior.
Furthermore, the cause for the arising of consciousness within the three realms must be universal;
therefore, this [cause] alone is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that because the six bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are preeminent, they subsume two types:
the six bases subsume both the six sense organs (ṣaḍindriya) and the six consciousnesses (ṣadvijñāna), as these two are conjoined;
or alternatively, the six sense organs themselves subsume the other two—the [six] consciousnesses and mental objects (dharma).
Therefore, while it was previously stated that the objects are distinct,
it is now stated that the objects are common;
this is because contact is their proximate cause.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"That is to say, the aspect of being agreeable and so forth, which is grasped by contact (*sparśa*);
and the aspect of appropriation and so forth, which is grasped by feeling (*vedanā*)."
Because they are proximate and induce a superior state,
just as through the power of feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, one seeks either union with or separation from a similar object.
This means that the object of sensation resembles the object of craving:
one craves for union with the object of pleasant sensation,
and craves for separation from the object of painful sensation.
It is called a "similar object.
Therefore, it is said that craving has the branch of sensation (*vedanā*) as its condition.
Ignorance, however, pertains only to the characteristics of arising and ceasing within the two types of internal and external sensations.
Not knowing things as they truly are,
one is unable to restrain the mind and gives rise to modes of activity that lack clear understanding.
Affection that is not intimate or compliant is not said to function as a condition.
However, if affection arises from delusion even toward those who are distant,
it still possesses the sense of being a condition.
It is not like the "feeling" (vedanā) that is taught in the treatises as a condition;
rather, because it arises from longing, it is able to activate latent tendencies (anuśaya) during the time of pursuit.
This is because craving seeks the union with desirable objects and the separation from undesirable ones.
And it perfumes the seeds,
giving rise to the proclivities (*anuśaya*) and the phenomena conducive to grasping (*upādānīya-dharma*),
because craving and grasping are predominant.
It is stated that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) serve as conditions.
Question: It was previously stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as the condition for the arising of karmic existence (*karma-bhava*).
Are these wholesome and unwholesome karmas already moistened or not yet moistened?
All are designated as "existence" (bhava) because they are capable of producing results; here,
we rely on that which, having been moistened, is capable of immediately producing a result.
It alone receives its name.
Prior to moistening [the seed], the initial formation that departs from increase is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*).
Based on their distinct meanings, each receives its own name; however,
here, based on the general meaning,
it is said that ignorance gives rise to karmic existence (*karmabhava*).
This is precisely the path of action (*karmapatha*).
Regarding the second classification,
the phrase "three are the paths of affliction" (*kleśamārga*) and so forth means:
The *Cheng weishi lun* states:
"Ignorance, craving, and grasping are subsumed under the category of afflictions (*kleśa*)."
This refers precisely to these three.
Conduct constitutes one part;
it is subsumed under karma.
This refers precisely to these two.
That [text] corresponds to this [work], which states:
"In some places it is said that karma completely encompasses existence."
One should know that this is because it is taught based on the existence [of consciousness] through karma;
as the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"In some places, it is said that consciousness is subsumed under karma."
Because that [text] states that the seeds of karma constitute the link of consciousness,
the "remainder" refers to the other seven links;
for it is taught that when combined, these constitute the path of karma.
The *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) states:
"Seven [of the eighteen elements] possess one part that is subsumed under suffering."
Because the five kinds, beginning with consciousness,
transform and are termed "existence," there are two stages within the third [section], the analysis of cause and effect.

First, regarding the twelve links in their sequential order as cause and effect: three are exclusively causes—namely ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—because they are the fundamental roots for the initiation of karma and the moistening of rebirth;
two are exclusively effects—namely birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
This is because it is the fruit produced by the preceding ten members.
Furthermore, this is based on the three types of defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and the causal relationship between seeds and manifestations;
since the perspectives from which they are viewed differ, the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are collectively subsumed under the categories of cause and fruit.
Briefly, there are five stages.
First is the stage of origination (*samutthāna*),
which means that each preceding factor serves as the cause for the subsequent one.
The subsequent ones serve as the results;
thus, this first statement—that the very first is solely a cause and so forth—is the second [point], namely, the cause and result of the beginning and the end.
This second [point] is also [included therein].
Because afflictions are the root,
these three are exclusively causes and so forth.
Below this, it is also stated that the first six links, as well as craving, grasping, and becoming, constitute the causal portion.
The latter two factors constitute the fruit-portion.
Feeling (vedanā) pertains to both types [of cause and fruit].
Furthermore, cause and fruit are distinguished according to their fundamental and derivative aspects. Third, there are causes and fruits that are either matured (vipāka) or non-matured (avipāka).
Fifty-sixth: Furthermore,
there are five factors subsumed under the results of the present life,
and two factors subsumed under the results of future lives.
This is collectively termed dependent origination subsumed under the category of results (*phala-saṃgṛhīta-pratītyasamutpāda*).
One should know that the remaining members are dependent origination subsumed under the category of causes (*hetu-saṃgṛhīta-pratītyasamutpāda*).
The *Madhyāntavibhāga*, first fascicle, also states:
Defilement by cause refers to the categories of afflictions and karma;
defilement by result refers to...
This refers to the remaining portions: the four causes and effects, both matured and unmatured.
The Abhidharma-śāstra states:
"At the time of the cause, there is that which projects and that which is projected."
That is to say, the aforementioned seven branches;
at the time of the fruit, there is that which produces and that which is produced,
namely the latter five branches.
This means that because craving and grasping are matured by ignorance and increase through it,
the six links beginning with volitional formations are termed "existence" (*bhava*) as they reach maturity; thus,
the two links of birth and old age are what are matured— this constitutes the fivefold sequence of cause and effect.
As stated previously regarding the two causes that project [the result]:
"The projecting cause and the producing cause together constitute the ten links as the cause."
The latter two members are the fruit.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states:
"The ten causes and the two fruits are necessarily not of the same temporal period."
Although the five meanings explained through various approaches differ because their respective perspectives vary,
there is no contradiction in principle.
Regarding the statement that "the four [links] are of individual characteristics while the three are of combined characteristics," the *Cheng weishi lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra) states:
"Ignorance, craving, and grasping are explained [as being of combined characteristics]."
It is called "unique characteristic" because it does not intermingle with other factors;
the others are "mixed characteristics," meaning they are those capable of inducing desirable or undesirable results.
Its substance is the member of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*),

because prior to being moistened, it is termed the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*). Furthermore, that which is able to produce the distinctions among the realms of rebirth (*gati*) is the member of existence (*bhava*).
Because it is moistened by the formations (*saṃskāra*),
it is further designated as "existence" (*bhava*),

for it is that which can produce the [subsequent] members. As for the fact that consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and a portion of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) possess mixed characteristics:
This shows that these three branches have two kinds of intermingling:
first, when manifesting as a result,
they intermingle with future results.
In the subsequent sections, these are mixed;
as for the mutual relation of the two causal factors,
their own natures are likewise mixed.
Now I ask about this matter:
namely, that a single consciousness receives three distinct names— name-and-form, the six sense bases, and contact—
but feeling is not consciousness.
Therefore, it does not inquire into the "mixed" [factors], but rather relies on those that are "defiled.
This refers to the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna-anga*), as stated in the preceding text.
Due to misconduct, the mind becomes inverted;
once the consciousness that manifests through inversion has perfumed the seeds, this is called the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Regarding the time of moistening:
That is, the seeds of consciousness,
moistened by craving and grasping,
at the initial stage of linking rebirth.
Regarding the limb of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and its dependent transformation:
at the time when the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise from this very name-and-form,
it is called the limb of the six sense bases.
The six sense bases and so forth are not entirely and exclusively consciousness, because they all possess consciousness;
therefore, they constitute a mixture. To specifically reveal the characteristic of suffering:
The five types beginning with consciousness,
in their state of manifest activity,
reveal the characteristics of the three kinds of suffering.
Birth, aging, and death are so named because the characteristics of suffering in the present cause have not yet become manifest;
these are termed the five [aggregates], beginning with consciousness.
Upon reaching the stage of actualization,
these five types of factors that have induced the production of results are distinguished according to their preceding and succeeding stages,
and are termed birth, aging, and death.
Therefore, in explaining the sūtra, it is said that the causes for the distinctions between the manifest and the induced— namely,
dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and that which arises from conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*)— are brought together through their conjunction.
That which is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) refers to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) that causes all conditioned formations (saṃskāra) to arise.
The nature that brings about the arising of these formations is termed "dependent origination," while that which is produced is termed "dependently arisen" (pratītyasamutpanna).
Therefore, the Abhidharma states:
"The cause is called dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda);
the result is called dependently arisen (pratītyasamutpanna)."
Within the inclusion of the five truths,
these seven factors are said to be the truth of suffering;
the remaining five factors have already been explained.
It is only the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) that is so described,
for the purpose of clarifying the distinction between the essential natures of the two truths;
it is not the case that all five factors constitute the Truth of Origination.
The *Cheng weishi lun* states:
"All are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering,
because their nature is that of the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*)."
The five [aggregates] are also subsumed under the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*),
because they are of the nature of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Oppression" is the meaning of suffering (*duḥkha*).
All are suffering,
because they summon maturation and because they possess the meaning of origination.
The fifth is also the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Among the four ways in which the various members (*aṅga*) serve as conditions for one another,
the first is being a condition by way of sequential order (*anupūrva-pratyayatā*).
Second, the explanation of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
Third, the question regarding the extent of their karmic functions.

Fourth, the question regarding the breadth or narrowness of their conditions. That is to say: "By means of ignorance, with respect to the phenomena that accord with the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), etc. and so forth.
Unwholesome mental formations are called "conformable formations";
they arise simultaneously with ignorance as their momentary origination.
Therefore, it is called "simultaneously obscured and obstructed.
Due to the five wrong views, indulgence, and negligence, it is associated with ignorance;
this condition arises from those views.
Because it is not associated with wholesome conditions,
it serves as the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for unwholesome bodily and verbal conduct;
or alternatively, it arises through ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).
It acts as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) that directly induces the various formations (*saṃskāra*).
If these wholesome formations are induced by ignorance (*avidyā*), [they arise].
This serves as a long-term condition;
due to delusion regarding that result, the first two types of volition arise,
and only subsequently does the formation of karma arise.
Thus, it constitutes a condition for cessation that persists over a long duration and establishes future fruits;
this explains the meaning of the distinct arising of the two types of formations.
It may also serve as a co-existent condition for wholesome conduct;
however, because it arises momentarily and does not directly initiate karma,
it is not mentioned here.
These and other such meanings should be understood by analogy.
As for the fact that formations (*saṃskāra*) serve as the co-existent condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*) for consciousness (*vijñāna*),
it is because they bring about its gathering through their distinct natures.
Manifest activity serves as the immediately preceding condition for the seeds of subsequent consciousness,
whereas seeds do not serve as conditions for manifest activity.
Because they are always co-existent,
consciousness, in relation to name-and-form and so forth,
is explained entirely from the perspective of their manifest activity and their status as future fruits.
If that were not the case, there would only be simultaneous conditions; feeling would serve as a condition for craving only by way of having ceased long ago.
That is to say, based on the object of feeling, craving subsequently arises and moistens it, whereby the fruit of the future is produced.
Therefore, it is said that one establishes [the state of] being difficult to liberate in the future and so forth. Regarding craving as a co-existent condition for grasping:
it refers to the desire and attachment established toward phenomena conducive to grasping, which proceed together with greed.
That is to say, craving and the act of grasping do not actually exist simultaneously; rather,
there is that which is grasped, the purpose for which one grasps,
and the causal conditions for grasping.

Because craving co-exists with grasping, craving serves as the co-existent condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*) for grasping; grasping serves as three conditions for becoming; furthermore, the capacity to project that fruit constitutes the distant condition (*parokṣa-pratyaya*).
This refers to the initial arising [of craving],
not to its subsequent continuity;
it is the craving for self that arises in relation to the various realms at the very moment of birth.
Because there is an interval of exactly one moment of death, it constitutes a distant condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*). Because there is an expectation of rebirth, it constitutes three conditions.
As for what is called "perfuming and activating those seeds": [it refers to this].
Because the seeds within consciousness and other factors have been perfumed by past karma, they are now called "existence" (bhava) as they produce manifest results;
thus, they constitute simultaneous existence (sahabhū). Although these seeds perished long ago, the result nevertheless arises.
Just as the initial moistening of a seed is transformed into the first produced fruit,
it constitutes a remote cause of cessation that acts as a projecting condition.
Because it is separated from the moment of death itself,
among the two types of existence-constituents (*bhavāṅga*),
the former consists solely of karmic existence (*karmabhava*).
The latter six constitute existence (*bhava*).
Because they are moistened by grasping (*upādāna*), they are further designated as existence;
this is termed "appropriation" (*parigraha*).
Regarding these very functions and all their respective functions within their individual spheres of activity as appropriate,
the Abhidharma-śāstra states that the member of ignorance has two kinds of function.

First, it causes sentient beings to be deluded regarding existence; second, it serves as a condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) up to birth (*jāti*). Regarding karma, there are two types: first, it causes the arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth in sentient beings.
Second, it serves as a condition for aging and death.
Thus, each of these links has two functions;
such is its second function.
This very functional activity refers to the three kinds of conditions explained above,
as well as all activities pertaining to their respective arising objects.
That is precisely what constitutes the first karma.
He further explains that old age and death also consist of two types of karma:
first, that which repeatedly causes the transformation of the temporal stages of sentient beings, thereby bringing about their deterioration, diminution, and decay.
Second, because it causes the lifespan of sentient beings to undergo change and destroys their life-span.
In this context, it is said that only the preceding member serves as a condition for the succeeding one;
therefore, there is no condition for old age and death.
This is not contradictory.
Seventh, the explanation of the sūtra:
"Because this exists, that exists," and so forth, in four propositions.
First, it is shown that dependent origination is without agency;
the resultant phenomena arise solely by virtue of the existence of conditions.
It is not the case that conditions possess a real, functional activity capable of producing a dharma as its fruit;
therefore, it is said that by virtue of the non-cessation of conditions, the meaning of further production arises.
Second, this reveals dependent origination as impermanent.
A small produced phenomenon cannot be established by taking a non-arising phenomenon as its cause.
The latter two clarify the meaning of dependent origination in terms of its dynamic power and function;
that is to say, although the third [verse] states that all phenomena are without agency,
and the fourth states that all phenomena are impermanent.
However, all effects do not arise by depending on any single phenomenon as their condition,
because the functional capacities of phenomena differ.
It is stated as follows: first, the refutation of causal arising through functional activity;
second, the refutation of eternalist causal arising;
third, the elucidation of causal arising through dynamic power.
The fourth [point] refutes the fallacy that, due to unequal conditions, what is produced by another would be experienced as a result by oneself.
Within the eightfold four-line analysis,
it is not necessarily a constituent factor.
Because it speaks of that [state] in a general sense,
the second phrase regarding ignorance does not mention the fruit of karmic retribution for obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) actions.
Because it is abbreviated.
Next, the second phrase:
"The same applies to the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) consciousness. Or, there may be that which is craving but not conditioned by feeling.
That is to say, one who seeks excellent liberation and, relying on wholesome desire (*kuśalacchanda*), abandons other forms of craving—

this category of wholesome desire for the Dharma is called "craving for liberation" (*mokṣarāga*). Furthermore, it refers to all wholesome desires that involve the wearying abandonment of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
It does not arise conditioned by a feeling that is favorable to craving,
nor does it coexist with such a feeling, nor does it precede it;
for there is no feeling that is favorable to craving.
To say that it is not a condition is not contradictory; in fact,
according to the true principle, one should here follow the latter part of the statement.
All that is craving necessarily arises conditioned by feeling.
However, there are instances where something is conditioned by feeling but is not craving;
this refers to the subsequent remaining links [of dependent origination].
9. Regarding "ignorance and the mental formations arising from it, if there is even a single part [of them]," these constitute the twelve links.
All of these obstruct right view, right thought, and so forth; here, however,
we speak of the preeminent obstacles,
mentioning only ignorance and the defiled mental formations.
Furthermore, there are the mental formations that obstruct right view and so forth,
as well as bodily formations,
vocal formations, and one portion of form.
Regarding the hindrances to right speech and so forth: as for right mindfulness and right concentration, those that act as predominant hindrances to the remaining factors of existence are as follows:
namely, with the exception of ignorance and formations in their entirety and one part, the other nine factors and a small portion of one factor [act as hindrances].
They obstruct right mindfulness and right concentration.
What is now called "the remainder" refers to the complete exposition of the nine factors.
There are two explanations for this.
The first states that because the preceding three factors describe the body of right wisdom and the body of morality,
the remaining nine factors are collectively termed "obstacles to right concentration" and so forth by virtue of their association with them.
In reality, one should speak only of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*);
these two obstruct the path of detachment, namely right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Furthermore, it is said that "the body of concentration" refers to the training of the mind (*citta-śikṣā*).
The link of consciousness is mind (*citta*).
Name-and-form, the six sense bases, birth, and old age and death all possess the essence of mind.
Furthermore, the two links of contact and feeling are mental factors (*caitta*).
The intermediate form together with the five preceding bases are collectively called the "body that obstructs right concentration" from the perspective of consciousness.
The two links of craving and grasping obstruct the path of detachment;
they specifically obstruct the body of meditative concentration.
This explains that right view, right intention, and right effort constitute the training in wisdom;
while right speech, right action, and right livelihood [constitute the training in ethical discipline].
The training in higher ethical discipline consists of right mindfulness and right concentration;
these constitute the training in higher concentration.
In the *Cheng weishi lun* (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*),
regarding the inclusion of the six *pāramitās* within the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*),
it is sometimes stated that diligence (*vīrya*) is included in all three because it universally exerts them.
Alternatively, this is discussed from the perspective of a beginner;
thus it says that diligence consists solely of precepts,
because one guards the precepts.
Now, based on long-standing accomplishment,
because insight is seen to be superior when aided by diligence,
it consists solely of the body of wisdom.
Because right mindfulness gives rise to the factors of right concentration,
it is subsumed under the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*);
this is because mindfulness maintains clear recollection and the mind remains focused.
The fourteen factors that belong exclusively to the category of affliction (saṃkleśapakṣa) are ignorance, craving, grasping, and consciousness,
because the mind is inverted.
That is, the seeds of consciousness, due to being perfumed by karma;
or, the fourth [member] is old age and death.
Within the state of old age and death:
Because they cannot be cultivated and studied,
the five factors beginning with consciousness are given the name "defiled" (kliṣṭa).
According to the explanation of the auxiliary factors (*upaniṣad*),
these six factors are in reality neither defiled nor pure.
The name "cause" is applied according to the fruits of collective and individual karma.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The third consists solely of the defiled."
Because they are of the nature of afflictions;
and seven are exclusively non-defiled,
because they are the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
This text states that within the seven stages,
it is possible for defilement to arise.
The designation "provisional" applies to both [types of craving]. The others apply to both kinds as well.
Therefore, it is only the defiled [craving] that is described as having four branches.
Whether it be consciousness or old age and death,
they are provisionally designated by the name "defilement";
however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is only consciousness.
Nor is this contradictory.
What eleven types of ignorance are absent such that, in their absence,
there are three kinds of active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and ignorance?
Initiation refers to the ignorance that initiates karma;
this encompasses both associated and non-associated envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
This refers to the ignorance that moistens rebirth;
it is mostly associated [with other mental factors],
and these two both manifest simultaneously.
The seeds perfumed by these are called the latent tendency of ignorance (*anuśaya-avidyā*).
This is because the ignorance that initiates action takes all forms of ignorance as its root.

In this context, it is explained generally that ignorance (*avidyā*) moistens rebirth; furthermore, among the members of dependent origination, "formative forces" (*saṃskāra*) correspond to "existence" (*bhava*), while "ignorance" corresponds to "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) and "grasping" (*upādāna*).
Therefore, this is explained generally. Moreover, these three types function as the general initiators.
Within this, there are two types:
the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Because they are discussed both collectively and individually, they are called the "three kinds."
The essence of their arousal is associated with the unshared [factors];
thus, the four become three,
because these three are collectively extinguished.
That [ignorance] which gives rise to formations ceases;
because that ceases, formations cease.
This explains how ignorance, in its general description, is what gives rise to all formations.
If it were not so, why would the ignorance that moistens rebirth— which has not yet been extinguished—
be extinguished immediately upon its activation? Furthermore, there are three kinds.
The latent tendency of ignorance that gives rise to the outbursts (paryavasthāna) functions in two ways:
first, it can give rise to the outbursts;
second, it can give rise to their associated states.
Third, they are able to give rise to what is not shared.
These three are all *paryavasthāna* (envelopments);
the first envelopment is the general one.
The latter two are specific;
therefore, there are three types of underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of ignorance that manifest in this way.
Because these three underlying tendencies of ignorance are extinguished, [the path arises].
The manifestation of ignorance ceases;
because the manifestation of ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease.
Furthermore, there are three [aspects].
This refers to the three realms.
Within these three realms, because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of entanglement that manifest have ceased,
manifest ignorance (*avidyā*) ceases.
Because ignorance is now extinguished, all volitional formations are extinguished.
Among the formations, ignorance alone is singled out as the primary factor for the three realms.
That which has already been performed and not yet ceased within one's own continuum refers to mental formations (*manas-karman*).
Furthermore, because of mental formations, bodily and vocal formations arise;
these refer to the two types of formations, bodily and vocal.
Regarding the statement, "By means of these three formations, consciousness exists; because they are absent, that condition for consciousness is also absent," this refers to the seed-consciousness,
which takes formations as its condition.
Because formations (*saṃskāra*) are absent, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is absent.
If formations are entirely non-existent, that consciousness is also non-existent;
or rather, because this seed-consciousness is entirely non-existent.
The manifest consciousness also does not exist.
Regarding the principle that because such-and-such feeling does not exist, craving does not exist, and so on up to the application of the condition of consciousness:
it is asked, "Feeling is the fruit."
Craving is affliction;
volitional formations are karma;
consciousness is the fruit.
They are not similar at all.
How can they be said to be analogous?
Answer: It is because of their activity and consciousness.
Because the fruits and karmas are distinct,
their natures are mutually different; thus,
one now experiences the fruit of feeling and the fruit of craving.
Or, although they are distinct in nature,
because they are identical [in function], one points to them as being non-distinct;
just as the maturation arises from karma.
The afflictions arising from maturation are not contradictory in meaning because they belong to the same category.
This is so within the inclusion of the twelve and eightfold gates of dependent origination.
"The three gates are what is manifested by that" is the general statement.
Regarding these three:
The second is that which is manifested by a single portion; namely, the gate of the arising of internal consciousness and the gate of the performance of its own karma.
Regarding the gate of the arising of internal consciousness:
consciousness arises in dependence upon the sense faculties.
That is to say: the gate of the essence of these various consciousnesses; the gate of what is produced by one's own karma.

Since karma invites maturation (*vipāka*), and because there are cases where it consists solely of individual retribution (*pratyeka-vipāka*), it is said to be "one part. There are three types of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
First is dependent origination by way of its own nature,
which refers to the eighth retributive consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*),
because it is the very nature of that which arises dependently.
Second is the dependent origination of experience,
which refers to the six groups of consciousness,
because they experience objects.
The three types of craving arise conditioned by the path of the agreeable and the disagreeable;
this is precisely the twelve links.
This is the gateway for the arising of consciousness.
Relying on the faculties and taking objects as conditions,
it initially appears to be the enjoyment of dependently arisen phenomena;
this is the gateway of one's own karma.
At first glance, it appears as though arising from self-nature and conditions;
in its entirety, it is both the path of the agreeable and the disagreeable,
and externally, it is the ripening of crops.
The vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) and the three types of sustenance (*āhāra*) that support them are all external vessels; therefore,
they are not of the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Pure sovereign power is contrary to the nature of dependent origination; therefore,
it is also not included.
Although the wholesome factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and so forth are called "gates of purification" (*viśuddhi-mukha*),

they are not included [in the category of the outflows] because they act as adverse conditions that oppose the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*), and furthermore, because they do not accord with or benefit it.
The meaning of reversing the flow [of dependent origination] is as explained in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
Regarding the thirteen faults:
first, the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is the root.
Consequently, the views arising from this— namely, the denial of the three time periods and the view of eternalism,
together with false views—
constitute three [categories] among the sixty-two views.
According to their respective dispositions,
they take the three periods of time as their object and give rise to views of eternalism, nihilism, and false views.
Therefore, in this fifth [view],
one regards this very view with fierce intensity and firm attachment as supreme;
one fears that nirvāṇa will not be attained in the present.
This refers to the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) or the five theories of attaining nirvāṇa in this very life (*dr̥ṣṭadharmika-nirvāṇavāda*).
These five possess these faults.
