This refers to the final three [links].
The *Cheng weishi lun* states:
"Because the six links already moistened are combined to constitute 'existence' (*bhava*)."
That is to say, because the five [aggregates] beginning with consciousness have distinct states of the three characteristics,
they are designated as "birth" and so forth;
that which is of inferior grade is called "craving."
The superior grade is called "grasping" (upādāna).
Therefore, all are real.
In the fifteen [categories], five are each a single entity.
Regarding the statement that "the others are not a single matter," it refers to the five factors— ignorance, consciousness, contact, sensation, and craving.
Among these sixteen, one is the cause of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It was previously stated that the twelve links are subsumed under afflictions, karma, and suffering.
Having already distinguished all twelve as belonging to the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Whether it be the one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions and so forth,
the karma produced by them,
or the fruits obtained therefrom.
These are all afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
therefore, they are not inquired about here.
Only the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are questioned.
This refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because ignorance serves as the cause for the non-defined wisdom that clings to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*),
it is called the cause of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
In reality, both the cognitive obscurations and the afflictive obscurations have ignorance as their cause.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Because that [ignorance] actually takes this as its basis,
it is now said that the ignorance which initiates karma increases due to delusion regarding the principle (*li*)."
Because they coexist,
they do not contradict each other even as causes for the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, because this ignorance initiates karma and brings about rebirth,
there subsequently arise the obstacles to the known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
They arise and increase through successive stages;
ignorance is the root, and it alone is declared to be the cause. Among the seventeen [factors], five are capable of producing suffering.

That is to say, ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) constitute the five [factors]. The "suffering of the embryonic matrix" refers to the five seeds, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding the eighteen [factors], the first six, as well as craving, grasping, and existence, constitute the causal portion (*hetubhāga*).
With sensation as the fruit,
it constitutes the stage of being the cause that gives rise to and moistens the delusions of rebirth.
It is said that [contact] arises from touch.
Since the two limits are distinct,
it alone is termed "mixed."
Furthermore, since the fruit exists in the future birth while the cause exists in the seed,
the two temporal limits are distinct.
In each successive birth, he possesses distinct characteristics, whereas others do not;
all are purely cause and effect.
This is because cause and effect are distinguished according to their fundamental and derivative aspects.
The nineteenth [point] states that the first six members can produce subsequent effects,
such as desirable and undesirable objects.
This refers to agreeable and disagreeable objects;
the feeling that takes these objects as its conditions is designated as the "fruit.
This is because desirable and undesirable objects serve as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Birth is able to take feeling as its object;
therefore, feeling is called the fruit.
That is to say, the preceding six members serve as the cause.
Because it can produce the fruit of this sensation,
it is not the object of sensation; yet,
the first six [consciousnesses] arise with respect to it.
This means that formations (saṃskāra) serve as the cause for sensation (vedanā).
Ignorance (avidyā) gives rise to consciousness (vijñāna), name-and-form (nāmarūpa),
and the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), which in turn serve as the basis for sensation.
Contact can give rise to feeling;
it is said to "give rise" to it because it corresponds accordingly.
There are three types of craving and grasping.
That which is capable of moistening and that which is moistened act as the cause,
producing the effect which is the substantial body of the five destinies;
this consists solely of the single link of sensation (*vedanā*).
It can produce two kinds of results:
namely, once the seeds to be experienced in the present have been moistened,
they can produce the manifest experience of feeling.
This is called the fruit produced prior to birth;
it is the seed induced by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) that gives rise to the personal existence (*ātma-bhāva*) in the future.
That which gives rise to subsequent fruits is called "producing subsequent results.
Alternatively, that which causes similar types [of dharmas] to arise from preceding to succeeding moments is called "producing initial results."
While the seeds have not yet been moistened,
[ignorance] acts as a remote drawing cause (ākṣepahetu) for the production of birth and old age and death in a future life.
This is called "producing subsequent results.
Regarding the phrase "twenty [factors] associated with pleasure, excluding two, and the rest," this refers to the statement "only consciousness" (*vijñaptimātra*).
Ten [factors] are associated with pleasure and equanimity.
This is because feeling does not associate with itself,
and because in the stage of old age and death, there is mostly an absence of pleasure and the possibility of equanimity.
Eleven [factors] are associated with suffering;
this is because they are not associated with feeling.
Old age and death involve much suffering.
Therefore, eleven [factors] are taught.
As for the essence of their seeds,
they exist simultaneously with their respective states.
Just as with the factors [of dependent origination] and so forth,
one should reflect according to reason upon all seeds arising together with other seeds.
"Both" refers to co-existent [factors].

Regarding the "twenty-one," such as the factors associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā-sahagata*) and a portion of the factors not associated with feeling (*a-vedanā-sahagata*) that are subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), he says:
Eleven [of these] are subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
In the stages of old age and death, pleasant sensations (*sukha-vedanā*) are generally absent;
since the suffering of change is established based on pleasure, it is not mentioned here.
This refers to those factors that do not coexist with the factor of feeling (*vedanā*),
specifically those that coexist with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*);
these are established as "perishing" based on pleasure.
Therefore, it is said that one part and twelve sub-parts are comprised within the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Because painful feeling exists within all the factors [of existence],
the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā) is established based on that painful feeling;
therefore, it is said to be "one part."
The twelve [links] in their entirety,
comprising all contaminated phenomena, are subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Because all are characterized by the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), they are explained in terms of the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
There are eleven minor categories.
Excluding the factors of old age and death,
there are only ten that are associated with neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Now, by adding the factor that is not associated with feeling,
it is said to be "a portion of eleven," according to the actual meaning explained previously.
Thus, within these various sacred teachings,
the explanations are not fixed according to the predominance of particular characteristics;
that is to say, there are differences between the two texts of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
As stated in the eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*:

"Regarding the fact that in the twenty-two [levels], such as the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the attainment of non-thought (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), and those possessing form (*rūpin*), the factors of form (*rūpāṅga*) can be obtained"—
this is based on the six consciousnesses.
The statement that there are no non-material factors (arūpīṇa-aṅga) follows the Sarvāstivāda method of exposition;
it is not the ultimate truth.
That school also maintains that sleep is not a state of being without mind;
the same applies to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This is according to the ultimate meaning (*tattvārtha*).
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
all factors (aṅga) are complete;
in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), only the present manifestation of form is excluded.
Therefore, it was stated in the previous fascicle that in the formless realm, consciousness relies on the seeds of form.

Regarding the twenty-three [types of reliance], this refers to relying on the factors of the higher stages while being detached from the factors of the lower stages; this constitutes only one branch of such reliance.
He says: The factors of the path of the higher stages can subdue those of the lower stages;
these consist of the six types of mental aspects, namely coarseness, suffering, and so forth.
Because one who seeks rebirth in a higher realm initiates it there,
it arises only in the first [meditative] stage of a higher level,
and not elsewhere.

Nor is it the entirety of the formations; therefore, it is said to be "one part. Regarding the phrase "twenty-four are the three defilements, while the remainder are of two kinds": (Note: This refers to the classification of the twenty-two faculties [indriyas] within the five aggregates. Twenty-four—namely, the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life, female, male, suffering, joy, grief, equanimity, faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"—are associated with the three defilements (kleśa). The remaining eight—the faculties of mind, pleasure, indifference, and the four factors of "having known," "final knowledge," and "the one who has fully known"—are of two kinds: both associated with defilement and dissociated from defilement.)
Regarding those [factors], ignorance, craving,
and grasping are exclusively unwholesome or obscured-neutral;
these three defilements alone [constitute them].
In the preceding fourth section,
four types of defilement were explained;
here, three are mentioned.
This is actually prior and provisional;
because their meanings differ, among the unwholesome [states],
there are both those that are defiled and those that are non-obscured-neutral.
That cloud-like movement consists only of the wholesome and unwholesome;
it also extends to the wholesome, unwholesome, and non-obscured neutral [states] during the seven stages.
Because it also arises as both wholesome and defiled, it is said to "pertain to both";
yet in reality, it is neutral (avyākṛta).
Since it depends on the five [faculties] that are about to arise, there is no fault.
Regarding the twenty-five [factors] bound to the three realms:
all those of the desire realm,
and a portion of those of the higher realms, and so forth.
Although those clouds all pertain to the three realms,
some are partial and some are complete;
the desire realm possesses two natures.
Ignorance, volitional formations, craving,
and grasping are of the nature of existence;
one is karma and seven are fruits.
The first consists of a single nature;
the second consists of two natures, namely ignorance, formations, craving, and grasping;
the third consists of one karma and seven fruits.
Therefore, it is said that "one part" [is so].

Regarding the statement that "all twenty-six [factors] are exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner," this is because one becomes a learner (*śaikṣa*) only after entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
Because all those in the stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are not learners (śaikṣa).
As stated previously in the ninth fascicle regarding the "action of a learner" (śaikṣakarma):
This refers to all wholesome karma within the mental continuum of either an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) or one in training (śaikṣa),
as stated in the Abhidharma-dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra, chapter four.
All wholesome dharmas belonging to one who seeks liberation have the meaning of "training" (śaikṣa). Herein,
it refers to the realization of the supreme training.
Nor is this contradictory.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The contaminated wholesome karma produced by noble ones (*ārya*)."
Because it has illumination as its condition and because it contradicts the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*),
it is not subsumed under the factors of existence.
From this it should be known that noble ones (ārya) certainly do not perform karma that brings about further existence (punarbhava),
because they are neither deluded nor seek after the fruits of future suffering.
By practicing the meditative absorption of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna*),
one utilizes residual karma from previous lives to be reborn in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) and other such realms.
This is not contrary to principle;
it clearly demonstrates the ordinary person's factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
All those capable of inducing or projecting a fruit are subsumed within the members [of dependent origination].
The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, lower fascicle, states:
Regarding external phenomena, for ordinary beings,
the four kinds of ignorance serve as conditions to give rise to meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations.
Regarding internal dharmas,
for an ordinary person who is heedless,
they exclude one type of unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
The remaining ignorance,
having induced negligence as its condition, gives rise to volitional formations among ordinary beings within the internal phenomena.
For those who practice with diligence and heedfulness,
as well as for noble learners (śaikṣa),
there are three kinds of ignorance.
It induces forgetfulness and serves as a condition for non-merit;
however, it cannot lead to rebirth in the three evil destinies.
This is not merit.
I do not say that it is formations conditioned by ignorance;
rather, my intention is to distinguish it from non-heedfulness.
Furthermore, the non-meritorious [karma] of the noble ones (ārya) invites only the distinct ripening fruits of the human and celestial realms;
it does not invite the general ripening fruit of the miserable destinies (apāya).
Since it is not a member of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*),
this non-meritorious [action] is not said to have the member of ignorance (*avidyā*) as its condition.
That sutra further states:
As for the non-associated ignorance,
even those ordinary persons within the internal [Dharma] who practice with diligence have not yet been able to abandon it.
The noble ones in training should know that [these] are to be abandoned forever; furthermore, for ordinary persons within this Dharma who are not negligent,
if they perform meritorious formations or immovable formations,
these are produced by a virtuous mind associated with correct attention to the True Dharma.
Liberation is the basis;
for it is by turning toward liberation that [the path] is brought forth.
Although it brings about a distinguished rebirth within the happy realms,
ignorance does not serve as its predominant condition; rather,
[wisdom] can act as the predominant condition for its abandonment.
This demonstrates that although ordinary beings prior to the path of seeing generate merit and the imperturbable through the three types of ignorance and their non-common seeds,
[they do not produce the formless realm].
It brings about the general resultant fruit (*vipāka-phala*) for the realms of humans and devas;
it does not serve as a predominant condition for the arising of ignorance,
because ignorance has been ultimately extinguished.
It is not because they are directly induced by the three types of ignorance and so forth;
rather, it is because their seeds exist,
or because they can induce them even remotely.
Nor does it negate that ignorance conditions meritorious and immovable formations;
it only negates that non-meritorious [formations] have ignorance as their condition.
Therefore, that sutra speaks only of noble learners (*śaikṣa*),
because, having eternally abandoned the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*),
they do not create new karma.
Because it has already been stated that the unique ignorance of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) no longer arises,
they do not create new karma.
Their subsequent wholesome desire for the Dharma constitutes the wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) factors of the body of an ordinary being.
Because it falls within the cycle of transmigration,
and since it is not yet the state of one in training (śaikṣa),
it is capable of inducing rebirth.
Regarding the inclusion within the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*),
the passage beginning "twenty-seven [types of] stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) abandon one part of all [defilements],
but not entirely," is explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* as follows:
There is an interpretation that ignorance is severed solely by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),
because it must be deluded regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*) in order to motivate the performance of karma,
and because noble ones (*ārya*) certainly do not create karma for future existence (*punarbhava*).
The two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
because they moisten rebirth by seeking future existence.
There are nine types of death-moment consciousnesses.
Because they are associated with innate craving (*sahaja-tṛṣṇā*),
the remaining nine are all subject to abandonment through both the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
This refers to all those abandoned by a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
Speaking in terms of the majority,
the *upādāna* (clinging) link is also to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
This master asserts that clinging is simply craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in its predominant form.
Therefore, they are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). According to one interpretation, all [factors] are common to both types of abandonment;
this is explained at length.
[This includes] the three members: ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
It is also common to both what is abandoned by seeing and what is abandoned by cultivation;
however, it is the factor of ignorance that primarily instigates the process.
It is abandoned solely by insight;
its auxiliaries are not fixed.
As for the two links of craving and grasping, they are what directly moisten and produce [rebirth].
It is abandoned only by cultivation;
its auxiliaries are not fixed.
Furthermore, it is an afflicted dharma.
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) should be abandoned;
it is not a defiled phenomenon (*kliṣṭadharma*).
Abandonment is explained in terms of these two meanings.
First, because they are free from bondage;
second, because they do not arise.
Thus it is said that the twelve links are common to both types of abandonment.
It should be understood accordingly.
This statement applies to all twelve links; as for the mention of "a portion," it refers to [the specific case of] ignorance.
If one abandons them by way of their intrinsic nature,
it refers to the afflictions and karma of the three evil destinies;
if one abandons them by way of non-arising:
Together with those various fruits and so forth,
what is said to be abandoned by the stream-enterer is called "one part."
The twenty-seven preceding sections have completed the ninth [section],
the "Analysis of Dependent Origination.
Now begins the tenth section, which subsumes [the teachings] from various sūtras.
There are fifteen sections.
First, the six kinds of discourse in direct and reverse order.
Both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) possess both direct and reverse order; regarding those that are partial or complete, it is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
there was a certain Brahmin by birth...
Eleven members are taught,
excluding birth (*jāti*),
because the capacity [of the recipient] awaits [the teaching].
Although it is also a part,
it is not what is being discussed here.
What is being discussed here is as follows:
This refers to observing the dark category (kṛṣṇapakṣa),
where one turns back at the stage of consciousness; thus,
one observes only ten links, or [the sequence] from name-and-form (nāmarūpa) up to entry into the womb.
Observing only nine factors is called "one-branch observation.
If one observes the white category (śuklapakṣa), [it is likewise].
One contemplates all twelve [links] together;
one fully extinguishes the twelve,
and cultivates the path to their extinction.
It is called "possessing all branches.
A single portion of this is termed the "dark side" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*),
because it contemplates suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
This complete portion is called the "white category" (*śuklapakṣa*),
because it contemplates cessation and the path.
Defilement and purification are the contemplation of the mind.
Therefore, it is not mentioned here.
Second, the profound nature of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) should be understood through ten aspects.
Regarding the meaning of impermanence (anityatā), there are six points.
The seventh is the meaning of suffering.
The eighth is the meaning of emptiness.
The ninth is the meaning of non-self.
According to ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
although the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all phenomena is inexpressible,
it is said that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena can be expressed as the tenth.
The first nine are established according to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) as various classificatory gates;
the final one is according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
The gateway of forceful verbal expression:
first, although one’s own seeds are powerful,
they still depend upon external conditions.
Because it is not produced by itself;
secondly, although the power of external conditions is predominant,
it still depends upon its own internal seeds as the cause.
Because it is not produced by Brahmā or others.
Third, although it arises from seeds and conditions,
[it is distinct from] those seeds and conditions.
Regarding the phenomena of this birth,
there is no agent, no purpose,
and no process of movement.
It is not like the "self" (ātman) of the Vaiśeṣika school, which performs actions;
rather, it consists of the categories of dharma and adharma within the category of quality (guṇapadārtha),
along with the category of action (karmapadārtha).
The assisting [condition] has practical utility,
causing the resultant dharmas to function; furthermore,
it is not like that of the Sarvāstivādins.
There exists a real activity that causes the resultant phenomena to arise;
now, however, there is nothing capable of acting.
Nor does it possess any karmic function;
although the fruit arises later,
there is no actual movement or transition.
Therefore, both [extremes] are negated.
The four [conditions] possess the capacity to produce;
they are not without cause.
Fifth, they arise anew at every single moment;
they do not possess a fruit through transformation (*pariṇāma*) as the Sāṃkhya school maintains.
Sixth, nevertheless, they appear to manifest the characteristics of both stability and motion.
Unlike the Saṃmitīya school and others who maintain that there is arising and ceasing within a single lifetime, regarding the meaning of suffering:
all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are by nature constant suffering (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
It is of a single flavor and without differentiated characteristics;
although it appears as if there is suffering or pleasure at certain times,
in reality, such pleasure does not exist.
Because there is no interruption of suffering and so forth, that which relies on the meaning of emptiness is,
in its causal nature, free from the self as an agent according to the Vaiśeṣika school;
and in its resultant nature, it is free from the self that experiences various sufferings according to the Sāṃkhya school.
However, that which appears not to be separate from the meaning of selflessness is as follows:
it is free from the essence and characteristics of a self,
and emptiness is free from the functions of a self.
These are the two distinctions.
The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, lower fascicle, states:
"That which is devoid of a real self-nature within the truth of suffering is called emptiness."
That is to say, the characteristic and nature of non-self within the Truth of Suffering is called "selflessness.
The sixth chapter of the *Abhidharma* states the same as the Sūtra;
although there is a difference in their respective perspectives, they are not contradictory.
Furthermore, this meaning of emptiness is free from the agent, the experiencer, and the essence of a self;
the nature of phenomena is the meaning of non-self and lacks the characteristic of a self.
It is the same as that [which was previously stated].
This statement "there is no mark of a self" uses the word "no" not in the sense of non-existence, but rather in reliance upon ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is inexpressible;
now, by explaining dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the tenth [topic] is established. According to the Abhidharma treatises, there are five kinds of profundity.
This refers to "the profundity of causes" and so forth,
which differs from this [present case].
See the lower fascicle of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra*.
Fifteen kinds of profundity are taught;
the first five are the same as in the Abhidharma (*Abhidharma-piṭaka*),
while the latter ten differ slightly.
As stated in those sūtras and śāstras, the wisdom that abides in the three dharmas consists of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*),
the wisdom of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), which refers to reflection (*cintā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Ordinary beings observe profound meanings as those in training do— either through the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna) or through the wisdom derived from hearing (śruta-mayī-prajñā)—
which constitutes their knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna).

The noble ones possess three types of wisdom: either the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna) and the knowledge of the diversity of bodies (nānātva-kāya-jñāna), or the knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna) and the noble body-knowledge (ārya-kāya-jñāna).
This is because they abide in the teachings and other such dharmas.
Because they know according to the true meaning, these two are distinguished. Regarding the four abodes:
by means of unerring phrases and syllables.
This nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is explained as follows:
the words and phrases that express it are called the "abiding of phenomena" (dharma-sthiti).
Therefore, this abiding of phenomena has the nature of phenomena as its cause.
Therefore, this dharmatā is called the dharmadhātu.
"Dhātu" has the meaning of "cause.
Alternatively, this refers to the present text as well as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras.
That suchness is called the "abiding of phenomena" (dharmasthiti).
It is called the "abiding of phenomena" because it is that which is expressed by the teaching,
being the very essence of the abiding of phenomena.
There must be the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) to serve as the basis for the teaching;
taking its essence as the cause and its meaning as the fruit,
if these five types of arising did not exist, [the teaching would have no foundation].

This means that while the five branches beginning with consciousness produced from seeds may be said to exist as "arising without location or abode," it is the arising of the six active consciousnesses in the present life that takes name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as its condition.

Regarding the statement that "because consciousness arises as a provisional designation at the stage of birth, it serves as a condition," and that "in subsequent states, consciousness serves as a condition":
when name-and-form arise, they must necessarily depend upon consciousness for their origination.

This explains that the present and the future act as mutual conditions for one another: the present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) depends upon consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the arising of future consciousness likewise depends upon name-and-form. Why is this so? [As follows: *The Sūtra says:* "Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form. If there were no consciousness, would name-and-form come to be in the mother's womb? No, World-Honored One. Therefore, it is known that consciousness is the condition for name-and-form. Furthermore, the *Sūtra* says: "Name-and-form is the condition for consciousness. If there were no name-and-form, would consciousness arise in the mother's womb? No, World-Honored One. Therefore, it is known that name-and-form is the condition for consciousness. Thus, these two dharmas—consciousness and name-and-form—are mutually dependent conditions, like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other. (T16, no. 717, p. 840a25–b03) *The Commentary says:* "The *Sūtra* states that 'consciousness is the condition for name-and-form. This means that the present consciousness is the condition for the present name-and-form. Name-and-form refers to the four aggregates (*skandha*) excluding form; these are collectively termed 'name,' while the aggregate of form is termed 'form. Together they constitute name-and-form. Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form because it is the cause of its production. Furthermore, the *Sūtra* states that 'name-and-form is the condition for consciousness. it does not refer to the concentration associated with the "attention at the culmination of application" (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*), nor to the concentrations of other uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*). This is what is meant by the phrase "samādhi and so forth."
This explains that the preliminary application (*prayoga*) occurs in the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*);
based on the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*), one gives rise to the untainted path of uninterrupted transition (*anantaryamārga*).
The paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) induced by these two [paths] follow.
Within the concentration associated with liberation (*vimukti-samprayukta-samādhi*),
that which is capable of severing the afflictions is called "associated with liberation.
This does not mean that the two preceding types of tainted attention (*sāsrava-manasikāra*) can suppress the afflictions.
The remaining paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) are so named;
this [path] is not a path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) induced in conjunction with meditative concentration (samādhi),
nor does it enter the fundamental stages (maulabhūmi).
Regarding the statement that both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are called "preparatory means" (*upāya*):
that which has not yet attained the fulfillment of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) is termed a preparatory means,
because it is taught that the abandonment of afflictions constitutes liberation.
This explains the joy born of separation from the first [dhyāna];

by this, the joy born of the other concentrations and so forth can be understood. Alternatively, these "concurrent" phrases refer to the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-bhūmi*).
It is called samādhi;
because it can liberate one from hindrances,
it is called liberation (vimukti).
It is distinct in essence from the three preceding samādhis and liberations;
therefore, it is designated as a "concordant category" (yuganaddha-pada).
Because their respective objects of focus differ,
there are two [aspects] established within the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
First, the characteristics of the hindrances are explained.
Next, the covering and eating are explained.
There are two aspects of the characteristics of the covering.
First, they are presented and enumerated.
The subsequent detailed explanation consists of two parts: first, the individual explanation of the characteristics within the hindrance of lethargy and drowsiness;
second, the reason for establishing them together as a single hindrance.
"Not guarding the sense doors" and so forth are as explained in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*.
"The mind being extremely dull and narrow" is as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Their inclusion within the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is established based on their functional correspondence.
The first two sections provide an exegesis;

the final section establishes the meaning of their sequential arising. Regarding the hindrances of restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*), the first part provides a separate explanation of their two characteristics.
The subsequent explanation establishes the reasons for their being grouped together.
Within these reasons, there are two further sequences.
The first explanation states that they are grouped because they share the same locus, such as relatives and so forth, which serve as their common objects.
They are established together as a single hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).
Later, because their characteristics of being resolved (*vimokṣa*) are similar, they are established together as a hindrance.
Regarding the previously explained characteristics of remorse (*kaukṛtya*), there are three periods.

Regarding the passage beginning with "When I was first in the secular world, by what cause did I leave home at such a young age? and continuing with "At the time of my initial renunciation, it may have been due to recollecting past experiences," etc.:
[This refers to] the period when one first went forth [into the religious life]. It may be that, on account of recollecting things previously experienced in the past, and so forth.
Regarding the period after having gone forth, there are likewise three textual passages concerning the similarity between the understanding and the practice.
These explain the first two periods, from the tasks that ought to be performed up to performing what should not be done.

Regret regarding what should have been done, what should not have been done, what was not done, or what was done contrary to what should have been done, all pertain to those who were formerly householders at the time of their initial ordination; next, one eliminates the mental distress (*kaukṛtya*) arising from such prior remorse.
And there is the arising of a specific form of remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
The second [interpretation] explains the remorse that arises at a time subsequent to having gone forth: "excluding the remorse and so forth that arose from prior regret."
Setting aside the remorse that arose while he was still a layperson— this entanglement of remorse which he has not yet been able to abandon—
and the remorse that arose at the time of his initial renunciation which he has likewise not yet been able to abandon, there subsequently arises further remorse characterized by sorrow and longing.
This arises because one recalls past instances such as frivolous laughter and the like;
furthermore, this is a specific type of *kaukṛtya* (remorse) occurring after one has gone forth into the religious life.
The two types mentioned above encompass all forms of *kaukṛtya* pertaining to the three preceding periods of time.
In the case of a layperson, remorse may arise regarding its object;
it can share the same objective sphere as restlessness (*auddhatya*).
However, for one who has gone forth, the initial arising of the mental aspect of remorse should not occur.
Therefore, it is called "regret regarding what is improper" (*agatya-kaukṛtya*).
Thus, the third section of the treatise concludes by stating:
"Next, the regret regarding what is improper that arose previously."
Furthermore, the regret that arises after one has gone forth into homelessness,
although its locus is not identical to that of restlessness,
is nevertheless similar in character to it.
It is not merely that they share the same object;
remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and longing (*daurmanasya*) are established in conjunction with restlessness (*auddhatya*).
After one has gone forth, these two have different objects.
Because remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is also characterized by anxiety and attachment, it is established as a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).
Restlessness (*auddhatya*), however, is not itself the essence [of a hindrance] because it does not pervade all defiled minds;
nevertheless, its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is predominant.
At this time, it does not exist;
since the locus of its description is not equivalent,
it does not contradict the principle of *vijñapti-mātra*.
Regarding the section on doubt:
"In relation to the Teacher" refers to the two jewels of the Buddha and the Sangha;
"in relation to the Dharma" refers to the principle.
The learner practices;
the instructor teaches;
the realized one attains the fruit.
These are the four jewels of doctrine, realization, practice,
and fruition. Because one harbors doubts regarding the Three Jewels,
one is unable to enter the path of truth (*mārgasatya*) through courageous skillful means.

Furthermore, "right abandonment" refers to the truth of cessation; alternatively, "expedient means" refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), "right abandonment" refers to the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*), and "tranquility" refers to the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Below, food and non-food are explained.
"Food" has the meaning of sustaining growth;
it is the condition for the increase of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
"Non-food" is the dharma that severs and extinguishes the hindrances. If one can remain detached from defiled thoughts and the like regarding these...
This merely sets forth the reason for the pure and wondrous marks. As for the nine grounds for resentment, they are as explained in the fifty-eighth [chapter].
Regarding the "light of the Dharma," it refers to a certain person who, according to what he has received, reflected upon, or encountered, [attains realization].
The wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation are assigned to them in that order.
"Examining all phenomena" applies generally to these three wisdoms. Furthermore, it is said that the realization of examination can counteract lethargy, drowsiness, and darkness.
Realization refers to the cultivation of the wisdom of the Dharma;
it is called realization because one touches and realizes [the truth] within meditative concentration through the light of the Dharma.
The wisdoms of hearing, reflection,
and so forth eliminate delusion and doubt;
in the stage of cultivation, they are able to eliminate torpor.
Because it can clearly reveal the nature of all phenomena, it is called the "light of the Dharma" (dharmāloka). Regarding "non-nutriment" (anāhāra):
this refers to cases where there is someone who, either through expository discussion (vyākhyāna) or through synthetic discussion (samāsa), and so forth.
To speak explicitly is called "opening the discourse" (*ārambha*).
To speak cryptically by means of metaphors is [the opening].
To bring these together so that they may be understood is called "synthesizing the discourse" (*nigamana*).
Opening the mouth and smiling is called "revealing the teeth.
Producing sound from within the throat is called "gurgling" (*āṭa-āṭa*).

Regarding the nine types of mental abiding (*navavidha-cittasthiti*), they are explained in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*, the tenth chapter of the *Abhidharma*, and other texts, as found in the thirtieth fascicle. As for those who maintain that there is an objective referent for dependent origination (*sālambana-pratītyasamutpāda*):
That which has conditions refers to resultant phenomena;
dependent origination refers to causal phenomena.
Within the fourth section on the establishment of the members, there are three parts.
First, the number is established based on the stages;
next, the inclusion and exclusion [of factors] are explained;
finally, they are distinguished through questions and so forth.
This shall be analyzed by means of seven gates: first, the explanation of the names.
"Aṅga" (limb) refers to a constituent part, as in the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) or the limbs of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
The Sarvāstivādins say:
"Samādhi is both meditative absorption (dhyāna) and a factor of meditative absorption (dhyānāṅga)."
The others are branches of meditative concentration (dhyānāṅga),
but not meditative concentration itself.
According to the true meaning:
Just as a fourfold army each serves as a counteragent,
so too are the three factors: equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension.
Based on the state of meditative concentration,
that which is equally capable of removing hindrances is called internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
Because they purify all hindrances.
The remaining names are easily understood. Second, regarding the essential nature:
although the number is eighteen, the essence consists of only seven.
First, vitarka;
second, vicāra;
third, vedanā.
Fourth, concentration;
fifth, equanimity;
sixth, mindfulness.
Regarding the seven wisdoms:
the bliss of the first two dhyānas is the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*),
and is not pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
The universal mental factor is one, namely sensation (*vedanā*).
The object-specific factors are three, namely mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
The wholesome factors are one.
That is, equanimity;
and two indeterminate factors,
namely vitarka and vicāra.
Due to internal purification, the sixty-third [factor] is stated to be equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension;
therefore, the number is exactly seven, with neither addition nor subtraction. There is a distinction in the types of these three stages.
Only the pure, untainted [meditative absorption] possesses these factors;
it is not the case for defiled concentration.
Within defiled concentration, [these factors do not exist].
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, fascicle 28, states:
"In the first defiled dhyāna, there is neither joy nor bliss,
because it does not arise apart from the afflictions."
In the second defiled dhyāna, there is no internal clarity,
because it is disturbed by afflictions.
In the third defiled dhyāna, there is no right mindfulness or wisdom.
Because they are deluded by defiled pleasure,
there is no purity of equanimity and mindfulness within the fourth dhyāna;
because it is defiled by afflictions.
Now, this may also be so regarding the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*).
In the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the first and second dhyānas,
all [faculties] may be present except for the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Or it may rely solely on the fundamental [dhyāna],
because concentration and wisdom are in equilibrium;
thus states the Abhidharma-śāstra.
The factors of meditative absorption are not established within the formless realms because of the single-flavored nature of śamatha. Regarding the five types of abandonment of hindrances,
in each of the first three dhyānas there are five factors, with two being excluded.

The four factors excluded by each of the four dhyānas are as follows: the reason for the increase and decrease of the six, five, and four branches is that within the first dhyāna there is no mindfulness, clear comprehension, or equanimity;
in the second dhyāna, these are termed internal serenity.
The fourth dhyāna is designated by the name "purity," as explained in detail in the sixty-third [section].
As for why correct knowledge (*saṃprajanya*) is not established in the fourth dhyāna:
Because it is eclipsed by sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant, and because clarity and darkness, or sharpness and dullness, are mutually contradictory.
Question: Why is the agitation and leaping-up of joy in the two meditative attainments called "inner serenity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), given that it is capable of obstructing?
In the fourth dhyāna, since the equanimity and sensation are dull, they obstruct right knowledge and are thus not pure.
Answer: In the second dhyāna, afflictions arise due to joy.
The three [defilements] that obstruct the universal [factors] are termed "internal impurities.
The fourth dhyāna obstructs only equanimity and sensation;
it does not obstruct equanimity and mindfulness.
It is called "pure.
The mode of activity of equanimity is dull;
it obstructs clear and sharp wisdom.
Therefore, correct knowledge (*saṃprajanya*) is not established in the fourth dhyāna,
because it does not arise due to the abandonment of mindfulness and equanimity caused by the obstruction of afflictions.
Thus, two purities are taught among the seven points of establishment and exclusion.
In the sixty-third [chapter], as well as in the Abhidharma and the Daśabhūmika Sūtra,
it is stated that in all cases, vitarka and vicāra serve as the antidotes to joy and bliss,
and they take the benefit of meditative concentration as their basis.
Regarding the statement here that "vitarka and vicāra take the object as their objective support":
this refers to observing the appropriate object in order to counteract [the afflictions].
Concentration serves as the basis;
joy experiences what has been attained;
and bliss removes heaviness and rigidity.
The mental experience of pleasure is called joy (*prīti*);
that which can gladden the body is called bliss (*sukha*).
The former is coarse and resides in the body.
The arising of pleasure and the cessation of that [suffering] is called "removal" (prahāṇa);
it does not refer to the removal of lower-level afflictions.
Because the elimination of the lower afflictions occurs solely through vitarka and vicāra,
this demonstrates that the factors mentioned in various contexts possess two meanings.
First, experiencing the attained object;
second, removing the obstacle of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*);
and third and fourth, the meditative concentrations experience what has been attained.
The removal of the heavy burden (*dauṣṭhulya*) has no separate essence;
for it possesses two capacities:
it gladdens the sense faculties and abandons the heavy burden. "Benefit" (*anuśaṃsa*) refers to the quality of grace.
Since these very factors all provide benefit to one who cultivates meditative concentration,
there are many repeated sequences among the sixty-three [factors].
Fifth, regarding the establishment of its specific names,
there are five: first,
the "Higher Mind" (adhicitta).
Second, dwelling in happiness in the present life;
third, nirvāṇa as a part thereof;
fourth, distinguished nirvāṇa.
The fifth section, "The Matters of the Abandonment of All Sensations," is divided into four parts,
because the third and fourth are combined for analysis.
Regarding "the mind of superior resolve" (*adhicitta*), the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is termed "mind."
Because it is able to collect the mind;
alternatively, that which is the basis is called "mind," and meditative concentration is indeed able to collect the mind.
The supremacy of the mind is called "higher mind" (adhicitta). Within the dwelling in happiness in the present life,
first "happiness" is explained,
and subsequently "the present life" is explained.
Regarding the reason why the formless realms are not designated as "experiencing" after [the explanation of the form realm]:
"experiencing joy and bliss" refers to the feelings of joy and bliss; "bliss of tranquility" refers to the bliss of *praśrabdhi*;
and "bliss of equanimity" refers to the bliss of *upekṣā*.
The feeling of equanimity is pleasant;
that which accords with and gladdens both body and mind is all termed "pleasure.
As for "pleasurable abiding," it refers to dwelling in a state of joyful contentment.
The sixty-third discourse states:
Because the mind is bound within and does not flow outwardly,
abiding in that which can induce bliss is called "abiding in bliss."
According to these words from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
contaminated pleasure (*sāsrava-sukha*) is bound to the three realms,
whereas uncontaminated pleasure (*anāsrava-sukha*) is comprised within that which is unbound.
Now, based on the fact that there are four types of bliss pertaining to both body and mind—
namely, the bliss of joy, the bliss of rapture, the bliss of tranquility, and the bliss of equanimity—
the four dhyānas receive the designation of "abiding in bliss."
In the desire realm, the latter two do not exist;
in the formless realm, the first two do not exist.
Therefore, although pleasure may manifest there, [it is not considered a faculty].
This is not called dwelling in bliss; furthermore, the joy and pleasure of the first and second dhyānas constitute bliss,
the peace and happiness of the third dhyāna constitutes bliss,
and the bliss of equanimity of the fourth dhyāna constitutes bliss.
Regarding "bliss of body and mind":

this distinguishes [this state] from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which is not a dwelling in bliss. Thus, forest-dwelling bhikṣus raised a critique, saying: "I now question him regarding the peaceful liberations that transcend both form and the formless, yet he cannot provide an answer," and so forth.
This means that the formless attainments are called "transcending form," and the untainted attainments are called "transcending the formless."
These two are called the peaceful liberations that constitute dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Therefore, it is now explained that the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are not for the sake of dwelling in happiness;
rather, the four dhyānas of the form realm are what are termed "peaceful liberations."
This is an abiding in happiness in the present life;
because one portion of the active afflictions has been severed,
yet their seeds have not been severed.
Because it subsequently regresses and arises again,
and is not definitive,
it is called "nirvana with remainder" (or "partial nirvana").
If one establishes untainted dhyāna or has not yet attained it,
this is also called "nirvāṇa pertaining to that part" (tad-aṃśa-nirvāṇa);
furthermore, it is conditioned (saṃskṛta).
It is not the unconditioned ultimate nirvana;
it is called "differentiated nirvana" because it involves the abandonment of only a portion [of defilements].
Pure concentration and a portion of the untainted [concentration] that suppress the afflictions are called "partial nirvana" (tad-aṃśa-nirvāṇa).
The untainted [wisdom] that abandons afflictions is not non-conditioned;
therefore, it is called "non-definitive.
It is a partial nirvana, and furthermore, it is not of the nature of abandonment.
One realizes non-analytical cessation;
this ability to realize meditative absorption is also called "nirvāṇa pertaining to that portion."
True nirvāṇa is called "nirvāṇa with remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa),
while conventional nirvāṇa is called "nirvāṇa without remainder" (nirupadhiśeṣa).
"Without remainder" (an-upadhi-śeṣa) carries the sense of being similar in kind to that [true nirvāṇa].
That which is conventionally categorized as such and resembles the ultimate reality is called "partial nirvāṇa" (tadbhāgīya-nirvāṇa).
It is also a differentiation of nirvāṇa;
it is called "differentiated nirvāṇa.
The fourth [section] explains, and within the fifth [section], which emerges from among the various matters concerning sensation (*vedanā*), there are four [subsections].
First, four points are set forth:
first, citing scriptural authority to establish the proof;
second, the mutual inclusion between the realm of renunciation and the five realms of renunciation.
Third, the explanation of the six elements of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇadhātu*) through three causes;
fourth, the explanation that being free from all faults is called the basis of renunciation.
Regarding the first [of these], there are three parts.
First, the four types of renunciation are presented;
next, the sūtra on renunciation is explained;
finally, the matter is analyzed through questions and answers.
There are three meanings of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*):
first, the meaning of non-engagement;
second, the meaning of the cessation of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Third is the meaning of freedom from defilement (*virāga*).
In the first dhyāna, there is freedom from sorrow;
thus, these three meanings are present.
The two meditative attainments (samāpatti) are free from suffering;
they possess only the sense of having extinguished the coarse heaviness (dauṣṭhulya),
because although it has already been abandoned at the initial stage of defilement, it still persists in the subsequent stages.
The latter three types of detachment possess both the sense of the extinction of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) and the sense of freedom from defilement;
they constitute detachment through the signless (*animitta*).
This pertains to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
In other stages, although there is separation [from defilements], it cannot be called "liberation.
Within the *Vimokṣa-sūtra*, there are two [types].
First, the *Vimilāśoka-sūtra* is explained;
subsequently, other sūtras are treated by analogy.
In this manner, one should understand that the text applies accordingly to the others as well. The initial section consists of four parts. First, how is the introduction (*nidāna*) to be understood?
The "introduction" refers to the root cause;
that which can produce the roots refers to the sense faculties, their objects, and so forth.
Regarding the "seeds of ignorance," it is because ignorant people give rise to much sorrow.
All of these are termed "preliminaries.
Even if they are not defiled sorrow, it is said that they arise from delusion (*moha*). Furthermore, they are the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
All are capable of giving rise to sorrow;
ignorance is their root.
This merely explains their seeds.
Due to this nature of the unwholesome faculty of grief,
it is impaired by delusion;
through the departure from desire, it is abandoned.
The remainder also ceases accordingly;
because ignorance has been extinguished,
even if there is conceptualization, it is not innate.
Detachment from desire is also relinquishment,
because it is accompanied by the concomitant faculty of grief and the category of relinquishment.
Within the question-and-answer section, there are three [points].
First, the characteristics of the faculties;
next, the explanation of the faculty of suffering;
and finally, the exposition of signlessness. Within the first dhyāna, the heaviness and rigidity (dausthulya) of the faculty of suffering have not yet been abandoned.
Because all roots of sorrow are induced by ignorance and non-equipoise,
they do not function at all when one is free from defilement;
the heavy residues (dausthulya) are also abandoned.
If one feels longing and grief for the unsurpassed Dharma,
yet lacks the guidance of knowledge,
one will abandon it through the renunciation of desire.
Because the various faculties of suffering are not necessarily induced by delusion,
as they still function even in those who are free from desire;
that is their state of grossness and lack of adaptability (*dauṣṭhulya-akarmaṇyatā*).

The two meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are precisely what extinguish [the afflictions]. Question: The faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) arises from the heaviness (dausthulya) of being separated from desire;
the second dhyāna extinguishes joy and bliss, and one is separated from the equanimity of the lower stage.
The heaviness is eliminated in the higher stages.
Answer: Because the basis for the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) and the presence of vitarka and vicāra exist in the first dhyāna, these are extinguished in the second dhyāna;
furthermore, there is no distinct basis for the support of joy (prīti) and bliss (sukha) to be induced.

When one is free from passion, the heavy burdens (dausthulya) vanish. If the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) has already been abandoned in the first dhyāna, then there would be no difference between the abiding resulting from the cultivation of experience for a practitioner who has entered the first dhyāna and that for one who has entered the second dhyāna.
This means that in the first dhyāna,
sorrow is extinguished;
in the second dhyāna, suffering is extinguished.
Consequently, although there is dwelling in happiness in the present life,
a distinction is nevertheless established;
for if suffering has already been extinguished within the first dhyāna, [how could it be said that suffering is not extinguished until the second?]
If there were no distinction between the two meditative attainments (samāpatti), there would be no difference in their dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*). However,
the Sūtra states that there is a distinction in their dwelling because of the difference in the experience (*vedanā*) upon emerging from dhyāna.
Furthermore, because there are distinctions in this abandonment of sensation,
in the first dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra are not yet stilled,
and the coarse and heavy (dausthulya) factors have not been abandoned or extinguished.
In the two higher meditative attainments,
tranquility prevails and the heavy burdens of affliction (*dausthulya*) are finally severed;
this is not the case in the first dhyāna.
The faculty of suffering has already been severed;
this [faculty] should not exist separately. Furthermore, regarding "the signless" (animitta), it refers to the concentration on emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi) entered by those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
It is called the concentration of the signless mind;
it consists of the seeds of outflowing equanimity and is bound by the afflictions.
The nominal latent dispositions (anuśaya) are termed "coarseness" (dausthulya);
when one enters this meditative absorption, they are said to be abandoned.
The manifestation of the nominal "envelopment" (paryavasthāna) of untainted equanimity still arises even while in meditative concentration;
it is not the case that those various feelings are defiled by afflictions.
There exists the presence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*);
these very latent dispositions are termed "coarseness" (*dausthulya*).
It is not the case that uncontaminated sensation (*anāsrava-vedanā*) lacks seeds.
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
and this faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) are said to depend solely on the higher stages;
because those stages increase [in refinement], they do not belong to others.
Regarding the second [point], the mutual inclusion between the five elements conducive to renunciation (*niḥsaraṇīya-dhātu*), there are three sections in the text.
First, the term "renunciation" is cited and explained.
Next, the resolution of objections.
Third, the miscellaneous explanation of the sūtra: "By means of the renunciation of desire, ill-will, and harmfulness, it speaks of the renunciation even up to the faculty of pleasure.
This refers to the three: desire, ill-will, and harmfulness.
Investigating that which constitutes the departure from impurity, compassion,
and equanimity is called "the ability to depart.
By means of these three contemplations, one acts according to what is appropriate for each case.
Since it exists throughout the four dhyānas,
the three renunciations are distinct from the four feelings.
Regarding the statement that "renunciation by means of form" refers to the renunciation of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) in the fourth dhyāna:
Because this attainment of the concentration of the sphere of infinite space involves detachment from the desires of the form realm,
it is the renunciation of the faculty of equanimity of the fourth dhyāna. "By the cessation of the view of a self-identity" refers to the concentration of the signless mind.
Being free from the defilements of the three realms, at the final moment of exhaustion, it is said that the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) emerges from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
These latter two types are collectively termed the "faculty of equanimity of renunciation. Regarding the phrase "conducive to renunciation" (*niḥsaraṇīya*), what is its meaning? Etc.
The meaning here is this:
ordinary persons and those in training cultivate the contemplation of renunciation,
yet they do not actually achieve renunciation.
Now, performing the five reflections is the practice of one who is beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Being already capable of transcendence is called "conducive to transcendence" (nairyāṇika),
because the fruit accords with the cause through the contemplation of transcendence.
It does not say that ordinary persons or those in training [possess this].
By performing this contemplation, one emerges from them;
thus, one has already emerged from the desires of the three realms.

Because this realm is taught for those who have attained the concentration of the signless mind and for those who seek the cessation of the transitory collection (*satkāya*), even though their various forms of renunciation occur simultaneously.
Regarding the specific distinctions in the cultivation of remedies at the time of correctly eliminating harm:
based on the distinct modes of activity and the stage of preliminary preparation (*pūrvaprayoga*), there is only one type of remedy above this [stage].
In the fourth dhyāna, equanimity is present;
free from the defilement of form,
it excludes [all else] and contemplates only the single category of the antidote that is space.
In the formless realm, there is equanimity;
regarding the body of the four aggregates,
one separately cultivates the specific antidote of the contemplation of emptiness.
These differ from the preceding three;
although they are abandoned simultaneously, they are established as three distinct types due to differences in their preparatory practices and modes of cultivation.
Because the latter two are not so, there is no distinction. Regarding the phrase "How are [the views] intense?
and so forth, this explains twenty-eight phrases found within the Sūtra.
The first thirteen phrases constitute the path of skillful means for abandoning desire;
the subsequent fifteen phrases, which are the opposite of these,
constitute the actual path for abandoning desire.
The intention of this sūtra is to clarify that the body of an arhat arises from the path of detachment through the aforementioned preliminary application.
Defiled craving does not function,
and the various delusions do not arise;
it is like water droplets that do not adhere to a red lotus flower.

Thus, the five contemplations are called "conducive to renunciation. Within the first thirteen phrases, the first eight constitute the contemplation of non-attachment to desire, while the latter five constitute the contemplation of weariness toward desire;
that is to say, they are by means of the mental application of observation.
This is a general statement;
the following two types of mental attention are specific statements.
Desiring to examine thoroughly whether the afflictions have been abandoned or not yet abandoned,
he further applies his attention and observes those signs of purity that are conducive to their arising.
Among these seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*),
the mental attention of investigation (*paryeṣaṇā-manasikāra*) is characterized by subsequent investigation into the mental attention of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-manasikāra*).
To repeatedly observe and cultivate the remedies with respect to superior matters is called the mental attention of intense application.
Therefore, it is said that because this refers to the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) prior to being free from the defilements of the three realms,
it is called "the attention of observation" (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*);
for this is the path of preparation for the "attention at the culmination of application" (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*).
For this reason, the "attention to the characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) and so forth are not mentioned here;
rather, it refers to the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) for the three realms that follows the abandonment of desire for the desire realm.
This is the mental attention of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*).
By implication, it refers to the three paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) through which one becomes detached from the desires of the three realms.
The mental application of observation (*mīmāṃsā-manaskāra*) is the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) for becoming free from the defilements of the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*). Here, however,
it refers to the Arhat’s ultimate freedom from desire.
Because he performs five kinds of contemplation,
according to this subsequent passage on the path of right abandonment,
his mind is explained as being "well-gone" (sugata).
It is said that when one abides in the mental attention of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*),
one correctly abandons all afflictions and shall attain the path of the ultimate sublime abiding of the mind.

He is named the Sugata. What is meant by "well-cultivated"? It means that because other forms of attention have been well-cultivated, one should know that this refers to the stage of abandonment and the stage of the path of the means for abandonment; that is, the stage of abandonment through the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) when this "attention at the culmination of application" (*prayoga-paryavasāna-manasikāra*) has been well-cultivated.
And when one has well cultivated the stages of the path of abandonment, such as the mental attention of prior observation (*pūrvaparīkṣā-manasikāra*),
one understands and becomes free from their active manifestation (*samudācāra*).
Liberated;
free from the bonds of signs;
released from fetters.
These three are distinguished by their separation from the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Because these three are abandoned, the underlying heaviness (*dausthulya*) is also eliminated. This refers to the various outflows (*āsrava*) arising from the conditions of sensual desires, with the exception of desire-greed (*kāmarāga*).
Because they have already become thoroughly weary [of them] during the preliminary preparations (*pūrvaprayoga*),
they are excluded. As for "impairment and deprivation":
Birth in the miserable realms is called "damage" (*upaghāta*);
being destitute of virtuous fruits is called "deprivation" (*vaikalya*). Regarding liberation from those states, transcendence, and dissociation, the sequence is as follows:
liberation from the fetters is called "transcendence" (*samudghāta*).
Liberation from the object of focus is called "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*);

liberation from latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) is called "disjunction" (*visamyoga*). Regarding the statement, "based on those about to be attained, those currently being attained, and the recollection of various objects of desire and so forth," this refers to the future, the present, and the past.
These correspond respectively to the various objects of sensual desire.
There are four parts to the explanation of the three causes regarding the scriptural passage on the six spheres of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇadhātu*).
First, citing scriptural evidence for explanation;
second, clarifying the specific modes of elimination;
third, resolving objections and difficulties.

Fourth, the explanation of the distinctions between the five and six elements: Therefore, the fact that loving-kindness and so forth are not the direct antidotes to ill-will and harm indicates that, at the stage of initial practice, one still gives rise to the conceit of "I."
Doubt has not yet been eliminated;
in order to subdue it and cause one to abandon all false attachments, [the teaching is given].
In establishing this realm,
there are two ways to exclude specific modes of activity (*ākāra*).
First, exclusion is categorized according to three types.
Subsequently, six lines are set aside for individual refutations. As for the establishment of the sixth [refutation] based on the observation of ultimate correct reasoning:
there is only the emptiness of the self as it is conceptually grasped within the reality of cause and effect.
This is called right reasoning (*yukti*).
By observing this, pride and doubt are extinguished. [The remaining afflictions are:
first, anger; second, harmfulness; third, envy; fourth, delusion; and fifth, greed and anger.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that these are, respectively, the four types of remedies: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
What is now referred to as "joy" (muditā) eliminates dissatisfaction.
This is precisely envy (*īrṣyā*). Regarding the abandonment of greed and hatred while not mentioning delusion (*moha*):
it is because the objects of love and hatred are not equal;
thus, one gives rise to the practice of equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward both within this context.
It is merely stated that the two objects [of perception] conducive to equanimity are removed;

for brevity, it is not explicitly stated that delusion (*moha*) is likewise removed. If one is free from the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*) regarding one's own liberation, one no longer clings to the conceit of "I," and thus turns away from the grasping of pride.
This is called liberation;
regarding the truths, jewels, and so forth that have been realized,
one is then free from doubt.
To resolve this objection, it is said: "These various modes of renunciation are certainly able to renounce all forms of ill-will and so forth.
This refers to the objection that one might say:
"One cultivates the six [immeasurables], such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and so on."
Since [the meditative absorptions] are definitively free from the six types of states to be abandoned,
such as ill-will (*vyāpāda*), why was it previously stated that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others do not directly eliminate ill-will, harm (*vihiṃsā*),
and so forth? This is now explained:
When these modes of renunciation are cultivated to the stage of perfection,
they will certainly enable one to transcend all forms of ill-will and the like.
Because they have not practiced well during the preceding stage of preparation,
faults such as anger may still manifest.
Regarding the previous statement that these do not directly counteract [the afflictions] but are included within the first four celestial abodes (*devasthāna*),
the two types— compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*)—
are both based upon the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
That which is called the "divine abodes" (devasthāna) relies specifically on the cultivation of the immeasurables (apramāṇa);
that which is called the "brahma abodes" (brahmavihāra) relies on them as well.

The fourth [section], the explanation of the name "departure from all faults," which is based on departure, has three parts: first, the heading stating that there are four kinds of bases for departure;
second, the detailed explanation of their characteristics and the reasons for them.
Regarding the three fetters, the four types, and the gains and losses across the four periods: the second section contains two parts.
First, it indicates that because there are distinctions among four types of persons, four categories are established.

Second, it provides a detailed explanation of their characteristics. As for the statement, "Because of their deceit and guile, they preach the Dharma based on [theoretical] principles rather than on actual individuals," etc.:
There are those who, being deceitful and fraudulent, consider the teacher to be superior;
they observe his physical appearance and deportment and then proceed to follow and learn from him.
Now, however, one must rely on the Dharma and not on the person.
One must debate with that opponent and reach a definitive resolution through one's own realization;
it is not by merely being in the presence of another person that one attains such realization.
Furthermore, regarding the distinctions within this very context,
there is a re-explanation of the aforementioned basis:
the Buddha, conforming to worldly convention, employs two kinds of discourse.
There is the person and there are the teachings;
now, I command that you rely on the teachings and not on the person.
One must not hear the Buddha’s words and, following the person who spoke them,
likewise rely upon that person; rather,
one should follow the conventional expressions used by the Buddha in accordance with worldly discourse.
"Because one should not rely on or cling [to them]," and "Furthermore, dharmas are of two kinds," etc.,
explain the second reliance.
This is because it accords with worldly convention.
Words are spoken to express principles and meanings;
one should not merely hear words that conform to worldly conventions.
This constitutes the ultimate [meaning].
Therefore, it is said that one should rely on the meaning. Regarding the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, some are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and so forth;
this explains the third reliance.
Although one is instructed to rely on the meaning,
one must not follow one's own views and grasp them as superior; therefore,
one relies on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

The four levels of definitive meaning are explained as in the chapter. Regarding the statement that "the World-Honored One at times proclaims the reliances (*pratisaraṇa*) and so forth," this explains the fourth reliance.
He speaks of consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the cause for humans and devas.
Nirvāṇa is explained by means of wisdom (*jñāna*).
In the sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) is taught for those who have newly begun their practice,
while wisdom is taught for those who have practiced for a long time.
There are those who, upon hearing of the initial cultivation, immediately grasp it as the ultimate.
To preclude this, it is said that one must rely on wisdom,
in order to attain the final goal.
Regarding the third bond, it is stated briefly that [the distinction between] loss and non-loss depends on four periods.
At the time of attaining the Dharma,
knowledge of the Dharma (*dharmajñāna*) arises.
Do not rely on others;
uphold the meaning according to the time,
and you may maintain it through the letter.
Because of the dhāraṇī that upholds the meaning rather than the letter,
when examining the meaning,
one relies on the definitive sense and not the non-definitive sense.
Because the wisdom of non-doubt arises, one practices "the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma. Here,
"Dharma" refers to the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya),
and "in accordance with the Dharma" refers to the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya).
When practicing the path of renunciation,
one relies on wisdom and not on consciousness;
these are the four reliances mentioned above.
From the initial practice to the final practice,
from the cultivation of the coarse to the cultivation of the subtle,
it reaches ultimate fulfillment.
In this sequential order.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "it should be known that the establishment [of the categories] has already been explained," the five gates in the preceding verse state:
This concludes the general summary and the presentation of the distinctions between the characteristics of mental attention (*manasikāra*),
which encompasses the essential points of various sūtras and their final miscellaneous meanings.
The general summary and the presentation have now been explained.
The third section below provides a combined explanation of the two gates of mental attention (*manasikāra*) and characteristics (*nimitta*).
Regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*) therein:
Because it is precisely that characteristic.
The text is divided into three parts;
first, the introduction.
Next is the specific explanation;
later comes the general discussion.
This is the first [of these].
In the detailed explanation,
first the mental attention (*manasikāra*) is explained,
and subsequently the object of focus (*ālambana*) is explained.
The beginning has three parts.
First, the seven types of mental attention (manasikāra) are listed by name;
second, the forty names of mental attention are given.
Next, the characteristics of the forty modes of mental attention (*manasikāra*) are explained individually;
subsequently, these forty modes of mental attention are subsumed under the seven modes of mental attention.
The characteristics of the seven modes of mental attention (*manasikāra*) are as explained below in the thirty-third fascicle;
their characteristics are further elaborated upon three times.
This is also subsumed under the four types of remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
The same applies to the ninth chapter of the *Abhidharma* (Jñānaprasthāna),
as well as the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth [chapters].
The seven types of mental attention and the four types of mental attention,
as well as the three kinds of yoga and so forth,
are all subsumed [within these categories] in detail, just as explained there.
Fearing prolixity, I shall not describe them in detail.
The forty modes of attention (*manasikāra*) are divided into twelve categories;
the first two concern the meaning of the teachings.
Second, the four foundations of mindfulness;
third, the two categories of the provisional and the real;
fourth, the three classes of ordinary beings and noble ones.
Five are the three categories of abandonment: initial, intermediate, and final;
six are the two categories of śamatha-vipaśyanā;
seven are the two categories of existence and emptiness.
The eighth is the sixfold cultivation and realization for the departure from defilement;
the ninth is the four paths;
and the fourteenth is the cultivation of the stages.
Eleventh, the fourfold wisdom-concentration (prajñā-samādhi),
which attains mastery by being free from hindrances.
Twelfth, the fourfold causes and effects of the three vehicles (triyāna).
Of all the modes of attention (*manasikāra*),
the first four categories constitute a general cause;
the latter eight categories exist only among those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
It serves as a specific cause;
the essence of this mental attention (manasikāra) is itself among the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika).
When cultivating concentration and wisdom, [it functions as such].
Because the function of attention (*manasikāra*) is predominant,
the Abhidharma states that for one whose benefit is increased by attention, it is said to be "conducive to *śamatha*.
This means it is wholesome and well-aligned with *śamatha*.
Because of vipaśyanā.
However, in this context,
attention (manasikāra) is supreme at the time of cultivating meditative concentration.
The Abhidharma also states:
"Mental attention (manasikāra) means holding the mind upon a single object so that it remains fixed;
[this occurs] in the stage of meditative equipoise (samāhita-bhūmi)."
The forty modes of attention (*manasikāra*) are clarified;
