although these modes of attention pertain to both concentration and the distracted state, they are for the most part cultivated based on that state of meditative concentration. They take phenomena (*dharma*) as their object.
That is to say, the wisdom arising from hearing takes meaning as its object;
the wisdoms arising from reflection and cultivation each rely on many objects, and their objects are not limited to that alone.
Because hearing [the teachings] takes the meaning of the few conditions as its object, and cultivation likewise takes the teaching as its object.

Regarding "attention consisting of resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣika-manasikāra*), the eleventh chapter of the *Abhidharma* states that it is exclusively mundane attention (*laukika-manasikāra*). Regarding "attention to reality" (*tattvamanasikāra*):
The Abhidharma states:
"It is exclusively supramundane,
as well as the attention subsequently attained therein."
That is, the fundamental wisdom and the subsequently attained wisdom.
Regarding what is said here— that one contemplates all phenomena through their specific and general characteristics—
this refers to the subsequently attained wisdom.
The fundamental wisdom that takes the principle of true suchness as its object is the mental application of universal knowledge;
it is the remote path of preparation. The mental application of correct abandonment is the proximate path of preparation.
And regarding the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that has already abandoned [the afflictions] refers to the remaining two paths:

the mental attentions of conceptualized and non-conceptualized images (*savikalpa-avikalpa-pratibimba-manasikāra*). These are the mental attentions that take the conceptualized entity as their object.
That is to say, the mind and mental factors of the three realms.
By means of the name "discrimination," one subsumes all phenomena of the three realms within these five dharmas.
The [first] is the discrimination of signs and names;
these two types of attention have the same objective essence.
They are divided into two types because of the distinction between *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
The eleventh chapter of the *Abhidharma* states:
"The object of focus consisting of a conceptualized image (*savikalpa-pratibimba*)."
The object of focus for concentration and wisdom when employing attention through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) is the non-conceptual image (*nirvikalpa-pratibimba*).
The object of focus for concentration and wisdom when employing attention to reality (*tattva-manasikāra*) is the [actual] object itself.
When one relies on that contaminated mental attention for śamatha and vipaśyanā,
it is called the "discriminated image.
This is because its essence is false conceptual construction.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) are called "non-conceptual images" (*nirvikalpa-pratibimba*),
because their essence is not false. Herein,
they are categorized according to their objects of focus (*ālambana*).
It is named the essence of discrimination;
it can take śamatha and vipaśyanā as its objects and is divided into two types.
Therefore, it is not contradictory to the limit of phenomena (*vastuparyanta*) or to the accomplishment of what is to be done;
however, it is contradictory to the Abhidharma and the following twenty-six [points].
Upon reaching that point, the *ālambana-manasikāra* of the limit of phenomena (*vastuparyanta*) shall be explained.
Regarding the *ālambana-manasikāra* of the accomplishment of what was to be done,
there are two interpretations.
One interpretation is identical to that of the Abhidharma:
namely, the former is the nature of all that exists (*yāvadbhāvikatā*),
while the latter is the nature as it is (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
The nature of the extent of all that exists refers to the essential entities and phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases,
for there are only so many.
The nature of things as they are refers to the sixteen aspects of the four noble truths and suchness:
that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
All conditioned phenomena are suffering;
all dharmas are without self;
nirvana is tranquility.
Emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness—
these are solely the principle of truth, or rather,
they are categorized by way of the doors of truth.
Either by means of the gateways of practice,
or by means of the summaries (udāna) of all phenomena,
or by means of the gateways of liberation.
Regarding the aforementioned aggregates, elements,
and sense bases, one understands the principles through their distinctions in meaning.
It is called "the nature as it is" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
The essence of the accomplishment of what is to be done is precisely the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*);
this reveals the first essence.
The nature of all that exists is known solely by subsequently attained wisdom;
the nature of things as they are is [known by fundamental wisdom].
The fundamental and subsequent wisdoms,
through their perfected activity,
constitute the twofold transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti): namely, awakening (bodhi) and nirvāṇa.
Among these, the object of focus regarding the limits of phenomena consists of body,
sensation, mind, and dharmas; that is, both the extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and the mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
The task is accomplished;
this is the twofold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). That is to say:
"I contemplate such and such" refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) taking the intrinsic nature of phenomena as its object. If I contemplate in such and such a manner...
Subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) takes the differentiation of phenomena as its object, thinking, "It shall be such and such";
fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) realizes the intrinsic nature (svabhāva), determining that "it is thus and thus."
This is the distinction realized by non-conceptual wisdom.
Although the nature of suchness is not a differentiation of phenomena,
it manifests two distinct modes of activity through the application of preparatory effort.
It is subsequently realized by correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), which is also said to be twofold:
"I have reflected in such and such a manner," referring to the cause, which is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); and "I have reflected in such and such a manner."
The cause of fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) is that "this and that shall come to be";
the result of subsequent wisdom (pṛṣṭha-jñāna) is that "such and such shall be discerned"—
this is the result of fundamental wisdom.
The above summarizes the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of enlightenment.
The pure object of focus (*ālambana*) is the transformation of the basis that is nirvāṇa.
Although this interpretation accords with the Abhidharma, [it is not the ultimate view].
Regarding the inclusion of the seven types of characteristics in the *Anuloma-vibhaṅga*, the second explanation states:
"This differs from the perspective of the *Abhidharma*.
As for the 'limit of phenomena' (*vastuparyanta*):"
This refers to that which is accomplished by reaching the limit of the phenomena (dharma) and principles (naya) regarding the body, sensation, mind, and dharmas as they occur in the present.
That is to say, it concerns the principles and matters currently being performed that are to be accomplished in the future.
Regarding this, there are three explanations.
One version says:
"When I contemplate in such and such a manner, this is the object of a distracted mind; if I contemplate in this and that manner..."
This is the object of concentration.
By means of this mental activity of scattering thoughts,
there will ultimately be such and such a result of decisive resolution.
Because one focuses the mind in this meditative concentration,
one will ultimately achieve decisive discernment and fulfillment; the phrase "contemplating thus and thus" refers to the objective essence as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Due to this volition,
there arises a determination and the fulfillment of such and such results, thinking, "If I contemplate in such and such a way," which is the characteristic of the mental image (*pratibimba*).
By virtue of this volition,

one should distinguish the three aspects of the accomplishment of such-and-such a resolution: namely, "I contemplate in such-and-such a manner" refers to the intrinsic nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-dharma*).
Due to this volition,
there arises a definitive result such as this or that; "if I contemplate in such and such a way," refers to the meaning of the differentiation of conditioned phenomena (*dharmas*).
Due to this volition,
one should distinguish how such and such a result is definitively accomplished; this above passage generally demonstrates the accomplishment of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
even though it may contradict the Abhidharma.
This accords with the textual phrasing of the inclusion [of these factors] within the seven subsequent [stages].
Regarding the phrase "the attention that takes the purification of the object as its object," there are two interpretations.
First, it is said that one attends to True Suchness (tathatā) as the object;
second, it is said that one takes this untainted (anāsrava) attention as the object,
because it serves as the focal point.
This refers to the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that takes pure objects as its focal point. Regarding mental attention consisting of resolute conviction and analytical investigation:
this refers to one who initially investigates all phenomena;
it is the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). It is preceded by calm abiding (*śamatha*).

Regarding the attention to tranquility through the investigation of resolute conviction during the state of meditative equipoise: this refers to the stage of wisdom consisting of reflection, wherein one first settles the mind internally;
it is characterized by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that settles the mind, with insight (*vipaśyanā*) as its primary factor.

This means that during the stage of cultivating wisdom, one cultivates meditative equipoise (*samāhita*); by means of the mental attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) and analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), one purifies knowledge and vision, for wisdom serves as the means and because wisdom is brought to fulfillment;
and by means of the mental attention of tranquility (*śamatha*), one generates pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

Because concentration serves as the means for the fulfillment of concentration; because of the cultivation of mental attention (manasikāra) both partially and fully; because of the mind attaining liberation from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) through uninterrupted and earnest mental attention; and because of the mind attaining liberation from the fetters (saṃyojana).
The five hindrances and nine fetters actually encompass both the manifest and the seed states; however,
they are designated as such because their manifest activity is predominant.
Now they are specifically taught as "hindrances" (nīvaraṇa) because their seeds are difficult to sever,
as their characteristics are submerged and subtle.
Now, these are specifically taught as fetters;
therefore, it is said that they are abandoned individually through the mental application of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-manasikāra*),

which encompasses the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), as well as the [mental applications] conducive to purification and analytical investigation.
The two paths of further progress at the proximate limit,
or pure knowledge,
are not included within the four paths. As for the six recollections:
This refers to the recollection of the Buddha and so forth, as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Regarding "spontaneously functioning attention," this refers to the four occasions, the first of which is the occasion of attaining attention.
Regarding the mutual inclusion within the lower [stages]:
this refers to when one attains the sixth and seventh mental orientations (*manasikāra*),
thereby becoming free from the ninth category of defilement.
1. At the time of the path of immediate liberation (*ānantarya-mārga*); 2. at the time of correctly entering and having already entered the fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*);

these two preceding times constitute the preparatory application (*prayoga*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); and 3. at the time of the actualization of cultivation (*bhāvanā-abhisamaya*).
Through the aforementioned preliminary application,
one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
practicing clear realization (*abhisamaya*); this is the fourth stage.
The stage of arhatship is "presently attained," which refers to the path of uninterrupted realization; it is "already attained," which refers to the path of liberation.
The third [section] concerns the inclusion of the seven mental orientations (*manasikāra*) within the forty mental orientations.
Within this, they are analyzed by means of five gates; first, the characteristics of the seven mental orientations are distinguished.
The attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) is able to discern the coarse characteristics of the lower stage and the tranquil characteristics of the higher stage.
This is the initial application of attention (*manasikāra*),
in which hearing and reflection are still intermingled.
From this point onward, it is exclusively the characteristic of cultivation (*bhāvanā-nimitta*).
Repeatedly contemplating these signs of coarseness and tranquility and repeatedly giving rise to resolute conviction is called the mind of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manas*).
By practicing this,
the path of initial abandonment arises;
one directs the attention associated with it.
This is called the mental attention of distancing;
therefore, all superior-grade afflictions and coarse heaviness [are abandoned].
Having completely severed [the lower fetters], he then further delights in the higher severance;
seeing the merit of that higher severance,
he has already touched a small portion of the joy and bliss of seclusion.
In order to eliminate lethargy and drowsiness,
one further repeatedly cultivates calm and sublime mental attention to gladden the mind.
This is called the attention of "delighting in practice.
In this way, the practitioner applies skillful means to the side of virtue.
Because it serves as a support,
it causes the afflictions, entanglements, and stains associated with the desire realm that are comprised within the medium grade [to arise].
They no longer manifest. For this reason, desiring to examine thoroughly whether the afflictions have been abandoned or not yet abandoned, he further applies his attention and observes;
that gives rise to a sign concordant with tranquility.
This is called the attention of investigation. In this way,
the practitioner repeatedly investigates and advances in the cultivation of remedies.
In order that all afflictions of the desire realm may attain dissociation for a brief period of time.
This attention associated with the path of counteraction is called the "attention of the culmination of the preparatory stage" (*prayoganiṣṭhā-manaskāra*),
because it is the final preparatory application of the first dhyāna.
By means of these weak-grade afflictions of the desire realm,
which no longer function at all, one immediately thereafter realizes the fundamental first dhyāna;
this is the mental attention (manasikāra) that accompanies the first dhyāna.
This is called the mental application that is the fruit of the culmination of preparatory effort (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala-manasikāra*).
Among these, it is because the path that abandons the superior grade of afflictions is difficult to initiate at first.
With the two types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) as the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
one abandons the subsequent lower grades; even so,
it is difficult to reach the fullness of the stage (*bhūmi*).
Because it is not the initial cultivation.
First, mental attention serves as the preparatory application (prayoga),
immediately following the preceding stage.
Because there may be the sense of preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the subsequent categories,
the three middle categories of abandonment are not said to involve preparatory application.
In the subsequent category,
there may be the sense of the path of liberation belonging to the preceding category;
it does not state that the [afflictions] of the preceding six categories are abandoned.
There is also a path of liberation that abandons the final three categories [of afflictions],
because one enters the fundamental [dhyāna] once the stage is complete.
The seventh mental application is said to be the path of liberation,
as explained in detail in the ninth chapter of the Abhidharma.
The thirty-third [chapter] below explains these seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*). Among them,
the first is that which discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*).
The wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation are all involved;
the remaining six are exclusively the wisdom of cultivation.
This refers to the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*).
Because it comprises the attention that takes phenomena as its object (*dharmālambanamanasikāra*).
This attention taking phenomena as its object is the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayīprajñā*). Furthermore, thirty-three [types] are taught.
Since these all belong to the higher stages, they do not extend to the stage of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*).
According to one interpretation, they consist solely of wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*);
however, at the outset, they are still interspersed with wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*) and reflection.
Its essence is not that of hearing or reflection;
this is stated in the Thirty-three [Sūtras].
By means of the concentration of the first dhyāna.
There are seven kinds of mental attention;
it should be understood that there are likewise seven kinds of mental attention for each stage up to and including the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
because there is no wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā),
it is also not the case that the fundamental stage (maulabhūmi) has not been attained.
First, because one immediately gives rise to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Second, the distinction between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) is explained in the eightieth [chapter].
All are common to both the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the three categories of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth,
the first and the seventh are common to all three types.
The remaining five [factors] consist only of the first two;
this is as explained in the subsequent section on the mutual inclusion of characteristics.
There is a fourfold classification of the paths.
The first, second, and fifth [mental abidings] pertain to both the path of preparation and the path of excellence;
they involve the mental application of "separation."
Only the path of uninterrupted transition;
the attention of relishing is common to all four paths.
The preparatory ultimate mental attention (*prayoga-niṣṭha-manasikāra*) encompasses both the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*);
it is the seventh mental attention.
It is solely the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
This refers to the cultivation of the four paths by those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*),
including all subsequent preparatory practices (*prayoga*) and the path of immediate succession (*anantarya-mārga*).
This is because [the previous categories] all belong to the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) as described in the preceding chapter;
for the Bodhisattva, however,
this is not the case, as it is possible for him to possess all four [paths] in each and every moment (*kṣaṇa*).
The meaning should be understood by analogy.
Now, based on the universal [application] that transcends all stages and realizes their characteristics through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*),
it is universally superior and progressive.
The attention that induces the immediate [attainment] and the attention of investigation also pertain to the stage of application (prayoga).
Because the subsequent category is a superior progression from the preceding category,
it is stated that the sixth [category] also applies to superior progression.
In general, the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) are distinguished based on the nine stages (*bhūmi*);
such is the actual meaning.
The sixty-two [types of] "understanding through signs" (*lakṣaṇapratisamvedī adhimokṣa*) are subsumed under the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).

The mental application of detachment (*vairāgya-manasikāra*) and the mental application of the culmination of preparation (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*) are subsumed under the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The mental application of delight (*rati-manasikāra*) is also included therein.
Regarding the inclusion within the fourfold path:
it is the contemplation of mental attention included within the path of superior progress.
This refers to the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga) for the specific separation from higher defilements, based on having already abandoned the defilements of the desire realm.
Because it proceeds with leisure toward superior progress,
it is not said that the subsequent category constitutes an uninterrupted path;
rather, it is the preceding path of superior progress.
Therefore, the attention of the culmination of the preparatory stage is exclusively immediate,
while the attention of observation is [distinct].
Based on the abandonment of the medium-grade [defilements], it is taught that one enters the path of cultivation;
this is described solely as the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*),
and it is not stated that what follows constitutes the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
Nor is this contradictory.
Regarding the seventh mental application (*manasikāra*),
its meaning as the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) may be understood by analogy.
Therefore, the treatise does not mention it.
Fifth, the three types of yoga practitioners are subsumed as follows:
first, the beginner (ādikarmika).
Second, those who have already practiced;
third, those who apply attention through crossing over.
Regarding the first, the stage of initial practice, there are two types.
First, regarding those who are beginners in the practice of attention (*manasikāra*),
they should abide in a single object and diligently cultivate attention.
Until one has attained the attention that has been cultivated,
one is still unable to touch and realize one-pointedness of mind.
Second, regarding the purification of afflictions for a beginner:
this refers to one who has already attained the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that was cultivated,
[and applies it] toward the various afflictions.
Desiring to purify the mind,
one correctly and diligently cultivates the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*).
A practitioner who has already trained in yoga refers to one who has thoroughly cultivated the five intermediate mental attentions (*manasikāra*).
The yoga practitioner who has transcended mental attention (*manasikāra*) refers to one who dwells in the seventh mental attention,
having surpassed the results of cultivation attained through the application of effortful practice.
It is said that these three types of practitioners alone,
as well as twenty-eight others,
possess the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
The stage of "beginning practice" is called the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*); the stage of "already practiced conduct" is called [the stage of] cultivation.
After the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*),
it is called the "attention that has crossed over" (*tīrṇamanasikāra*);
this signifies that the characteristic of manifestation resides in liberation.
The next five mental engagements belong to the stage of the aids to penetration;
the seventh mental engagement belongs to that same stage.
If this statement is made after the clear realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya),
then the three [stages] beginning with the learner (śaikṣa) are included within the forty mental orientations (manasikāra).
The text concerning mutual inclusion states that [these] contradict the seven types of mental attention and all pertain to those in training (śaikṣa).
The first and the seventh [stages] also pertain to those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
From this, it is known.
The three types of yogācāras are assigned according to their respective stages; thus,
their relationship with the seven mental attentions (*manasikāra*) differs in meaning.
The two gates are distinct;
one cannot subsume the three types of yoga practitioners within the seven modes of mental attention.
This clearly shows that the three stages of the seven types of attention are likewise so;
one should not give rise to further conceptual proliferation regarding this.
However, there are three types of yogācāras.
Among the twenty-eight [mental abidings],
seven modes of attention (*manasikāra*) are collectively assigned;
these seven modes of attention are not assigned according to the three stages.
Just as in the state that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
one possesses seven types of mental attention;
so too, in the stage of provisioning within the path of training.
There are those who possess all seven modes of attention,
because they first rely on the mundane path to progress toward the departure from defilement.
There is also the path of accumulation (sambhāramārga),
because one does not cultivate the seven mental orientations (manasikāra) and does not cultivate meditative concentration (samādhi).
Within the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*),
one fully possesses the seven mental attentions (*manasikāra*),
because one is progressing toward the departure from the nine grades of defilement of the desire realm.
After attaining clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
one also gives rise to the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) in order to further abandon the defilements of the higher stages.
Having distinguished the seven types of attention (*manasikāra*),

one should now distinguish how the forty types of attention are subsumed [within them]. Regarding the subsumption of the "attention that discerns characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) as having the dharma and the meaning as its objects,
there are two interpretations.
One explanation states:
because the wisdom of understanding (parijñā-prajñā) encompasses both hearing (śruta-mayī) and cultivation (bhāvanā-mayī),
it subsumes these two types.
One interpretation states:
"The comprehension of characteristics consists solely of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
This teaching asserts that when cultivated wisdom first arises, it likewise takes phenomena (*dharma*) as its object.
Therefore, it is said that these two are subsumed.
What was previously described as "conditioning dharmas" (dharmālambana) refers exclusively to the wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā).
This explanation applies to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
The former is narrow and the latter is broad;

thus, there is no contradiction. Regarding the inclusion of the three—resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), the ultimate fruit, and thorough comprehension—within the attention of reality (*tattvamanasikāra*): it is as follows.
The penetration of characteristics occurs during initial cultivation,
as well as during all initial cultivations of those beyond training;
for the most part, it consists solely of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
The cultivation of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and so forth is for the most part real;
since resolute belief (*adhimukti*) serves as the proximate path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
The principle applies to both the provisional and the real;
the attention to the ultimate fruit resides within the fundamental stages.
Regarding the statement that "the principles of the provisional and the real apply to all times and stages, while the mental application of observation encompasses only resolute belief":
this is because these constitute the three grades of the path of superior progress;
thus, one first cultivates through provisional understanding.
It is not said that [this] penetrates the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

This is because the principle of the subsequent preparatory application (*prayoga*) also penetrates the ultimate. As for the statement that "the other three mental orientations (*manasikāra*) encompass only the ultimate," this is because the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) predominantly contemplates the ultimate.
Regarding the phrase "this is according to the preceding gate; as for the remaining gates, it should be understood accordingly," one should know that this applies as appropriate to each case.
This refers to the inclusion of the characteristics of the seven previously mentioned modes of attention within the two [characteristics].
Regarding other distinct meanings,
the "discernment of characteristics" consists for the most part solely of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
Because it is the initial commencement of cultivation;
because the ultimate fruit is exclusively the true reality,
as it is the path of liberation.
The mental engagement of observation pertains to both resolute conviction and reality,
as it serves as the path of intensified effort for further advancement.
The remaining four are as before;

therefore, it is said that one should understand them accordingly according to other categories, for it is not stated that all seven types are distinct from those previously mentioned. Regarding the statement that "two kinds of attention also include the attention of one beyond training":
This is based on the fact that, having already attained the fruit, one repeatedly gives rise to revulsion;
thus, there is the aspect of discernment,
which relies upon the path for abandoning the afflictions.
Regarding the five mental applications mentioned in the middle [section], they no longer exist for those beyond training (aśaikṣa);
therefore, it is not said that they exist [for them]. As for the observation that encompasses all-encompassing knowledge (sarvajñatā):

Since observation also pertains to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), although the mental application of observation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*) includes that which involves conceptual discrimination (*savikalpa*),
wisdom (*prajñā*) arises predominantly within the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
It is by means of this partial explanation that the accomplishment of what is to be done is achieved, rather than through the absence of dualistic conceptualization.
Regarding the attention to the object (*ālambanamanasikāra*), if it is to be encompassed by all [stages] according to the first door,
this is based on the initial reflection:
"in such and such a manner," up until the point where it is analyzed as "thus and thus."
Because it is accomplished through cultivation based on conditioned results,
it is generally subsumed under the seven [categories]. Regarding the second classification, it is subsumed solely under the "result of the culmination of application" (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala*).
This refers to the aforementioned second type of attention, which takes pure objects as its focus;
it operates solely within the unconditioned state of the Buddha-fruit, because it is established based on the ultimate.
It is not subsumed under either the initial attention of resolute conviction or the attention of analytical investigation.
This is based on the initial investigation of all phenomena,
which occurs solely with a distracted mind; thus,
this is exclusively the wisdom consisting of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā).
Therefore, it is not subsumed within the seven [stages]. Regarding the statement, "If the initial tranquility is thus, one should know that it is likewise for the subsequent stages":
the initial tranquility refers to the stage of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), wherein the mind is stabilized through meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding the initial stage of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) and analytical investigation (*pravicaya*):
the seven [types of] non-included [mental applications] and the first six mental applications (*manasikāra*) encompass both partial and complete cultivation (*bhāvanā*), etc.
Among these, there is the one liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*).
Cultivated wisdom is not necessarily meditative concentration;
while ordinary beings may attain fundamental concentration,
they do not necessarily possess cultivated wisdom.
The mental application regarding the ultimate fruit is explained according to the preeminent [practitioner] as encompassing the complete cultivation.

Regarding "because those liberated by both [faculties] cultivate the complete factors" and "the attention that accords with reality is subsumed under the first two," the term "attention that accords with reality" (ānulomikamanasikāra) refers to...
Because it involves the repudiation of the object of focus,
it is subsumed under the first two;
this is the attention of antidote (*pratipakṣa-manasikāra*).
For the sake of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
it includes the preparatory stage of withdrawal (*vairāgya-prayoga*) up to its culmination,
as well as a portion of the stage of delighting in cultivation (*ruci*).

The attention of "embracing joy" (ratisaṃgrāhaka-manasikāra) pertains to all four paths; as for the attention of "conducive to purification" (viśuddhyānukūla-manasikāra), it comprises only a portion of embracing joy,
because it constitutes the path of superior progress (viśeṣamārga).
Although it is also included within the mental application of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-manasikāra*),
since it is combined with this path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
They are not mentioned because they are easily understood.

This is explained in terms of the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*); as for how it should be understood in terms of the remaining [antidotes], there are two interpretations. The first says:
This explains only the abandonment through conformable observation; it does not explain the abandonment of the mental attention that has not yet been abandoned,
nor the reason why it is subsumed under the mental attention of mere observation.
This is explained according to the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) that serves as the antidote for abandoning the middle grade [of defilements] mentioned previously;
if one considers the remainder,
it is because it is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the subsequent path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
It is also comprised of the three: the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*), resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika*), and joy in cultivation (*ratisaṃgrāhaka*).

If explained in terms of the antidote for abandoning the inferior grade, it is also comprised of the mental attentions of the application (*prayoga*), the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭha*), and the fruit of application (*prayoganisthāphala*).
Therefore, it is said that they "accord with what is appropriate. Second,
it is said that the four preceding types of attention (*manasikāra*) are collectively included within those previously mentioned.
This refers to the specific abandonment of the three grades;
it is explained in terms of the predominance of the antidote that abandons [the afflictions],
while relying on the sense of being "endowed" with the remainder.
The attention that accords with reality (anulomamanasikāra) pertains to the first two stages and the stage of "gathering joy" (ratisaṃgrāhaka),
as it also extends through the subsequent stage of application (prayoga).
It is also comprised by the investigation of accordance with purity;
it is the abandonment through accordance with investigation,
together with the mental attention toward what has not yet been abandoned.
It also encompasses the application of effort for the sake of delight and the fruit of the culmination of application;
the meaning of "encompassing" is as previously explained.
Therefore, it is said that those [mental engagements] which involve forced exertion are not included.

Because it is included within the attention that operates with intervals and effort due to the scattering of thought and wisdom— ranging from the attention of "operating with intervals and effort" up to the attention of "gathering joy"—
there are twenty-eight types of attention with intervals.
Having explained what is subsumed under the characteristics,
because it occurs between hearing and reflection, there are twenty-eight types of attention involving effortful application.
The subsequent five [types of attention] are said to be subsumed [under this category],
because they all involve the exertion of effort.
Among these, the attention of "delighting in the practice" (*abhirati-manasikāra*) extends throughout the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
Therefore, it is not explained in detail,
as the observation of superior progress is the same.
By means of the mental application of the culmination of preparatory effort (*prayoga-niṣṭha-manasikāra*).
Because one is able to attain spontaneous operation,
it is called "spontaneous operation";
it does not mean that one is already spontaneously operating at that very moment.
Twenty-eighth:
It is said that only the fruit of application is called "functioning without effort.
Among these twenty-eight [points],...
That which involves effort is called "uninterrupted" because it is contrasted with what was previously interrupted;
that which proceeds spontaneously is called "effortless."

Regarding the inclusion of the attention of investigation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-manasikāra*) within the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisamvedī-manasikāra*): this is because, by relying on the initial gateway of cultivation, one predominantly gives rise to wisdom (*prajñā*). As for the inclusion of the attention of effort (*ābhoga-manasikāra*) within the attention that overcomes opposing forces (*balavāhana-manasikāra*): this is because it involves the application of effort toward those opposing forces.
"Not included by others" means that it is subsumed under the attention of internal resolve;
this is based on the gateway of the initial, immediate internal object, and is not included by anything else.
"Subsumed under the investigation of pure attention" means... [it is] subsumed under the investigation of pure attention.
Examining whether afflictions have been abandoned or not is for the purpose of clearing away obstacles to purification; it is not,
however, truly subsumed within them.
Because it is neither a correct uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) nor included among the expansive mental orientations (*manasikāra*),
the nirvana without abiding (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*) is established through compassion and wisdom.
The two benefits are practiced extensively;

they are not included among the seven [types of attention] because the seven are solely for one's own benefit and are not extensive practices. Regarding the first, the universally pervasive mental attention (*sarvatraga-manasikāra*), it is subsumed within the ultimate fruit.
Regarding the previously mentioned universal [attainment], there are two types.
The first refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One; the second, "all-inclusive," refers to all bodhisattvas.
It is cultivated by both vehicles because they possess self-benefit.

Regarding the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) and the attention established by others (*parapratyaya-manaskāra*), these include everything up to that which serves as the condition for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
One interpretation states:
Because they encompass both the understanding of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the cultivation of hearing (*śruta-bhāvanā*),
they are subsumed under what has been established by others.
The second [master] says:
Although its nature consists solely of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*),
it nevertheless arises by taking external teachings as its object.
The inclusion established by others.
Second, within the detailed explanation of the distinctions among objects of focus (*ālambana*), there are two parts.
First, the object of focus as the characteristic itself (*nimitta*).
Second, the specific clarification of the characteristics (*nimitta*).
Because this object of focus (*ālambana*) is the objective field for all mental activities,
it is therefore the characteristic itself.
Because they equally take the object of concentration as their domain,
among the specific characteristics explained separately,
the four characteristics are explained first.

Next, the thirty-two marks are explained. Regarding the "characteristic of the object" (*ālambana-nimitta*), this refers to the essential characteristic of the objects to be known (*jñeya-vastu*) as they are conceptually differentiated.
The "essential nature of conceptual differentiation" (*vikalpa-svabhāva*) refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that act as the subjects of cognition.
The aspect of conceptualization (*vikalpa-nimitta*) is the objective aspect (*ālambana-bhāga*).
Because the concentrated mind takes this [conceptualization] as well as the objective aspect as its object,
it is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya-nimitta*), which refers to the requisites for meditative concentration (*samādhi-sambhāra*).
That is to say, it refers to the causes of non-regret, joy, tranquility, bliss, and so forth. Regarding the four [factors] such as not guarding the doors of the sense faculties:
these are as previously explained.
First is not guarding the doors of the sense faculties.
Second, not knowing moderation in eating.
Third, being constantly awake during the first and last watches of the night,
diligently practicing meditative cultivation.
Fourth is dwelling in non-reflective awareness (*asamprajanya*).
This is explained in detail in the lower Śrāvaka-bhūmi. The characteristics of laxity (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*) are as their names imply;
they are precisely those attachments to signs (*nimitta*).
Its essence has ignorance as its nature;
or it has craving as its nature;
or it has all afflictions such as views and doubt as its nature.
Among the thirty-two marks, there are two parts:
first, the individual explanation of the thirty-two marks;
second, their identity with the four marks. What is the mark of the basis? It refers to the characteristic of the discriminated essence.
That is to say, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) are to be assigned accordingly. What are the characteristics of the arising of the mind?
There are two such characteristics:
first, the characteristic of the arising of all minds.
As stated immediately prior, attention (manasikāra) is a single characteristic;
all mental states arise by means of attention.
Second, the characteristic of the arising of the eighth mind:
this refers to the mind among the twelve links that takes formations as its object.
Furthermore, because it arises conditioned by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). What is meant by "characteristic of its own kind" (*svasāmānyalakṣaṇa*)?
It refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*);
their "kind" (*jāti*) is distinct for each, and their "own characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) is as follows: [the specific defining feature of each].

This refers to each individual aggregate (*skandha*), because the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the eye and so forth are distinct. Herein, for one who has already attained liberation but does not apply the means for further abandonment, there is the contemplation of those possessed of craving and so forth.
Those who have gone forth are said to have attained renunciation.
There are two categories among them:
one category consists of those who do not cultivate the means for nirvāṇa.
One contemplates those with greed and those without greed, those with hatred and those without hatred, those with delusion and those without delusion, and so forth.
Those of one class who cultivate the means for attaining nirvana contemplate the contracted mind,
the expanded mind, the depressed mind, and the uplifted mind.
Up to the well-liberated mind and the poorly liberated mind—
these are the characteristics of non-defilement.
The first three pairs of contemplations are not necessarily conducive to world-transcendence;
the latter seven pairs are conducive to world-transcendence.

Alternatively, it is explained that those who accord with meditative concentration cultivate the skillful means, whereas those who do not accord with meditative concentration do not cultivate the skillful means;
this does not necessarily pertain to the supramundane. Furthermore, another interpretation of "not cultivating the skillful means" is as follows:
This means that because a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) has already attained liberation and no longer cultivates further skillful means,
they simply observe the three pairs of minds, such as those with attachment and so forth.
If one practices skillful means,
it refers to those in training who contemplate the seven pairs of mental states, such as the concise and the inferior.

Because it conforms to the departure of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). What is the sign of light? It refers to when someone, in order to remove darkness, [perceives] either a physical light or the light of the Dharma.
This was previously mentioned among the "nutriments" (*āhāra*) for the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
It is said that there are three luminosities;
these correspond to the first two. Regarding "dwelling in contemplation while seated" and so forth:
in the future, this is called "seated."

Out of consideration for the shame of others,
one avoids falling away from great benefit;
having a profound understanding of causes and conditions, one’s resulting increase in shame and faith is called "loving reverence."
Because one lacks love and respect for the Triple Gem,
it is called "losing great benefit.
Alternatively, one may give rise to three [faults] in each of the three places.
There is no need for further allocation.
Regarding the three kinds of supreme unsurpassedness:
first is the unsurpassedness of wisdom.
That is to say, among the three knowledges, the knowledge of selflessness is the root,
while the first two knowledges serve as the preparatory means.
Because of these three ways of entering the contemplation of the truths,
two types of practice are specifically taught as supreme;
namely, the four paths of practice.
The third unsurpassed liberation is the unshakable liberation of the mind.
Regarding liberation in the mundane and supramundane,
liberation for those in training and those beyond training,
and timely liberation.
That immovability is the liberation of the mind,
for it is the most unsurpassed.
Within the fourfold increase of the gates,
there are forty-six gates,
which also contain mutual contradictions.
Because they constitute a single gateway,
the essence of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is precisely wisdom (prajñā).
Because wisdom abides in its object only through associated mindfulness.
As for the four kinds of bonds:
Because it obstructs and confines the mind, it is called "bondage" (*bandhana*);
however, it is not necessarily of the nature of the afflictions (*kleśa*),
as it arises from the mind's reliance on grasping.
Taking the body as its own essence,
the body then binds the mind;
through the mind, one experiences [suffering] together with it.
Deeply apprehending the object of focus,
it binds the mind together;
for by means of the mind, one discerns form and so forth as its objective domain.
The objects that are cognized are dependent upon the mind,
just as in the case of [the perception of] other bodies and so forth.
The three factors associated with the afflictions are called "bonds" because they defile and afflict the mind.
Taking the four [objects] as one's domain,
one develops a profound sense of weary detachment; thus,
the four foundations of mindfulness are established.
The internal body, which is the basis,
binds the mind, which is that which depends upon it;
both are associated with feeling.
Distinguished by five states,
it is always concomitant with the mind and cognizes its objects.
The fetters are established as four because they are able to cognize the mind and its various afflictions and defilements,
as these are all associated with the mind.
Furthermore, there are four kinds [of practices] that take diligence as the precursor and lead even to the attainment and increase of wholesome dharmas;
these are the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*) for the manifestation of unwholesome dharmas.
This refers to the abandonment of the restraint and the abandonment of its fetters; that is, the abandonment of abandonment.
This is because unarisen unwholesome dharmas are termed "fetters," and one is thus able to attain wholesome dharmas.
This refers to the abandonment through cultivation and that which can increase [the roots of merit].
It refers to the abandonment through protection.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of mental concentration and mental abiding.
Distinguishing the stage of scattering is called "mental concentration" (*citta-samādhi*).
Abiding inwardly on a single object is called "mental abiding" (*citta-sthiti*).
Those bound by the fetters of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) are preceded by four types of perception (*saṃjñā*).
Because it relies on the seven realms of those with perception,
it excludes the immeasurables of the Peak of Existence;
the word "only" indicates that it excludes desire-greed.
As in the twelfth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
it is explained that the knowledge of the distinctions of others' minds encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the contaminated knowledge of others' minds:
One does not know the untainted mind,
nor does one know its self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) which takes that as its object,
nor does one know the wisdom that cognizes it.
This is because one's own mind cannot perceive itself.
The untainted knowledge of others' minds (anāsrava-paracittajñāna) is able to know both tainted (sāsrava) and untainted (anāsrava) minds.
One also knows the wisdom that is capable of knowing;
because the latter three parts of the Buddha-wisdom are collectively capable of knowing itself.
However, this does not necessarily constitute the four modes of practice of the Path.
Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that this applies to other persons.
Regarding the statement that "there are four dharmas capable of exhausting the outflows of the higher realms" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-āsrava*),
there are three explanations.
One explanation states that these are the four tracks of the Dharma;
within the seven stages of preparation, the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning,
they are able to exhaust the outflows of the higher realms.
Regarding the "footprints":
as for the second point concerning the four footprints,
the first is the attainment of tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*).
This refers to the seven stages of expedient means (saptavidha-upāya) and the stage of the path of vision (darśana-mārga),
wherein all afflictions (kleśa), karma, and their resultant phenomena have already been eliminated.
Third is the stage of the path of cultivation,
wherein all matters of the afflictions are permanently severed without remainder.
Fourth is the path of no-more-learning.
Having eternally severed all matters of the afflictions without remainder,
one further cultivates those very matters of the afflictions according to the path already attained.
Excluding the outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*), it applies to the three aforementioned locations.
A third [interpretation] states:
first, outflow-tainted wisdom.
This is the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
Second, the absence of all afflictions is the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Third, it is deficient in various functions.
This is because the path of liberation eliminates all coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) as well as its resultant phenomena.
Fourth, it is for the sake of abandoning all afflictions without remainder;
as previously attained, it is further cultivated and practiced,
which constitutes the path of superior progress.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of protection.
First is the protection of life,
which means not begrudging one's own body or life.
They uphold the True Dharma,
or protect the life-faculties of others without causing them harm.
Alternatively, one protects one’s own right livelihood and does not give rise to unwholesome karma. Regarding the second power of protection,
this refers to protecting wisdom.
To crush the hosts of Māra’s enemies,
or to protect one's own strength,
for the sake of benefiting others.
Alternatively, it is the protection of the five powers,
crushing enemies without yielding; as for the protection against mental afflictions,
it is the guarding against all defilements.
With an undefiled mind,
for the sake of protecting the True Dharma,
one gives rise to various afflictions.
He expels those who are evil persons who destroy the True Dharma and protects through right means.
He skillfully practices the True Dharma through expedient means.
Furthermore, there are four kinds [of practitioners] who are able to attain right view up to single-pointed concentration on a single object.
Not following after objects means not being greedy for them;
not opposing objects means... [not being averse to them].
He does not harbor anger;
he acts with clear comprehension;
he is not deluded.
These three types of practice purify one’s conduct when engaging with various objects;
they focus the mind single-pointedly on a single object.
It is right mindfulness.
The latter type is purity at the time of abiding.
Furthermore, there are four modes by which one can realize and attain liberation:
first, mindfulness;
second, the eye.
The three types of wisdom,
the four bodies,
and the clear knowledge of past lives.
The clarity of the divine eye,
as well as the two liberations,
and the exhaustion of the outflows.
In sequence, they are able to realize the body,

Regarding the fourth [element], its nature is lightness and so forth, characterized by mobility.
This means that wind can produce both primary and derived [elements];
because it resembles lightness, it is called "lightness, etc.

the nature of wind is to be able to move.
It is not through mental attention.
There are four factors that enable sentient beings to subsist,

Four factors constitute the tracks of consciousness;
that is to say, the four stations of consciousness. Having seen them, one proceeds toward them:
the five faculties and form are grasped as objects of perception.
The six objects—visible form and so forth—are co-existent with their respective bases and spheres;

these are assigned respectively to the five sense organs, the five dusts (sensory objects), and the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). Regarding the four types of questions and their corresponding modes of answering: [the first is] the categorical response (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇa*).
This refers to the four types of discourse, such as categorical exposition (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇa*).
Regarding the four ways of answering questions concerning the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
If one asks whether the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya is the true nature of awakening (tathatā), etc.,
one should give a categorical response, saying: "It is so."
When someone asks about the relative superiority or inferiority of the fruits of human existence,
one should answer by means of analytical distinction:
compared to those of the devas, they are inferior.
The remaining [categories] are considered superior.
This refers to questions that are obscure rather than explicit,
nor are they of a categorical nature.
When asked about the relative superiority or inferiority of persons,
one should respond with an interrogative answer:
"To what do you compare them?"
In this manner, they proceeded by turns,
scrutinizing those devious intentions and cross-examining them endlessly.
Question: Regarding the question of whether there truly exists a sentient being who is an agent and an experiencer, it should be set aside as an answer.
Among the four types of answers regarding phenomena, this concerns the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
If one asks whether *tathatā* is eternal,

If one asks about the karmic fruits within the bodies of sentient beings, [it should be answered analytically].
Will its maturation necessarily arise?

For those whose delusions have not yet been exhausted,

one observes their deceitful intent as they inquire and request the teaching of the Dharma.
One should merely pose a counter-question rather than providing an explanation. One should ask:

One should set aside the answer;

Kind speech,

The stages of the Not-yet-arrived (*anāgamya*) and the Formless Realm (*ārūpya*) are called "painful," because they are biased toward either meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*).
The fundamental dhyānas are called "bliss" because they proceed by way of both paths;
although the stage of "not-yet-attained" (anāgamya) is said to possess joy and bliss, it is not so designated.
Because they are not yet perfected,

However, the Bodhisattva-bhūmi differs from this [text] in its distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones.

Regarding the phrase "pleasurable but not beneficial" and so forth:

The distinctions in meaning regarding worldly benefits, fame, profit, and so forth should be understood by analogy.
This refers, for example, to kings and the royal horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
Those various kings constantly harbored anxiety and fear regarding the subjugation of enemies and adversaries.
Because it enables both oneself and others to endure suffering,
the lord of sacrifice, though possessing supreme sovereignty, [remains subject to it].
To sacrifice horses and other animals for ritual offerings causes both oneself and others to suffer and results in demerit.
The four kinds of faults of speech are:
namely, falsehood and divisive speech.
Coarse, foul,
and impure;
these increase within the five gates.

There are twenty-four gates. Regarding the five causes for the loss of gains and offerings, such as conduct, these correspond to the five types of stinginess (*mātsarya*) taught in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
If one enjoys gains and offerings in such a manner [characterized by stinginess], [the gains are lost].
That which is stinginess regarding the place is "stinginess regarding the location.

That which is obtained from someone is "stinginess regarding the family," also called "stinginess regarding the donor. That which is the object obtained is "stinginess regarding the gift. That which is for the sake of obtaining it is "stinginess regarding the purpose."
One praises stinginess, thinking: "If it is obtained in this way, it means there is stinginess regarding the Dharma and stinginess regarding one's dwelling place, [thinking]:
'I alone shall dwell here.'"
I do not employ others;
even if there are others, I am always the master. This refers to one who is stingy regarding their household.
"I alone possess this house;
no other person shall enter it.
Even if others should come,"
Among these, I am the most excellent; as for those who are stingy regarding material gifts,
I alone shall take this object and will not give it to anyone else.
"If he gives to others,
I alone am superior and more excellent; he praises the stingy,
yet he praises me alone."
Do not praise others;
even if you must praise others, do so in such a way that they do not surpass me. As for stinginess regarding the Dharma:
[the thought] "I alone am able to know the meaning of the various sūtras and teachings."
Do not let others know [of this].
Even if there are those who might know, they are all estranged from me.
Furthermore, there are five factors that cause a practitioner to first destroy their pure precepts and so forth.
These are the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*):
the first two destroy pure ethical discipline (*śīla*),
and the latter three destroy one's reputation.
The inability to receive [the teachings] due to a deficiency in śamatha and vipaśyanā is the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness (styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa).
Forgetting [what has been heard] is the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa).
Indeterminacy is not the hindrance of doubt.
Regarding the teaching that there are three fetters based on the lower portion of the path of vision:
because one does not transcend the evil destinies, the view of extremes follows the view of a self-identity.
The adherence to views follows from the adherence to precepts and rituals;
because false views arise following doubt,
three fundamental [afflictions] are taught.
Thus, the six derivative [afflictions] are subsumed; delusion (moha) pervades all three realms, while hatred (dveṣa) and greed (lobha) increase specifically in the desire realm.
Therefore, only greed and hatred are explicitly mentioned.
This includes delusion as well, because it does not transcend the lower realms;

therefore, only five are taught as the fetters of the lower realm (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*). Furthermore, this is because the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) prevents one from proceeding toward liberation.
Through the clinging to precepts and observances,
one becomes deluded regarding the right path and follows a wrong road;
through doubt, one harbors uncertainty concerning the true path.
Regarding the obstacles to liberation,
only the first three [fetters] are taught as causes for rebirth in the evil destinies among the five higher fetters (*pañcordhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Regarding the fetters without distinction:
they are distinguished according to the realms (dhātu),
not according to persons.
The first is distinguished by name;
the remaining three are distinguished by the persons upon whom the fetters depend.
There is a difference in terminology;
for those who practice dhyāna are themselves human beings.
From craving, agitation arises;
from the conceit "I am," other forms of conceit arise;
and from doubt, ignorance increases.
The fetters that have distinctions in name lead to rebirth in the higher realms by means of the fetters that lack such distinctions.
Due to the presence of differentiated fetters,
those who have attained meditative absorption through birth do not abandon the higher realms because of three types of affliction.
Since all differentiated [afflictions] are abandoned through cultivation,
with the exception of views and grasping,
delusion is taught [as the root] because there is no doubt.
Because the Arhat has abandoned them.
Regarding the five kinds of lack of faith and respect,
the first is toward the Great Teacher.
Second, with respect to ethical discipline;
third, with respect to the mind;
and fourth, with respect to wisdom.
Fifth, toward one's fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*),
there is no faith or respect;
these are the five types of wrong practitioners.
First, giving rise to anger toward enemies;
second, causing dissension among friends;
third, constantly desiring to cause them sorrow and suffering.
Performing harmful deeds;
fourth, violating one’s own ethical discipline (*śīla*);
and fifth, engaging in the three types of unwholesome conduct (*duścarita*). Among these, the three kinds of consequential faults (*niṣyanda-doṣa*) are as follows:
Because of hatred and resentment,
there will be many enemies; because of the destruction of kinship, there will be many adversaries.
One is separated from dear friends because performing unbeneficial deeds gives rise to suffering; thus,
there are various forms of sorrow and pain.
These three are constantly present before one.
These are the three kinds of outflowing results (niṣyanda-phala) in future lives: first, the outflowing fault of manifest phenomena, because it destroys one's own ethical discipline (śīla).
Regarding the fault of the maturation of the subsequent state, which consists largely of regret at the time of death:
because one has practiced the three types of unwholesome conduct,
one subsequently falls into the evil destinies.
The fool regarding time is deluded concerning time;
he perceives as permanent that which is impermanent, arising and ceasing moment by moment. The fool regarding states is likewise deluded.

The delusion regarding the states of the three feelings consists in conceiving suffering to be pleasure; the delusion regarding intrinsic nature consists in being deluded about the nature of the five aggregates.
To conceive of a self where there is no self, the fourth being the pursuit of gain and honor, and the fifth being the seeking of livelihood—
these are called the five factors to be remedied.
As for the two superior practitioners:
First, the superior practice of meditative concentration;
second, the superior practice of wisdom.
There are four types of the superior practice of meditative concentration.
First, by hearing the noble discourse based on the truths,
one correctly understands the meaning of the Dharma;
second, by means of vast vocal sounds.
First, reading and reciting the sūtras;
second, elucidating the subtle meanings for others;
third, dwelling in secluded places.
Reflecting with careful discernment,
these latter three cases are analogous to the first.
Therefore, it should be understood that the correct understanding of the meaning of the Dharma— just as when one hears the vast sound of the causes regarding the causes—
is likewise so for the practitioner of superior wisdom.
Contemplating in order to eliminate superior degrees of sensual desire is the fifth.
These are the five types of practitioners who cultivate insight meditation.
Equally believing in awakening and nirvāṇa constitutes the two types of intentionality;
these are practiced with uninterrupted and earnest devotion.
The third is the cultivation of right knowledge,
which consists of the wisdoms derived from hearing and reflection.
Practicing śamatha with uninterrupted and earnest diligence is the fourth.
Practicing vipaśyanā with uninterrupted and earnest diligence is the fifth.
This refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
The latter three are called the "perfection of skillful means" (*upāya-saṃpad*).
Second, those who attain parinirvāṇa immediately after being born for the first time in the first dhyāna.
The Abhidharma treatises state that once one has been born into the form realm (rūpadhātu), the noble path (āryamārga) manifests;
this is said with reference to those who have not previously abandoned desire for the form realm.
It is not fixed as being only thus;
in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*,
it is constantly and extensively analyzed, as explained in the *Abhidharma-kośa* and other treatises.
There are three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*).
Having attained their respective fruits, they immediately enter parinirvāṇa without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
Why is this not the case for the other four types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*)?
Having attained the state with remainder,
one does not immediately enter the state without remainder;
this refers to the three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
For what reason do those of these three types,
having attained the five aggregates with remainder,
immediately enter the state of no-remainder?
Answer: It is because, due to the remaining four types [of fetters], both the arising and the fetters have not yet been exhausted;
thus, the duration of birth is long.
Because its momentum is strong,
once one has first attained the state with remainder,
one does not immediately enter the state without remainder.
The non-returner who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state has exhausted the fetters of birth;
although the fetters of arising still remain.
Its force is weak;
how much more so for those born in the intermediate state,
as their force lasts for only seven days.
That [person], being weak and inferior,
having attained the state with remainder, then enters the nirvāṇa without remainder.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 36, states:
Regarding the non-returner who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, there are four types of minds:
the first is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Second, those in training;
third, those beyond training;
fourth, neither those in training nor those beyond training.
Entering into nirvana.
The first [type] is the contaminated mind at the initial moment of rebirth and so forth.
The second refers to all untainted minds prior to the vajra-like samādhi.
The third refers to...
The various untainted minds subsequent to the path of liberation—
these three categories together encompass them all.
Entering the nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
in accordance with the teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school,
[the mind] consists of the unobscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) states of maturation (vipāka), deportment (airyāpathika), and so forth.
Because one enters into nirvana without remainder,
this fourth [category] is spoken of alone as "neither-learner-nor-non-learner" entering nirvana. Furthermore, this is according to the gateway of ultimate truth.
The very last moment is likewise only the eighth consciousness, unobscured and indeterminate,
as one enters the nirvana without remainder.
Therefore, in this fourth [case], it alone is said that one enters nirvāṇa;
the other three are not said to enter nirvāṇa. Furthermore, that sūtra also says:
Among the four kinds of mind,
two are nirvana and two are not nirvana.
One enters the state with remainder by means of the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣacitta*);
one enters the state without remainder by means of the fourth mind.
This is because the former two are not so. Furthermore, as stated below in this treatise:
It is taught that one who wishes to enter the nirvana without remainder must first enter the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*);
this is precisely the sixth consciousness, the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
That which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner is precisely the eighth consciousness.
If one enters the meditative absorption of cessation, only then does one enter nirvana.
Precisely because of this,
there are five types of practitioners who cultivate meditation:
those characterized by desire, ill-will, harmfulness, purity, and impurity.
There are three;
the meditative attainments of the form and formless realms constitute the fourth.
The characteristic of nirvāṇa is the fifth.
Within the section on the increase of the six gates:
There are sixteen gates in total; that is to say, the eightfold distinctions regarding the affairs of sentient beings are proclaimed based on the six characteristics, namely:
the six sense faculties and the six objects.
The six consciousnesses,
the six contacts,
and the six feelings.
The six perceptions,
the six volitions,
and the six cravings.
These are called the eight things: the distinction of the things upon which I depend, which are the six sense faculties;
and the distinction of the things that are their objects, which are the six objective spheres.
The distinction of the intrinsic nature of the object refers to the six consciousnesses,
because they grasp consciousness as the intrinsic nature of the self. The distinction of the object as the cause for experience...
The six contacts are so called because they are the causes of feeling; the six feelings are so called because they differentiate the objects of experience;
[the six perceptions] are so called because they differentiate the objects according to how they are expressed.
The six [bases] are perceptions (*saṃjñā*), because they are the causes for verbal expression.
The differentiation of the activity of affairs is the six groups of volition (*ṣaṭ cetanākāyāḥ*). The differentiation of the activity of aspiration is [the six groups of contact].
These are the six groups of craving (ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya).
They are also called the six desires,
for they have desire as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

Below this section on the distinctions among such matters, it clarifies the teaching of the eight topics based on the six characteristics: "I rely upon the eye and so forth" is the first characteristic;
"I [perceive] objects such as form" [is the second].
This is the second characteristic.
That which conceives consciousness as the self is called the "differentiation of the intrinsic nature of things."
Among the faculties, objects, and so forth,
each should be explained according to the third characteristic, namely through contact and feeling.
Based on a single characteristic, one speaks of the phenomena of contact and feeling; such is the name, and so forth, up to the arising of conventional expression—this is the fourth characteristic.
It consists in performing all actions, whether righteous or unrighteous.
This is the fifth characteristic. Not dwelling even in the diminution of desirable things—
this is the sixth characteristic.
Regarding disagreeable matters:
that which has not yet been obtained is not desired;
even if it is obtained, one does not dwell upon the desire for it.
Furthermore, regarding the six types of contempt for the Three Jewels and so forth, which lead to dwelling in rarity and decline:
within the context of the Three Jewels...
One should believe or not believe accordingly.
Regarding the three trainings, one may attain or fail to attain them; yet due to harsh speech, one attains nothing at all.
That is to say, regarding the loss of all wholesome dharmas due to the failure of superior ethical discipline:
one should believe that what ought to be attained will not be attained, and what ought not to be believed will indeed be believed.
Furthermore, regarding the "six kinds of supreme purity" and so forth, these refer to the six constant abidings (*ṣaḍ-ābhoga-vihāra*).
As for the statement "the four great elements, the space element, and the consciousness element":
the basis of form refers to the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
That which is the support for form is the consciousness element;
that which is the support for movement is the space element.
Therefore, it is said that only these six constitute a sentient being.
Based on this initial statement, there are briefly six kinds of bases upon which the various material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and their respective physical locations depend as appropriate.
These are the factors that can obstruct the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Truths.
That is to say, within the previously mentioned five expanded gates,
three delusions give rise to three inversions,
which constitute the three [types of craving]: namely, the seeking of gain and offerings.
The fourth is for the sake of [long] life;
the fifth is for the hope of longevity.
The five [points] are the same as before.
The distinction here is that, below,
the sixth hindrance is explained.
Because it did not exist previously, it is said:
"Therefore, this is spoken of as being within the stage of illumination (*āloka-bhāgīya*) and not within the stage of liberation and maturation (*vimukti-paripāka-bhāgīya*).

Thus, these seeds do not possess distinct characteristics within the six sense bases; therefore,

As explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
