Recalling past laughter, play, and the like;
following regret (*kaukṛtya*);
and [recalling] the three periods of time and so forth.
This follows the doubt.
The treatise answers the question of how many obstructive factors one cultivates within the mind while walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), stating:
"By means of a mind accompanied by clarity (*āloka*) and a mind accompanied by light (*ābhā*)."
That is to say: water and fire;
the stars and the moon;
medicinal herbs.
Jewels are the condition for light;
this mind of light is called the "mind associated with light."
Only the sun is the objective condition for this light;
the mind associated with this light is called the "mind conjoined with light."
The sun is able to emit light that reveals hidden places so they may be seen;
other luminaries, such as the moon, do not do so. Thus says the treatise.
Answer: Regarding the statement that one cultivates the mind while sitting in meditative seclusion,
it means that one either contemplates the bones or contemplates the skeleton.
Alternatively, one may contemplate the gaps between the skeletal bones.

The *Śāstra* further states that the "characteristics of the meditative concentration of the virtuous and good" refers to the characteristics of the meditative concentration that abandons these four hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
The *Śāstra* on the Differentiation of the Resolving of Doubts and the Coverings states: "It is called the 'excellent concentration of the wise' (*viduṣaḥ kalyāṇa-samādhiḥ*)."
Regarding the question of whether something existed or did not exist in the past,
what is intended here is that the initial statement constitutes improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
Thus, all three periods are raised and lowered;
one may doubt that the three periods exist as well as their causes and conditions,
yet all three periods are raised.
Regarding the doubt concerning existence and non-existence,
why is it that, among the three time periods, one speaks only of the past and not of the present or the future?
What is the intention behind this?
The commentary states:
As is shown by the brief reflection of the extensive treatise,
both the preceding and following sections cite all three time periods.
In this context, only the past is explicitly mentioned;
the present and future are understood by implication.
They are not stated because the treatise is concise. Furthermore, the present is actually existing.
One must not doubt whether they exist or not;
future phenomena are indeterminate,
and their existence or non-existence is difficult to infer.
Furthermore, it is said that one now attains right view because the future fruit is already severed; therefore,
there is no need to doubt whether the future exists or not.
Because the past is not the same as the present and future,
one specifically doubts its existence or non-existence;
in reality, however, it pervades all three periods of time.
When one reflects, "In the past, what did I exist as? How did I exist?
there are two types of reflection herein:
first, reflecting on what dharmas existed in the past.
Second, he reflects on where past phenomena come from; that is,
first he asks about the substance of phenomena,
and subsequently he asks about the function of phenomena.
The past being thus,
the two other time periods are to be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, the treatise states that [the practice] is for the sake of preserving bedding and furniture, and for conforming to worldly decorum and so forth.
The meaning here is that during the first watch of the night,
one should walk back and forth until exhaustion.
In the latter part of the night, do not allow him to practice walking meditation;
during the first part of the night, he may practice walking meditation,
but do not allow him to go far away.
Or, when reaching the place for walking meditation (caṅkrama),
one might fear that thieves would steal or lose the bedding and requisites;
therefore, one advances the bedding so that it may be used during the walking meditation.
Furthermore, although it is the middle of the night,
one's deportment must remain correct;
therefore, in accordance with worldly etiquette, one practices walking meditation during the first watch of the night.
Furthermore, the worldly practice is to perform walking meditation during the first watch of the night,
and the communal practice of the Saṃgha is likewise to perform walking meditation during the first watch of the night;
because this accords with worldly custom, they are the same regarding the first watch.
There are two reasons for walking meditation (caṅkrama):
first, to protect and maintain one's bedding;
that is why it is not performed at a great distance.
In accordance with worldly etiquette, the scriptures divide [the practice] into walking meditation and sitting meditation;
the treatises explain that one should arise from thought and employ skillful means when lying down. Thus it is said:
Regarding those who are like wild deer in the forest:
wild deer, fearing they might be wounded or killed by humans,
do not sleep in peace.
There is a skillful means regarding the time for lying down; it is the same for people today.
The treatise states that "the latter part of the night" refers to the period following one-quarter of the night having passed, which is called the final portion of the night.
The night consists of only four parts;
once the final part has passed,
it is already dawn.
What is meant by "night"?
In this context, it refers to the final portion [of the day] that has passed.
This means that among the four parts, entering the final part is called "transgression" (*atīta*).
It is not because the final part itself no longer exists that it is called a transgression.
There are two kinds of transgressions.
First, it is called "past" as soon as it enters [the present];
this refers precisely to the passage in this treatise.
Second, it is called "past" once its function has been completed.
It is like the passing of a night;
here, "passing" (atikrānta) refers to entering [the next state].
If it is capable of encompassing four parts within three periods of time.
The latter part refers to the subsequent time;
among the four parts of the night,
that which has passed by taking one part from the preceding is called "passed."
The latter portion moves forward;
it does not move backward.
Therefore, regarding the text on the middle watch of the night:
It is said that when one quarter of the night has passed out of the four quarters of the night,
this is the middle period;
it has passed the first quarter of the time.
Furthermore, since the middle period encompasses the middle period,
it also exceeds one part; thus,
one takes the greater portion of the second part.
The third section primarily establishes the middle section.
In the commentary on "dwelling with clear comprehension" regarding going and returning,
there are four points of meaning.
First, full awareness while going and returning;
second, full awareness regarding what should be gone to and returned from;
third, full awareness of the proper time for going and returning.
In these four ways, one should thus go and return.
Among these, this refers to the second [way] in which one should go and return.
And as for the fourth [case], "in this way and that way one should go and return," what is the distinction?
This is explained again below in the commentary.
It is said that regarding their appearance, movements, conduct, rituals, and deportment, they should proceed and return in this manner;
this is distinct from what was stated previously.
The second [point] concerns only those such as his family members.
One may go to and return from [such families].
There are five kinds of families one must not go to or return from;
the fourth is the last.
If one must visit households,
there are established rules and protocols for such visits;
one may proceed accordingly.
Non-existence implies that there can be no coming or going;
this constitutes the distinction. In the subsequent sections on "Beholding" and so forth, each likewise possesses four [aspects].
Following this method of composition,
the second line is identical in all cases:
"In that house, it may be so, or it may not be so."
The fourth phrase clarifies the renunciation that arises from what is permissible in the second phrase.
Regarding the *saṃghāṭī*: [text continues]
This refers to the "upper garment," which is the robe worn on top,
like an outer wall.
This robe is also like that:
it is worn most outwardly and worn most upwardly.
This is called the "upper robe.
According to the treatise, it may range from sixty strips down to nine strips.
Among the various schools, this robe does not exist;
this treatise is based on their combined accounts,
with the maximum limit being sixty [units].
Regarding the nine citations, these are stated provisionally based on what is commonly accepted by all schools;
however, there may be sixty citations,
or even more, up to one hundred and fifty.
Question:
Each treatise mentions that there is either a middle robe or a lower robe.
The commentary states:
The inner robe is the *uttarāsaṅga*;
it was previously called the *yītúluósēngjiā*.
It is also referred to as the "seven-strip robe."
What is now called the "middle robe" (chūnyì) is so named because it is worn beneath the outer robe (dàyī) and above the five-layered undergarment.
It is also called the "middle-layered robe" (*antaravāsaka*),
because it covers the body and is worn in the middle.
The lower garment (*nivasana*) consists of five folds.
Because this section follows immediately below that,
the rules for the three robes (tricīvara) are explained again;
furthermore, these robes are categorized as either middle or inferior.
Therefore, they are called the middle and lower robes.
If that is so, why are there no "upper robes"?
It is clearly understood that the three robes are the subject of discussion here.
The upper garment is the saṃghāṭī.
Regarding the discussion on chewing and tasting:
for what reason are cakes and the like considered "chewed" food?
Milk and the like are tasted.
That which can be chewed is called "tasting" (svāda);
that which cannot be chewed is called "eating" (bhojana).
Solid foods such as cakes and the like that can be chewed or sucked are called "eating" (khādati);
those that cannot be chewed or sucked are called "tasting" (svādayati).
Alternatively, one might speak in a general sense that there is no difference between eating and tasting;
this is because [the distinction] must be established according to worldly convention.
Thus, it is said in the sequence of the commentary’s exposition.
Furthermore, there are households where one should not go: those that are exclusively slanderous and incorrigible,
meaning they are determinedly devoid of affection,
or those whose roots of goodness have not yet matured.
Regarding how one should proceed according to the commentary’s explanation:
it is said that one does not fall upon the mountain peaks. As for "mountain" and "peaks": [the former refers to the general mass, while the latter refers to the specific elevations].
What is meant by "falling"?
In this context, "falling" refers to falling into a state of abiding.
It does not mean falling;
it does not cause one to fall from a mountain peak.
Regarding the argument that this should follow the analogy of the moon:
That is to say, just as the moon can cool and benefit people,
when one enters the home of a donor,
one's body possesses a refreshing coolness.
It benefits the donor,
just like the moon;
this is discussed from the perspective of maintaining one's own mind.
The statement, "It is not that they lack wisdom; rather, having explained at length, they must act with speed and not with delay," means that in this context,
each of them goes to the house of a donor.
Why must one hope for a reward?
It is not that they lack wisdom in giving,
but rather that they proceed immediately.
One should not practice such unwise giving;
that is, being stingy and failing to give.
If one does not give, one will not go [to a higher realm].
One should not do this.
It is not that one does not go because the gift was not given wisely;
rather, when going, one must proceed with great speed and not with delay.
The Commentary states that "one should not untie the knot" means that one should not leave the knot unfastened.
The Dharma Master says:
There is a toggle at the bottom of the robe;
it should not be left open but should be fastened.
Furthermore, it should neither be pulled up too high nor hang down too low.
The robe is not excessively loose.
The treatise states that it is not like the trunk of an elephant.
That is to say, one should not let the corner of the *kāṣāya* hang down like the trunk of an elephant;
rather, it should be draped over the shoulder like the flower-cluster of a *tāla* tree,
which emerges from its sheath as the tree blossoms.
The same applies to the corner of the robe;
in neither case should it hang from the neck of the dragon,
even if it is draped over the shoulder.
The corners of the robe must not be raised as high as a dragon's head;
one must not be fidgety or restless.
The *kāṣāya* should be placed within the crook of the elbow.
It is like a ball of beans.
Question:
According to the treatise, one should not eat food by biting it off.
This refers to instructing one to eat with the hands held open.

In the commentary’s explanation of the sequence beginning with "coming and going" and so forth, it starts from the passage: "Suppose there is someone who relies upon such a village or town," and so on.
Having thus finished the begging, one returns to one's original place.
This explains the two methods of going and returning;
one should know for oneself the procedures for going, returning, and so forth.
Each has four modes of action.
For now, we shall treat the "going" and "returning.
These are the sequential rules for going and so forth.
Down to the case of *dṛṣṭi* (viewing) and so forth, one does not perform them in their entirety.
This may be understood by analogy with going and returning (*gamanāgamana*) and the like.
By analogy with a small portion of *dṛṣṭi*, one also performs [the action].
The remaining [passages] are to be read in sequence: furthermore, from "in such [a place]" down to "not subject to turning back," one understands the places where one should not go;
next, down to "or the house of a merchant leader."
One should go when one understands the proper place to go; next, even down to the time of angry contention, one should not go.
One should go when there is understanding. Next, down to the point where one accepts and makes use of things while being firm in resolve and modest.
The explanation should correspond to what has been traversed.
The preceding section has already completed the explanation of going and returning.
Next, below this, it concerns the time when one has already gone or is currently going, and so forth.
Up until the point where they are able to encompass the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and cause all evil discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) to cease manifesting,
one clearly perceives and contemplates two dharmas;
therein are two [factors].
First, it clarifies what should be seen;
second, it clarifies what should not be seen. Regarding the clarification of what should be seen:
That is to say, from what has already passed in the past down to that which one ought not to contemplate,
it is explained by analogy that these should not be looked upon.
The following should be observed:
furthermore, one should not sway the body, swing the arms, shake the head, and so forth,
down to sitting with dignified composure.
This passage generally clarifies the two dharmas of contraction and extension;
herein, it merely judges what is improper,
rather than explaining what constitutes proper action.
Construct it according to the above instructions.
Furthermore, one should not leave the ties unfastened, nor should the lower part be tucked up or spread out.
This applies even when coming from places such as pits, ravines, or precipices.
This explains the two dharmas of maintaining robes and maintaining the alms-bowl.
Within this, there are two parts;
first, it explains maintaining the robes.

The following clarifies the practice of holding the alms-bowl.
Furthermore, it begins with "one should consume food and drink in due order" and continues down to "one should not eat by biting off pieces."
This clarifies the four dharmas of eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting;
herein they are explained collectively rather than individually,
so one should reflect upon them according to the text.
Furthermore, from the time of returning from the house of a donor to one’s own dwelling during the latter part of the day or night,
until the time for periodic pauses to practice walking meditation,
one should clearly maintain the two dharmas of abiding and walking.
Furthermore, from "in this way, in one's own place of residence, in one's own courtyard,
in one's own room" down to "sleeping and resting in accordance with the Dharma," the first section clarifies the two practices of sitting and reclining.
Within this, there are two parts.
The first clarifies sitting, dwelling, and reclining, from the passage beginning with "In this way, regarding oneself...
down to "...and sits in quietude."
The above clarifies sitting;
the following clarifies lying down.
Furthermore, this applies to the daytime portion as well as the initial portion of the night and thereafter.
From the time when [the Buddha] practiced seclusion and silent meditation for the sake of cultivation and abandonment,
he briefly elucidated the two dharmas of speech and silence.
Within this, there are two parts.
First, speech;
second, silence.
This may be understood according to the text.
When contemplating the Dharma,
from the time one begins its uninterrupted and earnest cultivation until its thorough mastery,
the matters of speech and silence are extensively elucidated.
The textual passage also consists of two parts, which may be understood by referring to the above.
Next, it continues with the section beginning "Furthermore, at the time of the stage of Extreme Heat... and so forth.
From "until all [faults] have been completely eliminated" onwards,
it explains the cultivation of exertion (*vyāyāma*).
Furthermore, from "regarding the category of the wholesome (*kuśalapakṣa*) where one has not yet previously entered" onwards, [it explains the remaining stages].
Thus, up to this point, it is called "dwelling in right mindfulness.
Herein, the intent is to clarify that prior to full maturation, one is merely said to possess "clear comprehension" (*saṃprajanya*);
from the point of its accomplishment onward, it is called "dwelling in clear comprehension."
Examine this according to the text;
this was not composed by the Master himself.
Furthermore, one should understand that within this passage, from "if one goes" (*yadi gacchet*) onwards...
The two dharmas of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) and conduct (*caryā*) subsume all the preceding categories;
these are the dharmas that perform the subsumption.
It is not that which precedes movement that is called "abiding. That which abides while performing an action is called "movement";
it is not that which abides while stationary that is called "movement."
The term "abiding" (sthiti) refers to the state of abiding;
it is not the same as the "abiding" mentioned previously.
Therefore, there is no contradiction in its encompassing of phenomena.
Regarding the treatise’s statement that mental action (*manas-karman*) occurs when one is lying down, silent, or standing:
herein, lying down should properly be included within bodily action (*kāya-karman*).
However, because volition (*cetanā*) directed toward the clear signs (*nimitta*) arises first at the time of lying down, it is designated as mental action.
That which is not lying down is the mind.
According to the treatise, there are four types of action during the states of walking, standing, and sitting;
right mindfulness constitutes one of them.
Heedfulness is one;
performing what ought to be done is one;
being blameless in both the present and the future is one.
The first consists of accumulating the provisions for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained;
now, these twenty kinds of perception are assigned according to the text as found in the twenty-fifth fascicle.
As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
the treatise further attests that while three fruits are mentioned,
the fourth fruit is not explicitly named because the supernormal power of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) is already accomplished within the fourth fruit.
These are discussed collectively here, though not individually.
Regarding the three types of supernormal transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*):
first, the supernormal transformation of psychic power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
First is the supernormal power of the body;
second is the supernormal power of declaration,
which is the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others.
Because it discerns and declares the minds of others,
it is the third path of teaching; that is,
the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).
This may be called the three types of action (*trividha-karman*).
As explained in the first fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*,
the treatise analyzes instruction (*avavāda*) and admonition (*anuśāsana*).
It differs from other sections;
namely, the four types of instructional activity.
This is explained here in general terms.
The remainder shall be discussed separately.
There is no contradiction regarding the four types of instruction and so forth;
this is as explained in the clarification of the meaning of the four instructions.
Regarding the statement,
"The treatise proclaims that which is associated, accompanied by auxiliaries, and conducive to purity":
"Associated" means being in accordance with reason.
The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is precisely this wisdom.
The accompanying factors (*sahāya*) are the simultaneous mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
The conforming factors (*anuloma*) are the contaminated preparatory wisdom (*sāsrava-prayoga-jñāna*).
Because it accords with right knowledge, it is pure and sublime;

it is the avoidance of turbid and confused speech. That which is "useful" refers to speech that is consistent with and not contrary to the attainment of *nirvāṇa*. It should conform to names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and so forth.
Regarding all languages, the treatise states that they are matured by these eight factors; this refers to the following passage:
"Furthermore, this discourse should be delivered at the appropriate time," and so forth.
Alternatively, regarding the first interpretation: if one can admonish and raise [the issue], the eight [factors] therein constitute the question.
The *Śāstra* says: "One should know that it is by virtue of these causes and conditions"—this refers to the four [factors] immediately preceding, as indicated by the word "and" (*yǒu zì*).
The Commentary states: "A true person" (sappurisa) refers to those on the four paths and those who have attained the fruits.
This refers to the four fruits. What is meant by "hearing and reflecting upon the sublime Dharma"?
It refers to the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Below this, the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) will be explained in detail.

5. Contemplating joy while breathing in and out;

these four observe feeling.
Ninth, observing the mind entering and exiting with the breath.

fourteenth is the contemplation of relinquishment as the cessation.
The fifteenth is the contemplation of the cessation of desire for inhalation and exhalation;
the sixteenth is the contemplation of the extinction of inhalation and exhalation, etc.
These are the four methods of contemplative practice.
Regarding the fourfold explanation of the body in the treatise,
the fourth section provides a further explanation of the practice of calming bodily formations (*kāyasaṃskāra*).
Bodily formations refer to inhalation and exhalation.
To cause these to be stilled and eliminated is called "stilling bodily formations. Furthermore,
regarding the statement in the treatise, "one who thus clearly understands joy, one who clearly understands pleasure," and so forth:
In this context, regarding the understanding of mental formations (*cittasaṃskāra*):
there may arise deluded thoughts such as "I" and "mine," pride, or the notions "I shall exist" or "I shall not exist," or "I shall have form" or "I shall be formless," and so forth.
These views are called "provisional" because they arise from deluded thoughts.
This is not a view among the sixty-two views. If one were to rely on a view among these sixty-two views,
thinking "I shall exist," this would be the view of eternalism.
There is no scriptural authority stating that those who have realized the Truths give rise to false views, nor that those practicing the Path give rise to the view of permanence.
Therefore, what delusion could possibly manifest here and now?
Furthermore, this [delusion] arises while one is still at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

There is no contradiction because the truths have not yet been seen. If that is so, how can those who have previously seen the truths give rise to views such as eternalism while performing these sixteen superior practices?
The meaning is as follows:
These sixteen modes of practice are also performed by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
As for the previous mention of those who have "seen the truth" (*dṛṣṭasatya*),
that was stated with reference to those who have actually realized the truths.
It is not that it does not apply to ordinary persons;
in fact, it does apply to ordinary persons.
This arising of views such as eternalism is itself superior.

Regarding the statement that "the seven sufferings constitute the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā)":
according to the actual reality,

the remaining six types of suffering are also suffering due to change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*),

Furthermore, there is a passage in that [text]:

the training in concentration (samādhi-śikṣā) is explained solely in reference to the four untainted dhyānas.
How is this known?

The subsequent passage states: "However, it is by relying on dhyāna that one is first able to enter the clear observation of the Noble Truths and the state of rightness and departure from birth; it is not the case that one can accomplish this matter while being entirely devoid of all dhyānas."

This is a further explanation of the previous first interpretation, which states that the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) is designated solely in reference to the four dhyānas. Regarding the second interpretation:

furthermore, all formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) as well as all other meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) are also called the training in concentration.

That is to say, the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and all other remaining contaminated concentrations (*samādhi*) and meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) belonging to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) are all termed the training in concentration (*samādhiśikṣā*).
This includes both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Why is it that the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*) is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*),
while the training in meditative concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) is both tainted and untainted?
The explanation is as follows:
That concentration is also exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
As for the previous mention of "furthermore,

the formless concentrations," this refers to the statement regarding untainted concentrations as well as all other meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*), which are also termed "training in concentration" (*samādhi-śikṣā*).

This refers to the untainted meditative concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*) of the four dhyānas that are capable of inducing the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Regarding the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*), it is currently exclusively untainted;
as for the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*), its meaning is equivalent [to the former], and there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, meditative absorption (samādhi) is both with-outflow (sāsrava) and without-outflow (anāsrava);
wisdom (prajñā) is likewise.
This statement is made in reference to that which is superior, namely the outflow-free state.
There is no impediment to using different ritual implements for the rite;
this accords with what follows below.
If one possesses both precepts and meditative concentration, [one may proceed].
It is not necessarily the case that there is wisdom;
however, where there is wisdom, there must be both ethical discipline and meditative concentration.
Therefore, the former interpretation is superior.
Since one takes the acquisition of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) as the training,
what prevents the training in wisdom from being exclusively untainted, while the trainings in ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) may be both tainted and untainted?
There is no impediment to the fact that their breadth and narrowness are not uniform.
In the lower section of the treatise, among the ten dharmas such as contrariety and so forth, it says:
"In this present context, the intended meaning is to take those obstructive dharmas which hinder the yogic attention (*manaskāra*) that contemplates all phenomena in order to sever [afflictions]."
This should be understood according to the preceding explanation regarding light;
although there are four types,
the intended meaning here refers to the dharma-meaning (dharmārtha).
The second light is able to sever the factors that obstruct the yoga of contemplation (*cintā-yoga*).

As for what the treatise calls "the loss of the meditative object (*yoga-viṣaya*) already attained," this refers precisely to tainted states of meditative concentration (*sāsrava-dhyāna*) and the like.
The treatise states that "disciples who turn back" are so called because they follow those teachings; thus, they are termed "turning.
The treatise further states that there are four types of skillful means (*upāya*).
First, ethical discipline;
second, mindfulness;
third, heedfulness.
Fourth is concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*).
This can be understood according to the text.
Regarding the characteristics of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*) in the treatise:
The phrase "whether produced by humans or produced by non-humans" refers to learning to recognize the signs of distraction;
this is the interpretation of the Dharma Master.
Furthermore, examining the preceding and following passages,
this is not the case; for in the sections concerning "separation from the middle," all state that it is "due to causes and conditions."
Therefore, one should know that these conditions are precisely the causes and conditions for the arising of greed and the like.
Thus, the subsequent passages all state that [things] arise "due to causes and conditions" or "produced by effort."
This arises from the distraction caused by such preparatory application (*prayoga*).

If, however, vipaśyanā is weak, it explains the causes and conditions for non-distraction; as for the characteristics of the subsequent causes and conditions following extremely intense insight (*vipaśyanā*):
One should then cultivate and accumulate the provisions;
regarding the causal conditions for their final fulfillment,
one should understand them by analogy with the lower and middle stages.
In the commentary on "limited and inferior resolve" (*adhimokṣa*), it says:
"That which is called 'limited and inferior intentional understanding' (*manasikāra-adhimokṣa*) with respect to the object (*ālambana*.
This refers to the concluding text [of the preceding section].
It is said that this is because its objects of focus are narrow and limited;
thus, it belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
If it belongs to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), its objects of focus are called vast and immeasurable.
This refers to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The treatise states: "That which functions when what is to be accomplished has been brought to completion" means that when that which is to be accomplished has been perfected, its basis is purified.
Because the basis is purified,
and because it causes the pervasive love and joy to be purified,
it is said that it transforms at the time of accomplishment.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are explained in detail as in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*;
their names are listed among the seven limbs of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), etc.
Regarding the presence of the word "equal" (等) in all [the cases],
the Dharma Master says:
"This 'equal enlightenment' (等覺) refers to the seven limbs of the Tathāgata."
Because they are able to bring about perfect enlightenment,
all [of these] include the word "perfect" (samyak).
If that is so, the same applies to the final eight branches of the Noble Eightfold Path.

The first five stages raise objections that hinder this interpretation. According to another view, the seven factors of enlightenment pertain to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while the eightfold [path] pertains to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);
the path of seeing is signless (*animitta*).
The cultivation of the path is a form of discrimination;
because it involves discrimination, there are signs.
Because it is signless, it is equal, and because it is awakened, it is called "equal awakening."
This meaning is consistent throughout the preceding and following sections.
In the *Śāstra*, while explaining the body within the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*),
it states that the "thirty-five kinds of body" are termed "bodily form" (*kāya-rūpa*).
In this context, "body" (*kāya*) refers to the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
When referring collectively to the bodies of ancestors and the national body,
these specifically denote the bodies of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Because one's ancestors have come down through the generations,
all hope for the sacrifices performed by their descendants;
all harbor this wish.
Because it extends back to one's ancestors,
it is called the "ancestral kingdom.
A detailed explanation is as found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Furthermore, the treatise states: "The intermediate body manifests the lower body.
It also says: "The inferior body and the intermediate body.
What is the distinction between these two intermediate bodies?
The internal body is called the "middle body" in relation to the manifest body;
it is termed the "middle" because it stands between the three categories.
This refers to their relative positioning within the three grades.
The treatise explains twenty-one types of feeling,
as listed above. Regarding the "nine kinds of feeling," the Dharma Master says:
That is, each of the first three positions is itself a triad;
thus there are nine.
These nine encompass all feelings completely.
There is no other separate opening of gates. Furthermore,
it is explained that the "nine types" consist of the three feelings— pleasure and so forth— as three [categories].
1. The three feelings associated with the body and so forth that are pleasant;
2. Feelings associated with the mind that are pleasant;
3. Those accompanied by relish (*sāsvāda*).
Seven are without flavor.
Eight depend on worldly attachment;
nine depend on renunciation.
Combined, they constitute nine;
when expanded, they become ten.
The treatise asks: "What is meant by 'dharma'?"
Therefore, the mind was explained previously;
here, the dharmas are explained.
Regarding "greed, the Vinaya, and so forth":
Vinaya is called "subduing"; that is,
through non-attachment, one subdues attachment.
The *vinaya* of greed is simply non-greed.
The treatise states: "If these various feelings are conducive to nirvana, and so forth."
This refers to all unconditioned phenomena that accord with decisive discernment;
that is, all untainted mental factors,
whether categorized according to the realms.
That is to say, the outflowing phenomena (āsrava) of the three realms are called "the relish of craving" (āsvāda).
As for the outflowing phenomena of the two natures in the higher realms,
they are [comprehended] through the hearing and reflection [wisdom] of the desire realm.
For those who have gone forth from the household life and so on,
it is based on the precepts of renunciation;
as for the dharmas of the two natures belonging to the lower realms.
And the essence of the five types of sensual desire is called "addiction.
The treatise states: "It should be understood that these six mental states all arise during the time of active engagement."
This means that when the first six moments of mind are in the process of active engagement, they are designated as the "time of activity" (*cāra-kāla*);
it is not during the stages of abiding, dwelling, and so forth that they are called the time of activity.
Since this is the case for the time of activity:
The time of abiding should be understood according to what was previously explained.
The time prior to entering meditative concentration is termed the "time of activity."
The phrase "arising while abiding in meditative concentration" refers to the period of abiding.
As for the commentary’s statement, "based on the pure coverings (*pariṣkāra*) and so forth," this explains the fourteen moments of mind during that period of abiding.
Before attaining the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) of meditative concentration,
while abiding in the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
it is called the stage of purifying hindrances (*viśuddhi-āvaraṇa-bhūmi*).
One gives rise to eight kinds of minds;
relying on the uninterrupted path of meditative concentration,
one abandons the fetters of affliction.
Arising from those six minds. Question:
Why are the first eight called "purifying the hindrances" (*śuddhaka-vītarāga*)?
They are the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for meditative concentration (*samādhi*), not the immediate [attainment] (*anantarya*).
The latter six are pure.
Alternatively, one [attainment] is exclusively the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The commentary states:
Furthermore, for example, greed, hatred,
and delusion are the hindrances to be remedied,
while non-greed, subjugation [of hatred], and so forth are the remedies that counteract them.
This refers to the grasping of the six sense-fields.
The three objects to be remedied are the three hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
This occurs at the time of practice.
The following are the eight types of abiding:
whether concise or dispersed.
"Concise" refers to the characteristic of cessation (*śamatha*).
"Scattering" refers to distraction.
"Sinking" or "lifting up"—
the former is dullness (*styāna*).
To raise is to raise the characteristic;
if there is agitation, one is separated from agitation;
agitation is itself restlessness.
Regarding whether one is at peace or not at peace:
that which is called "remorse" when it pertains to what was poorly done is termed "not at peace," while that which pertains to what was well done is termed "at peace."
Furthermore, doubt is not quiescence;
that which is definitive is called quiescence.
Moreover, the preceding path of antidote, taken together, is termed quiescence.
Taken together with what was previously treated as "non-quiescence," each has its own specific antidote;
this is called the stage of purifying the hindrances (*nīvaraṇaviśuddhibhūmi*).
This refers to the five hindrances;
as for the eighteen types that follow,
they are described in terms of their general characteristics.
There is nothing else to be remedied;
to attain the latter six periods,
one must necessarily have attained the former.

Only after the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) have been purified can one enter the fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*). If that is so, since the object to be overcome (*pratipakṣya*) and its antidote (*pratipakṣa*) must necessarily be simultaneous, why are the hindrances considered the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*)?
"Concentration is the uninterrupted path.
The meaning is as follows:
for instance, it refers to the aforementioned remedial paths such as those of tranquility (*śamatha*).
If it is the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
the various hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are suppressed but not permanently severed;
furthermore, the preceding stage that is capable of suppressing them constitutes the path of preparation.
The cessation of that which is to be abandoned occurs simultaneously with the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and is severed by that path of immediate succession;
for it is only when the antidote arises that the abandonment of the object to be countered occurs.
The treatise states: "Having attained liberation from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), one enters the fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*).
Within this path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantaryamārga*), the non-concentrated mind is precisely that which is to be overcome."
Because the first eight have distinct antidotes,
they involve the mind of analytical observation during the path of preparation;
the subsequent path of uninterrupted transition involves observation of the general characteristics.
Some say it refers to the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Furthermore, it does not necessarily clarify the eight moments of mind preceding the path of uninterrupted realization, which constitute the stage of skillful means (*upāya*).
Those that are to be remedied are all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
There are also specific objects to be remedied by the latter six types [of antidotes].
Although this is not the removal of hindrances (*āvaraṇa*),
it is a general severance of all afflictions (*kleśa*);
such is the sequential order of the immediate application (*anantarya-prayoga*).
The eight [applications of mindfulness] merely suppress the afflictions;
they are not the "uninterrupted" path.
This is discussed in the section on the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) within the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.

If it is said that "the thorough knowledge of the self-nature, causes, defects, and remedies of all defiled phenomena as they truly are is the application of mindfulness to phenomena," this should be compared with the preceding text.
There is no separate interpretation of these four types;
there is only their intrinsic nature, their defects, and their remedies,
with no other causes or conditions.
If one follows the previous citation,
the obscurations (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth that are to be remedied are termed its "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
The preceding statement spoke of knowing that there are fetters (*saṃyojana*) within the sense-sphere of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*).
Because faults are designated as "faults," the preceding path that remedies them is called the "antidote.
Furthermore, there is no separate textual passage providing the causal conditions for this interpretation.
If the meaning is established, there is no impediment;
that is to say, during the six stages of practice,
the three unwholesome roots are termed the causes and conditions of all afflictions.
The various delusions arise from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, the seeds of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) themselves are called causes and conditions.
Moreover, by what means [do they arise]?
Conditioned by which bases does the self-nature arise? That is called the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, depending on the eye up to mental attention (*manasikāra*), the arising of afflictions with respect to the eye and so forth is called the causal condition.
In the initial explanation of the foundations of mindfulness regarding feelings, mind, and dharmas within this treatise,
the intended meaning here is:
if one generates the foundations of mindfulness of feelings, mind, and dharmas by taking the internal body as their object.
Taking these feelings, mind, and mental factors as objects is called the internal contemplation of feelings, mind, and mental factors.
The same applies to the external and so forth.
In this context, regarding the body as an object,
there is no distinction made between the primary elements (bhūta) and the derived elements (bhautika), such that it takes both as its collective object;
however, in the fourth lower stage, it takes only the primary elements and not the derived elements.
Therefore, they are distinguished.
In the fifth treatise, in the explanation of the cultivation of the contemplation of the body, it says:
"If one takes as an object the form of a body that was once conscious but is now unconscious, regarding its past state of being conscious, and so forth."
The meaning here is this:
when one clearly perceives a corpse, it had once possessed consciousness in the past;
this present corpse is termed "external."
When consciousness is present, it is called "internal.
Taking as its object the existing body with consciousness and the future body without consciousness—
internal and external are likewise so.
Because there is consciousness in the present and no consciousness in the future,
there is the similarity of dharmatā and the equality of dharmatā.
They are of one characteristic and without difference;
this applies even to the past.
This is from the sixth explanation.
It is said that if one takes one's own intermediate body as the object of focus,
then "one's own internal body" is what is meant by "intermediate body";
it refers precisely to one's own internal intermediate body.
In the section on the refutation of the four inversions,
explaining the meaning of the impurity of the body,
it speaks of the four charnel grounds associated with impurity.
In the second section of the treatise,
"Explaining Perversions," regarding the statement "experiencing suffering and pleasure," this is based on the explanation in the subsequent section on "Covering."

It is said that the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) is established because those who encounter [the teaching] are deluded regarding the self as a substantial entity within the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
they thus conceive of this very mind as the self.
This is contrary to the first [position].
As explained in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the First Volume of the Abhidharma),
in the section explaining the meaning of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
it states that the two factors of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It is the same as in the Abhidharma.
In the Hīnayāna, mindfulness alone is taken as its intrinsic nature;
now, in the Mahāyāna, both dharmas are included.
It constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Since all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) serve as its accompanying entities (*sahāya*),
they are said to be "intermingled" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*).
The twenty-ninth fascicle of the treatise states: "What are called all wholesome dharmas?
That is to say, 'if they are the antidotes to those [unwholesome factors],' etc.
This first phrase refers to the general definition.
The first two phrases are the general [statement], while the latter two phrases are the specific [explanation].
Regarding the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "capable of treating that," it refers specifically to that which was mentioned in the specific [explanation].
This refers to those hindrances and fetters.
Furthermore, while the preceding [section] explained unwholesome dharmas,
the present [section] concerns their respective antidotes.
The latter two phrases specifically identify the remedies,
while the first phrase provides the general overview.
This is explained within the treatise’s discussion on "exertion" (*pragraha*).
If it is said that [the mind] takes as its object past things that are not currently perceived and present things that are currently perceived,
why is the future not mentioned?
Furthermore, the past is not currently perceived.
That which has already arisen and that which has not yet arisen are both not directly perceived;
thus they may be said to be "not directly perceived.
There exist present phenomena that have not yet arisen and are not directly perceived.
What is meant by "the present" being called "directly perceived"?
The meaning is as follows:
that which exists in the past and present, yet has not [yet] arisen.
Because all [factors] exist in the future,
one does not explicitly mention the future;
by citing the past and present, the meaning of the future is already implied.
If one gives rise to a yet-to-be-arisen dharma by taking a presently perceived object as its condition,
the apprehension of that object is termed "presently perceived."
It is not that dharmas which are neither present nor yet arisen are called "directly perceived.

Regarding the statement in the treatise that [cognition] arises solely through the power of conceptualization and not through the power of an objective realm, this refers to those who, while dwelling in the present, contemplate the past and so forth.
This means not proceeding toward objects,
having no proceeding toward objects,
but rather taking the past and future as its conditions; therefore, it is called "abiding."
Regarding "the power of discrimination and the power of the object":
this means that engaging with an object is called "activity.
When the power of an object of unwholesome dharmas arises, [it is likewise so].
Because there must necessarily be conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*),
this partial phrase [of yours] does not hold;
conceptual discrimination is itself the mind.
The phrase "and [the arising] of unwholesome [states], etc.
constitutes the first partial statement;
it refers specifically to the arising [of such states] in the past and future.
The second "concurrent" phrase arises regarding present objects;
it is the opposite of the first [phrase], which was explained as the exertion of diligence through application.
The treatise states: "The restraint that abandons."
Discipline (*saṃvara*) is called "preventing transgression" because it prevents already arisen evil from increasing;
as stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*.
Furthermore, the precepts are well-purified through ten causes and conditions,
as stated in the preceding twenty fascicles; namely,
there are ten factors conducive to training (*śikṣānulomika-dharma*).
First, being free from the company of women;
second, being free from attachment;
third, being free from indolence.
Fourth, being free from the view of a self;
fifth, being free from craving for the flavors of edible food;
sixth, being free from craving for discursive speech.
Seventh, one is free from the eleven faults.
Eighth, one is free from the savoring of meditative absorption.
Ninth, one is free from distraction.
Tenth is patience.
The essence of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) is concentration;
they are designated by their causes, namely desire and so forth.
Furthermore, concentration is the "foot" for supernormal powers;
therefore, it is called a "basis of supernormal power" (*ṛddhipāda*). Moreover, concentration itself is termed "supernormal" (*ṛddhi*).
These four are the bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*).
The "spiritual power of the mind" (*cittarddhipāda*) is the sovereign of the mind (*cittarāja*).
The Dharma Master says:
Furthermore, it may also be a fixed [position],
as stated in the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*.

It is said that by the predominant power of these four samādhis, one has already distanced oneself from the envelopments (paryavasthāna) and further brings about the permanent destruction of all evil and unwholesome dharmas. At the time of this correct cultivation, there are eight applications of abandonment (prahāṇasaṃskāra); they function with distinctions for the sake of permanently destroying the latent tendencies (anuśaya), and for the sake of attaining the perfection of samādhi. Thus it is stated.
This is raised to clarify the basis for the eight formative forces of abandonment (*aṣṭau prahāṇasaṃskārāḥ*).
These eight formative forces were formerly known as the "eight provisions for action" (*aṣṭau karmasambhārāḥ*).
To clarify the intended meaning, two gates are opened:
first, for the severance of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
second, for the perfection of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This accords with the subsequent explanation of the two types of factors that can sever the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Therefore, the following text states: "By means of two causes and conditions, one analytically understands the abandonment of the latent dispositions;
namely, by means of direct perception and reflection."
And because of the relinquishing of what is not directly perceived,
one is able to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) through these causes and conditions.
This should be understood by analogy with the explanation of "exertion" (*pragraha*) at the beginning of this fascicle.
It is said that if one takes past or future objects as conditions,
it is called "conditioning what is not presently visible"; if one takes present objects as conditions, [it is called "conditioning what is presently visible"].
It is called "conditioned by what is presently perceived," which means that thought considers only the present and relinquishes objects belonging to the past or future.
If that is so, why does the explanation regarding equanimity state:
"It refers to the equality of mind that accords with all evils throughout the three periods of past, future, and present"?
Furthermore, let us divide volition (*cetanā*) into one lifetime and relinquishment (*tyāga*) into two lifetimes;
the reality of this is as stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Abhidharma* (*Abhidharmapitaka*).
The antidote consists of volition and equanimity;
because these enable one to distance oneself from even those lethargy and excitement that have already arisen,
they thus pertain to the abandonment of [defilements] across the three periods of time.

Since the two factors of reflection (*vitarka*) and relinquishment (*praśrabdhi*) are called the abandonment of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the remaining six [factors] should be understood accordingly as the perfection of samādhi.

Furthermore, the subsequent text states: "If these eight types of exertions (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*) now mentioned are fully accomplished for the sake of permanently abandoning all latent tendencies, they are collectively termed 'desire-samādhi' (*chanda-samādhi*)."
Examining this general text,
it appears that all eight [types] possess both functions,
and furthermore, they subsume the four yogas.
Because all four yogas sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, volition (*cetanā*) is able to initiate body and speech,
giving rise to wholesome bodily and vocal karma.
One ceases evil physical and verbal actions.
Since body and speech are form (*rūpa*), volition (*cetanā*) is designated by way of that form; thus, volition is directly perceived.
Equanimity (upekṣā) exists solely in the mental faculty;
it is not the same as volition (cetanā).
Therefore, it is called "equanimity that is not directly perceived" (aparokṣopekṣā).
It is not necessarily the same as the text at the beginning of this fascicle.
Those eight formative forces of abandonment (*aṣṭau prahāṇasaṃskārāḥ*) are [discussed] in fascicle twenty-eight.
The four yogas can sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
these are desire, diligence, faith, and skillful means.
Although the Abhidharma explains four types of inclusion (*saṃgraha*), [the four yogas] encompass them.
Yet they are entirely different and cannot be reconciled;
such is the sequence herein.
That which differs from the four yogas among the twenty-eight is that,
herein, the eight stages arise sequentially according to their textual order.
Among those four yogas, faith is the first;
this is likewise the case in the Abhidharma.
Therefore, that treatise states:
Faith is the cause of desire.
This means that when one exerts diligence, one does not depart from faith;
faith and mindfulness are present at the outset.
Because there is faith in the Buddha and so forth,
desire and other [mental states] subsequently arise;
now, because one does not depart from that faith, [desire arises].
Therefore, faith is mentioned last;
this is consistent with the text of the Abhidharma itself,
as it follows the sequence of arising explained in the *Catuḥyoga*.
Therefore, faith is primary.
In the discussion concerning the causes and conditions for attaining the name "basis of supernormal power" (*ṛddhipāda*),
it is said that they are called "bases of supernormal power" because one is able to reach [the goal] by means of them.
The ability to go and return, and so forth, is termed the supernormal power (ṛddhi-pāda);
it is the fruit of the meditative absorption (samādhi) realm,
with desire and other factors serving as its causes.
Because one is able to attain this supernormal power of meditative concentration,
it is called "supernormal power" (ṛddhipāda).
This is explained in the treatise within the section on the five faculties (pañcendriya).

Regarding the statement, "As for the wisdom that can give rise only to supramundane dharmas as its predominant condition (*adhipati*)," this explains the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) therein; here,
the "predominant condition" is the faculty.
Faith has two types of predominance:
first, it can give rise to supramundane dharmas,
thereby acting as a predominant condition.
The two [faculties] can successively produce subsequent dharmas;
they are called "faculties" (indriya) because they act as predominant conditions (adhipati).
The first four possess both meanings.
Therefore, while diligence and the others previously functioned as preparatory practices,
wisdom now has but a single meaning:
it serves as the predominant condition solely for the arising of supramundane dharmas.
There is no capacity for successive stages to give rise to subsequent meanings.
The treatise states: "It should be understood that herein, the faculty of concentration and the power of concentration are precisely the four dhyānas...
up to the realization of the fruit of non-returner, and so forth."
Among these, the first two fruits are attained only through the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage];
proceeding from there in sequence, one reaches the fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Having attained the four dhyānas and generated supernormal powers (abhijñā),
they are mentioned specifically for this reason.
The fourth fruit is not mentioned because it is not sequential and because it is implied by its shadow.
Furthermore, because it is stated briefly,
among the four dhyānas, supernormal powers are produced;
thus, "as one wishes" is mentioned, while other concentrations are not.

The Commentary states: "By means of precisely these faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*), through gradual cultivation and so forth, one is able to give rise to the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) in their superior, middling, and inferior grades.
Regarding the faculties and powers herein, they are as explained in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*.
The faculties (*indriya*) are present in the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*);
the powers (*bala*) are present in the two subsequent stages.
It is precisely for this reason that it is now said: "by means of these faculties and powers."
Regarding those who have produced the stages leading to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*):
these faculties and powers are the specific [factors],
while the stages leading to penetration are the general [category].
Because the particular gives rise to the universal,
it is called "arising"; that is,
they occur simultaneously rather than at different times.
This is because that which arises before and after is termed "initiation.
There are those who wish to maintain that there is untainted [wisdom] prior to the path of seeing;
this will be addressed in the passage immediately following in the treatise.
Since supramundane, untainted noble dharmas arise immediately thereafter by the power of the faculties,
one knows that what precedes this is tainted;
it cannot be called untainted.

The Treatise says: "If one seeks clothing, food, drink, and so forth, up to the requisites for maintaining the body, at the time of seeking—this is what is sought at the time of seeking. "Whether going or returning," and so on.
Even when abiding, this is what is performed during the time of abiding;
it is the opposite of the twenty-two [aspects].
This may be verified by the *Śāstra*, which states:

"By the predominant power of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one attains right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) comprised of nine types of non-erroneous modes of activity; the mental abiding that is encompassed by these nine types of modes of activity is called right mindfulness and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*)."
The meaning here is that,
with the four foundations of mindfulness as the cause,
nine kinds of mindfulness arise simultaneously with the concentrated mind.
The nine kinds of mindfulness are identical to the nine kinds of mindfulness that abide in equipoise and are associated with meditative concentration;
in all nine cases,
they take meditative concentration as their auxiliary companion.
Concentration is also of nine kinds.
It takes right mindfulness as its primary factor for inclusion;
those that serve as its auxiliaries are not included.
In this context, mindfulness subsumes the opposites,
as explained in the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* regarding the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
It is said that only those among the gods who are destined to take rebirth do so;
such a person, having resided in the heavens for one interval,
takes one existence among human beings.
One who does not return to be born again in the heavens is also called an "Anāgāmin" (Non-returner). Here,
the practice is based on the human realm.
This is named after its fruit, for at the stage of the cause, it is not yet called "non-returner.
The treatise states: "Furthermore, herein [are included] greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and so forth."
Furthermore, regarding those who diligently apply themselves through the power of differentiating their objects of focus,
the intent here concerns persons characterized by attachment, aversion, ignorance, and so forth.
This has an antidote;
first, in the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana*),
concentration arises by the power of the distinctions among the objects of focus (*ālambana*).
For one who follows the practice of greed,
the mind dwells in tranquility only after practicing the contemplation of impurity with diligent cultivation.
Those who practice through the balanced temperament possess all [faculties];
according to their specific conduct,
they are able to practice them all.
As stated in the treatise:
"Just as one who practices according to their specific disposition has their mind abide within the five objects of stabilization (pañca-viṣkambhanā-citta)."
It is not that his conduct is pure.
Some say it also involves severing delusions, but this is incorrect.
According to the old exegesis, one practices the contemplation of each breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*) to eliminate the two categories of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Now, with the exception of *vitarka* (applied thought), it is said that they "only" consist of the activity of *vicāra* (sustained thought);
this does not exclude *vicāra*. Question: Why is this so?
Why is this? Because it is not eliminated;
for one investigates with careful attention when explaining.
Vitarka then leads to distraction;
therefore, it is said that one must eliminate vitarka.
This is explained in the treatise within the section on the characteristics of persons with balanced temperaments (*samabhāga*) and others.
It is said that while those who act out of greed possess all the various modes of conduct, those who act from a balanced temperament (sāmya-carita) do not excel them;
thus, when a person of balanced temperament encounters conditions, they immediately give rise to greed and are then designated as one who acts out of greed.
It is the same for those of equal parts (samabhāga):
whenever they encounter conditions, greed and so forth arise;
such a person is called one who acts out of greed (rāgacarita).
It is similar to [the obstruction of] greed and so forth.
In the commentary on the obstruction of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*), it says: "As for the place of birth..."
This refers to the places where [the noble path] arises; in those places, the noble path does not arise.
That is to say, in the three miserable destinies (*durgati*), the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) arises.
That is, the maturation of evil arises in those places.
It is not the basis for the noble path (*āryamārga*).
In the commentary on the initial purity (*ādipariśuddhi*), it says:
"One should understand, as previously explained, that the precepts are well-purified by means of ten causes and conditions."
As for the twenty-eight [types of persons], they accord with those dharmas by means of ten dharmas.
First is the avoidance of the mother’s domain and so forth,
as previously explained.
Those śramaṇas who live by the Way sustain their lives through the Way;
thus they are called "those who live by the Way."

The treatise states: "If there were no Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas for the sake of awakening, nor even Śrāvakas who perpetually uphold the Tripiṭaka, they could not be called 'Śramaṇas who preach the Path.'"
This discussion is for the time being based on the case of śrāvakas when no Buddhas or bodhisattvas are present.
If Buddhas or bodhisattvas were present,
this assembly of śrāvakas would instead be called the "Superior Path."
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called "Śramaṇas who preach the Path.
Now, in the absence of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
the Śrāvakas are called "preachers of the Path."
It is for the sake of ensuring that the eye of the True Dharma is not severed from its seed.
In the commentary on the "Śramaṇas who destroy the Path," it says:
"Because they destroy the very root of the original right path, etc."
The meaning here is as follows:
ethical discipline is the root of the Noble Path;
because one now violates ethical discipline, it is called "destroying the root of the path."
The treatise states: "The World-Honored One, relying on that, made such a statement as far as 'the external teachings of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are empty and non-existent,' and so forth.
The meaning herein is as follows.
The Blessed One, relying on the true teaching, spoke thus regarding the four kinds of śrāvakas.
He made this statement:
There are external teachings such as those of the śramaṇas;
these are false teachings that even destroy the Path.
Furthermore, there is nothing [of substance] therein;
for it is only by receiving the true precepts that their destruction occurs.
Since those [precepts] are, in fact, false precepts.
Regarding the establishment of the path that is both destructible and indestructible,
it is explained in the *Brahmaṇaparīkṣā* (Examination of the Brahmins):

"Those called 'Brahmins by designation' refer to those in the world who are designated as 'Brahmins' through conventional speech based on conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and common designation (*samājñā*)."
Regarding this, there is an explanation:
it is like a kṣatriya whom his parents have given the provisional designation "brāhmaṇa."
Although his physical substance is that of a kṣatriya,
he is designated by the name "brāhmaṇa" because of his conception;
furthermore, it is due to this conception.
Regarding those who are designated by such names and concepts:
it refers to those in the world who, based on these common perceptions and designations, are called "brāhmaṇas.
This refers to the third type, the truly virtuous brāhmaṇa.
The Brahmin named Jñātiputra is so called because he has purified his will;
this has already been explained as before.
In the commentary on the explanation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), it states:
"Those who sever the holy life refer to the noble ones who have attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) and so forth.
Why, in this context, are the first two fruits not explained?
Furthermore, regarding the second holy life (*brahmacarya*) mentioned previously,
why is there no discussion of being free from desire for the form and formless realms?
The meaning is that it does not refer to the first two fruits of the path.
Taking as the basis the complete abandonment of desire for the realm of desire,
one who has temporarily severed [desire] through the holy life (brahmacarya) accomplishes temporary holy life.
It is because it refers specifically to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, for what reason was it not stated in the preceding second [section] that "desire" refers to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth?
This shadow reveals [the meaning].
By analogy, one should understand that this applies to Arhats and those who have attained the fruit of Non-returner;
it should be known that the mundane path is also discussed in contrast to these.
One should say that it is the abandonment of desire for both the form and formless realms.
This shadow-like manifestation of the meaning is not contradictory. As for the term "ultimate" (*atyanta*):
it is called ultimate because the seeds [of defilement] have been severed by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
The fruit of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is not called "ultimate.
In the commentary on the term *bhikṣu*, it says:
"Regarding 'self-proclaiming' and so forth..."
The first refers to those who constantly beg for alms and so forth;
these are those who call themselves bhikṣus while being violators of the precepts— those known as "bhikṣus by name and concept" (saṃjñā-bhikṣu).
That is to say, one who has not yet received the precepts,
but possesses only the conceptual designation of being a bhikṣu,
yet does not yet possess the precepts.
The treatise states: "To know yoga well is to know skillful means well.
This is because one knows that practice accords with principle;
through the wisdom of such practice, one is able to be in accord with the fruit.
Therefore, it is known as the "expedient means" (*upāya*), which is also termed "concordance" (*yoga*).
The treatise states: "If there are any individuals whose characteristics are not yet matured, and so forth."
Regarding the statement, "Even if the second faculty has matured, one does not yet skillfully know the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and so forth," what is the difference between these two?
The meaning is as follows:
The former has not planted roots of goodness at all;
the second, although having planted them to some small extent,
differs in that it lacks skillful means.
The treatise states: "Due to three causes and conditions, emptiness has no fruit;
that is to say, it is the fruit of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), not a worldly fruit."
How is this known?
It is stated below that although one has attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is no instruction (*avavāda*).
Because the true instruction is not followed, the untainted [state] (*anāsrava*) does not arise.
Therefore, emptiness has no fruit.
This is the third section of the thirtieth fascicle;
it begins with one verse.
Within this, there are two main points:
first, the enumeration of three general categories;
second, [the discussion] within the third category.
This is further divided into five sections.
Now, these four lines of the verse consist of twenty characters;
the first eight characters enumerate the three general categories.
The twelve characters below are separately divided into five parts:
"going to offer congratulations and inquire" constitutes one;
"seeking out" is the second.
It is established as the third [category]. Within this establishment, it is said that there are five gates:
guarding and nurturing is the first;
renunciation is the second.
The nature of the object is the third;
the purification of obstacles is the fourth;
and the cultivation of mental attention is the fifth—according to the prose section below.
This is divided into three parts: first, from "If one cherishes oneself" down to the conclusion of the explanation of the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), it is called "going to offer greetings.
Second, from "Having thus maintained right mindfulness after leaving the teacher's presence," and so forth.
The section beginning with "Regarding the second, seeking" clarifies the inquiry;

the section beginning with "When about to inquire" clarifies the method of inquiry; and the section beginning with "Having thus inquired and being well-versed in yoga" clarifies the third, the formal establishment.
To clarify the formal establishment [of the ritual],
first the method for the master to establish the disciple is clarified. Below the section on "The Yogin," the formal establishment of the ritual method is clarified.
The Treatise says:
Having asked in this manner, if the other should respond accordingly, one must subsequently seek out the four bases through four causes and conditions.
First, one seeks out the four bases by means of the first cause and condition.
For those of sharp faculties,
one further establishes the three lower causes and conditions to seek out the four locations.
For those of dull faculties, it is further explained: "How is this known?
Below this, three causal conditions for its arising are presented, which emerge spontaneously from within the search for the four locations.
Therefore, in the logical analysis and verification of the lineages (gotra) of the three vehicles,
it is not stated that those who shed tears and so forth upon hearing the Dharma of the three vehicles [possess such a lineage].
This discussion is based, for the time being, on those of determinate nature;
it is examined within the context of practice.
Regarding the statement, "If there is one whose conduct is characterized by desire, and they hear skillful words and discourses being spoken for them,
they will immediately give rise to the most supreme, pure love and delight," the intended meaning here is as follows:
Those whose temperament is dominated by greed, being greedy for wealth and pleasure,
develop the most supreme pure faith and so forth upon hearing discourses on how the Buddha-fields are composed of the seven precious jewels and are pure and sublime.
External objects of desire are not called "pure and sublime," because they cannot give rise to the most supreme pure faith.
Furthermore, desire and so forth are separately identified as the grasping of craving.
In the commentary on delusion (*moha*), it says:
"As it was explained for those of dull faculties, the same applies to the manifestation of their conduct."
That is to say, for those of dull faculties,
coarse teachings are expounded;
they must exert effort in their search before they can understand them.
This person of deluded conduct,
upon hearing such expressions as "nirvāṇa," experiences fear regarding transformation and decay.
It is said that one does not feel fear even when subsequently given false instruction;
it is like a person of dull faculties who only understands after exerting great effort.
Treatise.

Regarding the statement, "Having correctly sought by means of four causes and conditions in four locations, one again [seeks] appropriately in five locations," the following clarifies the five gates within the section on establishment (*vyavasthāna*).

The "cultivation and protection of meditative concentration and so forth" refers to those items listed in the first verse. What is meant by "cultivation and protection"? This refers to the first [point].
What is meant by "separation"? [This refers to the second point.]
This is the second [section]. What is one-pointedness of mind?
This is the third.
In this context, it is explained as being associated with blameless joy (*prīti*).

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, by means of that mindfulness, one dwells in extreme stability without defilement toward the object of focus, proceeding in association with the maturity of the path and pliancy," this is the intended meaning here.
Because it can eliminate defilements,
one attains the path that brings about ultimate peace and security.
Because it is associated with a state that is inherently pleasant and agreeable, it is called "faultless.
This is explained in the treatise regarding the nine stages of mental abiding (*navākārā cittasthiti*).
It is not necessarily that this is the "centered mind";
it is simply that abiding in a single object is what constitutes it.
This is because, from the very beginning, one withdraws the mind and so forth.
Because it does not necessarily entail the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
what was previously described as belonging to the category of *śamatha* is not,
in every case, *śamatha* itself.
As it is summarized in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*:
In the commentary on the section concerning tranquility (*śamatha*), it says:

"That is to say, various unwholesome discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) such as desire, ill-will, and cruelty, as well as the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), cause the mind to be disturbed."
This is because one generates revulsion by first citing these faults; thus,
it speaks of the "hindrance of sensual desire" and so forth,
as well as the various secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*, Chapter Seven: "Whatever are afflictions (*kleśa*) are all secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
even the root delusions (*mūlakleśa*) are secondary afflictions."
There are secondary afflictions that are not primary afflictions;
these refer to the twenty types of derivative afflictions,
which arise only in dependence upon others.
This is not the fundamental [affliction],
because greed and the others arise in dependence upon other factors.
These are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
In the treatise’s explanation of how these nine are subsumed within the six types of power, it states:
"The first [power] arises from the two powers of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*), through repeated hearing and repeated reflection, and so forth."
Up to and including being thoroughly and universally established therein.
Among these, if it is the first [stage],
it is by means of the two powers of hearing and so forth.
That is to say: first, internal abiding;
second, even abiding;
third and fourth, settled abiding and close abiding.
By the power of recollection—
which is subsumed within the first two powers among the two types of textual passages—
it is further stated: "And one thoroughly abides in this very continuity through the application of means and the application of purification."
This seems to also include the third stage of abiding (*anusthāna*).
It is clear that the previous explanation of abiding also occurs below the first two powers.
Regarding how the third and fourth [powers] are identical in their power of recollection,
the commentary states:
"In reality, the third is abiding."
This is subsumed under the first two powers.
