Regarding the terms "abiding" (*sthiti*) and "closely abiding" (*upasthiti*) mentioned within the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*),
this is the intended meaning here.
One abides in close placement (*upasthāna*) by the power of mindfulness;
it is not that both the power of mindfulness and the state of close placement are the two factors [of abiding],
but rather it is simply the single factor of close placement itself.
This is the power of mindfulness. Furthermore, the treatise explains:
"In the beginning, it arises through two powers: hearing and reflection.
Thus, internal abiding is the first and is singular.
Internal abiding and equal abiding constitute the first two powers;
that which is stable abiding is the power of mindfulness.
As it was stated previously that "disciplined" (*dam pa*) and "calm" (*zhi ba*) refer to two types of concentration (*samādhi*),
so too the present mention of "abiding" (*gnas pa*) and "closely abiding" (*nye bar gnas pa*) should be understood as likewise encompassing these two types.

This is not understood as being established within the state of close abiding (*upasthāna*). If so, why does it say, "and precisely within this continuum, through the means of purification and so forth, one dwells in universal stability"?
The commentary states: This abiding encompasses three powers.
If contemplation has not yet been perfected, it is subsumed under the first two powers.
If the practice of contemplation is accomplished,
it is gathered through the power of mindfulness;
for when one first records the mind within, at that time—
Binding is the means for the continuity and clarification [of the mind];
furthermore, it is not yet the attainment of stable abiding.
This is the initial cultivation of the mind through the contemplation of abiding.
Subsequently, one abides through the power of mindfulness;
once observation is accomplished, there is the power of mindfulness.
Furthermore, regarding the expression "equally and universally abiding":
This refers merely to abiding in equanimity as a single category;
it does not mean abiding in the sense of grasping,
because equanimity pervades all coarse and agitated states of mind.
It is established as pervasive.
One does not take "abiding" (sthiti) as the first two powers.
The treatise states: "The four kinds of vipaśyanā, which comprise wisdom through the three gates and six matters."
Each of these types of wisdom penetrates the three gates and six matters. In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*,
within the section explaining the investigation of principles (*yukti-paryeṣaṇā*),
it explains the principle of nature (*dharmatā-yukti*).
Regarding the phrases "establishing the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as inconceivable," "the nature of phenomena abiding," and so forth:
just as by virtue of being produced (*kṛtakatva*),
one establishes that sound is impermanent, so it is here.
This establishes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Like karma, medicinal herbs, and incantations,
this nature of phenomena is inconceivable.
This refers to the nature of the distinctions between the three vehicles, which is the seed that exists by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This is called "abiding in the dharma-nature" (*dharmatā-pratiṣṭhita*).
The treatise asks: how does one diligently cultivate the meditation on impurity?
This is the fourth purification of obstructions.
The treatise states: "Regarding 'bad odors' and 'arisen odors':
because they are subject to transformation and decay, their odor is termed 'bad odor'."
For example, regarding excrement and filth:
to smell them as soon as they arise is called "smelling upon arising.
This is like [smelling] leeks, garlic, and the like.
The treatise says: "Regarding 'born from a blood-pitcher,' this head is a *kumbhīra* (skull) or a blood-pitcher,
because it is capable of maturing blood."
In explaining this in the *Śāstra*, it says:
"Although these pure forms possess a pure appearance in the present world, they shall not be impure in the future, unlike the impure external forms of the present."
The phrase "there is no such possibility" means that it clarifies the pure matter (*rūpa*) of the present time.
In future lives, it will certainly become impure.
Having already observed external objects as impure, one observes the internal body, thinking:
"If [the body] were pure even in future lives..."
If the internal body were not impure as it is in the present,
then external impurity would be of only one kind.
This is impossible;
it must inevitably become impure.
It is not said that it "will" become impure.
In the *Treatise on the Investigation of Principles*, it says:
"In this way, one investigates principles by relying on the conventional, the ultimate, and causal conditions through the principle of dependence."
The aforementioned understanding that there is no self within is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, as it is said, from the contemplation of the livid corpse up to the chain of bones,
this is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
This present body of mine,
being drawn forth by prior karma and afflictions,
is the cause.
The union of the impurities of the father and mother and so forth are the conditions;
now, the conclusion follows the sequence of the discourse.
It is not established in sequential order; furthermore, the establishment in sequential order may be understood by analogy.
[End of] the treatise. Within the explanation of the principle of proof (*upapattisādhana-yukti*).

It means that one forms this thought: "How can the mental engagement with the remedial dharma now serve as an antidote for the afflictions that are about to arise within the objective sphere of what is to be remedied?"
The meaning here is this:
external objects of impurity are called "antidotes" because they counteract sensual desire.
Because one takes external impure forms as an object,
one will certainly be able to counteract the afflictions that arise toward pure objects of perception.
To state this formally:
When one takes impurity as an object, one is necessarily able to counteract sensual desire;
because it takes that which can counteract [desire] as its object,
it is just as when one takes the signless as an object, one is able to dispel the sign.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-lü-tsuan*, Scroll Eight. Completed on the fourteenth day of the fifth month of the eighth year of Kyōhō (1723), the *Kibō* year. By the śramaṇa Kōhon, age sixty-nine.
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-lü-tsuan*, Scroll Nine. Composed by the śramaṇa Ki, who translated the treatise, for Scrolls Thirty-three and Thirty-four.
The Root Treatise (*Śāstra-mūla*).
The first verse clarifies that each of the ten masteries possesses seven gates. The second line clarifies the seven mental orientations within the first gate.
First, to clarify the seven gates:
First, the cultivation of the mind;
second, the departure from desire;
third, the detailed exposition of the various meditative concentrations.
4. The two meditative attainments;
5. The five supernormal powers;
6. The distinctions of birth.
Regarding the seven characteristics,
they shall be explained separately below.
Within this fourth *dhāraṇī*, these [characteristics] constitute its essence.
In the second verse,
"observing the truths" refers to the first two types of mental attention (*manasikāra*);
"penetrating them as they truly are" refers to [the subsequent stages].
The mental application of distancing is for the purpose of severing the afflictions; it is extensively analyzed for the practitioner.
The others are mental applications that culminate in the final one.
This is the mental attention of the seventh fruit.
Among the first thirty-one [mental attentions],
it clarifies the purification of the fourth hindrance.
Now, the explanation of the fifth [topic], the cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*),
which constitutes the major section within the thirtieth [chapter].
This is explained in the treatise under the second [section], the "Renunciation of Desire" (*vairāgya*).
Question: How many types of persons (pudgala) herein do not, even when initiating application of effort, attain the supramundane path in this very life? Answer:
There are four types of persons.
As for the fourth person,
it refers to all bodhisattvas who delight in realizing great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) in a future life rather than in the present life.
This intent clarifies that the path to Buddhahood for a bodhisattva pertains to the future, not to the present dharma.
Although the mundane path can manifest the application of effort in the present life,
it only brings sentient beings to maturity within the cycle of birth and death.
Because he applies himself to the preparatory practices of the mundane path,
this person directs his mind toward the future fruit of Buddhahood.
One immediately gives rise to the preparatory application of the supramundane path.
Now, based on the former meaning,
the treatise explains the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*).

The attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) refers to being able to discern the coarse characteristics of the desire realm and the tranquil characteristics of the higher realms.
In the Lesser Vehicle, one must perform all six stages of practice;
however, in the present Mahāyāna, one attains it through a single stage alone.
It is not necessary to possess all six modes of activity;
rather, one may attend to any single one among those six.
This is explained in the treatise within the section on the common characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of the third characteristic.
It is said that "all desires" refers to the suffering of birth and so forth, up to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
The reason the eighth type, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*),
is not mentioned here is that this explanation is based on what is commonly known in the world.
This is stated according to what is commonly known as suffering in the conventional sense,
rather than in terms of ultimate suffering;
this [present case], however, refers to ultimate suffering.
Although all desires and various matters exist,
they are not mentioned because they are difficult to know.
This is explained in the treatise’s analysis of the coarse category of discursive investigation (*vitarka*).
Regarding the statements "like a chain of bones," "like congealed blood and flesh," "like a grass torch," and "like a single piece of charcoal fire":
herein, "like a chain of bones" means it is loathsome;
"like congealed blood and flesh" means it is unreal and disgusting.
It is like a torch of grass that is extinguished in an instant;

yet it is like a small portion of fire that can burn mountains and marshes—so too, even a small amount of desire and the like can burn away the roots of goodness. Furthermore, it is said to be like charcoal, where one part possesses fire and another part lacks fire.
It may be considered loathsome; however,
this interpretation is not correct,
for the first two types of attention do not speak of the severing of afflictions.
The third is the mental application of seclusion (*viveka-manasikāra*),
because it is able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the explanation of seclusion in the treatise:
It is said that the path of initial abandonment arises.
Question: As it is said that the two ends of a scale rise and fall simultaneously, why is it that one attains the perception of the form-realm mind?
There are still afflictions of the desire realm that have not been eliminated;
[Master] Shu says this refers to the stage prior to the "comprehension of characteristics" (lakṣaṇapraveśa).
Although those in the desire realm who practice hearing and reflection may cultivate revulsion toward desire,
they are not yet able to accord with the path that abandons the afflictions of the lower realms.
Because the resolution that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisamvedinādhimokṣa*) accords with seclusion and abandons the desires of the lower realm,
although this resolution that discerns characteristics cannot itself sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Yet delusion does not arise;
it is like a person at the stage of the first fruit who, while not yet free from desire,
attains the "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya) concentration through cultivation.
At present, the same applies to the realization of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapraveśa*):
one realizes the characteristics even while not yet free from the lower grades of afflictions (*kleśa*).
When the realization of characteristics arises, the secondary afflictions do not arise,
just as when a wholesome mind arises, an unwholesome mind does not arise;
it is not because they have been severed that they do not arise.
Because the attention of "separation" has been abandoned, [the afflictions] do not arise;
however, because the first two types of attention have not yet been abandoned,
they persist during those first two stages.
If desire or evil should arise in the interim,
the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* explains that among the latter two types of attention (*manasikāra*),
it is the attention of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*) [that counteracts them].

It is said that by means of these causes and conditions, the mind becomes dissociated from all afflictions bound to the desire realm; this occurs through the method of temporary suppression and abandonment, rather than through the ultimate and permanent destruction of the seeds and so forth.
This concludes what is called the "mental attention of the culmination of application.
Herein, one subdues the afflictions through the six modes of practice;
however, because one does not yet attain realization through the higher path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
It is said that they are "temporarily suppressed and severed.
Regarding this suppression and severance: does it suppress the manifest states (*paryavasthāna*), or does it suppress the seeds (*bīja*)?
Both must be subdued.
How is this known?
From the explanation within the first two types of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Regarding the second stage of mental attention (*manasikāra*), it is not interspersed with hearing or reflection;
although afflictions do not arise,
they have not yet been suppressed at their root.
The path of immediate succession has not yet been named;
however, by the third stage of mental attention (*manasikāra*),
the capacity for the seeds to produce manifest results is suppressed.
This is what is called the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*).
This is performed by means of contaminated (*sāsrava*) practice;
if one were to rely on uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) practice, it would necessarily sever the seeds [of defilement].
Only then is it called the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Although the subsequent mind does not arise,
it still constitutes the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
It is the same here as well:
the subduing of the manifest mind constitutes the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
while the subduing of the seeds constitutes the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).

The seventh mental application (*manasikāra*) is that which, immediately following this [sixth], by means of these causes and conditions, leads to the realization and entry into the fundamental first *dhyāna*; this very mental application concomitant with the fundamental first *dhyāna* is called the "mental application that is the fruit of the culmination of the preparatory stage" (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala-manasikāra*).
The intended meaning of this treatise is that the ninth path of liberation resides in the fundamental dhyānas.
The nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation all occur within the preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*); regarding this,
there are two interpretations.
One interpretation holds that from the first dhyāna up to the third dhyāna,
there are nine uninterrupted paths and nine liberations,
which may occur either within the fundamental states or in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
The ninth liberation may exist within the fundamental dhyānas;
if it is the ninth path of liberation from the fourth dhyāna upward,
it necessarily exists within the fundamental dhyānas.
The first eight liberations and the nine uninterrupted paths reside within the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*). Why is this so?
Below the third dhyāna,
there is joy and bliss in the fundamental stages;
in the preparatory stages (sāmantaka), there is equanimity.
Within the fundamental stages,
whether one is practicing contemplation or severing delusions.
In all cases, there is no neutral feeling (upekṣā-vedanā), because it is a dharma of darkness;
it is definitively non-existent.
Because they are characterized by joy, delight, clarity, and sharpness,
if one abandons the afflictions within their preparatory stages (sāmantaka),
[the abandonment is accomplished].
If one engages in contemplative observation,
there is always equanimity;
this clarifies that it is only through contemplative observation that joy and bliss can be attained.
Joy and bliss do not occur at the time of abandoning the afflictions;
they pertain to the three lower dhyānas. There are two types of individuals:
those of sharp faculties and those of dull faculties.
The path of uninterrupted liberation arises;
if the person possesses sharp faculties,
the ninth path of uninterrupted realization abides in the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*).
It is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) resides in the fundamental dhyāna (*mauladhyāna*) and is associated with pleasure (*sukha*) and joy (*prīti*).
If the person is of dull faculties,
the ninth uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) abides in the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) and is associated with equanimity (upekṣā).
Because the mind is dull, it cannot swiftly enter the fundamental absorption associated with joy and bliss;
thus, its ninth liberation resides in the preparatory absorption (*sāmantaka*).
It is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
As for the statement in this text that one enters the fundamental dhyāna through the seventh mental application (*manasikāra*),
this refers specifically to those of sharp faculties.
This seventh mental engagement is able to enter the fundamental state swiftly and is associated with bliss and other qualities.
One takes the three dhyānas;
if they are situated in the preparatory stages (sāmantaka),
they serve as the path of liberation (vimuktimārga).
It is associated with equanimity.
If there is a fundamental dhyāna,
it serves as the path of liberation.
It is associated with pleasure and so forth.
Regarding the fourth dhyāna and above,
there are the first eight liberations and the nine paths of uninterrupted transition.
All [of these] are within the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
If it is within the ninth liberation,
it must be within the fundamental absorption (*mauladhyāna*).
It does not abide in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*);

this is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that if one does not analyze it in this way, there would be nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for the preceding [stages].
Residing within the preparatory stage,
the ninth path of liberation serves as the fundamental meditative absorption.
Beginning from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is likewise so. What is the proof for the preceding meaning?
If one understands it generally without further differentiation, [it is established].
The first six mental applications (*manasikāra*) belong to the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*);
the seventh belongs to the fundamental stage (*maula*).
However, it is simply described as the location of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Furthermore, this serves as proof.
Since it has not yet been seen that the text takes "discrimination" (vibhāga) as its excellence,
the latter argument uses this very text as its proof.
The previous school interpreted this passage as explained previously regarding those of sharp and dull faculties;
it concludes in the section on the "empty space" below.
This shall now be explained in detail.

In the third section of the treatise, regarding the explanation of *manasikāra* (mental attention), it says: "Furthermore, when the *lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manasikāra* (mental attention that discerns characteristics) [arises], up to the *adhimokṣika-manasikāra* (mental attention consisting of resolute belief), one correctly initiates application for the purpose of abandoning [the afflictions] or for the purpose of attaining [the qualities]."
As stated in the *Twenty-eight Clouds*:
"The first two types of attention (*manasikāra*) both belong to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*);
here, however, it is liberation alone that constitutes the primary practice of the path of preparation."
This is because it is taught here based on a superior state,
a state adjacent to the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
and a state that is not interrupted by hearing or reflection (*śruta-cintā*).
It is taught that resolute conviction alone constitutes the correct application;
the preceding twenty-eight [categories] are discussed from the perspective of actual reality.
The "clear realization" (*parijñā*) is also a stage of application (*prayoga*). Furthermore, it is explained that this correctly initiates the application;
it does not necessarily exclude clear realization from being a path of application, because its resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is superior due to its proximity to the [fundamental] stage.
This explains the definitive arousal of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
For now, it describes resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) as the path of correct preparation,
without excluding the perception of signs (*nimittasamjñā*).
This accords with reality and contains no contradiction,
as is established in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*.

Regarding the statement that "through the mental application of observation, one can abide with the mind free from overweening pride (adhimāna) regarding what has been attained," why is it not said that one is free from overweening pride when abandoning the superior grade [of afflictions]?
Furthermore, it is not in the context of abandoning the third category that one speaks of being free from overweening pride;
rather, it is in the context of abandoning the middle category that one speaks of being free from overweening pride.
The commentary states:
The delusions of the first six categories are coarse and easy to recognize;
the delusions of the final three categories are subtle and difficult to discern.
Having completed the severance of the superior, middling, and lower grades of afflictions of the preceding stages,
one fails to recognize that the lower-grade afflictions still remain,
and thus gives rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This means that once all nine grades [of afflictions] have been exhausted,
one realizes the fundamental meditative absorption (mauladhyāna);
it is because one is now free from this conceit (māna).
Regarding the abandonment of medium-grade afflictions,
it is stated later that one is free from overweening pride;
this is not the case for the abandonment of superior-grade afflictions, which is mentioned later.

The treatise states: "Furthermore, the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) and the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika manaskāra*) are collectively termed 'conformable attention' (*anulomika manaskāra*), as they both proceed in conjunction with the antidote of repudiation (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*).
This is the intended meaning here.
It is subsumed under forty modes of attention (*manasikāra*) and four types of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
Regarding the forty modes of attention:
As explained previously in the eleventh fascicle,
regarding the application of attention (*manasikāra*) that accords with reality among the forty [factors].
There are twenty-five types of mental attention (*manasikāra*):
mental attention that conforms [to the object], and mental attention that brings about revulsion toward the focal object (*ālambana*).

Because they accord with the abandonment of afflictions, the first two types of attention are "concordant. Furthermore, the attention of withdrawal and the attention of the culmination of application are called "counteractive" attention, as they proceed together with the counteractive abandonment.
The attention of counteraction is the twenty-sixth.
As for the attention of counteraction:
This means that because it correctly abandons all afflictions and serves as the immediate path (*ānantarya-mārga*) for those two,

the "attention of counteraction" (*pratipakṣa-manasikāra*) is subsumed [under it]. Furthermore, the "attention of delighting in cultivation" (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manasikāra*) is also termed both the "attention of counteraction" and the "attention conducive to purification" (*viśuddhy-anukūla-manasikāra*).
There are twenty-seven types of attention conducive to purification.
Regarding "attention conducive to purification":
This refers to the cultivation of the six recollections,
namely the recollection of the Buddha and so forth;
it is also comprised within the mental attention of "delighting in practice."
Because it abandons the intermediate grade of afflictions,
it is called the "attention of antidote" (*pratipakṣa-manasikāra*);
by means of clarity, one cultivates specific joy through the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*).
The contemplation of pure nirvāṇa, the Buddha,
and so forth is also called the "pure specific object.
For this reason, it is explained in the same section as the "exclusive distancing" [from defilements] and other such qualities.

Furthermore, because the aforementioned "separation" (*viveka*) and so forth do not include the attention conducive to purification (*anulomika-pariśuddhy-amanasikāra*), these two [categories] together include it. Question: Why are the four remedies (*pratipakṣa*) not included here?
The commentary says:
Because it reveals the meaning,
this explains the severance of delusions.
One should understand that, like "abstention" and so forth, this refers to the antidote (*pratipakṣa*). If so, why is it not said to be "co-existent" (*sahagata*)?
The meaning is as follows:
The antidote is wisdom (*prajñā*);
mental attention (*manasikāra*) is the mind (*manas*).
The preceding text further includes the antidote.
Because the mind and wisdom proceed together,
they are called "concomitant.
In this context, however, only attention (manasikāra) is being clarified.
It is not the antidote to ignorance because it lacks wisdom;

therefore, it is not said to be "concomitant. Furthermore, if one observes that the mental application of investigation is called the "mental application conforming to investigation," [it is so designated].
Regarding the twenty-eight types of mental attention (*manasikāra*),
"mental attention of sequential observation" refers to observing which afflictions (*kleśa*) have been abandoned and which have not yet been abandoned.
Alternatively, one may contemplate the principles of the various dharmas previously realized;
these, in relation to what preceded them, are likewise the "distant-part antidote" (*viprakṛṣṭa-bhāga-pratipakṣa*) and so forth,
but they are not mentioned here for the sake of brevity.
In relation to that which precedes it, this is the path of progress;
therefore, it is called the "counteractive of distancing" (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*). In relation to the mental application of "delight in gathering" (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manaskāra*), [it is so called].
This is the path of liberation;
therefore, it maintains the antidote.
It is now explained following the stage of "delight in what has been gathered."
It is not said that the antidotes mutually include one another;
as previously stated, they do not subsume each other,
as is extensively reconciled in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*.
The Treatise says:

"In this way, it should be understood that the remaining four types of attention are subsumed within the six types of attention, namely, the conforming attention (*anulomika-manasikāra*) and so forth.
The commentary states:
The four modes of attention (*manasikāra*) are called "the remainder" because they are external to the seven modes of attention;
they are all included within the forty modes of attention,
and are now subsumed under the six modes of attention.
Therefore, it is said that [these] are subsumed within the six types of mental attention (*manasikāra*). Question:
Why is it not explained here how the seventh type of mental attention is included and so forth?
Answer: It is explained as follows.
The seventh mental application is the result;
these four mental applications,
together with the preceding six, are all causes.
Because they can be mutually subsumed as causes,
the seventh mental application (*manasikāra*) is not included as a result;
for within this context, the seven subsume the forty.
It encompasses only four;
in the text of the eleventh section below,
forty [factors] are used to subsume the seven.
That is to say, the meaning of the forty types of attention is fully subsumed within the seven;
now, the seven subsume the forty,
but the forty do not subsume the seven.
Therefore, they are neither fully exhausted nor gathered;
there are differences to be examined.
The treatise explains that the first dhyāna is coarse among the middling states.
Regarding the statement that "the nature of coarse mental verbalization is called *vitarka*," there are two interpretations.
The first states: "Speech" refers to the names of phenomena (*dharma-nāman*).
Its essence is coarse mental activity;
it is capable of investigating all phenomena because it resembles names and expressions.
"Speech" refers to the nature of verbal expression.
Furthermore, "name" (nāman) refers to the name of speech;
"thought" (vitarka) refers to the name of mental activity.
Because this is a conceptualization of names,
it is called "mental verbalization" (manojalpa).
In the Hīnayāna, vitarka and vicāra are associated with the fundamental [consciousness].
Some say: "The Mahāyāna is not like this;
investigation and analysis (vitarka-vicāra) exist only during the stage of expedient means."
Not so. Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere:
"In meditative concentration, there is no vitarka or vicāra."
There is no arising of verbal vitarka and vicāra,
yet it is not that subtle vitarka and vicāra are absent.
Furthermore, this distinguishes [the first dhyāna] from the five factors of the formless realm.
This is because the branches are established based on the fundamental dhyānas.
The treatise explains that [vitarka and vicāra] are included within the "place" (sthāna);
as for their inclusion among the external bases (bāhyāyatana), it is as follows:
This refers to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The treatise states: "If one abides in the superior" means that those of the lower stages abide in the intensification of suffering.
In the commentary on the Sūtra regarding the attainment of the joy and bliss of seclusion (*viveka-prītisukha*),
it is said that "secluded" (*viveka*) refers to having already attained the mental attention of the culmination of preparatory application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-manasikāra*).
It is said that "arisen" (*jāta*) refers to being produced immediately thereafter, with this [attainment] as its cause and its condition.
Regarding the statement, "Joy and bliss refer to having already attained the sought-after goal," this is based on those of sharp faculties during the ninth path of liberation.
Because this person has entered the fundamental dhyānas,
it is said that they give rise to joy and bliss;
this refers to one of dull faculties.
The ninth path of liberation can only give rise to joy and bliss upon entering the fundamental stage after one has already dwelt in the preparatory concentration (*sāmantaka*).
Regarding the treatise’s statement that "one can dwell correctly for as long as seven days and seven nights," it means:
This clarifies that one is able to enter meditative absorption and remain therein for seven days and seven nights.
Why is it not said to be for a longer duration,
but only for seven days and so forth?
Because that edible food of the desire realm lasts for seven days;
if it exceeds seven days, [it perishes].
Because their bodies perish immediately upon emerging from meditative absorption,
they cannot remain for a long duration;
furthermore, this is based on such a limited period of time.
Now, as he is about to enter the meditative absorption of cessation,
many months and years will not pass;
once seven days have elapsed, he will emerge from the absorption.
His body will then perish; however,
if he emerges from meditative absorption within seven days,
his body will not perish.
This discussion is based on the period when [the body] is not yet destroyed;

it simply states "seven days. Question: If he enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) after the seven days have passed, then upon emerging from that absorption, he ought to die.
The Master [Yì] said: "Not so.
Because he has entered meditative absorption for a long time and is sustained by the power of that concentration, he does not die."
Now he also emerges from meditative absorption and immediately enters the "consciousness-endowed" concentration;
therefore, he does not die either. Question: He also emerges from the "cessation" concentration.
Does the cessation attainment (nirodha-samāpatti) cause the body to perish or not?
The answer is: it perishes.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the explanation of the second dhyāna:
as for what is called "concentration," it refers to having already attained the *manasikāra* (mental application) of the culmination of preparatory effort;
this distinguishes it from the first dhyāna.
That is called "born of detachment" (vivekaja),
while this is called "born of concentration" (samādhija).
That [state] attains the name "born of detachment" because it is the first to be free from the fetters of the desire realm.
This refers to the fact that one has already attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) beforehand;
therefore, it is said to be "born of concentration.
This is explained in the treatise regarding the third dhyāna.
It is said that from the third dhyāna downward there is no such bliss (*sukha*) nor uninterrupted equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Below that, the essence of bliss is joy (*prīti*);
that which gratifies body and mind is bliss.
Now, within the third dhyāna,
mental satisfaction is also called pleasure (*sukha*),
because that pleasure is at its ultimate limit.
Therefore, it is said that the lower stages lack this bliss.
Although equanimity exists within the internal practice of the lower stages,
it is not specifically designated by that name.
Furthermore, because there is an interval, it is not that they are abandoned without interval; thus one says "non-existence.
It is not that there is no abandonment due to the presence of an interval; this is also called "non-abandonment."
In the commentary on the fourth dhyāna, it says:

"Furthermore, because the types of counteragents here are similar in their force, the counteragent that consists in the abandonment of pleasure (*sukha-prahāṇa*) is not explicitly taught; rather, only that which is produced by the counteragent as the abandonment of pleasure is mentioned."
In this context, equanimity, mindfulness,
and clear comprehension are termed the antidotes;
the bliss of the third dhyāna is termed that which is to be countered.
In the Sūtra, only the pleasure to be abandoned is mentioned;
it does not mention the equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension that perform the abandonment.
This is because the third dhyāna has already clarified the counteractive factors, such as equanimity and mindfulness.
It is called a "homogeneous class" (*nikāya-sabhāga*) because it resembles this fourth dhyāna as its antidote;
it is termed a "homogeneous class" because its name and essence are similar.
Both are capable of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*);
as these two states are similar,
they are said to be "similar in power."
This has been explained briefly.
This commentary does not clarify the reason why the fourth dhyāna is able to counteract [the lower states].

The treatise says: "Because one repeatedly cultivates this very state, one is able to abandon it so as not to remain [bound] within the third dhyāna; since the superior pleasure of the stage of the third dhyāna is thereby relinquished, it is said that 'due to the cessation of pleasure.'"
In this context, the pleasure associated with the third dhyāna binds the practitioner,
preventing them from attaining transcendence of the third dhyāna.
Being unable to attain that superior fourth dhyāna,
one now repeatedly cultivates equanimity and mindfulness,
thereby able to relinquish the bliss of this concentration.

The Treatise says: "By reason of these causes and conditions, whether it be what was previously severed or what is now being severed, they are collectively described as 'the severance of pleasure and the severance of suffering,' wherein prior sorrow and joy have subsided.
Herein, "the severance of pleasure" refers to that which is being severed now.
The remaining faculties of feeling (*vedanendriya*) are termed "previously abandoned.
Therefore, the lower and middle [levels] are covered and counteracted.
This is because, as it says, "up until the time of entering the first dhyāna, the feeling of mental grief (*daurmanasya*) subsides."
Regarding this, as stated previously in the eleventh fascicle:
"For what reason is the faculty of suffering said not to be abandoned within the first dhyāna?"
Because the heaviness (*dausthulya*) of that category has not yet been abandoned.
This may be the case for one whose body belongs to a lower realm;
but for what reason does the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), though not yet abandoned, not manifest in one born in the first dhyāna?
Because the various sufferings associated with their concomitants— which are subsumed under the faculty of grief—
have already been abandoned by him,
there remains only their coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Yet it has not been severed.
If the faculty of suffering were severed within the first dhyāna,
then that practitioner—
Upon entering the first and second dhyānas,
there would be no distinction in the states produced by feeling,
because both possess both joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*).
There should be no distinction;
however, because the coarse and heavy [defilements] have not yet been severed,
it is said that there is a distinction.
Yet the Sūtra states that there are definite distinctions based on the emergence from various meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*). Question:
Is it not possible to establish these distinctions simply by whether vitarka and vicāra have been abandoned or not?
For what reason must the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) necessarily be severed,
yet it is said that there is a distinction?
The meaning is as follows:
Since vitarka and vicāra do not constitute an obstacle to joy (prīti) and bliss (sukha),
one cannot speak of a distinction of joy in terms of the abandonment of vitarka and vicāra;
this is because the joy of the first dhyāna still possesses the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya).
The benefits have not yet been stated.
Because joy (*prīti*) in the second dhyāna has already abandoned suffering,
that joy is pure and superior.
If one were to explain the distinctions based on the conceptual investigations of existence and non-existence,
the dharmas of existence and non-existence are immeasurably diverse,
and thus their respective meditations could be differentiated.
Now, conversely,
it is objected that there would be no distinction between pleasure (*sukha*) and joy (*saumanasya*),
because the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*)— being identical to pleasure, joy, and so forth— is an obstacle to the characteristic of feeling (*vedanā-lakṣaṇa*).
If one does not distinguish the joy (*prīti*) of the first and second dhyānas from the faculty of the cessation of suffering,
then the joy and bliss (*sukha*) of the first and second dhyānas would be [nothing other than] feelings (*vedanā*).
There should be no distinction [between them],
because suffering has already been abandoned during the initial stage of the first dhyāna;
this [present abandonment] refers to the abandonment of *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness).
Its seeds are not said to be severed;
they still exist in the Arhat.
This is explained in the treatise concerning the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

Regarding the statement: "In all those various aggregates, conceptualizations of distinctions arise—such as the concepts of food, drink, jars, clothing, hanging ornaments, and so forth, up to the concepts of mountains and forests—in all these, no mental attention arises," etc.:
This refers to one whose body resides in the desire realm; when,
relying on the sphere of infinite space, they eliminate the perception of form,
[they do so] with respect to the objects of form within the desire realm.
Furthermore, it was for this reason that he previously spoke of the Jeta Grove and so forth;
it was not that his body had been born in the form realm when he wished to enter into space.
Yet this perception exists. The *Śāstra* states:

"It should be known that herein, from the stage of access (*sāmantaka*) up until one has not yet entered the actual fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*), one takes only space as an object. Once the fundamental absorption is attained, one also takes space as an object and likewise takes all the aggregates (*skandha*) belonging to one's own level as objects. Furthermore, within the stage of access, one also takes all the aggregates belonging to the lower levels as objects."
The commentary states:
From the fourth dhyāna upward, its ninth path of liberation consists of the seventh mental application (*manasikāra*).
It occurs only within the fundamental meditative absorptions (mauladhyāna).
At the very moment one first attains the path of liberation (vimuktimārga),
it lasts for that single instant.
The mind of the second moment takes as its object only the aggregates of its own level; however,
it is able to take the aggregates of the higher and lower levels as its objects.
This is because it is explained here with reference to the first moment of the path of liberation;
therefore, it is said that [the path] also takes the aggregates of its own level as its object.
As for the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) prior to the preparatory concentration (*sāmantaka-samādhi*):
However, because one generates revulsion toward the lower stages,
it is said that they also take as their object all the aggregates belonging to the lower stages.
This refers to the first eight paths of liberation.
It also takes the aggregates (*skandha*) of the higher and lower stages as its object;
however, because this is explained here with reference to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
it is stated that it "also takes the aggregates of the lower stage as its object."
However, it does not exclude the preparatory (*sāmantaka*) and fundamental (*maula*) stages;
rather, it takes as its objects the aggregates (*skandha*) of the higher, lower, and its own level.
This applies to the eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) within the preparatory concentrations (*dhyāna-sāmantaka*).
Because it does not mention the nine uninterrupted [paths],
it says that they take the lower aggregates as their object within the fundamental dhyānas.
This refers to the first moment;
it is stated that way because the second moment and those following are implicitly established,
and because it is said that [the mind] also takes the aggregates of its own level as its object.
In the treatise,
it does not say that [the mind] takes only the aggregates and so forth of its own level as its object;
rather, it says that it "also" takes them as its object.
These paths of uninterrupted transition and liberation are explained as previously [described] in the context of the first dhyāna; however,
if there is a contradiction with the second fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamudaya*, [the former should be followed].
As explained in the commentary of that Great Master,
there are three parts to the exposition on the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The first correctly clarifies the transition from the desire realm to the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
Having become weary of the sphere of nothingness,
one forms the perception of abandonment;
this is the beginning of the subsequent stage.
Up to the point where one is able to abandon even the perception of the sphere of nothingness;
this is the second explanation for the name "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Within this, there are two [aspects].
The first interpretation is that it is not characterized by perception;
the second interpretation is that it is not characterized by non-perception.
This begins from the point below where, due to these causes and conditions, one first enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness.
"Up to" means up to either the perception of existence or the perception of non-existence;
this clarifies that it is not the sphere of infinite consciousness and those below it.
This is the perception of "there is something.
The sphere of nothingness is the perception of "there is nothing.
Therefore, it is said that there is neither perception nor non-perception.
This is neither the perception of existence nor the perception of non-existence.
Now, within the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
neither of these two perceptions exists.
Within the state of non-perception,
there are two types of non-perception;
now, within the state of non-non-perception.
Nor is it non-dual because of the absence of ideation. Within the second major section, the second part clarifies that it is not the absence of ideation.
There are two types of the absence of ideation.
First, the attainment of non-perception;
second, the attainment of cessation.
In both of these attainments, the mind is entirely extinguished.
Now, the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is not like this; therefore,
it is said that it is not "without perception" (*asaṃjñin*),
which means it is not the two types of non-perceptual attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Because there is subtle perception within the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
the third [verse] clarifies the state of being at the Peak of Existence,
which transcends the lower levels such as the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
And entering the fundamental [dhyāna] from its own preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*);
that is to say, when one gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) right here [in the preparatory stage], and so forth.
In the *Śāstra*,
regarding the explanation of the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*),
it says: "In this way, those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have already become free from craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)," and so forth.
This is based on the attainment of realization through the severance of afflictions,
as reconciled in the commentary on the ninth fascicle of the *Abhidharma* (Dafalun).
This includes such states as the dwelling in tranquility (*śāntavihāra*).
That is explained in detail elsewhere in the text;
as for the statement that the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) first arises only in the desire realm (kāmadhātu):
This is based on the teaching of the conditions.
When first beginning to practice, one must necessarily rely on the desire realm;
however, when first arising [in a higher state] later on, the form realm may also be attained.
For example, a person on the path to the third fruit who had not yet attained this meditative absorption while in the desire realm attains it only after being born in the form realm.
It arises for the first time immediately;
however, because one first hears this teaching in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and only later is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu),
it is explained in the treatise among the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā).
The supernormal knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings also attains this wisdom associated with the divine eye;
it does so when taking as its object the events occurring after death in the present.
This is also the supernormal power of knowing death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda-abhijñā*), which is observed by means of the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
The treatise states: "As for *tūla* cotton..."
This refers to the silk from wild silkworm cocoons, known as *duroloma*.
In the commentary on the twelve perceptions (*saṃjñā*),
it is explained that the first five perceptions are the methods for cultivating the supernormal power of the psychic realm (*ṛddhividhi*).
Regarding the sequential cultivation of each of the remaining four supernormal powers (*abhijñā*):
within the cultivation of the supernormal power of the miraculous domain (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*),
the fourth method is that of cultivating through the body and mind.
This means that both body and mind are capable of transformation.
If it is a transformation, it is bodily action (*kāyakarman*);
if it is a manifestation, it is the transformative mind.
In the fifth treatise, within the explanation of the perception of resolve (*adhimukti-saṃjñā*), it says:
"To resolve the distant as near" means to contract the long into the short;
"to resolve the near as distant" means... [the rest of the sentence is missing from the source].
Lengthening the short and making the long, and the mutual transformation of the coarse and the subtle—
these are transformations of physical form; the earth and water elements acting upon one another—
these are transformations of the four great elements.
In this context, only the two transformations of form and sound are discussed,
without considering the other sense objects,
as explained in detail in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
The treatise states: "Regarding those who exercise mastery over a portion of the derived matter produced by the four great elements in the Brahma-world:
'a portion of derived matter' refers to the two types, namely visible form and sound."
Therefore, it is called "a portion" because it does not involve the non-reversing contact or the five sense faculties,
and because it consists solely of external objects; thus, it is called "a portion."
Furthermore, according to the transformations effected by meditative concentration, there are only two possibilities.
Because one part cannot transform the entirety of the Brahma-world,
it is said to be "one part."
In the commentary on the method for cultivating the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*),
it says: "As for 'a broad or long place,' this refers to a marketplace."
First, there is the place where the children play,
called the Vast and Long Place;
it is so named because that location is vast and extensive.
The assembly is also immeasurable;
"many" is used here to indicate a great multitude.
As for those in the first dhyāna heaven who are called "Brahmās":
"Brahma" has the meaning of "purity.
Because one is initially free from desire, it receives the name "pure.
As for the second dhyāna being called "light": [it is so named because]...
Because it is initially free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), it receives the name "Radiant" (*ābhā*).
As for the third dhyāna receiving the name "Pure" (*śubha*), it is because it attains superior bliss; this superior bliss is what is termed "purity."
In the fourth dhyāna, ordinary beings and noble ones dwell together in three heavens.
The first is named Anabhraka (Cloudless);
the others are named according to the increase of their merit.
Regarding the name of the five *anāgāmin* heavens,
the treatise explains within the section on the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that they exist "within the commonality of the group (*nikāyasabhāga*) of the devas who follow [the practice]."
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is no separate place for receiving retribution;
because one receives this retribution according to the three grades of conduct,
they are called "gods who follow their conduct" (anugāmin-deva).
The treatise states: "As for the distinctions among the activities performed while abiding, this refers to the specific differences in the karma performed while abiding in the three grades.
The thirty-fourth fascicle of the treatise states: "Having explained the four aspects of each of the Truths..."
This is what is called the "mental attention to the characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*).
Within this context, the seven types of mental attention encompass everything from the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) up to the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The resolution that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedin-adhimokṣa*) occurs prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Specifically, the discernment of characteristics pertains to the five preliminary applications (*pañca-sthāpanā*) and the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*);
the resolution mentioned below pertains to the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*).
"Distancing" (*dūrikaraṇa*) occurs from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) onwards;
"distancing" extends up until the sixteenth moment of mind within the path of seeing;
"observation" (*vīkṣaṇa*) occurs during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) up until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*).
All observation, whether of what has been abandoned or not yet abandoned,
and all cultivation— this is the attention of observation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*).
From the [stage of] Vajra onwards.
Up to the point of severing the eight grades of afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
all are termed "appropriating joy" (*ratisaṃgrāhaka*);
that is, all uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The culmination of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) occurs at the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*),
and its ultimate fruit resides in the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Since the present [treatise] intends to clarify that which precedes the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), [it focuses on this stage].
It is said that this is called the "mental attention to the characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*).
This will be explained below in the sequential discussion of the various stages;
one will understand it by consulting that [section].
The treatise states: "As explained at length in the *Saptāha-sūtra* (Seven-Day Sūtra)" refers to the *Kalpa-sūtra*,
which is called the *Saptāha-sūtra* because it describes events occurring over seven days.
In the treatise explaining the eight causes and conditions for transformation,
the seventh— drying by the wind— is as follows:
it refers to when great winds blow and fan wet clothes, wet ground, crops, and forests until they become dry.
Regarding those who are withered and parched:
it refers to having wet clothing,
or occasionally being on damp ground.
Alternatively, crops and the like may be fanned by great winds, causing them to wither, shrivel, and become parched.
"Shu" (𣌑) is pronounced as "chū" (初急反); it is as the world calls it.
This extreme refers to the state of being parched and withered.
In the treatise’s explanation of the fifteen kinds of transformative changes,
it says within the eighth section on the transformation of cold and heat:
Regarding the expression "dry speech," it means that because [the mouth] is hot, it becomes dry when speaking.
As worldly people say:
Dryness is the transformation of moisture.

The *Śāstra* states: "It refers to that which, through contact with a touch conducive to pleasant sensation, experiences the pleasure arising from the conditions of that pleasant touch, and is itself capable of discerning the state of the pleasant sensation."
For now, let us take contact (sparśa) that leads to pleasant feeling as an example;
since contacts leading to suffering and so forth have not yet been raised, it is said:
"By means of contact with what is conducive to pleasant feeling."
This refers specifically to feelings such as suffering and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "when experiencing pleasure produced by the condition of a pleasant contact," the "pleasant contact" is the object.
That which can produce a pleasant tactile sensation is this:
now, when the mind apprehends an object conducive to a pleasant tactile sensation and pleasure arises, it is able to cognize itself.
This refers to the state of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
At the end of the commentary on the sixteen kinds of transformation (*vipariṇāma*), it says:

"Of these, the first six are matters of what is appropriated (*upātta-vastu*); the latter ten are matters of the body and its requisites; and the six [of the former] are matters of what is appropriated."
That is to say: first, matters concerning the earth;
second, matters concerning gardens;
third, matters concerning mountains.
Fourth, matters concerning water;
fifth, matters concerning work;
sixth, matters concerning storehouses.
The ten types of bodily requisites are:
first, the matter of drink;
second, the matter of food.
Third, matters concerning the three vehicles;
fourth, matters concerning robes;
fifth, matters concerning ornaments.
Sixth, matters concerning dance, song, music, and so forth;
seventh, matters concerning perfumes and garlands;
eighth, matters concerning requisites.
Ninth, matters of light and darkness;
tenth, matters of men and women.
If one relies on the aforementioned list of names:
Food and drink are each distinct matters;
now, within this explanation, food and drink are combined into one.
The reason they are unified as a single category is as follows.
The *Śāstra* states: "Precisely by the power of such a dominant mental attention (*adhipati-manasikāra*) based on direct perception, one examines the nature of impermanence as transformation.
This passage serves as a summary and conclusion of the preceding section, extending up to the point where it says, "one should correctly infer," and so forth.
Regarding the various forms and so forth:
the disintegration of the primary elements is easy to know;
their momentary arising and ceasing is difficult to know.
Because [the subject] is subtle,
I shall now proceed to analyze it;
first, I shall initiate the discourse.
How is it inferred from below?
Up to the point where it is established that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) must necessarily undergo momentary arising and ceasing;
this is clarified by the fact that there exists a subtle and minute arising and ceasing.
One can perceive the occurrence of great transformations and arisings-and-ceasings;
it is not by seeing minor arisings-and-ceasings and the like that one knows the meaning of great arisings-and-ceasings and so forth.
From "because it exists due to the conjunction of this and that set of conditions" down to "having arisen,
it naturally perishes without depending on causes and conditions for its destruction."
This clarifies the refutation of the objection.
It states that cessation has causes and conditions.
That is to say, the objection is raised as follows:
Do you not yet understand that both arising and ceasing possess causes and conditions?
Now, it is explained in general:
this dharma arises because of the convergence of various conditions.
That which arises has causes and conditions;
that which perishes spontaneously without depending on causes and conditions is a phenomenon of cessation that lacks causes and conditions.
The treatise, from the point "In this way, by all such causes and conditions of transformation, it is able to cause conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)...
down to "...it is not the case that all of them do not arise at all," clarifies and resolves potential objections.
An objection is raised as follows:
Just as the sun’s heat scorches green leaves and turns them yellow,
does this not mean that it is precisely because of the sun that the greenness fails to appear?
This very day constitutes the condition for the transformation of blue.
To explain this now:
the sun can transform blue into yellow.
In this way, why do you say that the sun is the cause and condition for transformation?
This sun is the cause and condition for the subsequent arising of yellow;
it is not the cause and condition for the prior destruction of blue.
Why is this so? Because people perceive that after the preceding blue color has ceased, a subsequent yellow color arises;
this yellow is not similar to the blue.
Since this yellow production can be apprehended as existing,
we know that the sun serves as the condition for the yellow production,
and not the cessation of blue.
If, after being scorched by the sun, the green decays and yellow no longer arises,
then the daily destruction of the green may be considered the condition for the destruction [of the yellow].
However, since there is a condition for its arising, once the yellow has arisen, it immediately possesses arising.
The yellow that arises tomorrow and thereafter takes blue as its condition;
it is not the case that blue’s destruction serves as the condition, nor is it that all subsequent things are rendered unobtainable by it.
If blue were extinguished, then all subsequent phenomena would be entirely unobtainable.
This very day constitutes the condition for its decay and destruction;
this is the inverse explanation.
As the *Śāstra* says: "There may be certain conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) which, having already perished and been destroyed..."
This is the objection of the opponent: up until the point where even the final residual trace is no longer obtainable,
if this [preceding] has ceased and another dharma arises, [then what follows?]
This may be understood as before.
If, once this dharma has ceased, no other dharma arises,
what then will become of it?
Just as when boiling water, there is no water left at the very end;
so too, when the world is consumed by fire,
there is no ash or charcoal remaining at the very end.
Fire boils water; boiling water extinguishes fire,
and both the fire and the boiled water are exhausted.
Because they serve as conditions and so forth, we know that extinguished phenomena can possess causes and conditions.
The treatise states: "They, too, proceed through a successive succession of causes and conditions."
Regarding the statement "up until performing such deeds," the Master of the Treatise provides this explanation:
"The present explanation states as follows."
This is explained in the same way as the fire that boils water mentioned previously:
it merely serves as a condition for the successive arising of phenomena.
When there is finally no water, the absence of water is not due to the fire.
Now, since the power of water is itself absent,
it cannot serve as a condition for fire to arise later; therefore,
the presently ceasing phenomenon likewise lacks causes and conditions.
Now, Zhu Nan says: "On this very day,
it acts as a condition for that yellow birth,
and it also acts as a condition for the prior cessation of blue."
"Is it not so? He replied, "It is not so.
If a single cause and condition were able to produce both arising and ceasing,"
Arising and ceasing are contradictory;
therefore, how can the conditions for these contradictions be one?
If the productive condition were one, [the result would likewise be so].
The phenomena that arise should not be mutually contradictory;
they should also be one.
Furthermore, if the phenomenon of cessation were to possess causes and conditions, [it would follow that it is produced].
That which exists through causes and conditions is subject to cessation;
that which has ceased becomes the cause and condition for further existence through causes and conditions.
If that which is capable of arising is itself the arising of causes and conditions,
what does this have to do with the cessation of arising?
Therefore, one should know that phenomena subject to cessation cease spontaneously.
Regarding the objection concerning the Lord (*īśvara*) as the cause:

if it were the case that the Lord alone serves as the condition, then all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would have to exist simultaneously with that Lord; why then would they arise only momentarily?
The intent of this objection is as follows:
If Īśvara exists from the beginning,
there must also be a time when he is not Īśvara.
Thus, conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) exist.
Since these conditioned phenomena are simultaneous with the Sovereign Lord (īśvara),
it is known that conditioned phenomena are likewise inherently existent from the beginning.
If it were inherently existent,
it would be permanent and thus should not be designated as "conditioned formations" (saṃskāra).
Because, according to that doctrine, activity does not exist inherently;
having perceived this objection, the opponent then establishes further that Īśvara himself exists inherently.
Since all conditioned phenomena arise subsequently,
the subsequent treatise states:
"If one says that Īśvara and so forth exist prior [to them]..."
Seeing this shift in the opponent's position,
the author of the treatise further pursues the difficulty, saying:
"If [the result] arises only after the activity has ceased, [how can it be produced]?"
Thus, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) do not arise solely from a sovereign creator (*īśvara*);
they further depend upon other conditions.
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "These various conditioned phenomena do not arise with a sovereign creator as their sole condition," and so forth.
If one takes Īśvara as the condition,
then since various conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) exist at times [under his control],
they should all equally have existed from the very beginning.
If subsequent formations were to arise only later,
then those subsequent formations would only be produced by virtue of prayer.
If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) take the act of making a prayerful aspiration as their cause,
why then would only Īśvara be the cause?
Therefore, the subsequent treatise says:
If it is argued that Īśvara [acts] according to his own desires, such as through effort (prayatna) or prayer (prārthanā),
since he has already conceded that desire is the cause,
this must further be examined and refuted.
Therefore, the subsequent treatise asks:
"If that is so, does this desire have a cause? and so forth, provisionally assuming that desire has a cause.
If one takes sovereignty as the cause,
then since sovereignty is primordial,
desire should also be primordial.
Because whenever there is sovereignty (*īśvara*), there is also desire (*kāma*).
This is refuted by the same arguments previously applied to the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "If one says there is a cause, it would be like [the claim that] *īśvara* and so forth are the cause."
If one were to propose that the Sovereign Lord (Īśvara) is the cause,
once that has been refuted, there would still be other causes;
it is not the case that the Sovereign Lord is the cause.
If you wish to posit a distinct cause,
then just as the aforementioned formations have desire, effort, and aspiration as their distinct causes,
one might now say that they further take desire, effort, and aspiration as their causes.
If there were a separate dharma other than Īśvara acting as the cause,
then all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would arise from a distinct cause;
why then would one need to falsely imagine a useless Īśvara?
Therefore, the subsequent section of the treatise asks: "If it is said that this desire has further causes and so forth...

The treatise then states: "In brief, it is due to the power of three kinds of predominant mental attention (*adhipati-manasikāra*), up to and including the power of inferential mental attention (*anumāna-manasikāra*)."
As previously stated at the beginning of the preceding fascicle, the teaching on the nature of impermanence was cited to engender pure faith;
this is precisely due to the predominant power of the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of pure faith within this context.
As previously stated, the eight kinds of causal conditions,
as well as the fifteen or sixteen kinds of transformations and so forth,
are all directly perceived.
This refers to the second [stage], wherein, through the predominant power of the mental attention of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-manasikāra*),
one sequentially infers that within all causes and conditions, there is arising and ceasing at every moment (*kṣaṇa*).
However, because the dominant power of inferential attention (*anumāna-manasikāra*) is present herein, all of these are indeed the three types of attention within this context. The treatise asks:

"Regarding the five modes of practicing impermanence previously cited that accord with cultivation, the two modes of transformation and disintegration have already been explained; why, then, does one further contemplate the nature of impermanence by means of the mode of separation (*vibhoga*)?"
The beginning of the fascicle states that one enters into the realization of the Truth of Suffering by means of ten modes of practice.
Among the four modes of practice concerning suffering,
within the first five modes of practice:
One realizes impermanence.
Among these five modes of change, the first is the mode of transformation,
which consists of the eight types of causal conditions previously explained.
The fifteen or sixteen types of transformation and so forth constitute the second,
the aspect of disintegration (*vibhava-ākāra*).
This is because, as previously explained through inference, the momentary arising and ceasing and so forth are the aspect of cessation (*nirodha-ākāra*).
Having already explained two modes of practice,
how is it that the third now further contemplates the nature of impermanence by means of the mode of separation?
In the treatise’s explanation of the internal mode of separation:
It is said that one who was previously a master of others— neither a slave nor a servant, capable of enjoying things for oneself— and so forth,
later loses that status as a master and ceases to be a non-slave or non-servant, instead becoming a slave or servant to another.
This intention is like a person who, when formerly a master, was neither a slave nor a servant; later,
having lost the nature of a master, he no longer possesses the nature of a slave or servant,
but instead acquires the nature of another's slave and the state of being their servant.
One acts with mastery,
as in the case of those who have changed offices and so forth;
this is because one contemplates the nature of impermanence while discussing the practice of the dharma-nature.
Regarding the statement, "that which is called 'all that is subject to transformation, impermanence, and so forth,'" the intended meaning here is as follows:
it is like the present experience of pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*).
At the time of experiencing meditative absorption (*samāpatti*),
there is no impermanence of transformation;
rather, it is by means of the three modes of impermanence beginning with transformation that [impermanence is understood].
Contemplating present pleasant sensations at the time they occur,
although their nature of impermanence has not yet manifested,
it will do so in a future life.
Because these three types of impermanence are necessarily present,
one penetrates this truth in such a way:
that pleasant feeling will certainly be impermanent in the future life.
Although the nature of impermanence is not yet manifest in the present life,
it will be so in the future; therefore,
the treatise states that "union is impermanent."
It means that one contemplates present phenomena by means of the aforementioned three kinds of impermanence,
because they are conjoined with these three kinds of impermanence.
This is called the impermanence of conjunction;
that is, the aforementioned pleasant feeling in the present life.
These flow into these three types of impermanence.
The treatise states: "In this way, through the reasoning of proof and the cultivation of higher training, once one has attained certainty regarding the nature of impermanence," and so forth.
There are three types of reasoning for establishing proof.
First is establishment by means of authoritative scripture (*āptavāda*),
as stated at the beginning of this volume:
The ten lines are listed.

Subsequently, these ten lines are able to correctly observe [the truth] by means of the principle of logical proof (*upapattisādhana-yukti*); herein, first, according to the principle of authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), as the Blessed One said:
Having thus briefly explained the two types of impermanence—the internal and the external—it is said:

"In this way, for the time being, by the power of the superior attention of pure faith, based on the reasoning of the authoritative scriptures (*āptāgama-pramāṇa*), the practitioner of meditation... and so forth.
This is the authority of the ultimate teaching (*āptāgama*).
Within the authority of the ultimate teaching, two matters— internal and external—
are clarified, including sixteen kinds, fifteen kinds, eight kinds, and so forth, of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
This is the second direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The second [section], which was the detailed explanation of the sixteen aspects, has now concluded.
As it says below: "Precisely by the power of such a dominant mental attention (*adhipatimanaskāra*) based on direct observation..."
Having observed the nature of impermanence through transformation,
the passage beginning with "those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and so forth" clarifies the establishment [of this truth] through inference (*anumāna*).
These three constitute the principle of proof (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*) herein;
furthermore, the phrase "because of the cultivation of the predominant [factor]" refers to the principle of authoritative scripture (*āptāgama-yukti*) and so forth.

The subsequent passage states: "This is due to the power of the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of predominant pure faith, or due to the power of the mental attention of direct perception, or due to the power of such inferential mental attention," and so forth.
In this context, because he also cultivates the higher training,
he understands the authoritative scriptures (*āptāgama*) and so forth;
each of these [authorities] is examined individually below.
Mental attention (*manasikāra*) is itself the cultivation of intensification.
The treatise states: "Immediately following this, one enters into the practice of asceticism and reflects thus: 'All such conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent,' and so forth."
Regarding the passage, "Thus, by way of the aspect of the unattractive,

one enters into the contemplation of suffering," it should be understood according to the subsequent text as referring to those formations that are conducive to painful feeling, as well as to painful feeling itself.
By way of the aspect of the unlovely,
one enters into the suffering of suffering;
by means of this very aspect, one enters into the three types of suffering within that [suffering of suffering].
Within this category of the disagreeable mode of existence,
the preceding seven types of suffering are subsumed;
these seven sufferings are all, without exception, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).
If one follows the *Abhidharma* and other textual sources,
among the seven types of suffering, the first five are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*),
and the subsequent two are the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
Regarding those points that contradict this text,
it is explained for now as follows:
the first seven [types of suffering] are associated with the aspect of being undesirable.
Among the seven types of the unlovely (*apriya*),
the first five are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

Now, by means of these three modes of activity— the mode of being unlovely (*apriya-gati*), the mode of being bound (*saṃyojana-gati*), and the mode of being unstable (*anavasthāna-gati*)— [they are so designated].
Because it is subsumed under the three types of suffering through association;
that is, it is subsumed by way of association.
Although there is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) within that which is undesirable, [it is still categorized as such].
All these are subsumed under the gateway of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*),
because the few are included within the many; thus,
both types of suffering are the suffering of suffering.
Furthermore, because these lead to the arising of painful feelings and so forth,
all seven are indeed the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*). Why is this so?
Next, in the second clarification regarding the practice of fetters and bonds:
by means of the practice of fetters and bonds, one enters into the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*).
This occurs precisely at the locus of the fetters and bonds, such as craving and so forth.
The arising of craving and so forth gives rise to the entire mass of suffering consisting of birth, old age, sickness, and death; therein,
those seven types of suffering that accord with the experience of pleasant feeling constitute the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Therefore, one should know that the arising of painful feeling in accordance with [the nature of suffering] is the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā).
The arising of neutral feeling in accordance with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings is the suffering of conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).
The lower section concludes by entering into the three types of suffering.
As for the discrepancies between the preceding and following sections of the treatise,
these are resolved here by seeking the meaning through their essential nature and characteristics according to their contextual convenience.
Furthermore, regarding the distinctions among the categories of summarized meanings,
that treatise must correlate the three types of suffering with the eight types of suffering. Thus,
we know that five of these constitute the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
This treatise subsumes the eight types of suffering under three modes of activity.
The mode of being unlovely constitutes the first seven sufferings;
now, these three modes of activity are subsumed under the three types of suffering.
Therefore, it is subsumed under the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*). The aspect of being unlovely is the suffering of suffering;
the aspect of being unlovely is not subsumed by [the category of] the suffering of suffering.
The seven types of suffering included therein constitute the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
therefore, there is no contradiction. This is because they are distinguished according to their categories of inclusion.
The following clarifies the distinction between the two practices of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*anātman*):
emptiness refers to the absence of intrinsic essence,
while selflessness refers to the absence of functional agency.
