That is to say, they calculate that having an essence is "existence," and they use emptiness to dispel this; they take the function of existence to be the "self," and they use non-self to dispel this.
In the exposition of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*),
there are three successive expositions.
In the first exposition:
Regarding the understanding of the causes, accumulations, arisings,
and conditions: as for the statement that craving is called the "cause" because it is known to draw forth suffering,
consider, for instance, presently encountering an object conducive to pleasant feeling.
Within that, craving arises;
one should know that this immediately perfumes craving and so forth to form seeds.
At the time these seeds are formed:
Furthermore, it causes the seeds of future birth and so forth to grow therein;
for this craving is able to draw forth and produce those seeds of birth and so forth.
Therefore, it is called the "cause" (*hetu*). Since it has already drawn forth suffering and can further summon and assemble it so that it arises, it is called the "origin" (*samudaya*).
This refers to how the aforementioned craving (*tṛṣṇā*) moistens the constituent of formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, thereby bringing about existence (*bhava*).

It is called "accumulation" (*samudaya*) because this craving accumulates other factors that can produce future results; it is called "arising" (*samudbhava*) because, having drawn forth suffering, it causes that [suffering] to emerge.

That is to say, once craving has perfumed the seeds of suffering, it is able to cause the seeds of suffering to give rise to the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of birth and other forms of suffering.

Because craving can cause the seeds of birth and so forth to arise as actual manifestations, it is called "arising" (*utpāda*); furthermore, because it is able to grasp and sustain the seeds of future sufferings and sequentially draws forth the accumulation of all sufferings, it is designated as the "condition" (*pratyaya*).
Since craving is able to grasp and increase the seeds of future suffering through perfuming,
it is able to bring about the sufferings of future birth and so forth.
Arising in succession,
the origination of all sufferings is called "condition."
This first section, moreover,
is largely consistent with the sixth fascicle of the *Abhidharmapitaka*;
please compare them.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of "cause" in terms of its general and specific distinctions:
all forms of craving that are able to crave for a future self-substance are termed "attracting suffering";
this is the general definition.
The other three are distinct.
Having already cited suffering,
craving is called "origination" (*samudaya*) because it causes the fruits of the three realms and five destinies to manifest in the present and accumulate as future results.
Once the five destinies have been drawn together, craving causes the manifestation of birth for an individual within those destinies and so forth; this manifestation is called "birth.
Once birth has manifested for an individual within the destinies and so forth, [the remaining links follow].
Craving causes these various stages, such as birth and so forth, to arise within this person's body, manifesting in succession; this is called "condition.
These three [stages] thus arise individually in their respective order.
Consulting the sixth fascicle, it is the same as this.
The meaning of the second "furthermore" (punar) is that the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) serves as the cause for the link of grasping (*upādāna*).
The link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the origin (*samudaya*) in relation to the link of existence (*bhava*), because it is capable of accumulating all karmas.
Furthermore, it is by means of the link of craving that the link of birth (*jāti*) is brought to manifestation; this is called "arising" (*utthāna*).
That is, the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is able to draw forth the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) from afar;
its manifestation is called "condition" (*pratyaya*).
This is the third sequential explanation of the meaning.
One understands that the seeds of all afflictions are attached to the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as their basis;
one knows that the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) such as craving and so forth are called "causes" because they are the causes for future existence in a subsequent life.
To know that the seed of craving can produce future fruit is what is meant by "knowing.
Because of this single type of seed,
the subsequent three types of active manifestations are termed "craving."
Craving is called "origination" because it draws forth and gathers future existence;
with this craving for future existence as a condition,
it further gives rise to [craving] toward present objects.
The arising of craving accompanied by joy and attachment is called "arising" (*udaya*).
Taking this very craving that accompanies it as a condition,
the arising of various forms of craving for joy and pleasure toward future objects is called "condition" (*paccaya*).
Among these four kinds of craving,
the present craving that clings to one's own self is not mentioned here;
furthermore, this is simply the first of the four cravings, termed "craving" alone.
This craving is craving in its general sense;
its specific characteristics are difficult to discern.
It is now described by means of the term "seed."
In fact, this applies to all active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
Although the treatise speaks of "afflictions in general," its intended meaning refers specifically to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Because this craving can induce the production of future results,
it is referred to as "craving for the three" (*trṣṇā*).
Furthermore, this craving for renewed existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*) can further give rise to craving that is accompanied by delight and greed (*nandīrāgasahagatā tṛṣṇā*).
Craving accompanied by joy and greed arises in dependence upon present objects;
together with this craving, there arises craving for one's own future existence.
Because it can also give rise to craving toward present objects by means of the future body,
it is called "concomitant craving" (*sahagatā tṛṣṇā*).
With craving for future existence as the cause,
and because craving arises in connection with excellent objects in the present,
[one craves] for excellent objects in the future.
Furthermore, because various forms of craving and delight arise,
those various cravings and delights also have concomitant craving as their condition.
In the exposition of the four aspects of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*):
the complete exhaustion of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is termed "cessation" (*nirodha*);
the complete exhaustion of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is termed "tranquility" (*śānta*).
That is to say, the aforementioned two kinds are the foremost, supreme, and unsurpassed, and are thus called "sublime" (*praṇīta*).
Furthermore, the aforementioned two kinds are eternally abiding and constitute definitive emergence, and are thus called "detached" (*niḥsaraṇa*).
This concludes the explanation of the four aspects of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) in the treatise.
Regarding the object of the cessation of the knowable,
it can act as a path that enables the thorough seeking of meaning.
It is called the "path.
This is because the path enables one to reach the dharmas sought after;
and since that which is sought includes both the false and the true.
That which is sought through thorough investigation is real and not false; this is called "suchness" (tathatā),
as it distinguishes [reality] from the false.
Not only is one able to seek the truth within the Truth of Cessation,
but one is also able to know the Four Truths as they truly are through their respective gates.
That which can follow and turn accordingly is called "practice" (*caryā*),
because it traverses the Four Noble Truths.
Practice traverses the Four Noble Truths.
What is it that can bring about transcendence from birth and death?
It is called "transcendence" (*niḥsaraṇa*) because it has the sense of being able to proceed single-mindedly toward *nirvāṇa*,
and because it transcends all worldly afflictions (*kleśa*).

The Treatise says: "Since he has thus, within his own internal experience, directly perceived the aggregates and, based upon the principles of the truths, has engaged in unerring reflection and correct observation," and so forth, up until:
"he is able to permanently sever [the afflictions] and achieve ultimate liberation."
The intention here is that,
by means of the principle of the Four Noble Truths,
one contemplates the aggregates as they appear within this realm.
Having established impermanence and so forth,
one is able to use reasoning to infer and examine the aggregates that are not currently perceived within other, dissimilar realms.
That is to say, all conditioned and contaminated phenomena belonging to those other realms and so forth,
which pervade all locations within the three realms and exist within every category of the aggregates.
At all times throughout the three periods,
there exist such assemblages of factors capable of producing results; thus,
the truth of suffering arises from the conjunction of difficult-to-reconcile conditions, such as birth, aging, and so forth.
All things follow this principle of suffering and impermanence;
all phenomena, such as karma and afflictions, which constitute the truth of origination,
have the nature of being produced through causes, origination, and conditions.
If these formations possess the nature of cessation,
which is tranquility and bliss, this is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The path that exists therein is capable of severing all afflictions.
The ultimate transcendence of birth and death is the Truth of the Path;
this is the intended meaning of this passage.
The practitioner perceives this by means of direct observation in one direction, using it as an analogy for the aggregates and so forth that are not directly observed in other directions.
The treatise states: "This is the basis for the seeds of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)."
The intention here is that one practices these four truths by means of the five applications of mindfulness,
both collectively and individually.
This is precisely the locus of support for the seeds of subsequent untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Because a single tainted [condition] can serve as a condition to induce the untainted,
it is called the "locus of support for seeds."
This refers to the meaning of newly perfumed seeds.
Second, during the time of the five preliminary practices (*pañca-vastūni*),
one is also able to further increase the beginningless untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).
This type of cultivation, while situated within the stage of the five cessations (pañca-vyapakarṣa),
is also subsumed under the stage of the attention that discerns characteristics (lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manaskāra),
because it is capable of differentiating the essence and giving rise to the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (dharmajñāna-anvayajñāna) at the initial vision of the path.
This is called the basis for the seeds of the knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge (*dharmajñāna-anvayajñāna*).
In the commentary on "excellent attention" (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*), it says:
"Such attention takes only the truths as its object and remains exclusively in meditative concentration."
Based on this mental attention (*manasikāra*),
in order to sever the basis of the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*),
the subsequent text states that the coarse forms of *asmimāna* arise both intermittently and continuously.
Since this attention consisting of resolute conviction proceeds either intermittently or continuously with the conceit "I am," why is it said to be exclusively in a state of meditative concentration?
Is this not contradictory?
The meaning is as follows:
the aforementioned attention characterized by clear manifestation...
When a single virtuous mind takes a single object as its focus,
because it was previously interspersed with hearing and reflection upon that same object,
now, when resolute conviction arises, [it occurs].
It is exclusively wholesome.
When focused on a single object, it is not interspersed with hearing or reflection;
it remains continuously in meditative concentration.
This excludes the "characteristic-of-comprehension" [mental application];
therefore, it is said to be "exclusively.
This statement is based on the fact that for a long duration, one remains in a single observation within a wholesome state of mind.
It is not that he does not emerge from meditative absorption to give rise to the conceit of "I am," nor that he regresses and gives rise to other afflictions; rather,
the following passage intends to clarify his suppression of the conceit of "I am."
In reality, because one conceives of a self through pride,
[the afflictions] arise either intermittently or without interval;
however, in the present case, they are distinguished by being clearly understood through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
It is said to be "exclusively" [meditative] because one abides in contemplation for a long duration;
it is not like the "characteristic-discerning" [stage], where one cannot enter contemplation for a long duration due to the alternation between hearing and reflection.
Therefore, it is called "exclusive."
This is not contradictory.
In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, within the explanation of "limitlessness," it says:
"That is to say, the flow of birth and death and such phenomena are limitless, and so forth."
The meaning of this section is to clarify that the Four Noble Truths are boundless;
the details of the text may be understood accordingly.

The Treatise states: "Once one has understood that such pride is an obstacle, one is then able to swiftly penetrate it with wisdom and, by means of spontaneous engagement through mental attention (*manasikāra*), subdue all external objects of knowledge and enter into [the state of] mental attention."
This "conforming attention" (anuvartaka-manasikāra) is precisely the aforementioned "I-conceit" (asmimāna),
for by means of this internal self, one is able to enter into accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding "the attention of entry by way of following" (*anupraviṣṭamanasikāra*): as for "the attention of entry" (*praveśamanasikāra*),
it refers to that which has already long wandered through saṃsāra in the past and will likewise wander in the future.
Up to the point where signless suchness is itself signless;
that which arises by taking external objects as its objective support is called the "mental engagement of entry."
That practitioner, following this mental attention,
applies himself with diligence and continuity to contemplate the Noble Truths;
once this contemplating mind has ceased, it does so for a time.
Subsequently, one again gives rise to the immediate [state],
observing the flow and abiding of skillful means;
the preceding mind of observation then subsides.
Subsequently, one observes the arising of the mind;
using the subsequent mind as the object of the preceding mind,
one applies oneself with single-minded diligence without substitution.
For this reason,
it is impossible for a coarse form of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") to arise;
this is the intended meaning of the passage.

The treatise says: "In this way, the practitioner who diligently cultivates yoga observes that the continuity of the mind arises anew at every moment, differing from one to the next, either increasing or decreasing.
Here, "practitioner" (yogācāra) refers to the one who practices.
When practicing meditative cultivation,
if each moment of thought increases in excellence, it is called "increasing";
if it does not increase in excellence, it is called "decreasing."
Although there may be a momentary arising of something abrupt,
since there is both increase and decrease, as well as change and transformation,
it is clearly known to be impermanent.
Since this very mind of observation has entered into the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*),
it is clearly known to be suffering;
there is no such thing as a real calculation that these are truly dharmas.
However, the nature of suffering is what is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
One contemplates that the mind is suffering and that the very phenomena (*dharma*) it conceives of as real are suffering.
Because one contemplates the absence of a second phenomenon, they are not real.
The second [type of emptiness] is that all falsely conceptualized real dharmas are called empty.
That they lack autonomous function is what is meant by the "practice of non-self" (anātman);
this is the intended meaning here.
That is to say, one takes the Truth of the Path as the object of contemplation in terms of its impermanence and so forth;
this is because, from the perspective of the mind of contemplation that resembles [the path], it is the Truth of the Path.
However, according to the actual mind of contemplation, it is the Truth of Suffering.
Because it is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*),
this is now explained in terms of its conformity to the supramundane meaning.
Furthermore, within this stage:
Because it possesses the meaning of being untainted (anāsrava),
it is called the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya). Regarding this meaning:
It also takes the Truth of the Path as its object in terms of impermanence and so forth;
however, in terms of its actual nature, it is the Truth of Suffering,
as reconciled in the ninth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*.
The two [factors], namely "newly perfumed" (*navābhyasta*) and "natural" (*dharmatā*),
explain this passage within the treatise’s exposition of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
It is said that while its mind appears to have ceased, it has not truly ceased;
because non-conceptual wisdom is tranquil and subtle,
it is termed "cessation."
Now, this resembles that;
because it is not the actual wisdom of that [object], it is called "resembling cessation.
Furthermore, non-conceptual wisdom itself ceases.
To observe the discriminating mind is called cessation;
now, this which resembles that is called "resembling cessation.
Furthermore, the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is also named cessation.

Because it causes the mind to become subtle, it resembles that meditative absorption of cessation and is thus called "resembling cessation. Regarding its being "resembling the absence of an object of cognition while not lacking an object":
non-conceptual wisdom has no objective support consisting of mental images.
Now, although this is without marks or characteristics,
because it possesses an image resembling that [object], it is said to be "resembling" something even though there is no actual object of cognition.
Furthermore, because this object-possessing [consciousness] is present before one,
it is not without an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Although the mind is subtle, it appears as if it were without an object.
Yet it is not without an object;
furthermore, non-conceptual wisdom is free from conceptualization.
It is far removed from all signs and far removed from all afflictions;
because this [present state] resembles that [former state].
Although the words appear to describe detachment,
it is not true detachment;
this is explained in the treatise within the section on the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).

It is said that immediately following this, one gives rise to internal mental attention (*manasikāra*) regarding the principles of the Noble Truths previously contemplated; immediately upon that mental attention, there arises—in accordance with the sequence of the Truths previously contemplated, whether they were directly perceived or not—within those Noble Truths, a definitive knowledge free from conceptual differentiation (*avikalpa-niścaya-jñāna*) and a direct perceiving knowledge (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*), each arising in its respective order.
Immediately following the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) of the previous life,
and based upon the principles of the Noble Truths as observed during that supreme mundane dharma,
one now enters the gateway of the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
One gives rise to internal mental attention.
Immediately following this mental attention of the true path of seeing,
within the path of seeing through images:
In accordance with the truths previously observed at the time of the first dharma,
if these two are directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), while other things—
such as those in different realms or those not belonging to one's own sphere— are not directly perceived (*parokṣa*).
Within the various noble truths,
there exists an untainted, non-conceptual certainty that follows the sequence of suffering, its origin, and so forth.
Doubt and wisdom arise spontaneously from within oneself rather than being induced by others;
this wisdom is produced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
unlike the conceptual doubt that exists prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It arises from the stage of "comparable" (anuloma);
this is the intended meaning here.
Furthermore, it is proven that [the path of seeing] arises immediately after the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma).
The name [of this section] follows immediately from that.
Now, I intend to explain the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which is difficult to understand;
thus, I shall bypass the discussion of the semblance path of seeing (*pratibhāsadarśanamārga*).
However, the state from which one turns back toward the immediate [attainment] is precisely the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*); thus,
it now serves as the precursor to what follows.
This refers to the arising of internal mental attention (*manasikāra*) regarding the principles of the Noble Truths previously contemplated;
this occurs precisely at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Immediately following this mental attention—
Following the sequence of the truths previously contemplated,
within the path of insight (*lakṣaṇa-darśana-mārga*),
whether they are directly perceived or not directly perceived.
The arising of decisive knowledge (*niścaya-jñāna*) and directly perceived knowledge (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) is also the intended meaning here. The treatise states:

"Because this is permanently abandoned, if one has previously already become free from desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmadhātu*), then at this present time, having entered such a direct realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), they obtain the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*); it should be understood that they are no different from those previously described as being free from desire."
"Up to and including not returning again to be born in this world"—
this refers here to first employing the mundane path to suppress and abandon the desires of the desire realm.
Now, at the time of entering the Path of Seeing,
one who attains the fruit of Non-returning is a person who has transcended [the stage of] Non-returning.
For now, setting aside the discussion of non-returners who have already detached from the desire realm,
this extends up to those who have previously detached from the sphere of nothingness;
this detailed debate is excerpted and synthesized from the thirteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmapitaka*.

The characteristics of one who has abandoned desire for the world were not previously explained in the preceding fascicle—such as having serene deportment, speech that is grave and solemn, and being free from agitation and the like.
Now, because this [subject] resembles those [characteristics], [they are mentioned here].
It says, "One should know that there is no difference," and so forth.
Furthermore, although they are similar, there is a slight distinction:
namely, that a non-returner (anāgāmin) is not reborn in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
He entered parinirvāṇa right there;
this is not the case for those who have left desire behind in the world.
Thus, there is a distinction between them.

The treatise states: "Because the knowing wisdom and the known object are in harmony without contradiction, and are observed as being present before one, it is called 'clear realization' (abhisamaya)," and so forth, up to:
"It should be understood that this is likewise true for the brahmins and others."
When entering the path of seeing and realizing suchness,
because the object— suchness— is signless,
its cognition is likewise signless.
Second, there is the non-dual harmony of signlessness;
because the subject that perceives and the object perceived are free from the contradiction of signs,
and one observes them directly before oneself, it is called "clear realization" (abhisamaya).
To explain the meaning of the term "clear realization" (abhisamaya):
it is like a kṣatriya being in harmony with another kṣatriya in one place, without any conflict or contention.
Because they share the same lineage,
they constitute a single class;
this is also termed "clear realization" (abhisamaya).
Brahmins and others should know that it is likewise:
the signless path of seeing is the union of subject and object;
being signless, there is no discordance.
Therefore, it is called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*).

The treatise states: "This also attains numerous characteristics; that is to say, by realizing the clear realization of such truths, one attains the four knowledges," and so on, up until "fully accomplishing numerous characteristics."
Regarding the clear entry into the path of vision,
there are twelve kinds of characteristics;
that is to say, because one realizes the direct contemplation (*abhisamaya*) of the truths in this manner.
These two phrases apply throughout the following twelve bases.
One thereby attains four kinds of knowledge,
namely, regarding all mental engagements (manasikāra), whether in motion or at rest, and so forth.
Up to the knowledge of illusory phenomena (*māyākāryajñāna*).
This first illumination refers to the attainment of four knowledges upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
These four knowledges are:
First is the mere dharma-knowledge;
that is, when one was an ordinary person,
one falsely conceptualized a real self.
Now, upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one eliminates the notion of a real self;
there is only the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding the mere designation of dharmas.
During the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one falsely conceptualized [existence] as either annihilation or permanence.
Now, entering the Path of Vision,

That is to say, from time immemorial,
there exists the nature of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
which is the sense of that which can be severed.
What is called "lineage" (gotra) refers precisely to that locus where defilements can be severed;
therein exists the untainted seed (anāsrava-bīja).
When one generates the mind and takes up the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*),

the *bodhipakṣadharma* factors such as the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā*, *cintāmayī-prajñā*) that are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) are identical in meaning to those previously described.

The Commentary states: "Because all bodhisattvas rely upon and are established in their own vehicle's lineage (gotra), they possess the capacity for endurance and great power"—this is the first interpretation.
The "upholding of the lineage" (gotra-dhara).
The commentary states:
Now, in explaining this passage, we shall provisionally present two interpretations.
First, by virtue of relying upon the spiritual lineage (*gotra*),
one possesses the capacity and power to attain awakening (*bodhi*).
First, by means of the potential and power inherent in one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*),
one is able to establish great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
Second, by means of one's own vehicle lineage (*yānagotra*).
Because it serves as a basis,
one possesses the capacity to achieve perfect enlightenment.
Because the lineage of one's own vehicle serves as the basis for establishment,
it possesses great power and realizes great enlightenment.
The lineage (gotra) serves as the basis for these two explanations;

it is likewise explained in these two ways within the subsequent section on the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) that arise from the generation of the mind of awakening (cittotpāda).
Furthermore, there is another distinct explanation regarding the maintenance of the lineage (gotra),
namely the naturally inherent lineage (dharmatā-gotra).
This refers to the maintenance of the two initial stages of resolve prior to the ten levels of faith (daśa-śraddhā).
That is, from the stage of the ten faiths onward, it maintains the factors conducive to perfect enlightenment (*sambodhipākṣikadharma*);
that is, from the stage of the ten understandings onward.
Furthermore, it is said to maintain the lineage (*gotra*).
This refers to the ten stages of faith.
Second is the maintenance of the initial resolve,
which refers to the stage of tenfold understanding.
The "upholding of the factors of enlightenment" refers to the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*).
Although this interpretation has not yet been fully elaborated upon in the authoritative scriptures, [it is presented here].
Without a basis, how could there be a reliance?
Furthermore, there is the maintenance of the lineage,
which refers to the maintenance of the resolve for awakening (bodhicitta) that arises from the natural order of phenomena (dharmatā).
The initial generation of the mind occurs at the beginning of the one hundred thousand kalpas prior to the ten stages of faith;
it may also be attained by taking the first principle as the basis for the true generation of the mind.

The treatise states: "A person who abides in the state of lacking the spiritual lineage (agotra), because they lack such a lineage, is certainly incapable of attaining unsurpassed enlightenment, even though they possess the generation of the mind and engage in preparatory practices as their support."
The commentary states:
There are three interpretations regarding those who lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*).
In reality, there is no time when the capacity to generate the bodhicitta exists;
this is spoken as a provisional argument.
Therefore, although it is said that "one generates the mind" and so forth, [it is only in a conventional sense].
This is the first explanation:
those whose lineage of the two vehicles is fixed are also said to lack the lineage of the Mahāyāna.
Even though one may encounter the conditions to give rise to the bodhicitta,
because such a person is still incapable [of sustaining it],
it is said that although they have generated the mind and so forth.
This is the second explanation:
namely, those persons who by their very nature lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*).
Although they may in fact resolve to attain enlightenment, [they do not truly possess it].
In the end, they will surely regress and be unable to attain that unsurpassed bodhi.
This is the third explanation. Question: Generating the bodhicitta is not for the sake of seeking worldly fruits.
From what kind of seed does this manifesting mind arise?
The commentary states: it arises from seeds of merit-constituting virtue, not from untainted seeds.
Because they lack skillful means and untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*),
the treatise states: "They bring them to maturity solely by means of the roots of goodness of humans and devas," and so forth.
In the commentary on the explanation of its alternative names,
it is also called "the auxiliary cause," "the basis for the stages," "the precursor," and "the dwelling," because it assists in the accomplishment of the result.
Because it can produce a fruit;
because it relies on the attainment of a fruit;
and because it follows the conventional designation of a stage.
Because it guides the arising [of phenomena],
and because it contains and stores the fruit;
these are respectively correlated with the auxiliary causes and so forth.

The Commentary states: "As it has been said regarding the lineage (gotra), so too should one know the conduct and preparatory practices (prayoga) of the initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment (prathama-cittotpāda).
The Explanation states:
This means that just as the lineage possesses the sense of being preceded by auxiliary causes and so forth.
One should know that the generation of the mind and so forth are likewise thus. Question: What is the practice of application (*prayoga*)?
Previously, it was explained that maintaining the generation of the mind is called the practice of application.
Now, this is also called "the practice of application.
The commentary states:
the two types, "that which is practiced" (*pratipadya*) and "that which practices" (*pratipad*), differ in name.
The practice that is to be performed refers to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma);
it is the practice that is capable of performing [the task].
This refers to that generation of the mind;
therefore, the previously mentioned generation of the mind is called the application of practice (*prayoga*).
Here, according to the text, this pertains to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
This refers to the two distinct types of applied practice (*prayoga*). In the treatise,
it is explained that there are two kinds of spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
The original lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*) and the lineage of practice (*śikṣā-gotra*) are established according to the three meanings of "newly perfumed" (*navābhyasta*), as appropriate.
Some say that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla takes the name "practice" (*śikṣā*) to refer to the stages beyond the first ground (*bhūmi*).
Not so; for prior to the [ten] stages,
the ten faiths do not give rise to untainted seeds.
When that seed is produced, it is called the "cultivated lineage" (*abhyāsa-gotra*).
It is described as "produced" because it increases accordingly;
this is the distinct interpretation of the master Ratnacandra.
Only the *viśeṣa-mārga* (the path of excellence) establishes the sense of "family" (*gotra*) in terms of the function of severing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The "cultivated family" (*abhyasta-gotra*) refers to the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
It takes as its seeds the outflow-tainted [dharmas] such as hearing and reflection. Question:
What is the path of seeing for superior rebirth?
Explanation: The term has two meanings.

The Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma) serve as the predominant condition (adhipatipratyaya) for either the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti) or [the subsequent stages].
The patience regarding the dharma of the suffering of birth is,
among all conditioned phenomena,
the only one that is untainted.
It does not arise from causes and conditions;
alternatively, it arises with the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) as its cause and condition.
Because it has been practiced for a long time,
the contaminated wholesome [states] that can sever the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) are the most excellent;
this is because they possess the sense of being supreme.
This serves as the causal condition for the arising of the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*;
such is the intention of this master of the treatise (*śāstrakāra*).
Taking this as the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) is as explained later;
it is the superior condition (adhipati-pratyaya) arising from the principles established by our former masters.
Since this has been transmitted from antiquity,
and because one wishes to distinguish a particular meaning,
this formulation is established.
As for those whose intention is to ascend,
they do so solely to protect the meaning of the Dharma.
Some people say:
It is not the case that those who protect the Dharma have not yet separately planted the seeds during the stage of the ten faiths;
this has been explained extensively in other treatises.
As stated in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, there are distinctions:
prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), there are three minds.
The first is the mind of faith (*śraddhā-citta*).
Second is the abiding mind;
third is the firm mind.
Within the stage of faith, these are called the "abiding in the lineage of cultivation."
That is, the ten stages of understanding (*adhimukti*) and the ten stages of practice (*caryā*),
these twenty mental states combined constitute the stage of abiding mind (*vihāra-citta*) and the firm mind (*dṛḍha-citta*),
which is the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
I have searched for that sūtra in the western regions,
but have not yet heard of an original manuscript existing there.
Nevertheless, I shall now provisionally synthesize it.
To summarize the intent of that sutra:
the lineage of the stage of cultivation (*śikṣāgotra*) constitutes many lineages.
As that very sutra states:
The "nature of the stage of practice" refers to being within the state of faith; that is,
the stage of the ten faiths.
The "nature-lineage" (*prakṛti-gotra*) refers to the state of abiding in the mind.

In that sutra, the ten stages of understanding (*adhimukti*) and the ten stages of practice (*caryā*)—which are designated as the ten understandings and ten practices—are called the nature-lineage. Question: For what reason is this stated in that sutra?
First, the acquired surname (xi xìng) is clarified;
subsequently, the original surname (běn xìng) is clarified.
The commentary states:
At the very moment of initial cultivation,
it is called the "name" (xing);
once the subsequent cultivation is perfected, it is called the "clan" (xing).
This is because it is designated as the "nature-lineage" (*gotra*).

This sequence of before and after does not accord with the meaning of this treatise. Question: For what reason are those twenty mental states (*citta*) condensed into ten stages (*vihāra*) [in some systems], while in the *Avataṃsaka* and other texts they are expanded into twenty mental states?
The commentary states: This is to distinguish it from what precedes and follows.
Because the former initially gives rise to superior faith, it is distinguished as being different from what precedes.
Since they are not adjacent and because this is the first vision of the Path,
these are combined into twenty moments of mind.
It is merely designated as "one dwelling.
Therefore, that sūtra states that the ten dedications constitute the lineage of the path of cultivation (*mārga-gotra*).
Because the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*),
that which follows the path of seeing is called the lineage of practice (*caryagotra*);
such is the intended meaning of that sutra.
The intended meaning of this treatise is that,
logically, this cannot be so,
because their natures are each distinct.
In the *Śāstra on the Explanation of the Coarseness and Subtlety of Seeds*, it says:

"Furthermore, this lineage that has not yet practiced to fruition is called 'subtle' because the fruit does not yet exist; that which has already practiced to fruition is called 'coarse' because it coexists with the fruit."
The commentary states:
This refers to the initial perfuming of the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*).
Because the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) increase and double in strength, they are described as "coarse" and "subtle."
It does not belong to other stages.
How, then, can it be called "simultaneous"?
This is according to the interpretation of Dharmapāla.
Furthermore, it forms a distinct seed;
the newly arisen seed coexists with the old seed—
this may be explained in such a manner.
According to the interpretation of Candragomin,
it merely causes the old [seeds] to increase;
that is, they are the newly added seeds within the mental continuum (*manas*).
In terms of its meaning, it is explained as the fruit;
in the older version, the seed is explained as the cause.
Therefore, they are said to be "both."
Furthermore, when considering a preceding moment in relation to a succeeding moment,
although they are distinct moments,
the cause ceases as the effect arises.
Because the cause exists,
it is able to produce its fruit; therefore,
they are said to be simultaneous.
As in the meaning of the *Jayasena-sūtra*,
the seeds of beginningless contaminated wholesome dharmas are called the cause;
this is the causal condition at the initial stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
The untainted teaching perfumes and produces new seeds;
these seeds are the fruit,
while the beginningless seeds serve as the cause.
Because cause and effect are simultaneous, they are said to be "coexistent.
The treatise states: "Regarding those various mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, and so forth..."
The meaning here is this: one should not even allow others to deceive or mislead them, much less do so oneself;
for a person possesses various kinds of treasures.
Because the mind is deluded and inverted,
it is unable to collect [the senses] and unable to guard them.
Having first entrusted it to another,
because the mind was deluded and inverted,
one was unable to remember it.
The Bodhisattva is able to awaken others correctly;
he would not even allow others to deceive him,
much less do so himself.

The treatise says: "His nature is to delight in vast wealth and status; regarding all such extensive resources, his mind is inclined toward their enjoyment, and he delights in great undertakings rather than narrow or meager means."
This means that because the bodhisattva’s mind is vast,
they delight in utilizing it;
it is not a matter of meager wealth and status.
His nature is to delight in vast wealth and status,
because his undertakings are extensive rather than narrow or meager.
Furthermore, as previously clarified,
although the objects of giving may be few,
one is able to distribute them equally through the act of generosity.
It is vast rather than narrow or meager.
Now it is clarified that the nature of this [generosity] is to delight in bestowing great wealth and status,
and is able to distribute its activities equitably.
"Vast and not narrow or meager" refers to the distinction from the previous passage concerning "few things" and "many things" as objects of delight.
The treatise states: "Those who value the reception of the Dharma and value the future world."
This is one meaning:
it refers to the bodhisattva’s profound generation of faith and reverence toward the four dharmas of undertaking;
that is to say, deep faith.
The four types of feeling (*vedanā*) are explained in the fourth fascicle below:
namely, present suffering and pleasure, future suffering and pleasure, and so forth,
as well as retribution in future lives.
The Bodhisattva has deep faith;
because of this faith, their words are weighty.
Furthermore, they have deep faith in the acceptance of the four dharmas.
And because they believe in future lives,
they perceive even minor transgressions as deeply fearsome.
How much more so regarding many transgressions;
therefore, one should not commit faults within these precepts.
It possesses the four means of integration— loving speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—
which should be sought and applied accordingly.
Below, the ten paths of action are also clarified.
If one investigates this according to the text,
there are further three kinds of ethical discipline (śīla) throughout [the treatise],
namely: the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-śīla), and so forth.
One should seek this out.
Within patience (*kṣānti*), there is only the patience of enduring enmity and harm.
This is explained in the treatise within the section on diligence (*vīrya*).
It possesses three types of clarity:
beginning from "all bodhisattvas" below,
up to "one must ultimately accomplish the skillful means through discernment."
This clarifies the diligence of application.
Next, from "whatever one undertakes" downwards,
it extends to laziness, negligence, and despondency.
It clarifies the diligence of donning armor regarding all vast undertakings, let alone minor ones;
it clarifies the diligence that is free from cowardice.
Within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), there are likewise three types.
This begins from "As for all bodhisattvas...
and extends down to "...and having developed a deep yearning for detachment."
This clarifies the meditative concentration of skillful means (*upāya-dhyāna*).
Its nature is such that its afflictions are thin;
this is true even for those of the inferior grade, let alone for those of the friendly or neutral grades.
"Seeing or hearing [the suffering of others] below" clarifies the meditative concentration that benefits sentient beings;
"below" clarifies the meditative concentration that brings forth supernormal powers.
This explains the third [point].
The treatise states: "Regarding phenomena, one is able to receive them, uphold them, and contemplate them," as explained by Vasubandhu in the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*.
These are correlated with the three types of wisdom—those arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
"Hearing" refers to receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
"Reflection" refers to recollecting and contemplating [the teaching] without forgetting it.
This very volition is able to produce cultivation;
it is named after its cause,
and thus the wisdom of cultivation is called "volition."
This is another distinct interpretation; consult the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* further for its specific explanation.
Examine the intended meaning within the section on wisdom (*prajñā*).
There is no separate clarity; these three types are now correlated:
its nature is not dull or rigid, nor is its nature subtle or obscure.
Their nature is not deluded.
These three phrases correspond,
in sequence, to the three types of wisdom.
Regarding the aforementioned phrases, the treatise states that a bodhisattva is one who is able to mature only the innate wisdom (*sahaja-prajñā*)—
that is, the goodness acquired at birth—
and is also able to enter into all [levels].
The "fields of knowledge" (*vidyāsthāna*) are the objects of the sphere;
that is, skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
These two phrases constitute the general meaning.
These are correlated with the three types of wisdom.
The subsequent text also generally clarifies how the three types of wisdom are free from faults and possess the power of analytical discernment.
Furthermore, his nature is not dull or ignorant;
he should apply himself to the wisdom of application (*prayoga-prajñā*). This wisdom is capable of entering into all fields of knowledge (*vidyā-sthāna*) as its objective domain.
Subsequently, the innate wholesome [states] are matured;
because the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-prajñā*) gives rise to verbal expression,
it pervades each and every [object].
Having departed from states of negligence,
possessing the power of analytical discernment,
that non-conceptual wisdom.
Because it differs from what precedes and follows,
it will not be discussed again here.
Furthermore, this provides a general explanation of the bodhisattva’s wisdom.
It is not necessarily the case that the three types of wisdom are explained separately here.
As the treatise states: "One should know that this is called the coarse characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the bodhisattva lineage capable of inference.
This is because the subtle characteristics of the bodhisattva lineage are difficult to discern.
Now, because one can infer the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) by means of conduct,
it is said that one can infer the coarse characteristics of a bodhisattva’s lineage. Thus,
the opening passage of this section states:
By means of these marks,
others are made to recognize that he is truly a bodhisattva;
as for his subtle marks, they constitute the definitive, ultimate meaning.
Only the Buddha can know this;
herein, for the time being, we defer to the Buddha and do not say that I myself do not know it either.
The claim made by ancients that Maitreya was unaware [of this] is erroneous.
For the *Śīla-sūtra* states:
I have already briefly explained the coarse characteristics of the spiritual lineage (gotra).
As for all other actual meanings, [they shall follow].
As for "only a Buddha can know," even Śākyamuni would not have known it;
thus, one must acknowledge that this knowledge is attributed to the Buddha.
It is not that Maitreya does not know;
rather, he says that while the Buddha knows completely, he himself does not know completely.
How could such a principle exist?
If one were to state generally that Maitreya does not know [this], it would be an error.

The Treatise says: "Regarding the bodhisattvas of the lineage (gotrabhū), as long as they have not yet been defiled by the four secondary afflictions (upakleśa) that are contrary to the white dharmas (śukladharma)—whether these are present or absent... and so forth.
Among these, the "white dharmas" refer to the first six perfections and the four secondary afflictions,
which will be listed below in their respective order.
For those bodhisattvas of beginningless lineage who have not yet become fully endowed with the four [qualities],
or when they are not fully endowed with the four types of defilement:
The lineage is associated with these six perfections;
however, because it is defiled by those four secondary afflictions,
the white dharmas do not manifest.

The Treatise states: "If there is a person (*pudgala*) who lacks the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), one should know that even if they possess all [the conditions], in every way and of every kind, they will certainly not realize awakening.
Regarding this, the traditional transmission says:
Regarding "all" being of three kinds:
the first "all" refers to the Buddha; the second "all" refers to...
[the rest of the sentence is missing from the source].
This refers to the practice of training.
The third [category] is all [phenomena],
which refers to the three periods of time.

It is said that those of no lineage (agotra), despite having a Buddha and the practices to be learned, will certainly not realize bodhi throughout the three periods of time. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
"The first 'all' refers to the Buddhas."

The second "all" refers to having no inverted attachments regarding the practices to be studied. The third "all" refers to... [text fragment] ...the practices to be studied. The ninth "all" refers to the non-arising of all obstacles. The tenth "all" refers to the non-arising of all secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). The thirteenth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of transition. The fourteenth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of existence. The fifty-third "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of thirst. The fifty-fourth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of desire. The fifty-seventh "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of obsession. The fifty-eighth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of fixation. The fifty-ninth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). The sixtieth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of discursive thought.
