The ninety-third "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental perseverance. The ninety-fourth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental commitment. The ninety-fifth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental dedication. The ninety-sixth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental devotion. The ninety-seventh "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental aspiration. The ninety-eighth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental resolve. The ninety-ninth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental determination. The hundredth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental certainty. The one-hundred-and-first "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental conviction. The one-hundred-and-second "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental confidence. The one-hundred-and-third "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental trust. The one-hundred-and-fourth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental reliance. The one-hundred-and-fifth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental support. The one-hundred-and-sixth "all" refers to the non-arising of all forms of mental foundation. The one
This refers to expedient means that are rapid;
it is the reverse of the three preceding causes and conditions,
with the sole exception of those whose faculties are not yet mature and who lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*).
They may also encounter a Buddha and practice the teachings;
they must quickly make vows and so forth,
for there is no fourth stage of ripening the faculties.
One should know that they will certainly not realize bodhi.
Regarding the "Chapter on Generating the Mind," the second generation of the mind is maintained as explained previously.
What constitutes the essence of this vow?
This means that its essence consists of desire, faith, and resolute conviction;
alternatively, its essence is subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna).
Therefore, among the ten perfections, the first six constitute correct wisdom.
The latter four are subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*),
because they are situated in the eighth [ground] and take subsequently attained wisdom as their essence.
If one defines it by its essential nature,
then desire and faith constitute its substance;
however, this is as explained in two passages of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* itself.
If one follows the subsequent passage below,
its essence consists of definitive aspiration;
this aspiration is precisely the mental factor of desire (*chanda*).

The *Śāstra* states: "The first aspiration generated by a bodhisattva among all the correct aspirations of bodhisattvas is the initial correct aspiration, which is universally capable of encompassing all other correct aspirations.
The subsequent commentary on the section concerning the generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) states:
The initial generation of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) is able to encompass all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma),
because it is preceded by the most excellent roots of virtue.
The word "and so forth" refers here to the initial generation of the mind through right aspiration.
Because they are all intense and sharp,
they are able to encompass the other aspirational minds.
Furthermore, this initial aspirational mind serves as the foremost.
Since all other previously arisen aspirational minds and so forth belong to this same category,
they are subsumed within this initial aspirational mind.
The treatise states: "In this way, one should know that the initial arousal of the mind has five aspects; as for what is called its 'intrinsic nature,' this concludes the previous five points.
The particle "and" (又) signifies the meaning of a conjunction, which should be applied accordingly to each point in sequence.
The treatise states: "Furthermore, from the very first moment they generate the resolve, bodhisattvas are said to have entered the Mahāyāna;
thus, that which is subsumed under 'generating the resolve and entering' is what is intended here.
This passage clarifies the following meaning:
A bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind is said to enter the ranks of those who have entered the Mahāyāna;
this is stated in accordance with worldly convention.
For a bodhisattva who is entering the Mahāyāna,
this is not the true entry;
as for the true entry:
This refers to bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi onwards;
if such a bodhisattva exists,
that is the true meaning.
This is not a matter of worldly sentiment or conventional discourse.
The treatise states: "In this way, it should be understood that the initial generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*) is the root for entering and gathering [beings] toward enlightenment;
it is the basis for training that flows from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). This constitutes the fourfold formulation.
This concludes the explanation of the meaning of the four *ya* syllables.
The treatise states: "The four conditions (*pratyaya*), the four causes (*hetu*), and the four powers (*bala*).
Conditions are remote; causes are proximate.
With power as its auxiliary companion,
it generally clarifies two kinds of causes;
thus, there are three distinctions.
The treatise states that the "ten secondary afflictions" (upakleśa) refer precisely to the ten types indicated by the character "many" (bahula) below;
among these are sorrow, suffering, unwholesome conduct, and so forth.
These are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) because they arise in accordance with the primary afflictions. Thus,
they are named secondary afflictions.
Their essence is not that of the primary afflictions;
furthermore, they are designated as "secondary afflictions" because they are numerous.
Its essence is not that [of the primary afflictions];
it is subsumed under the category of secondary afflictions (upakleśa) and is thus called a secondary affliction.
In the commentary on the four causes,
the second cause states:
"Depending upon being sustained by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and virtuous friends."
How does this differ from the first of the four previously mentioned conditions? In that condition,
one merely observes the performance of supernatural powers,
but has not yet received instruction.
Because he now instructs and exhorts us as our kinsman,
this is the cause.
We have witnessed him performing a divine transformation.
This is because they are distant and do not provide instruction;
this is the condition.
Therefore, there is a distinction between the two.
The third among the causes:
one frequently gives rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings.
Regarding the difference between this and the fourth stage within the period of the intermediate kalpa during which one saves sentient beings: in the former case,
one merely initiates the aspiration for enlightenment oneself.
Causing others to resolve their minds [upon awakening],
and undergoing suffering on their behalf during the causal stage,
are causes because they are based on intimacy.
The treatise states: "Based on four objective spheres, although one has not practiced them habitually, one can give rise to lower, middling, and superior compassion without interruption.
The four objective spheres refer to the previously mentioned cases of others, oneself, and those suffering, and so forth.
Whether seeing it in oneself or seeing it in another,
one encounters suffering accordingly.
One gives rise to inferior compassion if one sees oneself or others encounter even a single suffering; one gives rise to middling compassion if one sees [them] encountering [any such suffering].
If one perceives oneself or others undergoing the great suffering of the Avīci hell,
one gives rise to supreme compassion to rescue them;
or alternatively, regarding the four objects.
Each [of these] is capable of giving rise to superior, middling, or inferior compassion.

The treatise says: If bodhisattvas generate the mind of awakening by relying on the four general and specific causes and conditions—whether through their own power, the power of past causes, or both powers combined—it should be known that this mind is firm and unshakable. Alternatively, if they generate the mind through the power of others, the power of application (*prayoga*), or both powers combined, it should be known that this mind is neither firm nor stable, yet it is not without movement.
The meaning here is that,
among the four causes and four conditions mentioned previously,
one may rely individually upon a single cause or a single condition.
Alternatively, there are those who generate the mind [of enlightenment] by means of all four causes and four conditions;
among these, regarding the four powers:
Furthermore, it relies on two powers,
namely the power of its own causes.
Within these two powers:
Whether generating the mind of enlightenment by relying on one power individually,
or by relying on these two powers collectively.
All of these are firm and immovable.
If one generates the resolve for enlightenment based on the power of others, the power of application,
or both powers combined, [it is likewise so].
This is not solid,
nor is it immovable.
Within these four conditions:
The initial object of focus refers to those who are in close proximity to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth;
this present passage, however,
concerns both specific and general objects of reliance.
All are firm and immovable;
other-power is likewise so,
meaning the power of others such as Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is then subsumed within that which is non-solid yet not without movement.
How is this not contradictory?
The commentary states: It is not so.
"Other-power" refers to kings and those who possess authority,
who compel one to generate the aspiration for enlightenment through coercion.
It is not like seeing the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
when one sees the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they spontaneously arouse the mind [of awakening],
for being gathered within the conditions, they are immovable.
Generating the resolve through being urged by others is categorized as "movement" because it is driven by the power of others;
furthermore, it includes the power of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
This is not something that is unstable, nor is it something that lacks movement;
it is like the second cause among the causes [for the arising of a sprout].
It is the gathering together by a virtuous friend.
"This is the firm and immovable withdrawal.
What is the meaning of this?
[The author] states: It is not so.
Being sustained by virtuous friends is the condition encountered when a bodhisattva engages in the practice of the teachings and so forth;
although one may encounter such a friend within the power of a superior person’s application of effort, [it is not sufficient on its own].
These are merely virtuous persons of the world and are not like Bodhisattvas;
therefore, there is a distinction between them.
Furthermore, for the sake of the meaning, let us consider this from one perspective.
In this context, it is judged as being firm, immovable, and so forth.
As for reality, within the causal conditions,
there is that which is movable and not firm.
Regarding the statement that "among the powers of his preparatory application,
there are the immovable [knowledges] and so forth," this is for the sake of distinguishing them according to one particular meaning.
This treatise is written for this purpose.
The treatise states that there are four causes and conditions that can cause a bodhisattva to retreat from the bodhicitta. What are these four?
They are listed as they appear in the text itself.
This is the opposite of the four causes mentioned previously;
it is simply their reversal. The treatise states:
"The faults of encompassing followers are of two kinds: namely, providing benefit or causing harm to followers, and being defiled by either compliance or opposition toward these two matters."
That is to say, defilement arises as a depreciation toward what is disagreeable,
and defilement arises as an exaggeration toward what is agreeable;
therefore, these are called the two matters.

The treatise says: "By virtue of this, the bodhisattva matures such merit free from affliction and harm, which is twice that of one protected by the protection of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), and is equal to twice the merit of a wheel-turning monarch."
That is to say, it is the merit such that malevolent spirits and demons cannot approach;
it is the merit of having no illness in one's remaining body.
The merit of acting with valor for the benefit of others;
the merit of teaching the Dharma without weariness;
and the merit of transforming the heavy burdens of the coarse aggregates into lightness.
The efficacy of mantras is proven by many instances of their blessings.
Regarding this, it is said:
"Mantra phrases and vidyā-phrases."
That is to say, it refers to a mantra phrase that is not an ordinary sentence;
it is a mantra possessing illuminating words,
or it is this very mantra.
There are those who possess the power of clarity and great majestic spiritual authority;
they are called "Sentences of Clarity" (vidyā-pada).
When ordinary beings employ it, there is no efficacy;
when Bodhisattvas employ it, there is immediate efficacy for the sentient beings they seek to liberate from affliction.
The merit of gentleness and patience;
the merit of having afflictions become thin and slight;
the merit of being free from calamities while in one's country.
The merit of swiftly escaping the miserable realms;
the merit of being able to weary of all sufferings;
and the sixteen chapters from "Chapter on Benefiting Self and Others" onwards.
This is the first maintenance;
it is the maturation of the third factor of enlightenment.
This is the one maintenance.
Within these sixteen chapters,
there are three major divisions,
as the treatise states:
Briefly stated, regarding the stages where a bodhisattva trains, the manner of such training, and the basis for being able to practice and train:
according to the former Master Yuanyuan,
there are two [aspects] to the maintenance of the resolve from this point downward.
The first five chapters clarify the dharmas to be studied;
the subsequent eleven chapters [clarify the stages of practice].
It clarifies their learning and conduct;
yet now it is said that this is not so.
According to this treatise:
There are three types of training grounds;
namely, the training grounds of the preceding five chapters constitute the first.
If one trains in this manner,
it constitutes the sixth and final category:
clarifying how such training damages the factors of training.
It constitutes the second [category].
If one is able to practice and study it,
then there are the remaining ten categories.
This clarifies the conduct for those practicing the training;
it constitutes the third [section].
First, the points of training:
There are five categories and seven dharmas.
What are the seven dharmas?
They are listed as they appear in the text itself.
What are the five categories?
They are formed by grouping the seven into five.
How are they grouped into five?
Namely: the chapter on the benefit of self and others,
the chapter on the meaning of reality,
and the chapter on power.
The "Chapter on the Dharma for Maturing Sentient Beings" and the "Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment" (bodhipakṣa-dharma) are combined as one,
being the first and second [chapters] respectively.
Because the five or six dharmas are grouped together as one,
they are designated merely as "five categories";
here, these are expanded into seven dharmas.
This should have been manifested in a separate location;
however, it is introduced here at the beginning of the "Chapter on Benefit for Self and Others" because it is listed first among the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
The factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) are maintained;
they receive their name from being maintained starting from the final chapter.
In the first section of the treatise, "Explaining Pure Benefit for Both Self and Others," the initial portion clarifies pure benefit for oneself.
Regarding the clarification of self-benefit:
First, the factors that obstruct self-benefit are clarified.
This refers to those bodhisattvas who,
regarding purely self-benefiting and altruistic [practices],...
This continues until one does not transgress the conduct appropriate for a bodhisattva.
Within this, there are two parts;
first, the explanation of the dharmas that ought to be abandoned.
That which constitutes a transgression of the Dharma and is not in accordance with the Bodhisattva’s conduct— what should be known and what should be abandoned—
is the second [point], clarifying that which one should practice and study so as not to overstep the precepts and to remain in accord with the Bodhisattva’s conduct.
One should diligently practice and study.
This concludes the general explanation of the two categories of dharmas: those to be abandoned and those to be studied.
Hereafter, the specific dharmas that constitute obstacles to self-benefit will be explained.
There are eight points that should be understood according to their meaning.
The treatise states in the second section, "Brief Explanation of Self-Benefit and Common Benefit for Others":

"If bodhisattvas, whether motivated by compassion as their primary impulse, or for the sake of dedicating [merit] toward unsurpassed enlightenment, or for the sake of rebirth in heaven, at all times cultivate generosity, patience, and so forth—up to self-benefit and common benefit for others."
The intention here is that,
because one gives rise to compassion and intends to benefit others,
one seeks awakening.
For the sake of benefiting others,
they are born in the heavens to benefit sentient beings and teach and transform them.
It is not like the former [category] of what should be abandoned,
wherein one clings to heaven as supreme bliss and seeks birth in heaven.
Now, for the sake of others, one is born in heaven;
this is because one takes compassion as the foremost principle and thus cultivates generosity,
patience, and the other perfections.
Seeking the joy of awakening and rebirth in heaven—
because all these are for the sake of delighting in benefiting others—
they are called "benefiting oneself while simultaneously benefiting others."
The *Śāstra* states: "Furthermore, excluding all such characteristics as previously described, and including everything else...
down to 'the bodhisattva should diligently practice and study therein.
Herein, this reverses the aforementioned obstacles to one's own benefit (*svārthavibandha*).
This should be understood as corresponding to "benefiting oneself.
Now, the treatise states:
"The opposite of the former is called benefiting oneself and benefiting others."
If one were to translate [the term] as merely "obstructing self-benefit" and practice only deeds for one's own benefit,
it would follow that this is solely self-benefit.
Because self-interest is an obstacle,
the bodhisattva does not engage in it;
this is what the present intention clarifies.
Because it involves the destruction of things shared with others,
although it is the opposite of self-benefit,
it nevertheless carries the meaning of benefiting others.
The same applies among the hindrances:
if one considers only the practice for one's own benefit,
then there are only hindrances to one's own benefit.
If one says that the desire to benefit others is also obstructed by the hindrance of benefiting others,
the following passage in the "Explanation of Benefiting Others Together with Oneself" states:
Furthermore, setting aside the aforementioned characteristics,
all other bodhisattva practices for the benefit of others that are contrary to those [characteristics] are included.
One should know that all these are termed "benefiting others together with oneself.
This is the opposite of the aforementioned [wrong practices],
specifically the cultivation of giving based on the wrong view that there is no cause and no effect.
Violating the precepts and departing from right practice while preaching the Dharma to others—
these two factors are obstacles solely to the benefit of others.
This is for the benefit of both others and oneself;
it should also be understood as the reversal of the obstacle to exclusively benefiting others,
in order to practice the conduct of exclusively benefiting others.
Now, the meaning is explained:
because there is the principle of encompassing others,
although it overturns obstructive practices, it extends to both self and others.
The two preceding passages are similar.
Since the bodhisattva takes the benefit of others as his primary principle,
only that which benefits others— and that which benefits both oneself and others— is not an obstacle.
Regarding those who seek their own benefit,
there are three obstacles within the practice of purely benefiting others.
First, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings...
Having abandoned the form realm, they are reborn in the desire realm for two reasons: first, to benefit sentient beings;
and second, to teach and transform those in the ten directions in accordance with the supernormal powers previously attained.
Third, because the fruit has already been perfected,
he has no further personal seeking;
he acts solely for the benefit of others.
Having completed the explanation of these three— performing deeds of great benefit, supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), and so forth—
one should diligently study them so as to sever the former two dharmas.
Regarding the "two dharmas," these refer to the two dharmas mentioned in the preceding section on the reversal [of the three natures].
The treatise states: "The category of benefit refers to the benefit of oneself and others."
It refers to practicing a single dharma oneself and causing others to practice that same dharma; because one practices this same single dharma for both oneself and others,
it is called a "category" (jāti).
The four modes of experiencing phenomena (catvāri dharmopavicārāḥ): namely, pleasure and pain in this world and the next,
which together constitute the four propositions.
These are called the four dharmas of reception.
In the treatise, the third and fourth dharmas are explained together. Question: This section clarifies the categories of benefit for oneself and others;
why, then, are the first and fourth dharmas [treated separately]?
Experiencing these in the next world brings benefit to neither;
they are all painful sensations.
Is this not clarified herein?
The commentary says:
The Bodhisattva does not accept the fourth dharma for the sake of benefiting himself and others.
If this practice were of no benefit to oneself or others,
the Bodhisattva would not intend it;
such is the case within the fifth category.
Regarding the statement that there is nirvana and the dharma of nirvana:
by attaining nirvana,
one achieves both self-benefit and the benefit of others, encompassing both the mundane and the supramundane.
This fifth cause cites the previous second and third matters to provide a general clarification;
the first and fourth intentions are not adopted.
Furthermore, one receives the Dharma through four dharmas for the sake of self-benefit.
Because they know what is feasible and what is not feasible,
they also share this knowledge with others,
and they themselves likewise know what is feasible and what is not feasible.
Since both oneself and others know what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced,
one practices the former and does not practice the latter; thus, both are benefited.
In the commentary on the explanation of the five kinds of happiness,
the essential nature is briefly set forth.
Regarding what is called "happiness caused by causes":
It has three factors as its essence:
namely, karma that results in pleasant fruit,
as well as the two factors of the faculties and their objects.
That which can produce contact conducive to pleasant feeling—
these three are the causes of the essence of pleasure;
they thus possess the nature of the five aggregates.
Because it takes as its object all karma that accords with pleasant results,
its associated and co-existent factors all have pleasure as their essence; collectively,
they take the five aggregates as their essence.
The second is the experience of pleasure,
which refers to the feelings of joy and bliss;
it encompasses both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
It serves as the essence of the experience of pleasure.
It is the pleasure that is the antidote to the three types of suffering,
as stated in the text.
That is to say, when sufferings such as cold and heat cease,
a sensation of pleasure arises;
one then regards that very pleasure as suffering by means of wisdom.
The antidote to suffering is the essence of happiness;
furthermore, the state in which suffering is absent is conventionally described as this happiness.
It does not possess a real substantial entity;
this shall be clarified and explained in the subsequent text.
Accordingly, it may encompass all five aggregates;
this is the essence of feeling, wherein the four types of feeling are the abandonment of suffering and pleasure.
Thus, the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling is taken as the essence of pleasure.
That is to say, the seed of the mind of aversion is established upon the basis as the meditative absorption of cessation;
within the state of the absorption of cessation,
all seeds of the mind of aversion [are present].
All these are the essence of happiness.
The treatise states that concentration constitutes the essence of happiness.
Fifth is the happiness free from affliction and harm.
The treatise is of four kinds.
First is the joy of renunciation,
which refers to those who have left the household life.
The subsequent text concludes by stating, "Because it is able to accord with [it]," which refers precisely to the joy of awakening (*bodhi*).
Second is the joy of seclusion (*viveka-sukha*).
This refers to the joy and bliss born of seclusion attained within the first dhyāna,
which has the category of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) as its essence.
Third is the bliss of tranquility.
The scriptural texts state that from the second dhyāna upward, the cessation of all vitarka and vicāra is called "the bliss of tranquility.
Thus, the meditative absorption (samādhi) of the second dhyāna and above is itself the essence of this bliss.
Because it eliminates applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*),
wisdom (*prajñā*) is also the essence of bliss.
This is the bliss of the four [dhyānas] and the three types of enlightenment (*sambodhi*).
This is precisely perfect awakening;
it refers to the bliss of non-conceptual wisdom,
or it may also include subsequently attained wisdom.
This constitutes the essence of bliss.
By severing the afflictions, one attains this wisdom;
that which is thus attained is the bliss of unconditioned nirvāṇa.
This is subsumed under pleasure (*sukha*).
It is called "cessation" (*śānti*) because it serves as the realization of cessation;
it is subsumed under mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*).
This is the essential nature of the five pleasures.
Furthermore, these five pleasures are all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
for they do not clarify the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
One does not grasp at the bliss of the tranquility of nirvāṇa.

The Treatise states: "That which is called the cause of pleasure refers to the two categories of pleasure—the sense faculties and their objects; when these serve as causes, they are contacts that accord with pleasant feeling."
Regarding the phrase "having pleasure as its cause":
that which serves as the cause for pleasure is called "having pleasure as its cause."
This means that because the two factors of faculty and object are able to produce pleasant sensation,
they are called "two factors";
they are the causes of pleasure.
Furthermore, the faculties and objects can also produce contact conducive to painful feeling;
here, we take those faculties and objects that produce contact conducive to pleasant feeling—
those faculties and objects which exist within the state of pleasant feeling.
Therefore, the *Bhavavarga* states:
"Furthermore, the explanation of the two categories of pleasure."
That is to say, within the nature of pleasure itself, there are two types: contaminated and uncontaminated pleasure;
furthermore, there are two types: physical and mental pleasure.
In the present text, it is stated that the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) act as causes,
capable of producing two kinds of pleasure— both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*)— pertaining to both body and mind.
The sense faculties and their objects are not treated as two separate things;
they are merely considered the causes,
while the "mind" (manas) refers to the resulting effect produced from them.
This refers to tainted and untainted pleasure.
It takes the cause that produces [pleasure]—
namely, the sense faculties and their objects— as the cause of pleasure.
Furthermore, there are two types of grasping regarding the category of pleasure (*sukha-varga*):
as previously stated, one is the grasping of the fruits of the mind and body, whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*);
the second is the grasping of both causes and fruits.
The two— the faculties and their objects— constitute the two categories of pleasure.
Although the pleasure of the result is mentioned,
the intent is to take the pleasure of the cause.
In the second section of the *Śāstra-vyākhyā* on the experience of pleasure, it says:
"By virtue of the three causes and conditions subsumed under the aforementioned cause of pleasure," and so forth.
These three causes and conditions are precisely the two: the sense faculty (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*).
And the karma that accords with pleasant results constitutes the third.
To provide another distinct explanation,
one should adopt the specific meanings as previously set forth.

In the *Tarkajvālā* (The Blaze of Reasoning), while distinguishing between those pleasures that are intrinsic and those that are not intrinsic, it states regarding the fourth type—the pleasure of the cessation of sensation:

"However, based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all sensations whatsoever are suffering; because this ultimate suffering is temporarily pacified when one abides in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is called 'pleasure'."
In this context, because the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is untainted (*anāsrava*),
the preparatory mind (*prayogacitta*) preceding it is also untainted;
yet, it is said that what is loathed is suffering (*duḥkha*).
This is spoken with reference to the contaminated states that are to be abandoned from afar,
just as in the case of those unconditioned phenomena;
in reality, however, the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling has already been attained through the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
After a long time, one finally attains that concentration;
at the moment of attaining it,
it is because it is obtained from the preceding path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
It is called the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling;
this case is likewise.
It is certainly an uncontaminated preparatory application (*anāsrava-prayoga*), not a contaminated one.
That which is loathed from afar is termed "loathing.
Although this is called "loathing suffering," even such a distant mental state is still tainted (sāsrava) and wholesome (kuśala).
From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is also suffering.
Furthermore, that it is equivalent to perception (*saṃjñā*), feeling (*vedanā*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is its great significance.
The Treatise states: "All other forms of happiness that are free from affliction and harm" refers to the happiness of renunciation,
the happiness of seclusion, and the happiness of tranquility.
Because this accords with the bliss of enlightenment,
and because it is a factor of enlightenment,
it is able to bring forth the bliss of enlightenment.
This may be understood as before.

The *Śāstra* states: "It should be known that all causes of happiness comprised within karma that yields desirable fruits in the present life and in the future—up to those things which are appropriate for sentient beings—should indeed be bestowed upon them. Thus it is said.
In this context, the first five types of pleasure are explained.
One should reflect upon and discern the meaning of what may or may not be given to sentient beings.
Regarding the first cause of pleasure:
Regarding karma that results in agreeable fruits,
the pleasure of the third, fourth,
and fifth [dhyānas] should be bestowed upon sentient beings unilaterally and without deliberation.
Within that cause of pleasure,
there are two categories: the faculties and their objects,
as well as the second type of feeling, which is pleasure.
One should observe whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to give before bestowing [it] upon sentient beings;
herein there is an obstacle,
as in the case of the third [type of feeling], the cessation of suffering which is pleasure.
There is a sentient being who,
previously being impoverished and suffering,

In order to pacify and eliminate suffering,
the bodhisattva bestows wealth and treasures;
once they have obtained that wealth and treasure, [they use it].
Even down to the commission of various sins through negligence—

For at the time of experiencing this pleasure, one is capable of generating all manner of transgressions.

The bliss of tranquility is the concentration of the form realm;

These are conditioned phenomena;
if they are bestowed upon sentient beings,
those beings will not abandon them once they have obtained them.
Although born in the realm of form, they give rise to craving for the flavor of meditative absorption;
they do not study the internal Dharma,
yet they reckon this state to be nirvana.
Later, they will again be reborn in the evil realms;
when sentient beings obtain this,
it is not without fault.
It is not that there is no defilement;
why then do they not experience pleasure equally? [The answer is:
One observes whether those sentient beings are worthy of receiving it or not.
He then asked: "Is it granted exclusively to all sentient beings?
Furthermore, within the nature of the experience of pleasure, does it encompass both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*)?"
Why is it not said that those with outflows [attain] it?
It is because one who discriminates and contemplates the outflow-free [state] is invariably granted the pleasure corresponding to its cause.
Karma that accords with pleasant results invariably bestows the pleasure derived from the sense faculties and their objects as its cause.
He does not grant it.
There are two kinds of pleasure resulting from this cause:
the pleasure of receiving what is given, and the pleasure of not receiving what is given.
Since there are these two kinds,
one should both give and not give.
Master Yuan said:
Karma conducive to pleasure is taught because it encompasses that which is certain to be bestowed;
it is certain to bring benefit.
If there are sentient beings who give rise to karma conducive to suffering,
the Bodhisattva does not grant it;
if they give rise to karma conducive to happiness, he does grant it.
Because it must necessarily be given;
that untainted feeling within the experience of pleasure subsumes that necessity.
Because those who should be benefited cannot be exhausted,
one must not speak of them partially;
for that which is to be done is immeasurable.
Just as in the case of the four dhyānas, one should give what is determined to be appropriate;

it is not so with untainted feeling (*anāsrava-vedanā*). Question: If there are those whose faculties are matured and who wish to enter the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), [how should they be treated]?
One who is capable of receiving the outflow-free [attainments] is also one whose destiny is fixed;
for what reason, then, would they not be granted them?
The previous interpretation is incorrect.
The meaning is as follows:
if one relies on the ultimate reality, [it is not so].
It is also obtained within the intrinsic nature of sensation (*vedanā-svabhāva*),
just as in the conceptualization of pleasure;
it is merely because of the distinction between the existence-nature and the non-existence-nature.
Untainted feeling (anāsrava-vedanā) should not be categorized exclusively [with one type];
furthermore, it may enter a stage (bhūmi),
yet it cannot be said to enter a stage.
Because they are distinct, one should not categorically state that [the teaching] is bestowed.
Even if it were granted to those who have entered the stages (bhūmi),
it should still be bestowed categorically.
Because it does not allow for the entry of opposition,
it is therefore combined as an illustration.
If that is so, then one abandons the experience of pleasure.
Regarding the happiness free from affliction and harm, how is it reconciled?
Answer: It is by contemplating the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because it is of a distinct nature of feeling.
For what reason is it not the same as pleasure?
Its essence is of three kinds.
One may make such distinctions;
furthermore, the granting of the cessation of pleasant feelings and so forth is bestowed exclusively upon those who have attained it in the present life.
One should know that this has already revealed the untainted (anāsrava) feeling;
it is also to be bestowed,
as it is indicated by the implication of the text.
It does not speak of experiencing pleasure.
This concludes the third major section from the lower part of the thirty-sixth fascicle.
The cause and the result are subsumed under self-benefit and benefiting others;
thus, within both cause and result,
there is self-benefit.
Because it also includes other practices, the treatise states:
"First, the ripening cause and ripening fruit; second, the merit cause and merit fruit; third, the wisdom cause and wisdom fruit.
This is to be understood according to the ripening causes and fruits, etc., mentioned in the subsequent text.
There are separate explanations of the causes and effects of merit and wisdom,
as well as combined explanations of these separate explanations.
Within the causes and effects of maturation (vipāka), there are three [aspects].
First, this explicitly clarifies the nature of the maturation (*vipāka*).
Regarding this nature of maturation,
it should be examined in light of the subsequent statement concerning faith, which describes it as being "endowed with great power."
It is not necessarily the case that all are the fruits of the indeterminate;
rather, at the time of fruition, there are dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*) or outflow fruits (*niṣyandaphala*) which are termed "ripening of the fruit" (*phalavipāka*).
If one is still before the stages [of the path],
it is induced solely by contaminated wholesome karma;
if one is on the stages, [it is induced by both].
Furthermore, the untainted (anāsrava) is also generally employed as the nourishment for karma;
moreover, if it is a resultant neutral fruit (vipāka-avyākṛta-phala),
it is exclusively tainted (sāsrava).
It is subsumed within the stage prior to the grounds;
it also extends throughout the grounds.
If it is a result of increase or a result of uniform outflow, [it is likewise so].
Just as the powers of faith, speech, and so forth exist on the level of the world,
they pertain to both the outflowing (sāsrava) and the non-outflowing (anāsrava), because they arise from subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna).
Such as these are the entities of maturation (*vipāka*).
Second, regarding the explanation of the cause of maturation (*vipākahetu*),
there are eight types according to the subsequent text.
If one is still on the stage prior to the grounds,
there is only contaminated wholesome karma;
if one is on the grounds, [there is both].
They encompass both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*). If a cause brings about a tainted fruit,
this cause is termed "tainted."
If it induces an outflow-free (*anāsrava*) fruit,
this cause is called "outflow-free";
this is termed the second ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Third, regarding the explanation of the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*):
it is not that the fruit induced by prior karma is called the ripening fruit;
rather, the very substance of the ripening is what is summoned by karma.
This is called the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Having obtained the maturation, one relies upon the substance of that maturation to give rise to various activities of body, speech, and so forth.
This is the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
That is to say, the body, speech, and so forth, which are produced by the maturation-entity as their cause, constitute the fruit.
This fruit exists both prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and upon the stages.
All of these may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);
this should be understood according to the underlying principle.
This is called the "intermediate" ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
The second [section], which comprehensively clarifies merit and wisdom (*puṇya-jñāna*), also has three parts:
first, it clarifies the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the two kinds, merit and wisdom;
second, it clarifies the causes (*hetu*) of the two kinds, merit and wisdom.
The three vidyās are the two fruits of merit and wisdom;
the six pāramitās subsume merit and wisdom,
serving as their essential substance.
To what extent the phrasing may seem contradictory, the text itself provides its own resolution;
it applies both to the stages prior to the bhūmis and to those within them, and encompasses both the outflowing (sāsrava) and the non-outflowing (anāsrava).
These causes of merit and wisdom also pertain to both the contaminated and uncontaminated stages, as well as those prior to and upon the grounds;
they are precisely the causes capable of producing merit and wisdom.
The fruits of merit and wisdom refer to the benefiting of things and the benefiting of sentient beings that arise based upon merit and wisdom;
these constitute the fruits of merit and wisdom.
Whether these are causes or effects and so forth,
they are all exclusively wholesome and encompass both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The rest shall be explained as the text proceeds.
Regarding the first [topic], the explanation of maturation (*vipāka*),
the fifth [quality] is the perfection of being trusted by others (*ājñeya-vākya-saṃpad*).
This refers to being one whom the multitude honors and trusts, who serves as a standard for resolving disputes, and who does not practice flattery, deception, or the use of false scales and weights.
...up to being endowed with trustworthy speech.
Sixth, there is great renown that spreads throughout the world,

In this context, it is not by means of an indeterminate dharma that the retributive fruit (vipāka) constitutes its essence;
rather, because it is produced from a prior cause,
it now obtains a fruit of outflow (niṣyanda-phala).
Because it arises from prior causes,
it is explained among the results of maturation (*vipāka*);
this is known from this passage.
It is present throughout the untainted stages (anāsrava-bhūmi).
Furthermore, it is known that within the category of maturation (vipāka), there is the presence of wholesome nature (kuśala-svabhāva) and so forth;
this is explained in the treatise regarding the causes.
Regarding the statement that "the light of the gift of wisdom and fresh, pure garments are called the causes of form and color":
as for "form," it does not refer to the form of manifest color.
If the form of manifested color possesses luminosity,
then it follows that the meaning of manifested color serves as the cause for the effect of shape-form.
Therefore, one should know that "form" (rūpa) refers only to the form of the physical body,
as it takes the manifestation of visible color (varṇa) as its cause.
Furthermore, since they are gathered together,
what contradiction is there in taking visible color as the cause that brings about shape?
Therefore, "form" may refer to the form that is the basis for manifest color.
This is the intended meaning within the discussion of the cause of complete possession of great magnitude (*mahāpramāṇa*).
Having made offerings to the Triple Gem, elders, and others,
one should form a great vow,
praying that in a future age:
One gathers and maintains various merits within one's own person;
this is due to causes such as making offerings and generating aspirational prayers.
The meaning here is that one will, in the future, experience the perfection of great power.
This is explained in the treatise regarding the perfection of human nature.
Regarding the statement that one bestows the nature of another upon someone due to two causes and conditions:
this refers to a man who, being attached to the female form of another’s wife, is about to undergo a change of gender and lose his male organ.
The Bodhisattva exhorts him to restrain himself and protect [his vow], so that he does not undergo the change of gender.
Furthermore, he preached the Dharma for them,
so that those women and men,
through the Bodhisattva’s exhortation, were inspired.
One who does not delight in the female body shall obtain a male body; however,
one whose gender has been transformed may, through the exhortation of a bodhisattva,
attain non-transformation of the gender organ.
In the third of the three distinct causes and conditions explained in the *Śīlaparivarta* (The Chapter on Giving to Others),
regarding the purity of the field (*kṣetra-pariśuddhi*), it says:

"It should be known that, in brief, that which correctly initiates such preparatory application (*prayoga*) and correctly abides in the fruit of this preparatory application is called the purity of the field."
This refers to that which is performed continuously and with constant diligence;
it occurs at the time of initiating this preparatory application (*prayoga*),
as well as upon attaining the respective stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth.
This subsumes the fruits desired through the preceding preparatory practices,
up to and including the Buddha as the ultimate fruit desired through each preceding stage.
These preparatory practices and so forth constitute cause and effect.
Because all are capable of being fields of merit,
they are called "pure fields.
This is explained in the third treatise (*śāstra*) within the section on the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
The fruit of being endowed with excellence of form and color refers to the fact that whatever words one utters are invariably listened to and accepted.
How does this differ from the "endowment with trustworthy speech" (*ādeyavākya*) among the results of maturation (*vipāka*)?
If this fruit arises based on that maturation,
it simply arises based on that;
why must the fruit necessarily have a specific locus of belonging?
Because of his upright appearance and demeanor,
all people place their trust in him.
Furthermore, this was previously mentioned in the context of trustworthy speech.
Because there is no discrepancy in matters such as weights and measures,
what is discussed regarding these things is accepted by all without doubt.
Now, because his physical form and features are so upright and refined,
all people believe and accept what he teaches; therefore,
there is a difference [between him and others].
It is not that a single statement provides clear and explicit explanation in two locations.
In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, within the explanation of the fruit of mastery (*vaśitā*), it says:
"How can one gather all sentient beings through generosity, and so forth?"
Question: Why is it that while the maturation (vipāka) includes the full possession of great wealth, a great retinue, and a great following,

The answer is:
Previously, when the actual practice was undertaken, there were great assemblies and so forth;
now, one employs the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Because the discourse on giving is fully endowed with a great multitude,
whereas giving alone lacks such a large retinue; therefore,
there is no contradiction.
In the discussion of the results of great influence (*mahābhoga*),
there are also mentions of "leaving" [the world],
all of which serve to inspire confidence and trust.
However, because their respective causes differ, it is said that they all act with conviction;
furthermore, according to those causes, their discourse also differs.
If the bodhisattvas themselves possess power, [they act accordingly].
Being unable to properly establish the sentient beings to be converted,
they do not accord with their own welfare while performing such benefit for others.

if one possesses the capacity oneself but has not yet been able to transform sentient beings.

Furthermore, the phrasing [of the text] is unobjectionable.

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, all that is mundane and supramundane pertaining to the parinirvāṇa of the dharmas manifested by the Tathāgatas," the intended meaning here is that the Tathāgata realizes parinirvāṇa.

Answer: This present self-benefit actually encompasses the benefit of others,
taking wisdom as its primary focus.
Taking compassion as primary;
because they differ in meaning, it is explained that [compassion] refers to one's own benefit.
Within no single dharma is there that which is exclusively for one's own benefit; if there were such a thing,

Within a single dharma,
there is only self-benefit and no benefit for others.
This is not like those obstacles.

The treatise says: If, within the desire realm, one is able to obtain the perfection of wealth and treasures in future lives, the perfection of one's own physical form, and so forth, up to practicing the subsequent dharma for the benefit of oneself and others; [this is what is meant].
The meaning here is that one dies in the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm.
Or they are born in the form realm;
having died in the form realm,
they are reborn again in the desire realm.
Regarding the acquisition of one's own body and wealth,
as well as the manifestation of sorrow and suffering,
one cultivates both types of wholesome causes.

it serves both for one's own benefit and the benefit of others in the world to come.
In the fifth chapter of this treatise, within the section on the "Gate of Ultimateity" (*atyantatā*), it is said:
"If all afflictions are forever severed, and if one relies upon whatever constitutes the Noble Eightfold Path to obtain mundane wholesome dharmas, this is called 'ultimateity' (*atyantatā*)."
Just as within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
through the dominant condition of the power of the eight untainted factors of the path (*anāsrava-mārgāṅga*),
tainted wholesome phenomena (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) arise.
It is called "ultimate" because this alone arises and because one has already reached the supreme fruit.
The Chapter on the True Meaning (*Tattvārtha-paṭala*) is the section containing the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharmāḥ*).
Among the sixteen chapters, it is the second.
Regarding the meaning of reality as it is elucidated according to the texts,
take for instance the three natures (trisvabhāva).
The nature of phenomena as imagined by the parikalpita-svabhāva does not exist;
the two [natures], the paratantra and the pariniṣpanna, are said to exist according to the two truths.
Now, regarding the statement "existence" and "non-existence": [it refers to these].
It is said that what is beyond designation should be taken as the true reality.
Now, to clarify this meaning,
it is called the "Chapter on the Meaning of True Reality."
Why is the "Chapter on the Meaning of Reality" explained after the "Chapter on the Benefit of Self and Others"?
It is because [the former] concerns the benefit of self and others.
Regarding the practice of the vidyā-mantras:
since practice must necessarily rely upon principle,
the true meaning is elucidated following the discussion of the benefit of oneself and others.
The sequence of the chapters is as follows;
the main headings are the same here.
For example, at the beginning of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, it clarifies practices such as compassion and non-killing.
Later, regarding the nature of the Tathāgata and so forth within the Four Noble Truths,
from the perspective of ultimate principle,
such sūtras as these [are taught].
Because the examples are not uniform, the latter part of the preceding chapter clarifies the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*).
The treatise states: "First, based on the nature of things as they are (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*); second, based on the nature of things in their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*)."
Furthermore, for example, the nature of the two wisdoms as they truly are (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*) is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*),
which is the wisdom that takes reality as its object.
Observing the objects of cognition according to their principles and in accordance with their true nature is the "exhaustive nature" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*),
which is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Taking conditioned phenomena as its object,
it exhausts the nature of all objective spheres and is able to contemplate them.
This understanding is largely distinguished by the wisdom of principle and phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma-jñāna*).
Furthermore, the contemplative wisdom that observes the Four Truths, the Sixteen Aspects, the three gateways of emptiness, and so forth,
is termed "the nature of things as they are" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
Although the eight contemplations of the mind are subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*),
they remain supramundane because their subsequently attained objects— the aspects of the path of seeing— possess the nature of true suchness (*tathatā*); therefore,
they are called "the nature as it is" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
If, subsequently, one attains a conventional wisdom that understands suchness through the gateway of differentiation— taking as its objects phenomena such as the permanent and the impermanent,
or the contaminated and the uncontaminated— this constitutes the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This is termed the nature of all that exists (yāvadbhāvikatā).
This refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna),
which is divided into two types of wisdom.
This refers to the subsequently attained [knowledge] of the mundane and the subsequently attained understanding of the supramundane.
The treatise states: "Furthermore, there are four kinds: first, the reality established by worldly consensus."
Regarding the fourth, the reality that is the object of purification from the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-gocara-tattva*):
the first refers to what is commonly accepted by the world as conventional;
this is based on the conventional reasoning of existence.
Because this phenomenon exists as that which excludes the phenomena grasped through conceptual construction,
it is called the "truth established by the world.
It is termed "truth" because it is commonly accepted [by the world].
That is to say, it consists only of conditioned phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava*) and unconditioned phenomena without outflows (*anāsrava*).
As for "the two kinds of reality established by reasoning," these are supramundane because they are established through reasoning.
This refers to those who possess wisdom, up to and including those who practice analytical investigation,
relying upon meanings established through reasoning such as direct perception, inference, and authoritative scripture.
This encompasses both contaminated and uncontaminated, as well as conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
As for the third [type], the reality that is the object of knowledge purified from the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇaviśuddhajñānagocaratattva*),
according to the treatises, it includes the preparatory wisdom (*prayogajñāna*) and so forth of the two vehicles.
This refers to the three types of knowledge attained by the three vehicles,
the objects of those three knowledges,
and unconditioned nirvana.
The dharmas such as the Four Noble Truths are the reality that is the object of the wisdom purified of afflictive obstructions;
they exist solely within the contaminated preparatory wisdom (*prāyogika-jñāna*).
The two untainted knowledges (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and unconditioned nirvāṇa constitute the reality of the true essence.
Regarding the reality of the sphere of purified knowledge regarding the four objects of knowledge, which is the purification of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): [it is as follows].
These are the non-conceptual wisdom and the subsequently attained wisdom—
the two types of knowledge obtained through the abandonment of the cognitive obscurations.
Furthermore, the unconditioned *tathatā* (suchness) attained through the severance of causes is the true essence of this; that is to say,
it clarifies the untainted (*anāsrava*) unconditioned.
Furthermore, regarding the latter two realities,
they refer exclusively to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) obtained through the abandonment of the two obstacles based on their causes;
they do not include wisdom (*jñāna*), meaning they are strictly unconditioned and do not extend to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
In the *Tattvārthapatala* (Chapter on the Reality of the World), it is asked:

What is the "worldly consensus reality" (*lokaprasiddhatattva*)? It refers to that which all people in the world perceive as having a common nature through their cognitive awareness, which conforms to conventional designations, habitual familiarity, and the understanding of various specific things.
This meaning clarifies that all people in the world,
regarding various matters, [act in this way].
It is the verbal expression arising from conventional matters,
which accords with what is commonly accepted by the community as being realized through mental comprehension.
It is listed because it is the true essence of this; that is to say,
"earth is only earth," and so forth—
meaning it is only this, and not otherwise.
That is to say, earth here is simply earth;
water is simply water;
they do not arise from fire, wind, or other elements.
Because they are determined by worldly consensus and have been transmitted from beginningless time rather than being a recent invention,
these are the true entities.
In the discourse on the resolution of principles regarding thoroughly established reality (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*),
it says: "Those capable of vitarka and vicāra, those capable of investigation, and those dwelling in the stage of vitarka and vicāra" refers,
for example, to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
There are those who do not give rise to vitarka and vicāra at any time;
if there are those who do give rise to these vitarka and vicāra,
they are called "those capable of vitarka and vicāra," and so forth.
If one contrasts the desire realm with the form realm,
it is called "dwelling in vitarka and vicāra"; furthermore, the statement that one is "able to vitark and vicār" clarifies the person at the very moment when vitarka and vicāra are arising.
"Abiding in the stage of vitarka and vicāra" refers to those persons whose vitarka and vicāra have matured.
"Dwelling in the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana)" means that noble ones (ārya) abide in the untainted (anāsrava).
They are not excessively distracted by much discussion of doctrines and the like,
because ordinary beings are generally prone to distraction and take great pleasure in such discursive debate.
This refers exclusively to those who abide as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, although noble ones (*ārya*) possess the vision of the truths,
they also possess inferential, direct, and authoritative scriptural knowledge (*āptavāda*).
It exists to a small extent,
because it has already been realized;
whereas ordinary beings have not yet realized it at all.
Because inferential cognition (*anumāna*) arises frequently,
and because it is extensively established through reasoning,
this clarifies the principles of ordinary persons' inference (*anumāna*).
Regarding the dharma that is universally established,
the *Treatise on the Explanation of the Third Reality* states:
"If one is able to induce uncontaminated wisdom..."
Because it is not a contaminated preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*).

Why is it that the reality which is the object of the knowledge purified of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara-tattva*) does not take unconditioned *nirvāṇa* as its object?
The commentary states:
The treatise says "not correct" because this refers to the wisdom that takes nirvāṇa as its object.
This [preparatory stage] induces uncontaminated wisdom that takes nirvāṇa as its object;
it is also called "preparatory application" (prayoga) and is included within this category.
The treatise states: "Because of repeatedly practicing the view that the person (*pudgala*) lacks intrinsic nature as something distinct from the aggregates.

This means that within the phenomena of form as conceived by the parikalpita (imagined) nature, there is no existence;
it is like the self-nature of form and so forth as they are grasped by the parikalpita.
It is not merely that the self-nature grasped as form and so forth is non-existent.
Regarding material phenomena (*rūpadharma*),
there is likewise no other nature of material phenomena such as odor, fragrance,
and so forth. As the *Arthavargīya* states:
The *Abhidharma-sūtra* states that this is the "Chapter on Meaning" (*Arthavargīya*).
The treatise identifies the speaker as Saṃtha Kātyāyanīputra;
that is, Kātyāyana is his clan name (*gotra*) and Kātyāyanī is his personal name (*nāman*).
He belongs to the Brahmin caste;
among the eighteen clans, he is of one specific clan.
This is like how, among the four castes, one might say "the Li clan."
*Santā* refers to a specific lineage within the [spiritual] dispositions (*gotra*).
It is like having many [varieties] within a single plum,
namely the various distinctions such as those from Zhaojun and Longxi.
The treatise calls it *Indra*.
This refers to Śakra;
Īśāna is Maheśvara, the Lord of the World and the King of Men.
The treatise asks: "What are the eight kinds of conceptualization?"
First, intrinsic nature;
second, differentiation;
third, collective grasping.
1. The self; 2.
What belongs to the self; 3. Craving.
Seven are non-beneficial;
eight are contrary to both.
The first three are the skillful means for grasping at dharmas.
Four or five [factors] constitute the means of grasping (*upādāna*);
the latter three constitute the means of the three poisons (*triviṣa*).
Furthermore, the first three also pertain to the two types of grasping.
The four and five [consciousnesses] grasp only persons as their objects;
these eight types of discrimination do not apprehend them.
When the grasping of dharmas and the grasping of persons arise in their true nature, [these consciousnesses do not apprehend them].
Because attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) does not itself induce karmic retribution,
and since it is said that it can produce the three things [the body,
speech, and mind], we know that the grasping of phenomena and so forth serve as the preparatory conditions (*upāya*).
If that is so, since the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) also possesses the nature of unwholesomeness (*akuśala*), why is it not grasped? [The answer is:
It is not grasped by one who does not hold to the view of self.
The remaining unwholesome [factors] are taken up;
the last three do not take up the root,
as they exclude the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) that can produce it.
Furthermore, there is a distinction between [the secondary poisons] and those produced from the root [poisons].
This clarifies that the latter three serve as the expedient means (*upāya*) by which they can give rise to the three root poisons.
This also includes the provisional means (*upāya*).
If these are subsumed within the sevenfold distinctions,
one should reflect upon them according to the text itself.
The first three [categories] are able to produce both the sense faculties and their objects;
thus, the treatise states that they are "the bases and objects of conceptual proliferation," which refers precisely to the sense faculties and their objects.
The treatise states: "Because it takes the objects of perception, such as form (*rūpa*), as its basis and condition," and so forth, up to "the various distinctions of many and manifold categories.
This refers to the objects of perception, such as form.
They are called "name,
concept, and thing" because they serve as the basis and the object [of cognition].
It is comprised of verbal expression;
it is manifested by names, concepts, and verbal expressions;
it is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and is not comprised within a single lifetime.
Thus, that which is comprised within the conditioned and comprised within names includes untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena as well.
Now, to provide another explanation:
regarding what was previously called "untainted," [it refers to]...
It is not produced by the three types of discrimination;
that which is produced is subsumed under the others.
That which is called the "retinue" refers to the dharmas such as the sense faculties and their objects. That which is manifested refers to these very same dharmas.
Because these are what are manifested,
the fourth and fifth [categories] are distinguished:
the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), which is the root that gives rise to all views, and the conceit of self (*asmimāna*), which is the root of all forms of pride (*māna*).
Because the view of self and pride serve as the root for all other views and prides,
if the latter three can generate the three poisons,
this is explained in the treatise’s analysis of the general grasping at conceptualization.
To speak of "I," "sentient beings," or "living entities" within the conceptualization of self and what belongs to the self (ātman-ātmīya) is likewise reckoned as the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi).
What is the difference between these?
The answer is: the former is a general grasping;
it is distinguished by the two types of grasping for "self" and "what belongs to self."
The distinction exists solely due to the grasping at a person (*pudgala*).
As for the analytical investigation and the knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) which pertain to both types of wisdom,
this is as explained in the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*.
In the section on the "knowledge in accordance with reality" induced by the thorough investigation of the provisional designation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā*), it says:

"One knows in accordance with reality and penetrates in accordance with reality that the provisional designation of intrinsic nature regarding the objects of perception such as form (*rūpa*) is not the intrinsic nature of those things themselves, yet is expressed as being the intrinsic nature of those things."
That is to say, one perceives that the dependent nature is not real, and that the imagined nature—
which appears as if it were the object of such imagination—
is unreal; thus, its nature manifests.
Regarding the "mirage-water" mentioned among the eight similes:
it refers to a mirage that resembles water.

Next, the "Chapter on Power" (Vibhūtipaṭala) is explained.
Previously, the object realized by true wisdom was elucidated;
since that which is realized exists, [this chapter follows].
It cannot be in vain;
that is to say, he brings sentient beings to maturity and manifests great supernormal transformations.
To cause them to give rise to faith and to attain the fruits of sainthood.
If there are bodhisattvas...
Benefiting oneself and others,
manifesting great supernormal powers,
and practicing the correct path.
They seek to realize the fruit.
If the Munis were to realize their own buddha-activities [for themselves], [they would not need to teach others].
Arousing the mind of great compassion,
one delivers sentient beings by manifesting such majestic power; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Majestic Power."

Because it possesses sovereign mastery through reliance on the ultimate reality,
it is explained next. Within the five categories and seven dharmas:
The first three [sections] have already been concluded.

The treatise states: "Regarding the third, the power of co-arising:

bodhisattvas possess both types.
What is now referred to as "innate power" (*sahaja-prabhāva*) is as follows:

In the treatise, among the fivefold distinctions of the categories of power that are expounded, [this is one].
The *Pūrvācārya-śāstra* states: "Regarding the aforementioned three powers, there are five kinds of eightfold classifications.

these are merely the categories mentioned previously.
