Regarding the meaning of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), they are as usually distinguished.
As for what the treatise says regarding how one can transform through the supernormal power of knowledge of the sphere of psychic travel (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*):
This supernormal power of the knowledge of miraculous feats is the object to be transformed.
How so in this case?

Regarding the supernormal power of the knowledge of the transformation of the environment (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*): it is called "transformative" because it is able to transform and produce such objects;
since the object is described according to its perception, it is termed "transformative."
Furthermore, although it mentions that which is transformed,
its intent is to manifest supernormal powers;
therefore, it is called "the transformer."
The capacity to transform belongs to wisdom (*jñāna*).
To cite the object transformed is to illustrate the function of that which transforms.
In the commentary explaining the eighteen transformations,
within the fifth transformation, it says:
"If one forms the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that the earth becomes water, it then becomes water exactly as intended and not otherwise," and so forth.
Just as the Buddhas, despite possessing supernatural powers,
cannot transform the faculties of the five sense objects so that they become true faculties capable of seeing forms and so forth.
These resemble the five sense faculties but are not the actual five sense faculties;
although earth, water, and so forth are external bases (āyatana), [they are not the faculties].
Since their essential natures are each distinct,
how could water transform into fire?
It can only be that the substance of water ceases and a distinct substance of fire arises.
Within that [fire], it is capable of undergoing transformation;
by the power of the Buddha,
he causes the nature of moisture to exist even within the fire.
If one were to take moisture itself as the substance of fire,
then by changing its nature into that [of fire],
the insentient would be transformed into something possessing sentience.
This is because the realm of sentient beings undergoes increase and decrease;
it is of an unchangeable nature.
Furthermore, herein one transforms and attains the five sensory objects.
The treatise states: "One should know that form, odor, taste, and touch are likewise so.
Thus, one knows that these universally transform the five sense objects as their actual functions.
This will be explained in detail below in the section on definitive discernment.
The treatise states: "Brahmapurohita" (First Beneficent Devas) is so named because they exist prior to the Mahābrahmā devas;
thus, they are called the "Devas Prior to Brahmā."
What is meant by "benefit"?
In the treatise's explanation of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that surpass others,
it refers to the supernormal powers possessed by a bodhisattva who is bound to only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) or in their final existence (*caramabhavika*).
This refers to those dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven who have only one more birth remaining;
having exhausted this single lifetime, they are called "those with one birth remaining" (ekajātipratibaddha) or "those in their final body" (caramabhavika).
This refers to one who has already been born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and attains the Path in this very body;
for this body is the final existence within the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra).
This is called the final body.
Furthermore, it refers to the bodhisattva who, upon attaining realization, sits at the site of enlightenment—
that is, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree.
From the time he had not yet attained the Way until his attainment,
it is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa);
therefore, these constitute the first three [stages].
The treatise states: "Regarding the ability to transform into a body or a realm and so forth," this is explained solely as the capacity for transformation (*pariṇāma*).

The treatise further states: "Moreover, the transformed body—whether one's own or another's, and whether resembling [the original] or not—consists solely of that which is created to resemble the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*), yet it is not actual sense faculties."
Because the function of the faculties cannot be transformed;
because there would be the fault of the realm of sentient beings increasing;
and because it is impossible for them to resemble the bases upon which those faculties rely.
This is because they consist of the internal and external realms within four or five *paramāṇus*.
It is possible to transform [them] so that they appear similar.

The *Śāstra* states: "If the transformed body is extremely similar to the Bodhisattva’s own body, it is called 'the transformed body being similar to oneself'; if it is not so, it is called 'the transformed body not being similar to oneself.'"
Because the Bodhisattva manifests himself through transformation,
the Buddha creates a transformed Bodhisattva that is extremely similar to him;
this is called "self-similarity."

It is not so; they are not identical. For there are some Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who, even after their parinirvāṇa, continue to manifest through the power of their sustaining presence (*adhiṣṭhāna*), such as Śākyamuni Buddha.
Although they have entered parinirvāṇa,
by the power of their sustaining presence,
they cause the Dharma to continue to turn until the present day; or there are those who, having brought about benefit for a time, then cease their transformative activities.
Just as Susīma,
having attained enlightenment on the seventh day,
entered parinirvāṇa immediately.
The Dharma will likewise perish along with it;
lacking the power of preservation,
it shall not be propagated hereafter.
Therefore, the activity of transformation ceases.
As the *Śāstra* states in the section on "Understanding the Language of Transformation":
"Like the voice of the kalaviṅka bird, up to being independent and inexhaustible."
The treatise says: "Furthermore, because one can recollect the sequence of activities performed in successive moments without interruption.
This means that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to remember the preceding moment.
All phenomena from the preceding moment,
extending back to the beginningless past,
are fully understood.
In a single kṣaṇa, one is able to know in this way.
As for what the Hīnayāna says:
The Buddha, by means of the wisdom of the first dwelling, cannot know the preceding two moments.
If one were to take a single moment as an object,
that moment would be immeasurable.
Therefore, it is not obtained through conditions;
after fifty or sixty days have passed, one reaches old age and death.
There is no sense in which [the self] is conditioned by moments.
Now, those of the Mahāyāna— Buddhas and Bodhisattvas— all attain this.
The treatise states that among the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*),
there are those that involve mental attention (*manasikāra*) and those that do not.
This refers to bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (bhūmi) downwards;
as for the Buddha and those from the eighth stage upwards,
they abide in the state of non-intentionality (amanasikāra).
It concerns the affairs of immeasurable worlds.
The *Śāstra* states that "Dhāraṇī-mi-tu" refers to the kingdom of Siṃhala.
This is the country of Siṃhala.
There is a mantra there called Dāramiṭa;
it is a great spell among spells and a vidyā-mantra that possesses divine efficacy.
Now, first of all,
among the forms seen by the divine eye,
there are those that are attended to and those that are not attended to.
As explained in the commentary on the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-abhijñā*):
one thoroughly understands the attainment of the exhaustion of outflows.
This is the untainted attainment (*anāsrava-prāpti*);
it is the attainment of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
It is the thorough knowledge of the skillful means for the exhaustion of outflows.
This is precisely the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
In the commentary on the fourth characteristic of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) among the four characteristics of the six perfections, it says:
"There are not many enemies."
That is to say, the encounter with those one hates;
and the lack of much separation from those one loves—
that is, the departure from those one loves.
There is no great sorrow or suffering, namely that sorrow and suffering produced by the meeting with enemies and the separation from loved ones.
As the old treatise says: "Since there is neither separation nor union, there is likewise neither sorrow nor suffering."
Because it arises solely from separation from what is loved,
the two— enmity with those one hates and separation from those one loves—
are now divided into three.
The four characteristics of meditative concentration are established.
Within the first characteristic,
it is said that one is able to sever the afflictions, speech, discursive thought, investigation, joy, bliss, and the perception of form.
That is to say: the first dhyāna abandons the afflictions of desire;
the second is free from vitarka, vicāra, and speech;
and so it is for the third and fourth [dhyānas] as well as the four formless attainments.
In their respective order, they are free from joy, bliss, and so forth.
In the commentary explaining the characteristics of the six perfections, regarding the first,
giving (*dāna*), it says:
One is able to benefit sentient beings by means of the practice of generosity as one of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*);
this is the sixth [point] among the practices of the four means of attraction.
In all four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), one benefits sentient beings through "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*); thus,
the four integrative methods are subsumed within the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
Why is it that among the types of giving,
one does not speak of exhorting sentient beings to practice;
rather, one gives in a manner identical to one's own?
This is called "acting in concert" (samānārthatā),
and it is also termed "beneficial conduct" (arthacaryā).
For now, we shall discuss it in terms of its predominant influence.
This is said merely as a conventional designation and not in accordance with the ultimate meaning.
As for the ultimate meaning:
What prevents each individual [moment] from possessing beneficial conduct and so forth?
In the commentary on the innate power (*sahaja-prabhāva*),
it explains the accomplishment of enlightenment through the eight aspects (*aṣṭākāra-bodhi*).
The eight traditional marks are:
first, dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven;

Third, dwelling in the mother’s womb;

Sixth, attaining the Way;
seventh, turning the wheel of Dharma;
eighth, entering parinirvāṇa.
If one follows the traditional interpretation,
there would be no characteristics of renunciation, nirvana, or entry [into the path].
This treatise now follows the traditional explanation.
There is no single characteristic for renunciation;
there are seven other characteristics,
which one should identify according to the text itself.
Furthermore, if one understands it such that spiritual transformation constitutes a single entity,
then there would be no renunciation.
In this context, it likewise possesses eight characteristics.
To explain these eight characteristics individually:
abiding in heaven is not the true dharma.
Not taking birth from the lower part;
this refers to those who are born directly from the intermediate state (antarābhava).

fourth, emerging from the womb;
fifth, leaving the household life.
Sixth, attaining the Way;
seventh, turning the wheel of Dharma;
eighth, entering nirvana.
Now, this does not possess the characteristics of one who has left the household life (*pravrajita*).

This is explained in the treatise as the first Bodhisattva dwelling among the devas.
There are three things that surpass those gods:
first, the lifespan of the gods.
This means that the lifespans of those devas do not depend on fixed numerical measures,
as they may die prematurely; here, however,
it is clarified that the Bodhisattva exhausts the full measure of his celestial lifespan.
Because their lifespan is four thousand years.
Regarding this, the preceding treatise states that they remain for the full duration of the lifespan of the Tuṣita Heaven.

Otherwise, there are two obstacles:
first, an obstacle regarding the text;

Regarding the statement that "words and phrases are obstructive," the treatise says: "Three matters eclipse those heavens.
First, regarding the lifespan of the first heaven:
Those gods all have a fixed lifespan;
the Bodhisattva does not outshine or surpass their lifespan.
Because this [latter] statement contradicts the former, it constitutes a textual inconsistency.
Regarding the contradiction with the meaning [of scripture]:
a sutra states that when a Bodhisattva descends to be born,
all those gods likewise descend to be born in Jambudvīpa.
There are beings currently being born there;
when the Bodhisattva descends, less than four thousand years have passed,
so they should not be born there following him.
If they do not arise accordingly,
that would contradict the sūtras of those Buddhas.
If one says that arising subsequently and descending constitutes an untimely death, [that is incorrect].
This constitutes the second logical objection;
therefore, the thesis is not established.
Furthermore, for what reason would those gods not suffer premature death?
Regarding the two aspects of the celestial color—

the Bodhisattva is superior.
Third, regarding renown:
the Bodhisattva’s fame pervades the worlds of the ten directions;

In the *Śāstra on the Exposition of the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma*, it is clarified that after he had realized awakening, Māra sought an opportunity against him for six years but was ultimately unable to find one; his constant mindfulness was ever present before him.

that is to say, the World-Honored One constantly observed his own body, sensations, perceptions, and discursive thoughts,
and now had no other thoughts.
By constantly contemplating impermanence, arising, abiding, change, and so forth,
and because one is accompanied by this mindfulness,

As stated in the *Purāṇa-bhūmi-vastu*:
"One contemplates the birth, abiding, change, and so forth of all sentient beings.
Now, however, it says: "One contemplates one's own body."
Because one contemplates one's own body, Māra finds no opportunity;
how much less could he find an opportunity by contemplating others?
Furthermore, it may also be that here one likewise contemplates all sentient beings.

Māra finds no opportunity.

Taking Buddha-activities as the primary focus.

The Chapter on Maturation is the fourth of the five chapters.
Among the seven topics, it corresponds to the fifth and sixth topics:
namely, the maturation of sentient beings and the maturation of one's own Buddha-qualities.
For what reason is it explained next that [the Buddha] manifests,
realizes the truth,
and possesses manifest power?
What is "majestic power"?
It refers to the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and so forth.
Having manifested these six supernormal knowledges, [he...]
What do you wish to accomplish?
It does not exceed two intentions:
first, to bring sentient beings to maturity.
The intention to benefit others;
the intention for self-benefit, which consists in maturing the Buddha-dharmas.
Although the Buddha is endowed with the virtues of benefiting both self and others,
because he perceives the realm of sentient beings to be inexhaustible,

Following the Chapter on Power (*Prabhāva*), the Chapter on Maturation (*Paripāka*) is explained.
In the treatise’s exposition of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of maturation, it says:

"Abiding in this state, whether one encounters a Great Teacher or does not encounter a Great Teacher, one possesses the capacity and great power to realize immediately the abandonment of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the abandonment of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)."
This refers to what is contained within the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (stages conducive to penetration).
How does the bodhisattva know this?
The treatise states that one is able to realize the abandonment of the two obstacles immediately thereafter.
Therefore, one should know that if this stage were prior to that point,
it would not be possible to be thus.
Furthermore, in the *Dṛṣṭānta* [section], it is said:
"For example, when an abscess has reached full maturity, it is immediately ready to be lanced.
Thus, one should know that those in the stages prior to the bhūmis have already reached the stage of maturity.
This also applies to the stage of the *nirvedhabhāgīya*.
If one has already entered the stages (*bhūmi*),
why is it that [the result] occurs immediately prior?
One attains a body and mind that are conducive to the purification resulting from the abandonment of the two obstacles,
until the culmination of correct application;
since there is already that which is conducive to the abandonment of the two obstacles.
Furthermore, because there is the mention of "possessing preparatory practice" (*sābhisaṃskāra*),

Moreover, if it were on the grounds...
One also attains right application,
which is the knowledge of application on the stages (bhūmi-prayoga-jñāna),
capable of conforming to the two obstacles.

one is able to accord with the second stage by severing obstacles and purifying the superior body and mind.

taking the previous interpretation is without hindrance.
In the third section of the *Śāstra-vyākhyā*, concerning the distinctions of maturation,
"maturation of the faculties" refers to the perfection of lifespan and the perfection of physical form.

as explained in the preceding fascicle.

The treatise states that "subduing" refers to deeply protecting oneself so as to remain free from defilement.
"Even to the point of personally guarding against and not giving rise to transgressions"—
the meaning here is that one deeply guards against one's own faults.

it refers to those who are being admonished or instructed,
as well as others of a similar class who practice the Dharma together with them.
One attains benefit and happiness.
It is "benefit" because it stops those faults;
it is "happiness" because it brings about [the person's] reintegration. This refers to the single case of expulsion.
Having now driven them away, one draws them back again,
so that they and all other people may attain benefit and happiness;
for by restraining evil, one brings them under one's care.
If, after having expelled them, one does not take them back into the fold,

then they will themselves practice restraint.

As for those who have been expelled:
The intended meaning here is that they cannot obtain benefit or peace and happiness.
Among those of superior faculties,

The meaning is not that all grave offenses can be accepted;

This encompasses both the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.

these six types each receive their names based on one predominant factor at the time of their initial attainment.
This does not mean that the former is absent in the latter, nor that the latter is absent in the former.
This differs from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*,
which makes a general distinction between these [types of persons] based on whether they have regressed or not from the three trainings.
Other treatises may be the same as the two preceding types,
or they may differ.
As in the middle [section], the remaining seeds are not mentioned;
this is a brief explanation of the causes.
Furthermore, according to what follows below, they correspond to the middle grade within the middle [section].
The purification of the superior intention refers to the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa;
it does not necessarily pertain solely to the first bhūmi.
This is just as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains regarding the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*),
which pervades all stages and is non-retrogressive;
this treatise [explains] falling into certainty (*niyata-patita*) up to the ultimate.

The treatise explains the three grades of śrāvakas.
When one abides in the stage of inferior maturation, at that time there is inferior aspiration and so forth;
this continues up to the third grade, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life.

In this context, the "inferior grade" refers to the stage prior to medium and inferior patience (*kṣānti*), during which one would still fall into the evil destinies (*durgati*) were it not for this [attainment].

it realizes that one will not follow the evil destinies.
This refers to those from the stage of "increased patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) upward.
If one were to claim that because a person lacks karma for the miserable realms,
they do not fall into those realms,
and instead obtain the fruit in their presently visible body;
This is also included therein;
for the present, this discussion is conducted with reference to those who undergo seven more births.
It is said that one does not attain parinirvāṇa in the present life; rather,
if one considers the superior [progress],
it may take four births or even up to sixty kalpas.
For the practitioner,
they enter nirvana even within this very body.
This treatise was not composed for that purpose; otherwise,

This should be understood accordingly.
If the first person is compared to a bodhisattva of the lower grade,
then everything prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) would correspond to that stage.
Now, since neither the literal text nor the underlying meaning supports [the previous view], it is explained separately.
Among those who are Pratyekabuddhas,
they must have attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.

they give rise to thirty-six moments of mind to proceed toward the fruit of a pratyekabuddha and so forth,
as described in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*.
In the *Treatise on the Explanation of the Bodhisattva’s Lower Grade*, it says:
"When a bodhisattva abides in lower maturation, at that time they possess lower-grade aspiration and lower-grade application, yet still go to the evil destinies."
This bodhisattva has, in fact, already departed from the karma of the evil realms and does not undergo rebirth in the evil realms;
nevertheless, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, [he remains there].
At that time, one intentionally goes to be born there;
consequently, defilement arises,
and because one undergoes that retributive destination, [the process continues].
At the beginning of the kalpa, there were births in the evil realms.
It was like a garuḍa entering the ocean to devour nāgas;
having finished devouring the nāgas, it flew upward into the sky.
Because he had taken up the dragon,
there was mud on his feet;
in truth, he had no intention [to do so].
Originally, he was to catch a dragon;
at the time of catching the dragon, he consequently became defiled by mud.
It is the same with the Bodhisattva.
Because they benefit sentient beings, they consequently become bound by defilements;
therefore, even during the first eon, they were born in the evil destinies. If that is so, then according to the sūtra you have cited:

Fascicle Thirty-Eight. Chapter Seven: On Bodhi. Regarding the "Chapter on Bodhi": [text continues]
This refers to the fifth of the five categories of training and the seventh of the seven dharmas.
As for the term "bodhi":
This is the enlightenment of the three bodies (trikāya).
Enlightenment (bodhi) means awakening;
having realized the ultimate reality, one is awakened.

The treatise states that there are one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*),

The eighty minor marks;
the four kinds of complete purity, such as the purity of the path leading out of suffering;
and the ten powers.
The four fearlessnesses,
the three foundations of mindfulness,
and the three ways in which he needs no protection.

one obtains one hundred and thirty-six unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma),
augmented by great compassion.
The quality of non-forgetfulness,
the permanent eradication of habitual tendencies,
and the knowledge of all aspects— because there are these four kinds.
This constitutes the one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
As the text itself clarifies, the treatise states:

Because the fourth dhyāna is immovable,
because it is devoid of suffering and pleasure,
and because it is free from the three calamities.
It is named "Immovable.
The three lower [stages] are not so;
therefore, the Tathāgata dwells in it most frequently.
Sentient beings have much suffering;
because they abound in the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), they dwell in a state of suffering.
[The Bodhisattva], abiding extensively in a mind of compassion, [acts for their sake].
Because it uproots the suffering of birth.
As stated in Nāgārjuna’s *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"It is superior to the first three abodes."
Adding one Buddha-abode makes four.
As for the "Buddha-abode," it refers to the immeasurable samādhi of Śūraṅgama.
Furthermore, the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), the unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*),
and so forth, are all abodes of the Buddha;
alternatively, they may be divided into sixteen.
There are eight celestial abodes,
namely the four of the form realm and the four of the formless realm.
There are four Brahma abodes.
That is, the four immeasurables.
There are four noble abidings:
wishlessness, [the signless], cessation, and meditative absorption.
Thus, there are sixteen;
if expanded, they are immeasurable,
as explained in that treatise.
The ten titles are called "merits corresponding to recollection" because one obtains merits according to the recollections of sentient beings; therefore,
they are named "merits corresponding to recollection."
It is said that the body of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is but one,
yet possesses ten titles. For example,
it is like the case of a Dharma Master.
Among the ten [categories], the last one is the general designation,
while the preceding nine are the specific designations.
Within these specific designations:
The first three [perfections] benefit both self and others;
the middle three benefit only oneself;
the final three benefit only others.
If that is so, as in the first and third [cases],
it merely clarifies that the ultimate reality (paramārtha) is devoid of false conceptualization;
where does it clarify that "benefit" is the word?
Words are not false;
principles do not exist in isolation from words.
There must be someone to receive them.
Therefore, within the Tathāgata’s [activity], there is also that which benefits others and so forth;
by analogy, one should understand that within what is purely for the benefit of others,
there is also that which benefits oneself.
This can be understood by analogy with the previous explanation.
As for the nine distinct titles according to the former Master Yuan:
The first five are names for one's own virtue;
the subsequent four are titles for benefiting others.
These correspond to the meaning of benefiting others.
How can one speak of one's own virtues? Furthermore, among the preceding five [aspects], they are divided into two pairs;
the first manifests the perfection of the Path.
The latter reveals the ultimate cessation.
Of the former three stages, the first consists of tranquility and insight;
the second is the perfection of their causes.
The latter is the ultimate fruit.
Now, speaking according to the meaning of the term:
"worthy" (arhat) carries only the sense of being worthy of offerings.
It is not for the benefit of others;
therefore, it is also for one's own benefit,
as Master Jing said.
Regarding the term "Tathāgata":
he is called the Tathāgata because his speech is free from falsehood.
As it says in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Zhìdù lùn) and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chéngshí lùn):
Because one comes by riding the path of reality as it is to achieve perfect enlightenment,
one is called a Tathāgata.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
Because he has come by means of the six *pāramitās* and the eleven kinds of emptiness, he is called the Tathāgata.
As for the statement that his every word is without falsehood,
this refers to the perfection of his clear understanding and practice.
Yunming states that the practice of the three insights (vidyās) is as explained in the sūtras regarding the two categories of śamatha and vipaśyanā,
the six perfections, the myriad practices, and so forth,
as stated in the Old Treatise.
The three types of knowledge (*trividyā*) are practiced as explained in the sūtras, namely the two categories of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
This treatise now reverses that [explanation].
The treatise states: "There may be many eons during which not a single Buddha appears in the world; or there may be a single eon during which many Buddhas appear in the world."
This is as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*:
after the Buddha had completed three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of cultivation,
he further cultivated the karma for the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) during one hundred *kalpas*.
By reciting verses for seven days and seven nights,
he surpassed the nine kalpas of other Buddhas;
thus, within ninety-one kalpas, [he attained enlightenment].
By cultivating the karma of the marks and signs,
he eventually attained Buddhahood.
In the past, he encountered the Tathāgatas Dīpaṃkara and Śikhin.

From this point onward,
no further Buddhas appeared in the world.

namely from Krakucchanda Buddha down to Śākyamuni Buddha.

they are called the Five Buddhas;
thus they have passed through this great kalpa.

we know that in the Bhadrakalpa,
many kalpas are treated as a single kalpa.

"In the past, he encountered the Buddha Susaṃbhava and made three thousand vows."
Because they resolved their minds for enlightenment in groups of one thousand each,

when the kalpa is about to be formed...
Within the great ocean there is a thousand-petaled lotus flower,

it shall now be the first.

Regarding the phrase "in such divisions" from the treatise, this is the explanation transmitted from the West concerning other Buddhas appearing in other kalpas.

this present assembly is the place."

for there are no two Tathāgatas in a single Buddha-world,
as there is a fixed measure [of their appearance].

and thereafter attains Buddhahood.

Fourth, this refers to thoroughly understanding the obstacles to the six perfections.
