In the *Vyākhyāyukti* (The Explanation of the Compendium), it says:

"To explain for their sake, it is said that this sutra does not state that all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely non-existent; rather, it states that the so-called intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is entirely non-existent," and so forth.
It is not said that the two natures, such as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and so forth, are entirely non-existent;
rather, it is said that the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of what is expressed by conceptual construction (*parikalpita*) is non-existent.

Although the treatise states that all things expressed by speech proceed based upon that [dependent nature] and thus linguistic expression functions, the expressible self-nature of those expressions, when considered from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), is not their actual self-nature and so forth.
Although there are objects of expression such as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
based on these objects, pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) arises;
such is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) expressed by these verbal designations.
Because it is like a rabbit’s horn;
according to the ultimate truth,
it does not exist as the nature of expression that is conceptually constructed.
To say "without objects" means that there are no objects of parikalpita (imagined nature);
it does not mean that paratantra (dependent nature) is non-existent.
The treatise states: "For example, within space there are many forms and form-activities that can accommodate all forms and form-activities.
This metaphor illustrates that True Suchness (tathatā) is like space.
The pervasive conceptualization is like form and so forth;
as below, one merely eliminates the pervasive conceptualization of all that resembles form and the activity of form,
thereby realizing the nature of emptiness that resembles true suchness.
The treatise says: "Furthermore, like an illusion or a dream, it does not exist in reality as it appears," and so forth.
What precedes this clarifies that True Suchness (tathatā) resembles space, while form and karma resemble the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
From this point onward, the metaphors—

such as that of the dependent nature being like an illusion— are intended to show that it does not exist in the way it is imagined by the parikalpita (the imagined nature), such as a real person and so forth.
The provisional similarity is not non-existent;
it is based precisely upon the other-dependent nature (*paratantra*).
As the treatise states: "These various phenomena are not as they are described by the habitual verbal conventions of foolish people," and so forth.
In summary, this clarifies that the dependent and perfected natures exist,
while the imagined nature does not,
according to the ultimate truth of the ineffable intrinsic nature.
These two natures are not non-existent; rather, these two natures do exist.
Through this skillful means, one awakens to and enters into the principle that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, for their nature is non-dual, like an illusion or a dream.
This concludes the three natures.
It is said that the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) is neither existent nor non-existent.
It is not existent, being like a rabbit’s horn.
It is not that false conceptualization does not exist;
the dependent nature is likewise [not non-existent].
Yet it is not existent in the manner of the imagined nature.
It is not that conventional designations do not exist;

the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is likewise not existent in the same way as the imagined nature (*parikalpita*), yet it is not non-existent in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Regarding the phrase "neither grasping at even a small portion nor abandoning even a small portion," etc.:
One does not grasp at the imagined nature,
one does not discard the two natures,
and one does not commit the error of deprecating the two natures.
One does not engage in the superimposition of conceptualizing existence;
this is called "non-destruction.
The Śāstra states that there are four kinds of dhāraṇī: first, dharma; second, meaning; third, mantra; and fourth, the capacity for patient endurance (kṣānti).
As explained below in the section on the *dhāraṇī* of phenomena (*dharma-dhāraṇī*),
taking phenomena as its object refers specifically to the linguistic expressions that signify them.
The *artha-dhāraṇī* has mindfulness and wisdom as its essence;
its nature is identical to that of the *dharma-dhāraṇī*.
Only the object differs.
What is this difference?
It means that the referent (the meaning expressed) serves as the object.
That is to say, the immeasurable meanings, intentions, and so forth,
which reside solely in the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), are dhāraṇīs;
they have meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as their essence.
By relying on meditative concentration to maintain the mantra,
one ensures it is not practiced erroneously;
thus, the mantra is taken as the object of focus.
One who is able to attain the dharani of patience takes non-conceptual wisdom as the essence of that patience;
this is the realization of suchness.
That which is able to attain patience (*kṣānti*) is precisely the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*);
it possesses the functional capacity for the recitation of mantras (*dhāraṇī*).
Because one realizes suchness.
The Dharma Master says:
"This has non-conceptual wisdom as its essence. If that is so, why is it said that one 'is able to attain patience'?"
In this stage of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
by maintaining mindfulness of this mantra,
one swiftly attains true knowledge (*tattva-jñāna*).
One realizes suchness; therefore,
in the subsequent section concerning the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*),
the treatise explains the attainment of the *kṣānti-dhāraṇī*.
Regarding the practitioner whose cause for maturation is naturally firm:
this refers to those prior to the stages (bhūmi),
who possess the cause of patience (*kṣānti*).
It is called "immovable" because it cannot be moved. One who possesses the perfection of causal practice and sublime wisdom refers to one whose sublime wisdom has matured toward the supramundane.
Alternatively, it refers to one who possesses sublime wisdom within the immovable causal practice and dwells alone in seclusion.
This refers to the dwelling place. It is tranquil and beyond verbal expression;
it is free from the clamor of speech and worldly distraction. That which has never possessed any substantial entity is one whose mind is characterized by the simplification of affairs.
One who possesses no remaining provisions and sees the path while traveling should not proceed;
for one must travel only when the signs of clear light have arisen.
It is said that one walks while seeing the path;
furthermore, wherever one travels, one must see the correct road.
Thus, there is no fault in being unstained.
That which is not excessive is called "dwelling in the wilderness.
According to correct principle, it must be called a "path.
One should practice in reliance upon correct principle.
It is called "walking on the path of vision.
It can be understood through such practices as eating with moderation and so forth.

Regarding the statement in the treatise that one who has attained the bodhisattva-patience (*bodhisattva-kṣānti*) as taught by the Buddha can correctly contemplate the words and phrases of various mantras— such as those beginning with "Etc."—
it means that these mantras possess no inherent meaning.
There are merely names;
that is to say, bodhisattvas prior to the stages recite this meaningless incantation,
desiring to eliminate their conceptual attachments.
These are merely names;
where is there any objective referent?
Therefore, one should know that all phenomena exist only as names falsely imputed.
Because there is no grasping at objects as they truly are,
one cannot give rise to grasping based on names.
This is due to such reflection.
One is then able to enter true contemplation and realize the patience (*kṣānti*) of a bodhisattva.
The treatise states: "One simply and as-it-isly understands that there is no object; this is the meaning of the phrase 'that which is called no-object'."
This explains that the aforementioned absence of meaning is the meaning of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
It is said that this mantra lacks anything to be expressed;
because there is no referent to be expressed.
One is able to realize the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) precisely because there is nothing to be signified by this mantra; that is to say, one understands these phrases as they truly are,
namely, as being without referential meaning.
And one realizes the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Regarding the various categories discussed in the treatise,
those which are not determined therein are so because they involve error and are also not firmly established.
"Because there is falling back, it is also not vast," because it possesses limits and is not like that which is boundless.
In the commentary on the five kinds of vows and so forth,
regarding the second section on taking birth,
it says: "in accordance with [birth in] the various happy realms that bring benefit to sentient beings."
Question: Why is it that in this context it is not stated that they "conform to birth in the evil destinies"?
Answer: There are two intended meanings.
First, it means that the benefits for those in the happy realms are many,
while the benefits for those in the miserable realms are few;
thus, they are not discussed here in brief.
Second, because the eight marks [of a great man] accord with [the conditions of] existence solely within the happy realms;
furthermore, because in the miserable realms there is no manifestation as a sovereign king or the like through supernatural transformation;
and furthermore, it is stated when discussing the happy realms.
This indicates that birth in the evil destinies is mentioned by way of the most prominent cases;
the treatise discusses only the good destinies.
In the commentary on the three samādhis,
regarding the question "What is the bodhisattva’s emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) and so forth?",
the meaning of "emptiness" (*śūnya*) here is as follows:
If it is the path of insight through characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mārga*),
there are only the two lower aspects of suffering;
this is the meaning of the text regarding the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
Because of the mention of "afflictions" and so forth,
there are only four aspects of the origin [of suffering] and two aspects of suffering.
Regarding the meaning of the passage on signlessness:
because it contains the terms "permanent cessation" and "quiescence," it refers exclusively to the cessation of the lower four [realms].
If one refers to the texts of other passages,
there are many distinctions;
one such passage is as previously stated.
Furthermore, the wishless (*apraṇihita*) includes the four lower modes of practice associated with the path;
the remainder is as previously stated.
There is a textual passage stating that the signless (*animitta*) includes the four lower modes of practice associated with the path.
The wishless [samādhi] is not like that.
The rest is as before; there is a textual passage [to this effect].
The three truths are as before.
The first explanation [of the verse] consists of the four lines beginning with "releasing the path" (*mārga-vimocana*).
These are subsumed under the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*), as stated in the second fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*. According to one interpretation:
Regarding the path of emptiness (*śūnyatā-carita*): if categorized by the abandonment of afflictions, it pertains to all four truths;
the rest may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the discrepancies among these various textual passages,
the intended meaning is as set forth in the *Abhidharma-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Dàifǎ-chāo);
the underlying significance may be understood by inference.
Furthermore, the intended meaning of this treatise is that within the context of true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*),
these three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) are established as distinct functional applications.
If the abandonment of afflictions consists solely of the practice of emptiness,
yet at the same time also possesses the meanings of wishlessness and signlessness,
then this is the intended meaning within the section on signlessness.

The mention of "afflictions" (*kleśa*) and so forth appears to apply only to the four aspects of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) and two aspects of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
According to the section on increase and decrease below,
the "wishless" (apraṇihita) is established generally with respect to all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta);
thus, the wishless applies to all three truths.
Furthermore, regarding this general statement,
if the intended meaning here is as previously explained,
the treatise says: "In this way, a bodhisattva who diligently practices and trains within these three types of samādhi..."
This is an exhortation to study. Herein, "one who establishes the thorough knowledge of reality as it is" concludes the preceding section by clearly elucidating the three doors of liberation.
Furthermore, it concludes the meaning of neither increasing nor decreasing. Regarding "thoroughly awakening to and entering other modes of appearance and samādhi":
Having thoroughly understood this gateway to liberation as it has been explained,
one enters into other aspects of practice in accordance with reality.
"Those who are able to fully understand them and establish the principles through authentic realization and entry" refers to those who first enter the three true gates of liberation;
"those who cultivate the principles and know them as they truly are" refers to those who practice and thoroughly comprehend the principles according to reality.
Because it exhorts the practice of the method for cultivating *samādhi*,
the following provides a further explanation: "Within this, the assembly of *śrāvakas* diligently trains,
which consists of training in conduct as well as its perfect realization."
This refers to immediate realization and entry.
For a further alternative interpretation,
one may understand it by reflecting upon it.
Fascicle Forty-six. Chapter Seventeen on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bodhipakṣadharma), Part Three.
The treatise states: "Furthermore, there are four types of *dharmoddāna*, which is translated here as 'exposition' (*śāsana*)."
This is what the World-Honored One constantly recites and explains.
If this is called an *uddāna*, it means "collecting the dispersed";
that is, summarizing the prose by means of concise verses.
What is now called "discourse" (vyākaraṇa) refers to constant recitation and exposition;
this meaning is similar to that of a "self-spoken discourse" (udāna) delivered without being questioned.
If these four kinds of essential natures emerge from the nature of phenomena,
they are understood through the truths of the conditioned and the unconditioned.
In the treatise, among the three meanings used to explain the uddāna,
that which is called the meaning of "correspondence with phenomena" refers to the manifestation of impermanence and so forth.
However, because it is not associated with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
and because this path of practice can lead toward great rebirth (*mahājanman*).
It attracts the fruits of the mundane realms of superior humans and devas,
as well as birth in the pure lands of the supramundane;
furthermore, it can also produce rebirth in the realms of form and formlessness.
It is called "Great Birth" because one is able to give rise to the True Dharma;
it is called "Great Birth" for this reason.
Furthermore, if one discusses this in relation to emerging from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), this "great arising" is indeed tainted arising (*sāsrava-jāti*).

The treatise states: "In this very context, the immediate cessation of the intrinsic nature of the preceding momentary formations, followed by the arising of the intrinsic nature of the subsequent momentary formations—correctly contemplating this as 'arising' and so forth."
"Up to the point of correctly contemplating it as cessation":
if one relies on the Hīnayāna,
birth arises in the future.
The three characteristics exist in the present.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna,
these are the three characteristics of arising and so forth.
That which exists in the present and that which has ceased in the past are as explained in the preceding text.
To say that what was originally non-existent now exists is called "arising," in order to distinguish it from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
To say that the unconditioned exists [is likewise a conventional designation].
Yet that which is primordially existent is now existent;
whereas conditioned phenomena were originally non-existent and are now existent,
that [other] is said to be primordially existent.
In the immediate succession following the preceding moment,
there arises that which is not of the same kind as before;
for instance, if a single material phenomenon (rūpadharma) ceases in the prior moment.
The subsequent thought arises;
this is extremely similar [to the preceding one].
How can you say it is not the same as the prior word?
The commentary says: If one does not say "resemblance," it would simply be that very dharma;
and if it were that very dharma, [the fault would follow].
That is the very essence of the single dharma;
this supreme practice is an eternally abiding dharma,
and thus it is subject to no cessation.
Because it is not the very same substantial entity as the preceding moment,
there is the expression "resemblance. Regarding the term "abiding," there are two interpretations in the Mahāyāna.

One school asserts that "abiding" (sthiti) refers to the capacity to draw forth the efficacy for subsequent results in the present. If this were so, why is the final mind of an Arhat called "abiding"?
Because it lacks the capacity to draw forth a subsequent mind.
The commentary states: Because of this obstacle, two [different] explanations exist.
The present treatise says that when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have arisen and have not yet perished, observing them at that very moment is "abiding" (*sthiti*).
It is not the case that once this arising has already ceased, it is called "abiding.
If that were so, then abiding would occur at a time distinct from arising; therefore, [the Sarvāstivādins] maintain that they are distinct, as in the Hinayana.
This statement should now be stated in the Mahāyāna:
"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), having arisen,
do not perish at that very moment," as in the fifty-second [verse].
Furthermore, it is established that the state of arising persists;
this is designated as "abiding. As for "alteration," if one were to say that the transformation and decay of this dharma at the moment of its arising is called "alteration," this too is not correct.
This is because it is distinct from the state at the time of arising.
If one were to claim that it is only called "different" when it undergoes change later, since it was not yet changed at the time of arising; [then this would be untenable].
Because it arises at a different time.

Now, one should say that this already-arisen conditioned phenomenon (saṃskāra), in relation to those previously ceased conditioned phenomena, has a momentary intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that merely undergoes a distinct change,
which is termed "difference" (anyathātva).
That which differs from the preceding moment is all termed "difference.
For this reason, arising and difference occur simultaneously.
As for cessation, if it were identical to the present moment, then it would be simultaneous with difference and yet be called "cessation."
Cessation is a non-existent phenomenon (*abhāvadharma*),
whereas duration and change are existent phenomena (*bhāvadharma*).
How could an existent phenomenon and a non-existent phenomenon coexist at the same time?
Therefore, this treatise states: "From these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), at the moment immediately following their arising, the very nature of these arisen conditioned phenomena perishes;
this is precisely what is called 'cessation' (*nirodha*)."
This is because the characteristic of cessation is established only when a phenomenon, having existed, reaches the past;
thus, arising and cessation, as well as light and darkness, do not occur simultaneously. Question: If this is so, then [all these] would occur within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
There are no four characteristics.
The meaning is that at the very moment this dharma arises, it is simultaneously ceasing.

Just as the two ends of a scale are equal and simultaneous, so too in a single moment there is both arising and ceasing. If this is so, why is it not said that ceasing occurs first and arising afterwards?
The commentary states:
Because it is taught from the very beginning, and because there must necessarily be arising at the initial moment, all cessations are not prior; rather, they are simply the ultimate cessation.
Subsequently, it arises. Question: In various sūtras, it is said that there are three characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*). What are these three?
The commentary states that there are two meanings:
first, subsuming "abiding" and "entering" within "difference";
second, subsuming "difference" within "abiding" and "entering."
Regarding the statement "abiding enters into difference":
it is because abiding is similar to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, if one hears that all phenomena have abiding...
Thus, one who is weary of the conditioned lacks a vigorous mind;
now, to say that it is "only different" means that the conditioned is profoundly worthy of weariness.
Because there is change, it is not the same as the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), which possesses duration; therefore,
the characteristic of duration (sthiti-lakṣaṇa) is subsumed within the characteristic of change (anyathātva-lakṣaṇa).
If one considers the perspective of the Hīnayāna,
because it is capable of destroying and disintegrating produced phenomena,
it is superior in its functional capacity regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The characteristic of duration (sthiti) is capable of drawing forth subsequent births;
since it has no efficacy regarding cessation,
it is subsumed within the characteristic of change (anyathātva).
The second explanation subsumes "difference" (*visabhāga*),
"arising" (*utpāda*), and "abiding" (*sthiti*). Because it possesses functional capacity distinct from its own moment,
that which has arisen but not yet perished is termed "abiding."
Therefore, there is efficacy;
for [the effect] differs from the preceding dharma,
as it has no efficacy with respect to its own recollection.
It subsumes the distinct [phases] of entering and abiding;
furthermore, it differs from the characteristic of cessation because its own nature is not manifest.
It subsumes the distinct [factors] into arising and abiding. If that is so, why does it not subsume the distinct [factors] into cessation?
The meaning is this: distinction is a phenomenon that exists (*bhāva*), whereas cessation is a non-phenomenon (*abhāva*).
One is of the past;
one is of the present.
Although their appearances are similar, [they differ].
It cannot be subsumed under the characteristic of cessation.
See the fifty-third fascicle of the *Viniscaya-saṃgrahaṇī* and the third fascicle of the *Maulī-bhūmi-vyākhyā*.

The treatise asks: Why is it that when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise, only these very same conditioned phenomena are perceived, and no other distinct arising, abiding, aging, or ceasing is found; and likewise, when these conditioned phenomena abide, age, or cease, only these very same conditioned phenomena are perceived, and no other distinct arising, abiding, aging, or ceasing is found?
Why is there such a difference?
The subsequent presentation of the four characteristics is for the purpose of subsuming phenomena and excluding phenomena.
If one were to point to the dharmas in mutual reference,
there would only be the statement that "conditioned phenomena arise," and so on,
up to "conditioned phenomena abide, age, and perish."
If one negates a phenomenon by means of a specific negation,
there are four aspects of its essential nature;
therefore, the phenomenon is universally negated.
Therefore, all four characteristics are mentioned collectively. Question:
For what reason, in the refutation of arising, do you not merely speak of "arising," but apply the same [method] even to abiding and cessation?
The commentary states: Because that which abides also possesses arising,
and because at the time of arising there is abiding and so forth,
the "great arising" gives rise to the eight factors and so on.
Therefore, it is a universal negation.

The treatise states, "Because such investigation finds nothing," which means that by refuting the production of the production of form through the passage beginning with "If one is apart from those conditioned phenomena such as form," etc.,
the production of form is destroyed.
There must also be "arising" (*jāti*), which refers to the minor arising within the Hīnayāna.

The treatise states: "If one says there is only one [arising], then to reckon that arising is substantially existent is futile; to say that there is a distinct arising as a real entity is not reasonable."
This refutes the "small birth.
If small birth were identical to great birth,
one would calculate that great birth exists as a substantial entity.
It would then be utterly wasted.
Why is this? Because great arising gives rise to material phenomena (rūpa-dharma).
If there were a "small origination" distinct from "origination itself," then "great origination" should likewise have a separate substantial entity.
[If that were so,] the small origination would originate the great origination.
The two types of arising are spoken of as one;
for the "great arising" (mahābhūta-utpāda) that gives rise to derived matter (rūpa-dharma) is identical with the arising itself.
To claim that there is a separate production as a substantially existent entity is merely a futile exertion;
it is not reasonable.

The treatise says: "If one says they are different, then it would follow that 'the arising of arising' is not the arising of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra). That 'the arising of arising' is not the arising of conditioned phenomena is unreasonable.
Here, "not the arising of conditioned phenomena" refers to the "minor arising" (anupapatti).
This arising of arising is itself the great arising.
If you say that the great arising and the small arising are different,
then the small arising should likewise resemble the great arising.
It should be able to produce matter (*rūpa*).
The Great Arising (*mahābhūta*) produces the dharmas of matter,
and it is also able to produce the Minor Arisings (*upapādaka*).
The minor arising gives rise to the major arising;
for it must also give rise to material phenomena (*rūpadharma*).
The minor arising cannot give rise to material phenomena by means of the arising-of-arising (*jāti-jāti*).
It must be that the "arising of arising" (jāti-jāti) is what produces the primary arising;
therefore, it is illogical for the two types of arising to be distinct.
The treatise states: "If a dharma that is ceasing were to possess a separate intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then as a real entity, this very cessation would itself have both arising and ceasing."
The Dharma Master has finished the first layer of refutation above.
Next, he proceeds to the second specific refutation regarding the characteristic of cessation.
He states: "This is not so."
If one has not yet understood how that "arising of arising" applies by analogy to the remaining characteristics,
the following section raises the subsequent "destruction" to refute it;
this constitutes one complete cycle of argumentation.
In our school, what is called "cessation" is a non-existent dharma; it is not distinct [from the entity itself].
If you claim that there is a separate characteristic of cessation, then because this cessation would be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it would necessarily have its own separate arising and cessation.
If cessation were produced by that which arises,
then all phenomena would necessarily cease spontaneously and without effort.
Just as when entering the meditative attainment of cessation,
once the characteristic of cessation has arisen,
it follows the mind and mental factors of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses.
They should also both be extinguished,
because they are characterized by the extinction of arising;
since these two are mutually contradictory.
Therefore, the remainder must be extinguished.
Since they are not extinguished,
it is clearly known that what I have said is true.
This dharma is never called "extinguished.
It is not that extinction gives rise to something else;
rather, arising exists because it possesses the characteristic of extinction.
That which is produced by what produces it can obstruct that which produces; therefore,
the remainder must be extinguished.
The dharma of cessation has cessation;
know this by analogy with the preceding example.
This is explained in the treatise’s analysis of non-self.

Regarding the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) among all phenomena: it means that the person is not truly existent as being identical to those phenomena, nor is there a truly existent person existing separately from those phenomena.
This refers to the refutation of the views that the self is either identical to the aggregates or distinct from the aggregates.
In the treatise’s explanation of the tranquility of nirvāṇa, the meaning of "first, the causes are eternally severed; later, the remainder is extinguished without residue" is as follows:
This refers to both *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, the permanent abandonment of the causes occurs during the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), while the subsequent complete abandonment occurs during the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Moreover, the permanent abandonment of the causes occurs first.
In the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), one suppresses the manifest [defilements];
subsequently, one abandons them without remainder by cutting their seeds. As for the others that never arise again, this refers to the non-arising of the fruit.
Because it severs the causes [of suffering], the treatise states:

"Whether it be the superior and most superior, the ultimate and highest; whether it be the profound and most profound, the excellent and most excellent; or whether it be inferior, superior, or the most excellent—these include the Dharma-teachings, correct teachings, instructions, and admonitions."
The three phrases beginning with "supreme" explain the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);
the three phrases beginning with "profound" refer to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);
and the three phrases beginning with "excellent" [refer to the wisdom of cultivation].
This is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Among the three types of wisdom, each has its own superior, middling, and inferior grades;
furthermore, the teaching of the Dharma and the correct teaching constitute the three phrases of the three grades, beginning with the supreme. This is instruction (*avavāda*).
These three phrases—“profound,” “ultimate,” and so forth—constitute the three grades of instruction.
These three phrases—“superior,” “supreme,” and so forth—also constitute the three grades.
Furthermore, among the three types of wisdom mentioned previously:
Each [of these] contains three phrases— “Dharma,” “Teaching,” and “Correct Teaching”—
which are to be applied sequentially.
In the "Chapter on Merit," "merit" (gong) refers to meritorious labor.
"Virtue" (de) refers to the Way and its Power (daode).
To acquire this virtue through the application of effort is called "merit" (gongde).
This is explained in detail herein;
it is titled the "Chapter on Merit. Question: Why is it explained immediately following this?
Answer: Because the preceding section elucidated *bodhi* (enlightenment).
The thesis (pakṣa) consists of the aspect of discernment regarding cause and effect;
these must necessarily have a basis when functioning prior [to the inference].
Therefore, following the chapter on [the Bodhisattva’s] qualities, the chapter on Merits is explained. Within the first verse, which contains seven sections, this is the second:
the five kinds of non-marvelous phenomena that are nonetheless called "accomplished marvelous phenomena."
Judging by the signs,
everyone can attain this;
receiving it is nothing extraordinary.
If we discuss it from the perspective of the mind,
not declining to engage in such matters is called a marvelous phenomenon (*āścaryadharma*).
Furthermore, when compared with those of its own class,
it is not extraordinary;
yet when compared with those of the two vehicles, it is so.
It is most extraordinary.
The second extraordinary thing is that he remains silent and speaks no words.
Silence is indeed the flavor of true bliss;
yet, for the sake of sentient beings, one preaches the True Dharma and enters nirvana oneself.
This silence is indeed the flavor of bliss.
For the sake of sentient beings, one preaches the True Dharma.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra*: "By means of five causes and conditions, one is able to perform unfailing applications toward sentient beings," etc.:
One should understand its characteristics up to this point.
This comprehension of understanding is of two kinds:
first, seeking to bring about benefit and happiness for all sentient beings.
Second, up to the point of knowing things as they truly are,
as described in the Chapter on Offerings:
if one generates [the resolve], there are five matters.
Furthermore, there are three ways of conforming to the teaching of the Dharma;
fourth, being free from weariness;
and fifth, impartial compassion. Next, the verse has six sections.

Regarding the absence of a Buddha during the initial stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), it is because a Buddha possesses no such preparatory application. Next, there are five gates in the verse;
within the fifth gate, there are four intermediate points.
The means of attraction through affectionate speech;
among all means of attraction, this is the foremost.
Because both the intimate and the distant are near,
it is able to lead them forth to transcendence and serve as the initial gateway for entering the Dharma,
thereby performing the work of transformation and gathering.
The others are not so. Next follow two verses, comprising nine sections in total;
the first verse contains four sections.
The second verse has five sections.
Regarding the first section, within the first *dharma-prajñapti*, it asks:
"What is meant by 'successively compiling, arranging, and establishing'?"
"Compilation" refers to the Sūtras;
"arrangement" refers to the Mātṛkā;
and "establishment" refers to the Vinaya.
Furthermore, regarding the teachings of the Three Vehicles:
first, their texts are collected in sequence;
second, their meanings are established and compiled.
The Method for Establishing the Various Rules of Training (Śikṣāpada): Within the Three Gates of Increasing Truths,
the Truth of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇasatya) refers to the essential characteristics of all phenomena.
The truth of speech refers to the teaching that expresses [the meaning].
Function refers to the activity of all phenomena. Among the five gates of increase, the first four are the Four Noble Truths.
The latter one is not an unestablished truth (*avyavasthāpana-satya*). Among the six gates of increase,
it is said that "one is the truth of truth and two are the truths of falsehood," which explains the matters of reality and falsity.
Furthermore, wholesome dharmas are called "truths," while unwholesome and other such dharmas are called "false truths.
Within the *Saptavastuka* (The Sevenfold Exposition), these are discussed under the categories of the gratification (*āsvāda*),
the disadvantage (*ādīnava*), and the escape (*niḥsaraṇa*).
This refers to the two truths of origination and suffering.
Renunciation refers to the truth of cessation,
or alternatively, it includes the truth of the path.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) refers to suchness (tathatā).
It is the truth of resolute conviction;
that is, it is the abandonment through resolute conviction.
Regarding the fruit, within the ninefold increase,
the first four are suffering;
these are the four lower modes of practice.
The next two are eternalism and nihilism.
These two views are also called craving,
because one craves these very views.
This corresponds to the truth of origination (samudaya-satya).
The seventh corresponds to the truth of the path (mārga-satya), namely,
the wisdom of application (prayoga-jñāna).
Eight or nine [factors] constitute the truth of cessation.
In the treatise’s explanation of the seven aspects of the śrāvaka,
these two are what this wisdom relies upon.
The Dharma Master said:
"This is the mind-king;
furthermore, this is meditative concentration."
The same applies to the Mahāyāna. In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*,
regarding the explanation of the immeasurable realms of those to be disciplined (*vineya-dhātu*),
it states that there are seven categories, the first of which is "contempt."
As in the case of Devadatta:
having entered [the path] through disparagement,
he was mediocre between the two extremes.
As when a multitude has gathered,
he tames them with the most gentle speech;
this is the third extensive teaching on wisdom.
Fourth is the brief exposition of knowledge.
This is for the purpose of distinguishing between those of dull and sharp faculties;
it is included among the nine expanded categories.
Regarding those who are to be subdued from afar or nearby:
this refers to long periods or short periods, such as years or months.
Because they are distinct.
The treatise states, "Thus, having diligently practiced and studied," which concludes the aforementioned maintenance of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
The third section of the initial text concerns the passage on "the one who is able to train.
The following text states:
"In ten ways, a bodhisattva [trains] in the bodhisattva training."
One is able to practice correctly;
beyond this, there is nothing further that can be practiced correctly.
This concludes the third section on being able to practice correctly, as mentioned previously.
Thus we know that the texts for the three types of prohibitions differ.
For example, regarding the training in upholding [the precepts],
the first prohibition applies to the first two cases.
There is the arising of existence but no fetter.
This is because one is able to correctly train in the non-arising of the fetters of existence;
thus, it is known that this is an abbreviated indication by analogy.
And it is not said that there are three divisions; rather, there is one exposition.

The first chapter of the second section, the *Yogasthāna on Following the Dharma*, titled "Characteristics of Bodhisattvas," within the forty-seventh fascicle, concerns the four bases (*dhāraṇī*) of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
This is the second [section].
The first [section] correctly clarifies the conduct to be studied;
it is not that there is no discernment regarding the person capable of studying it.
This practitioner of vidyādhara practice,
having mastered what is to be learned, manifests the characteristics of a bodhisattva and acts in accordance with the conduct of the teachings they have studied.
This is the Bodhisattva-bhūmi, the Section on the Yoga of Following the Dharma.
It begins with a listing of ten chapters;
the first is the Chapter on Sustenance (Dhāraṇa).
There are eighteen chapters,
divided into three sections:
namely, the lineage (*gotra*), the generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), and the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), as previously explained.
One attains the exclusive holding of the name;
this second type of holding has four grades.
This refers to abiding in the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) regarding the objective aspect (*nimitta*).
As for "aspect" (*nimitta*),
it is so called because it is the sign through which one enters the bodhisattva path by means of maturing this dharma.
The analysis of the [characteristics] and so forth is as explained at the beginning of the subsequent chapter.
Since this chapter precedes the second, "The Chapter on Holding" (Dhāraṇī),
it is called the first, "The Chapter on Characteristics" (Lakṣaṇa).

Regarding the statement in the verse of the treatise, "The fivefold application of true bodhisattvas should be known," the prose commentary explains that these are the five qualities beginning with compassion (*anukampā*). As for the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of these five,
they are comprised of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), as explained below.
Compassion has meditative concentration as its essence;
this is because great compassion arises based upon meditative concentration.
This essence is comprised within meditative concentration;
it is of the nature of the wholesome root of non-hatred,
yet it does not refer to the wisdom that can give rise to it.
The second is pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*).
It is subsumed under the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
This is because it proceeds from the observance of the vows (*vinaya*), and because it is generated through the guidance of wisdom; thus, these two [perfections] subsume it.

If one follows the previous *Dānaparivarta* (Chapter on Giving) or the *Saṃgrahavastu-parivarta* (Chapter on the Means of Attraction), then giving is subsumed solely under the means of attraction of generosity (*dāna-saṃgraha*),
while the remaining four perfections are purely subsumed under the means of attraction of acting in common purpose (*samānārthatā-saṃgraha*).
If one excludes generosity, the remaining three means of integration are all subsumed within the perfection of wisdom; why, then,
is it said here that affectionate speech is included within ethical discipline?
This is the correct practice based upon the precepts;
however, relying on the precepts— such as refraining from false speech and so forth—
is not separate from their essential nature according to that treatise.
Because all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are initiated by wisdom,
the third [perfection] is vigor (vīrya),
which is subsumed under the three categories of diligence, patience, and wisdom.
In reality, it is simply diligence,
because it is initiated by wisdom and involves the patient endurance of suffering over a long period of time.
Therefore, they are discussed together.
Fourth, extending the hand to bestow gifts is subsumed under the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Fifth, the ability to resolve profound meanings and intentional terminology (sandhyā) is subsumed under concentration and wisdom;
if one considers its essential nature alone, it is wisdom.
Because the wisdom arising from meditative concentration is superior,
and because it proceeds simultaneously with that which arises from the superior [concentration], it is termed "meditative concentration.
These five types are all matured by relying on the practice of the six perfections.
These are the five modes of entry into the characteristics of a bodhisattva.
Regarding the explanation of the self-nature of valor (*vīrya*) in the *Śāstra*, it states:

"The various bodhisattvas are resolute and firm, without any timidity or inferiority, and possess great power. Master Jing explains that the three—diligence (*vīrya*), patience (*kṣānti*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—constitute its essence.
These are assigned in successive order;
however, upon examining the meaning of the text, this is not the case.
It merely emphasizes diligence exclusively.
These correspond, in order, to the three qualities of donning armor, diligence, and so forth.
Among these, one cultivates non-illuminating patience and wisdom.
Because it grasps and defines its own essence.
Regarding the explanation of the "basis" (*āśraya*) in the treatise:
"basis" refers to the mutual dependence [of the support and the supported], specifically the locus from which the characteristics arise.
The locus of the conditioned is also the locus of the six causes.
Within the locus for resolving the profound meaning and the intentional terminology, it is as follows:
There are five meanings.
The first is "conforming to the profound and appearing as profound," wherein "profound" refers to conforming to *tathatā* (suchness).
The wisdom that takes suchness as its object appears profoundly deep, because it accords with suchness.
It is because it relies upon wisdom that True Suchness (tathatā) manifests.
This is the fourth basis.
Regarding the meaning of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*):
"designation" refers to the names that express [meaning],
while "meaning" refers to the phenomena that are expressed.
The fifth refers to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Regarding the second section, titled "Wing" (*yi-pin*):
it means practicing the four dharmas.
Just as a bird has wings,
it is therefore called the "Wings Chapter.
Now, however, this is not the case.
This refers to what was previously called the "practice of understanding":
entering the marks of a bodhisattva and cultivating both the two divisions of the lay and the ordained.
Because it is practiced by means of two parts,
it is called a "part" (bhāga); therefore,
it is termed a "category of parts" (bhāgīya).
For what reason is it that those belonging to the bright portion have already entered the marks of a bodhisattva,
which can be attained by both householders and those who have left the home life?
Therefore, it is explained next.

The treatise asks: How does a bodhisattva benefit others? It means that by relying on the four means of attraction—namely, generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and cooperation—a bodhisattva is able to provide benefit to a portion of sentient beings.

Regarding the statement that "some provide a portion of benefit and a portion of happiness," it means that each of these four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) can likewise bring about both benefit and happiness.
Although it is said that giving wealth to others causes them to generate the resolve for awakening and so forth,
which constitutes "benefit," once they have obtained and used the object,
it constitutes "happiness" and so forth.
In this way, each and every one is accompanied by the knowledge of what is conducive [to benefit].
If it were not so, then "beneficial speech" would be taught as increasing benefit,
while the remaining forms of giving would be for the sake of providing comfort.
Cooperative conduct (samānārthatā) pertains to both [wholesome and unwholesome], because it consists in acting together for the sake of both good and evil.
This is explained in the treatise within the section on non-perverted dedication (aviparīta-pariṇāmanā).
Regarding the accumulation through three doors:
"three" refers to the skillful cultivation of activities, namely,
first, skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Second, benefiting others;
third, these constitute the three gates.
The treatise states: "A renunciant bodhisattva is one who can exclusively practice the 'hook-and-chain' pure conduct (*brahmacarya*)."
The term "hook-and-chain" (gou-so) signifies the meaning of being constrained by grasping at signs.
For those who have left the household life, there are prohibitions and precepts;
because they prevent the three types of unwholesome karma, these are like hook-and-chains.
The lay bodhisattva is not like this,
because they are consistently heedless.
The Chapter on Superior Intention (*adhyāśaya*) is the third chapter within the second *dhāraṇī*.
Within this, the intentions of bodhisattvas who have entered and generated the resolve for awakening are clearly elucidated;
there are fifteen such types and so forth.
This is explained in detail herein in the chapter titled "The Superior Intention" (*adhyāśaya-varga*).
As for "intention":
It has faith, aspiration, and resolute conviction as its essence;
because this mental disposition is predominant,
it is called the category of the superior mental disposition (adhyāśaya-pakṣa).
How is this clarified?
It is because one who wishes to practice the bodhisattva path must cultivate and give rise to it by relying on each individual part.
Cultivating this involves the factor of aspiration (*āśaya*).
Since aspiration is synonymous with longing, it is explained next.
There is a statement regarding its predominance (*adhipati*).
It appears to exist only on the level of the *bhūmi*; however,
in terms of its function as an auxiliary support,
there is no contradiction in its being present prior to the *bhūmis* as well.
In the fifth section of the *Lunjie qixiang lianlian* (Commentary on the Seven Characteristics of Compassion), concerning the Dharma, it says:
"That which is called 'untainted' (*arāga*) is also called 'without object' (*anālambana*).
Not seeking [the recipient's] favor or reward is termed 'untainted.'"
Not praying for future results is "absence of conditions.
Furthermore, both types are termed "untainted" (*asaṃkliṣṭa*),
because "taint" (*saṃkleśa*) refers generally to both gratitude toward benefactors and the fruits of future worlds.
The same applies to their conditions (*pratyaya*).
The treatise states that there are both "powers of supernormal knowledge" (*abhijñā-prabhāva*) and "innate powers" (*sahaja-prabhāva*).
The powers of supernormal knowledge are induced from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding "innate power" (*sahaja-prabhāva*):
because it has been cultivated in previous lives, it arises immediately upon birth.

The *Śāstra* states: "Furthermore, the impure intention (*aśuddhāśaya*) of all bodhisattvas is called the 'intention that should be disciplined' (*vinayitavyāśaya*), because one must apply analytical discernment (*vicāra*) to this intention. Moreover, the pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*) and the thoroughly purified intention (*suviśuddhāśaya*) of all bodhisattvas are called the 'innate intention' (*sahajāśaya*), and so forth."
Before reaching the stages (bhūmi), they have not yet realized the Dharma, but they subdue beings by manifesting supernatural powers (ṛddhi) and so forth;
from entering the stages onward, [they act differently].
Having personally realized suchness and practiced it for many eons,
his supernormal powers are co-nascent with his body.
It is pure virtue;
it is a pure intention;
it is an intention that arises simultaneously [with the action].
Because it is established as thoroughly purified by the nature of pure intention (*āśaya*).
What is the meaning of "abiding in the categories of abiding"?
It refers precisely to the twelve abidings (*vihāra*) which serve as its causes.
It is that which can abide and that in which one abides;
whether conditioned or unconditioned,
because the bodhisattva dwells within them, it is called "abiding."
Because this section explains these matters in detail, it is called the "Chapter on Abiding.
Furthermore, as for why they are explained later:
they are what is sought through the three eons of superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
The practice of the teachings currently being enacted brings about the fulfillment of one's own practice;
this refers to the distinctions between the stages from the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of the ultimate fruit.
In total, there are thirteen bodhisattvas who dwell therein;
therefore, they are explained next.
This is the fourth chapter of the second section, "The Sustenance" (Dhāraṇī).
This is the fifth chapter among the ten chapters beginning with "Possessing the Marks.

The treatise states: "Thus, starting from the full possession of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), it is explained at length, up until the point of those bodhisattvas who, as previously described, apply themselves with right diligence to the training of a bodhisattva."
This clarifies the eighteen chapters within the first *dhāraṇī*:

from the initial chapter on the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) up to the chapter on the uncultivated qualities (*aguṇa-bhāvanā*), these correctly and fully manifest the various characteristics of a bodhisattva as they have been described.

This is the first chapter on characteristics within this *Dhāraṇī*. It is the chapter on the stages for those who apply themselves with right diligence in the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of the bodhisattvas.
Regarding the bodhisattva’s intention (*āśaya*) as it has been described:
This is the section on the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
In the commentary on the three stages of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), it says:
"It refers to those bodhisattvas who understand, as it truly is, that which is able to contemplate reality."
That is to say, within the fourth stage,
one contemplates the factors of enlightenment;
these factors of enlightenment are that which performs the contemplation.
In the fourth stage, one contemplates these analytical factors;
this is called "knowing truly as it is" the reality that is the object of contemplation. As for that which is the reality of the object of contemplation:
This refers to contemplating the Four Noble Truths within the fifth stage;
the Four Noble Truths are the objects of contemplation. Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings who, due to a lack of wisdom, [fail to realize] reality...
This explains the contemplation of dependent origination in the sixth stage.
In the seventh stage,
it is called "with application" and "with effort."
Regarding the "uninterrupted path proceeding in the signless abiding":
this refers to the fact that this stage is not separated by tainted (sāsrava) states of mind,
but is instead discussed as a continuity consisting primarily of untainted (anāsrava) contemplation.
Therefore, it is called "uninterrupted," yet it is not actually uninterrupted.
It is not so in the eighth stage. Question: From the eighth stage onward, it is truly real.
Since there is no interruption [in the flow of the mind],
how can the two commentators from the West state that at the eighth stage there are times when there is a mind with outflows (*sāsrava*)?
The Commentary states: These all refer to the majority of continuous states;
it is not that there is no arising of outflowing (āsrava) mind, for in the ninth stage one attains the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).

The treatise states: "Being able [to analyze] the various categories (*paryāya*) of all phenomena—that is, the analysis of phenomena (*dharma-prabheda*), the analysis of meanings (*artha-prabheda*), the analysis of etymologies (*nirukti-prabheda*), and the analysis of distinctions (*pratibhāna-prabheda*)—these are the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)."
The characteristics of the tenth stage, such as first illuminating the world and so forth, are explained in detail as they appear in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, "Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmika-sūtra*).

The treatise states: "Furthermore, regarding those bodhisattvas whose superior practices abide in a limited scope of cultivation, whose objects of conversion are narrow, whose objects of conversion are incomplete, whose objects of conversion are unstable, and whose attainments undergo regression, [the following applies]."
To say it is "narrow and small" means that what is performed is not extensive.
To say it is "deficient" means...
Their actions are not constant;
it is said that they violate the precepts through evil conduct of body and speech.
Their actions are not fixed, as their practice lacks steadfastness.
There is indeed falling away at that time.
The statement that there is falling away from what has been attained clarifies that the aforementioned [attainment] was not fixed.
Furthermore, those who are undetermined have impure conduct and may fall back.
They cannot advance purely;
this is the distinction between these two.
Furthermore, regarding that which is indeterminate:
Those who constantly harbor hesitation and retreat are unable to advance further, and thus they fall back.
The following passage explains that the dimensions are the reverse of those previously stated.
A question is asked: "From the eighth stage onward, what is the difference between [the qualities of] 'equal to the first stage' and 'non-retrogression,' etc.?"
The commentary states: In the first stage and those following, there is still effortful application (*sābhoga*), and thus one cannot advance moment by moment (*kṣaṇe kṣaṇe*).
Therefore, one must maintain focused application.
Those who have already attained this are said to be "non-retrogressive.
From the eighth stage onward,
because there is not a single moment in which they do not progress, they are called non-retrogressive.
This is the distinction between these two.
Furthermore, the treatise states that there are five kinds of fear,
namely, the fear of non-sustenance and so forth.
According to the subsequent antidotes,
that which is to be remedied by the five fears and so forth constitutes the essence of this fear.
What constitutes the essence of this? It is the fear of non-survival (*abhavyatā-bhaya*).
Its essence consists of the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-love (*ātma-sneha*), and craving for the means of subsistence (*upakaraṇa-tṛṣṇā*).
Therefore, it is said below:
When, through the cultivation of the wisdom of selflessness, even the conceptualization of the mark of a self no longer arises,
how much less could there be conceptualization of love for a self or love for the requisites of life?
Therefore, it is known that its essence consists of the view of self and craving.
The second is the fear of ill repute, which has sensual desire as its essence;
thus, the text below states:
Since he has no expectations from elsewhere,
he constantly generates such a desire and aspiration within himself:
"I shall bring benefit to all sentient beings."
Because he does not seek anything from sentient beings,
for this reason he has no fear of ill repute.
Thus, one should know that the third fear of death has greed and desire as its essence,
while the fourth has the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi) as its essence;
therefore, the subsequent text says:
Because one is free from the view of a self,
the notion of the self’s destruction does not arise;
therefore, there is no fear of death.
It is clearly known that the fear of the fourth miserable realm (apāya) has the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi) as its essence,
while [the fear of] the lower realms has delusion (moha) as its essence.
As the treatise below states:
Knowing for oneself that after death,
in a future life,
one will certainly encounter all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Because of this, there is certainly no fear of the miserable realms (*apāya*), nor the five types of cowardly fears (*pañca-bhaya*).
Since these have ignorance (*moha*) as their essence,
the subsequent treatise states:
From the perspective of his intention,
he saw that in all the world there was not even one person who was his equal.
How much more so for those who are superior?
Therefore, there is no timidity or fear when among a multitude.
This which is to be remedied has delusion as its essence.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*,
there ought to be a distinct entity;
examine this.
The treatise states: "Accomplishing the limited wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*)," and so forth;
this clarifies the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "at times losing [it] through delusion" and so forth:
This clarifies the faculty of mindfulness for a bodhisattva who has matured but possesses a practice that is difficult and slow.
This clarifies the faculty of intention for one who lacks intense aspiration for great enlightenment.
This reveals that desire does not diminish for one who exerts fervent diligence;
this clarifies the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*). That which is profound, firm, and pure is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).

The treatise states: "As for the phrase 'at times fully possessing mindfulness, or at times belonging to the class of forgetfulness,' it is called the class of forgetfulness because there are instances where one remembers and instances where one does not."
This is because it is not entirely devoid of deluded thoughts;
thus, the term "category" (*jāti*) is used.
The Treatise states: "Regarding all the aforementioned perfections of the bodhisattva training, those who have not yet been able to train universally [are included here]."

This refers to the first *dhāraṇī*, consisting of eighteen chapters. Regarding what was explained above, up to the point where the various marks (*lakṣaṇa*) of a bodhisattva have not yet all reached maturity—this refers to the chapter on marks within this *dhāraṇī*.
As for "and so forth" as explained above, it is as previously stated.

Furthermore, for those whose bodhisattva intention (*āśaya*) has not yet been purified as described above, the two aspects do not appear equally within the bodhisattva’s correct application (*samyak-prayoga*). That is to say, they belong to the category of partial practice.
This refers to that which has not yet been equally manifested within the two divisions of a bodhisattva’s correct application belonging to the category of superior intention;
that is to say, one is as yet unable to practice correctly in reliance upon those two divisions.
This refers to what has not yet been manifested.

The Treatise states: "When these bodhisattvas abide in the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and progress through the lower degree of patience (*kṣānti*), one should know that the aforementioned characteristics and signs of their practices are of the highest degree."
"Up to the point of their complete and permanent eradication without remainder" refers to the aforementioned faults prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*),
which exist during the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
This is called the stage of lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*).
This fault is of the highest degree (*adhimātra*) at this time.
During the stages of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) and the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), it is called middle patience (*madhya-kṣānti*).
The ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) and so forth are called "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*);
their faults constitute the "intermediate" and "inferior" [levels].
This is explained in the treatise within the section on entering the Abode of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*).
It is said that by abandoning those [former states], one initiates six kinds of new, virtuous, and resolute determination. What are these six?
The treatise states: "The Bodhisattva’s great vow, which is of the nature of internal realization and cultivation, surpasses all other pure and white vows."
This is the first vow.
The *Dìchí jīng* (Bhūmivastu) lists the numbers one, two, and so forth.
The *Shídì lùn* (Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya) states:
The first is called "Contemplating the Characteristics.
The Sūtra says "without separation," which means that in aspiring for Bodhi, one is without separation from that aspiration.
This refers to that which is observed by means of subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
If one obtains this text,
it speaks of the bodhisattva’s great vow as the nature of internal realization and cultivation.
The Dharma Master said:

The *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) states:
"The second is the reality."
The Sūtra states that it is "unobservable," which refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Therefore, the Sūtra states that "that which cannot be seen" refers to subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Because it functions to alleviate the suffering of all sentient beings, it is not shared with any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
this is the third vow.
The *Dilun* states:
"The third is supreme goodness.
The Sūtra says: "Vast as the Dharma-realm."
Subsequently, through subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to save sentient beings;

Furthermore, there is a distinct meaning, as explained in the fifth chapter below: although this vow arises in a single moment, its very nature (*dharmatā*) is such that it can attain the immeasurable, desirable fruits of a bodhisattva’s pure qualities (*śukladharma*).

The *Dilun* states:
"The fourth is based on goodness."

The fifth great excellence of the *Dilun* school is as stated in the Sūtra: "Encompassing all realms of sentient beings.

This is the third [of those].

The *Dilun* states:
"The sixth is fearlessness.

capable of bringing one to the final limit.

Furthermore, once bodhisattvas have aroused this mind, they transcend the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) among bodhisattvas; the following explains the specific benefits of the fourth arousal of the mind.

From the stage of entry onward,

"Generating a mind directed toward the goal" means generating a mind that aims at the goal of benefit and happiness;

This means that the ultimate means for all sentient beings to be liberated from all suffering [is as stated].

If there were wisdom that possessed the afflictive obstructions (kleśāvaraṇa), [it would not be non-conceptual wisdom].
It is because [wisdom] cannot bring sentient beings to ultimate liberation from suffering.
When one contemplates what constitutes the wisdom that can perfectly realize this ultimate means,
it is found to be nothing other than the non-conceptualizing wisdom regarding all phenomena.
Because the arising of affliction through the manifestation of conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena is that which is counteracted by non-conceptual wisdom,
[this wisdom] is able to counteract and fully realize it.
This contemplation can bring about accomplishment;
this right knowledge is first clarified through the contemplation of the supreme samādhi occurring simultaneously with it.
Simultaneously with that which is induced,
even all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*) arise entirely from the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Hearing comes first;
all have the hearing of the true Dharma as their causal condition.
This concentration and so forth are then free from the hindrances of the various fetters.
It is for the sake of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) in order to sever the afflictions;

thereby perfectly realizing liberation.

Because this treatise speaks of the equality of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is known that this is *tathatā* (suchness).

furthermore, one attains the essential dharma and attains the essence of the Tathāgata."

furthermore, the term "ten masteries" also refers to the essential nature of phenomena—
this must be examined.

The fifth stage:
the treatise explains ten kinds of pure intentions of equality (*samatā-śuddhāśaya*).

This means that the Buddha is the Peerless Awakened One (*asamasambuddha*).
This term "peerless" refers to peerless awakening.
[This is so] because of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

it is neither unequal nor is there anything equal to it.

since these six are one,

"It refers to precept, concentration, and wisdom.

The equality of doubt and views,

The purity of knowledge, vision,
and abandonment is the equality of the knowledge and vision of the abandonment of conduct;
these six are subsumed within the aforementioned factors of enlightenment.
As in the text of the *Dìchí* (Yogācārabhūmi) and its commentaries, there are differences;

I speak of the Four Truths;
because this designation applies universally to the preceding three,
they are combined to form six types.
Based on the present,

based on the future, [it is likewise].

its cessation and non-arising is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

the nature of the means for practicing that abandonment is the Path.

they consist of ten aspects as thus described.

within this single ground.

as understood above,

The treatise explains the ten kinds of equality of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*).

which refers to relying upon the principle of ultimate truth.
All phenomena are equal,
as in the old treatise.
Second, the equality of signlessness through the practice of non-discursiveness.
Because speech, conceptualization, and mental images are, in their ultimate nature, equal in being signless;
as the sutra states, this is the second equality of signlessness.

arise from perception (*saṃjñā*). Now,
this characteristic is also the equality of signlessness (*animitta-samatā*).

existence is a false arising.
As it has been said in the past:
Third is the equality of non-arising. It is said:

When the sutra speaks of "the equality of non-arising," its meaning is that it is precisely because this mental perception does not exist.
Suffering does not arise spontaneously;
furthermore, it is precisely by means of this that one engages in verbal expression and formative activity.
Because the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is equal [to emptiness],
that which is grasped as being produced spontaneously—
this spontaneous production does not exist.
However, because they arise from causes and conditions,
it is said that they are equal in being unarisen;
there is no such thing as spontaneous arising.
The former is superior.
