"Three arise based on five"?
Therefore, we know [this refers to] the levels of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
These are bound to the five stages of the desire and form realms;
for the first three preparatory stages (*prayoga*) constitute the levels of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
If the contemplations such as the five stabilizing mentalities (*pañca-viṣkambhanā-manaskāra*) were merely states of distracted mind, [they would not lead to penetration].
Because they are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth,
they pertain to all seven stages (*bhūmi*).
Since the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the others, exist only in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), [they do not pertain to the lower stages].
There is no contradiction between the three bases and the five bases either.

Regarding the point that "in this context, meditative concentration is certainly not the cause of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) and so forth," it is as explained in the third fascicle of the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra*.
Within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*,
three Western traditions are mentioned.
Jayasena says:
These roots of goodness, such as liberation,
are by nature contaminated (*sāsrava*) and are subsumed under the category of preparatory skillful means (*upāya-kuśala*).
Now, as the seeds of the wholesome factors conducive to merit (*puṇyabhāgīya-kuśala*) increase, they bring about the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).
That meritorious karma is like dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
If it arises from the negligence of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth, it is produced by the three types of ignorance; however, for one who is not negligent, it is otherwise.
It should be known that this arises conditioned by clarity;
I say it is not because of ignorance as a condition that one attains a desirable fruit.
Upon reaching the stages such as the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*),
which accord with the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state,
they can no longer directly induce the general retributive fruit of suffering within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
It is said that while it is not the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*),
it is not the case that it does not induce a distinct fruit,
as in the examples of Ratnacandra and others.
That is to say, by the power of the untainted seeds,
it causes the increase of two types of dharmas: the manifest skillful dharmas with outflows that serve as expedient means,
and the roots of goodness pertaining to merit.
This is also as explained by the Dharma Master in the *Abhidharmakośa-ṭīkā*:
it may be understood that the meaning is subsumed within the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) and so forth.
The treatise states: "Because all other mundane roots of goodness arise on this basis, they become increasingly bright and flourishing."
It is because of the stages of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and so forth that the practice of the wholesome qualities conducive to merit becomes even more manifest;
this is due to the repeated cultivation of preparatory wholesome states (*prayoga-kuśala*).
It is "clear" because it thoroughly understands cause and effect.
If one follows the view of Ratnacandra and others,
even the contaminated wholesome states of preparatory application (prayoga) would be so.

Regarding the phrase "and the portion of merit, etc., is clearly understood," and the subsequent passage from "by this causal condition, that which is embraced by it, etc. up to "is swiftly established":
herein, it is because the portion conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and so forth serve as the causal conditions.
It causes the seeds of worldly merit, virtue,
and so forth— termed "indeterminate seeds"—
to become capable of transformation.
The seeds of virtuous karma and so forth become increasingly potent;
they are the seeds of the roots of virtue conducive to liberation.
It is swiftly established.
To be established means that it is capable of increasing and producing superior fruits.
Furthermore, it causes the seeds of the merit-portion and other wholesome factors to be swiftly established.
Within this, there are two meanings regarding the new and original perfumings (*ābhyāsa* and *mūla*).
Moreover, by virtue of these seeds, those various wholesome dharmas arise with increasing clarity and vigor.
Because of the seeds of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and so forth, the wholesome dharmas that manifest spontaneously also arise with increasing clarity and vigor.

Furthermore, it is said that this is the manifestation of the wholesome factors conducive to merit (*puṇyabhāgīya*). If that is so, how does this differ from the previous [state of] "arising with even greater clarity and vigor"?
The commentary states: It is even more excellent than before, because it increases moment by moment;
furthermore, it can induce [results] in the future, as explained below.
This clearly explains the meaning of wholesome karma pertaining to the portion of merit (*puṇyabhāgīya*);
it does not refer to wholesome karma pertaining to the portion of liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and so forth.
Nevertheless, it is not the case that it does not bring about distinct retributions.
In this context, "Dharma masters" refers to those who possess the karmic fortune and the seeds of goodness;
"equipped with a teacher" is to be understood as previously explained.
Furthermore, following this section on the *ālayavijñāna* as the possessor of all seeds, the external objections are addressed.
This refers to what was stated previously: that because it subsumes all seeds, it constitutes the root of all defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
How can there be two kinds?
Therefore, he cites a sutra as proof:
the analogy of the cluster of akṣa fruits.
It is just like the *aśvattha* fruit.
In the commentary on the cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*), it says:
"If ordinary beings take the evolving consciousnesses as their object, and so forth, until they are bound by the fetters of internal coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*)."
In this context, the general explanation does not mention those who enter the path of vision of a pratyekabuddha;
this is omitted for brevity,
as their contemplative practice is the same.
It merely severs what is similar to the grasping at a person.
If it is said that the Śrāvakas have already been explained, this includes the Pratyekabuddhas as well.
In this context, "taking the evolving consciousnesses as their object" means:

This contradicts the *Śāstra on the Compendium of Ascertainment* (*Vyākhyāyukti*), which states: "When a bodhisattva first begins their studies, they should first study the causal conditions as they truly are (*yathābhūta-pratyaya*).
As for 'causal conditions as they truly are'..."
This is because it contradicts [the fact that] it is precisely the ālayavijñāna.
One interpretation states:
"In reality, prior to the Bodhisattva stages..."
It functions as the *ālayavijñāna* as explained in the *Saṃgrahaṇī*; however,
because it pertains to the practice prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) common to the three vehicles.
The name refers only to the observation of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
Because defilement exists within the evolving consciousnesses, they are able to take them as objects.
It is not that Bodhisattvas do not take the eighth consciousness as an object.
Furthermore, all take the eighth consciousness as the object-condition of their representation-only nature.
However, after entering the vision of the truths (darśanamārga),
they take the fundamental eighth consciousness itself as their object.
If one is able to perform the contemplation of consciousness-only,
this refers to subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna);
if one has not yet entered the vision of the truths (darśana-mārga), one takes the objective essence (bhāva-svabhāva) as the object.
Because it is not like the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*),
and because it takes as its object the image of its own sixth [consciousness],
it is called "taking the evolving consciousnesses as its object."
It is not meant that the eighth consciousness is not taken as an object within the essential nature (*svabhāva*).
The *Saṃgrahaṇī* (Compendium) speaks in terms of the essential nature, whereas here we speak in terms of the reflected image (*pratibimba*); thus there is no fault.
Śrāvakas and others,
like Bodhisattvas, practice dual contemplation;
having entered the vision of the truths (darśanamārga), they proceed further.
Only when subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) arises does it truly take the ālayavijñāna as its object;
otherwise, it does not.
If the preceding [moment] does not take the eighth as its object, how can the subsequent one do so? Question:
Do the śrāvakas also perform this contemplation?
The commentary states: If a śrāvaka of indeterminate lineage whose faculties have already matured must first enter the vision of the truths before proceeding toward the Mahāyāna,
then it is possible for this contemplation to occur.
For those of fixed lineage whose faculties are not yet mature,
it is not the case that they enter the path of seeing;
this text speaks with reference to those of indeterminate lineage whose faculties are already mature.
Furthermore, speaking in terms of the substance of the seeds,
the three vehicles all sever both the truths of origin and suffering.
If there were even a single dharma not yet penetrated or fully understood, [the path would not be perfected].
I never say that one attains the exhaustion of outflows [merely through this].
Once the truths have been realized through contemplation, the three vehicles contemplate them identically;
however, if categorized by name, they differ according to their respective meanings.
This "acting as a condition" exists only for the Bodhisattva who practices both [aspects] together;
it does not apply to those of the Two Vehicles. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises explain this in terms of their essential nature (*tattva*).
This is also like that;
therefore, everything is fully understood.
If one considers whether the meaning conforms to the name, then there is none.
Because the followers of the two vehicles contemplate only the self of persons (*pudgala-ātman*),
they eliminate all afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
Bodhisattvas eliminate both.
The contemplation of the two vehicles differs as previously explained;
their realization of the ālayavijñāna is no different from what was previously explained.
Furthermore, it is correctly understood that the Bodhisattva is able to know the eighth [stage],
whereas those of the Two Vehicles cannot.
Regarding the path of seeing for those of the two vehicles within this context:
relying upon and taking the evolving consciousness as their object,
they subsequently enter the vision of the truths and fully comprehend all defilements, fetters, and so forth.
Before the Bodhisattva stages, one truly takes the eighth [consciousness] as an object;
because it has not yet become an object of attachment,
it is called "taking the evolving consciousness as an object."
Subsequently, those who have entered the vision of the truths take the ālayavijñāna as their object;
however, this ālayavijñāna is not an object for the two vehicles.
This is established within the context of the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti).
The treatise says: "Briefly summarizing those formations,
even down to a single accumulation or a single collection—
this is the path of preparation."
This is as explained regarding the bodhisattvas' untainted [states] in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā*;
the same applies to the two vehicles.
Having thus unified them into a single aggregate:
Up until the attainment of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti),
this is the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) for the transformation of the basis; immediately following it,
one should say that [the afflictions] have been abandoned.
This is the path of clear liberation from all defilements;
herein, the originally existing seeds of the afflictions are severed.
The seeds give rise to their manifestations at a different time.
If a Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma is born at this time of excellence,
the same applies to the moment of their passing away.
Either the fruit of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) perishes,
or the fruit of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is exhausted;
as is commonly analyzed, this "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is of three kinds.
First, the transformation of the basis through the single mind,
which means that True Suchness (tathatā) is transformed to serve as the basis.
Second, the transformation of the path.
This is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
This is that which effects the transformation.
Third, the nature of cessation (*nirodha-svabhāva*).
This refers to the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). These various treatises maintain that it is precisely this analytical cessation [that constitutes liberation],
because the wisdom capable of taking it as its object can sever the afflictions.
It is established because it is attained through the cessation of true suchness (*tathatā*).
The phrase "it is not a real dharma" and what follows explains the objection;
each instance of its arising can be understood accordingly.
It possesses the nature of grasping,
which is precisely the grasping of shared fruits;
furthermore, it is the very transformation of the basis of craving.
Mastery over the three natures means that,
having attained the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), one attains mastery over phenomena by taking up or abandoning the three natures.
Otherwise, one lacks mastery over acceptance and rejection.
Within the eighth sign of cessation,
although the body remains present, [the mind is absent].
Just as with a transformation-body (nirmāṇa),
since the eighth [consciousness] has already been severed by the power of karma and afflictions,
it should not exist by virtue of the force of residual momentum.
There exists an unobscured-neutral aggregate,
similar to a magical creation;
it is not produced by karma or afflictions.
Furthermore, this refers to the discourse on turning the mind toward the Mahāyāna; that is,
by means of the power of aspiration and supernormal faculties,
one causes [the lifespan] to abide for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
This maintenance of life arises precisely from the power of aspiration and supernormal power (*ṛddhi*),
just as a transformation (*nirmāṇa*) also arises through the power of transformative supernormal power.
It is not so, however, in the case of a Buddha.
Regarding the four statements on the ālaya,
this is as stated in the second [chapter] of the Abhidharma:
"As for the ālaya..."
It is so called because it can store the seeds of all phenomena (*dharma*),
and furthermore, because sentient beings grasp it as "self," it is the object of the attachment to self (*ātmasneha*) and is thus named *ālaya*.
Now, we adopt the latter interpretation.
Therefore, in the eighth stage and those above, the name is abandoned but the essence is not.
Regarding the term "extinction attainment" (*nirodha-samāpatti*) mentioned in the first exclusive proposition:
This refers to those who have attained the third fruit and no others;
for others fulfill the fourth alternative.
This applies when [the recollection] concerns birth and death.
An opponent may raise this objection:
Why are the aggregates of birth and death not discussed here?
They are already included within the state of fainting.
Within the second partial statement, there are three positions:
first, because craving for coarse and manifest phenomena is exhausted,
the designation "abandonment" does not refer to subtle attachment to dharmas.
This refers to the second stage of those of the two vehicles;
it means that they have permanently suppressed the active manifestation [of afflictions] upon entering the eighth stage and beyond.
When the manifestation of craving for persons is forever suppressed so that it does not arise,
this is not a case of retaining delusions,
because one has given rise to the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
The third pair eliminates the coarse and subtle habitual tendencies of the two attachments to persons and phenomena;
this refers to those from the eighth stage of the Tathāgata onwards,
who are here termed "non-retrogressive."
Because they have not yet attained non-retrogression,
their wholesome dharmas necessarily and constantly increase; thus,
the first stage is called "Non-Retrogression."
This is called "having attained non-retrogression.
It is not the case that afflictions arise at times when one has not [yet] attained it,
because [at such times] there would still be outflowing minds and so forth.
The term "transforming consciousness" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) applies universally to both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*);
however, the name "ālaya" is narrow,
applying only up to the stage of the two vehicles in training (*śaikṣa*) and the eighth stage of the Mahāyāna.
The *vipākavijñāna* and so forth are broad in scope,
extending even to the Mahāyāna *vajra[-samādhi]*;
as for those of the two vehicles who have attained no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), if they enter the realm of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣadhātu*).
The fourth phrase within the Tathāgata’s manifestation of signs regarding the ultimate nature of the two vehicles—
referring to the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth—
is expressed in the treatise by the words "and the Tathāgatas, etc."
It is not that non-retrogressive bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas do not actually enter the nirvāṇa without support;
this is stated with reference to the six evolving consciousnesses.
It does not refer to the seventh [consciousness],
nor to the āmalaka-vijñāna,
which is here translated as the "stainless consciousness" (amala-vijñāna).
It exists only in the state of Buddhahood;
it is simply another name for the eighth consciousness.
Some say it is the ninth consciousness.

In this treatise, within the determination (*viniścaya*) of the first two levels (*bhūmi*) of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, regarding the reason for establishing the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the six consciousnesses, it says: "Furthermore, a certain class of consciousness arises with a variety of distinct intrinsic natures depending upon various respective conditions."
In this regard, the followers of Asaṅga explain that although the eight bodies are distinct,
they are all of one class of consciousness; because their bases and objects are each distinct,
they are designated by names according to their respective bases.
If one follows the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
those who differ from the disciples of Asaṅga state that the eight kinds [of consciousness] are one in essence.
Because consciousness depends on different sense organs,
eight names are established;
yet its essence is without distinction.
This very passage is taken as authoritative.
In the *Śāstra*’s explanation of the "group of consciousnesses" (*vijñānakāya*) regarding partial knowledge and so forth, it states:
"There are epidemics, untimely deaths, calamities, and afflictions."
As the Dharma Master said:
the first three are the three harms,
and the last one is mental anguish.
Furthermore, the first three constitute the three offenses,
while the last one constitutes mental distress and suffering.
Now, these four characteristics shall be assigned to them in sequence once again.
Furthermore, the first one constitutes three harms,
and the latter three constitute three offenses.
Moreover, the first three constitute three harms.
The latter one consists of three offenses.

The Treatise states: "One should distinguish the differentiation of skillfulness regarding the mind and the differentiation of skillfulness regarding the transformation of the mind," and so forth, up to:
"One should know the differentiation of skillfulness regarding the transformation of the mind."
Contemplate that which is conceptually imputed as being without coming or going,
its nature being primordial nirvana.
There is no time when realization occurs as a causal condition;
one who is able to know the mind of the *dharmatā* of *tathatā* as it truly is is called skillful.
It is called "differentiation" because it is not [identical to] the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and so forth.
When the mind takes the three natures as its object, this dependent phenomenon is not a non-existent thing;
one contemplates and knows that this mind arises in dependence upon others.
This is called the transformation of the mind.
One who can truly know this does not give rise to pervasive conceptualization; this is called skillfulness.
The name "differentiation" refers to being distinct from the previous contemplation.
Furthermore, it is explained as contemplating the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) as appearing to exist when it does not truly exist.
When these phenomena, which exist as mere designations,
are severed, one realizes suchness;
this is called skill in the transformation of the mind.
"Transformation" means the cessation that realizes suchness;
it is the cessation of the mind's other-dependent nature and its imagined nature,
which are non-existent entities.
When one contemplates that there is only mind, the objects grasped [by it] cannot be severed;
the non-arising of suchness is merely termed "skillfulness regarding the mind.
The treatise explains that these two bring about the fruit of benefit and peace.
This refers to one who has attained the bliss of awakening and possesses mastery over its causes;
such a person brings the mind under their own control and does not allow it to become negligent.
Furthermore, this occurs precisely through the prior cultivation of the mind.
Because one attains the ultimate at the time of fruition,
one exercises mastery over the three natures while within the causes of blissful peace.
The commentary explains that the application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) observes only the mind;
this alone severs the notions of pleasure, purity, permanence, and self,
because it gives rise to the realization of the actual impurity and other such qualities regarding objects and phenomena.
Some say that one attains the object through the mindfulness of contemplating the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).
While the preceding statement spoke of the thorough knowledge of the collection of consciousnesses (*vijñānakāya*),
the present statement refers exclusively to the mind.
Because of profound goodness and valor,
there is this difficult passage.
Regarding the four perversions, as stated previously in the eighth [section], it says:
Regarding the clinging to precepts and vows, this is the inversion of regarding what is painful as pleasant;
regarding the clinging to views, this is the inversion of regarding what is impure as pure;
and regarding the extreme views, a portion of these constitutes the inversion of regarding what is impermanent as permanent.
The view of self is the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).
The *Xianyang lun* states:
"Since all four inversions are inversions of perception, view, and mind, they are all eliminated for this purpose."
Therefore, those who abide in the three types of dwellings and practice the six right conducts possess the dwelling of liberation,
which is the gate of liberation of the Bodhi of the Three Vehicles;
they possess the dwelling of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, which are the gates of liberation.
As stated in the second chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*:
if one speaks of "emptiness" and so forth without mentioning "cultivation" and so forth,
it then encompasses all three types of wisdom— those arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
It encompasses both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
If one speaks of the three samādhis, such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*),
these are precisely the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).
They encompass both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
If they are the doors of liberation such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*),
they consist exclusively of untainted cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Now, as for these three gates of liberation,
they are entered only by those who have attained the outflow-free state through the vision of the truths;
therefore, among the six correct practices that follow, they are subsumed therein.
These are subsumed within the two paths of seeing and cultivation.
That which can lead to the abiding in the dharmas of the gates of liberation refers specifically to the seven preparatory stages (*saptaprayoga*) prior to entering the path of seeing.
Furthermore, there is the dwelling in liberation, the dwelling in the extinction of nirvana, and the dwelling in the gates of liberation;
this is precisely the nirvana of the Path.
Because one relies upon it to attain manifestation, it is called a "gate."
That which can lead to and abide in the dharmas of the gates of liberation refers to the three types of mundane wisdom (prajñā) prior to the stages [of the path of seeing];
it leads to the arising of the Middle Way and the Truth of Cessation within the realization of the Truths.
Among the six types of correct practice,
uninterrupted practice refers to the roots of goodness induced by the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) through diligent reception and reflection, the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*),
and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), as well as the three paths of seeing, meditation, and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Next, the first three types of wisdom are said to be subsumed within the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*).
Within the three dwellings (*vihāra*), they are subsumed within the final dwelling, which comprises both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
The three gates of liberation are subsumed within the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Liberation abides therein by reversing the previous three modes of abiding.
Furthermore, it explains the six right practices and uninterrupted practice.
That is to say, within the seven stages of preparation,
one cultivates the wholesome states of reception and reflection without interruption;
immediately after this uninterrupted cultivation, one enters the path of seeing.
Because one has now attained the untainted (*anāsrava*), it is said that "the wholesome [state] induced by cultivation is well-received and arises.
This means that because the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) arises based on cultivated roots of goodness,
one becomes free from the desires of the three realms within that cultivation.
This refers to the time when one becomes detached from the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Becoming detached from the desires of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is termed "discriminating through the practice of discerning the truths," which means discriminating by taking the principles of the truths as an object.
Becoming detached from the desires of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is termed "being free from overweening pride" (*an-adhimāna*).
For example, a bhikṣu with overweening pride attains the fourth dhyāna and claims it to be the fruit of arhatship;
yet this state merely involves detachment from the desire of the formless realm and does not constitute true outflow-free realization.
He does not give rise to overweening pride;
nor does he give rise to overweening pride regarding his own attainment of freedom from desire for the realm of form.
All of these belong to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
However, they receive their names based on their predominant characteristics within a single realm (*dhātu*).
This is not like the previous explanation, where the time of attaining the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*) is termed "right pure conduct" (*samyak-viśuddha-caryā*).
Because one attains the six modes of constant abiding (*ṣaḍ-āveṇika-vihāra*),
the preceding liberations (*vimokṣa*) may also be sequentially correlated with them; furthermore,
the first [liberation] corresponds to the four [factors] within the third [mode of abiding] mentioned previously.
This refers to the second [period] mentioned previously in terms of the time of increase;
the sixth refers to the first [period] mentioned previously.
Alternatively, these latter five [periods] collectively apply to both of the former two.
The treatise further states that there are two kinds of giving: first, giving by the recipient; second, giving by the giver.
Regarding "giving by the recipient," the Dharma Master provides two interpretations.
One interpretation states that it is like giving one's own body for another to receive,
just as when begging for alms;
for one relinquishes one's own body to others so that they may receive it.
The first is called giving by the recipient;
the second is giving after understanding that one has received another's wealth and then practicing relinquishment.
This refers to the transformation of material giving into the gift of the Dharma, which should be understood accordingly.
Among those who attain the two fruits [of stream-entry and once-returning],
the recipient obtains great wealth,
while the donor obtains this result of natural outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Furthermore, regarding the recipient who enjoys wealth by overcoming their own stinginess:
the act of giving away what one possesses to one's own person is called "giving to the recipient," which is equivalent to giving it to one's own servants.
Furthermore, because they all possess a mind of generosity,
they will obtain wealth in the future; this wealth,
which they then enjoy for themselves, constitutes the result of a dominant influence (*niṣyanda-phala*) arising from their superior resolve.
Second, by giving to others, one obtains great wealth.
Furthermore, the first two types of giving are explained as before;
through them all, one obtains great wealth.
It serves as the fruit of maturation;
therein, one is not stingy and is thus able to enjoy it once again.
This is called the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
In the treatise’s refutation of the theory that the past and future exist substantially,
this passage is intended to clarify the intrinsic nature (*svadharma*) of the three time periods.
First, the cause for that [position] is refuted;
the text of the sixth fascicle of the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* on the stage of vitarka and vicāra is not the definitive analysis.
This is the definitive analysis of the dependent nature and so forth;
therefore, in the subsequent objection, it asks:
"For what reason?"
General Refutation: It is not the case that a phenomenon which is without direction or location can have the sense of moving from one direction to another direction.
This refutes the first [position].
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
Form in future time must possess spatial location,
because it undergoes transformation and change,
just like form in the present.
Furthermore, dharmas of the future cannot be transferred to the present world,
because they lack spatial location,
like the horns of a rabbit and so forth; nor are they [identical to] dharmas that have not yet arisen or have already arisen.
This refutes the second [position]:
namely, that your future existence is definitively without death,
because there is no birth.

"One understands the precepts by means of guarding against what is improper."
Regarding the statement "there is morality that does not prevent wrongdoing," this is merely the name of what is unwholesome;
if it were explained according to the current interpretation, [it would be incorrect].
Thus, there is no fault.
It is like the case where the name "non-restraint" (asamvara) is applied similarly.
Furthermore, it is objected:
The nature of evil is not itself śīla;
rather, because one who practices evil possesses evil śīla,
it is called "evil śīla."
Furthermore, one should see that the essence [of the view] is not evil;
for those who commit evil detest that view.
This is called "evil view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The commentary explains that "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*);
both wholesome and unwholesome discriminations are termed "views."
Śīla is named "cooling" because the nature of evil is not cooling; therefore,
it cannot be cited as an analogous example for [the case of] views.
The essential nature of the restraint likewise consists of both the wholesome and the unwholesome occurring simultaneously,
and it is comprised of five categories.
In its essential nature, it is a provisional designation based upon the seeds of volition (*cetanā*).
Now, according to the text of the Mahāyāna,
it likewise takes the ten paths of wholesome action and the five aggregates (*skandha*) of volition as its substance.
Non-restraint is the opposite of this.
Regarding the timing of the arising of the precepts,
for the five groups of the ordained:
The precepts are obtained after the third *karmavācanā*.
However, for śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and the three groups of lay followers,
the precepts are obtained immediately upon receiving the Three Refuges.
If one belongs to the two groups of the ordained,
one must receive [the precepts] from another because they are subsumed under the category of *bhikṣu*;
however, those belonging to the three groups of the laity obtain them through spontaneous acceptance (*svayam-upasaṃpad*).
That is to say, having already performed the three refuges, one immediately obtains the precepts.
If the Bodhisattva precepts are received naturally,
they encompass all precepts without exception.
After having gone forth, one must receive [the precepts] from another;
here, we clarify that the precepts of the two vehicles are received from another in two ways.
The branch of maintaining through restraint refers to shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). Shame is that which arises from oneself;
dread of blame is that which arises from others.
Both proceed together;
however, because one is predominant over the other,
when one precept is present, the second is not.
It is not that there is no single [precept] at all.
If one receives the precepts from another,
seven branches are initiated by means of the body.
Regarding precepts such as approaching a teacher,
seven branches are initiated through speech,
such as when one speaks to request instruction from a teacher.
If it is acquired spontaneously,
there is only mental manifest action;
this does not take body or speech as its means.

It is solely by means of the mind as a condition that one acquires the non-informative (avijñapti) aspects of the seven branches of body and speech. Question: There must then be non-informative [action] that does not arise from informative (vijñapti) action, because there is no body or speech [to produce it].
Because there is a manifest action (*vijñapti*) produced by one's own intention.
If that is so, then at the very moment of receiving [the precepts] oneself,
one pays homage to the Buddha and speaks these words.
Is it not that manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) is what makes [the intention] known? Now, in explaining non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), because it is made known by others,
it is said to be "without body or speech."
It is not that one lacks bodily and vocal karma; therefore,
informative action (*vijñapti*) also arises,
as in the case of commanding another to perform an act.
Alternatively, because vocal karma and so forth serve as the manifest expressions of the body and so forth,
the body and speech can mutually manifest one another.
Furthermore, these [expressions] pertain to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Just as one who is gravely ill is unable to move the body or utter speech,
even though they receive [the precepts] from another, there is also non-informative matter (*avijñapti*),
which does not arise from informative action (*vijñapti*).
Alternatively, because one may generate the resolve by oneself and possess only the unmanifest (avijñapti),
this treatise was composed for that reason.
Among the three Western masters' expositions on the essence of the precepts within the hundred practices,
some speak of "one part" and so forth;
this is identical to the Sautrāntika school.
When one receives one or two precepts,
the precepts are likewise generated at that time;
the same applies to non-restraint and so forth.
Taking a vow for a limited time is also called non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
If one commits killing without having taken such a vow, [it is not classified as non-restraint].
These are merely designated as being "intermediate.
When categorized separately by time and by type of experience, there are ten in total.
Herein, a question is asked:
Now that we have been separated for what is but a brief moment, how is this any different?
Yet you speak of [a separation] lasting for a hundred years,
or even until the end of one's life.
What is the difference between the tenth [type of resolve] and that which one receives for oneself and teaches to others?
It is because there is a distinction in the object of focus, the intent, and the pursuit.
Furthermore, within this, there are three stages.
The first three positions are categorized by phenomena;
the next three positions are categorized by time;
and the final four positions are categorized by persons.
However, within the latter [section],
the third [topic], "one's own words," is divided into two parts;
thus, it says, "ethical discipline (*śīla*), freedom from regret (*avipratisāra*), and so forth."
As stated in the seventh chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*:
"Because one has accomplished ethical discipline (*śīla*), there is no regret;
because there is no regret, joy arises."
Because of the arising of joy, the mind becomes glad;
because the mind is glad, the body becomes tranquil;
because the body is tranquil, one experiences happiness.
Because one experiences pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated;
because the mind is concentrated, one contemplates reality as it truly is;
because one contemplates reality as it truly is, revulsion arises.
Through the arising of revulsion, one becomes free from desire;
through freedom from desire, one attains liberation;
and through liberation, one declares: "I have realized liberation; my births are exhausted," and so forth.
Regarding the dhyāna restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*),
there are here only the four fundamental [dhyānas],
as in the eighth chapter of the Abhidharma.
In the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu),
form (rūpa) or restraint (saṃvara) is not established in brief;
this is indicated in texts such as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
The formless realm also possesses the precepts associated with meditative concentration;
however, within the desire realm, these may be cultivated as either a preparatory antidote (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*) for the path of cultivation or the path of seeing.
In this context, because it follows the logical sequence of the gates,
the formless realms are not mentioned;
furthermore, there are also paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) within the future dhyāna.
This is omitted for brevity.
As for those who are untainted (anāsrava) and have previously attained meditative absorption (dhyāna):
Relying on the fifth stage, one enters the path of seeing and attains the fruit of non-returning;
one obtains the path of seeing characterized by the precepts and the nine paths of uninterrupted transition.
It serves as the path of counteraction for the unwholesome courses of action and so forth,
as well as the path of subsequent liberation and so on,
up to the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
The path of seeing is called the "counteractive of distancing" regarding unwholesome precepts;
as for the path of cultivation,
it refers to the subtle transgressions within the bodies of noble ones.
Depending on the respective first dhyāna and so forth,
the nine grades of the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) are called the "path of antidote" (pratipakṣa-mārga) with respect to the [defilements] to be abandoned.
The path of liberation is also called the counteractive agent of distancing (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*).
However, in the Mahāyāna, there is furthermore a synthesis of the three realms and nine stages,
whereby one proceeds from the first fruit directly to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
It serves as the antidote for the nine grades [of afflictions].
Regarding that abandonment, it continues in this manner until, depending upon whichever stage [it may be], [the afflictions] are abandoned.
One takes the nine grades of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) as the path of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-mārga*);
the remaining stages are called the path of distant separation (*dūribhāva-pratipakṣa*).
This excludes the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the intermediate dhyāna;
this is based on those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have first attained the third fruit.
It is superior because it abandons the afflictions that are to be abandoned;
this is likewise true for the gradual abandonment of the third fruit and those beyond it,
solely by virtue of the superiority of the counteractive agents.
One attains the speech of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
If one has suddenly severed the nine grades of the three realms,
yet has not yet attained the state of one beyond training.
The path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) is superior because it is that which abandons all that is to be remedied;
the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) is superior because it alone is capable of remedying what is superior.
Regarding the entry into the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*):
herein, the method for those who practice "leaping over" (*vyutkrāntaka*) is based on the four fundamental dhyānas,
while the method for those who attain the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) is based on the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*).
In fact, the future dhyāna can also attain the fruit of transcendence and obtain the seven modes of mental attention.
Based on the future attainment of the fruit of non-returning,
the seventh mental application— the culmination of the preparatory stage—
necessarily enters the fundamental state.
Now, this is discussed in terms of the fulfillment of the fruit;
this treatise treats it as a transcendence,
as in the case of one who attains the fruits in successive order.
The formless attainments can sever the seeds of transgressions against the precepts of the desire realm.
The Dharma Master says:
"The path of seeing relies upon six stages, including the intermediate stage."
Not so. According to the six types of clear observation (*abhisamaya*), they arise based on three or five dhyānas,
excluding the intermediate dhyāna.
Although other texts state that there is untainted [consciousness] elsewhere,
since the abode of Brahmā is characterized by much distraction,
how could it be comparable to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), where such untainted consciousness is said to exist?
It does not constitute the abandonment of afflictions,
as is extensively analyzed elsewhere.
However, this refers to the discipline associated with meditative concentration and the Path.
The Dharma Master says:
It is established upon the volition (*cetanā*) that manifests simultaneously with the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), because it is a form (*rūpa*) that follows the mind (*cittānuparivartin*).
Question: Why is it called "unmanifest [form] concomitant with the Path" (*mārgasamprayuktā avijñapti*)?
Just as right speech and right action give rise to verbal expression,
how do they function as informative intimation (*vijñapti*)?
Furthermore, this is according to the *Prātimokṣa* vows.
It is established upon the seeds of volition;
this [case] should also be understood in the same way.
Just as, for example, the Prātimokṣa vows persist from the moment they are received onward.
Moment by moment and instant by instant, they continue to grow;
yet when they encounter conditions and are relinquished,
the original seeds are not destroyed.
It is not like the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), where it is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) because [the precepts] have been severed;
rather, it is now called "abandoning the precepts" (*śikṣā-pratyākhyāna*) because the seven branches of the new moment do not arise.
The same applies to the precepts associated with the meditative concentration of the Path (*mārga-samādhi-sahaja*).
When there is a mind, it increases moment by moment;
the seven branches multiply.
If the mind has ceased and one is in a state of uniformity, [they do not increase].
It arises through the continuity of its seeds;
because there is no sense of new addition,
it is called "abandonment."
This is not like the Prātimokṣa vows, which continue to increase whether one possesses a conscious mind or not once they have been received;
therefore, it is called "the transformation that fulfills the intention. Question: How does this occur through active volition (*cetanā*)?
Regarding the determination of the essence of the precepts,
some say that it is established upon this seed.
One should establish it as being superior to the preceding path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
just as the volition (*cetanā*) that gives rise to the *prātimokṣa* vows;
for it takes up the karma of the volition of the preceding path of preparation.
In the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
this has not yet been established as an explanation;
it is like the preparatory path prior to the path of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mārga*).
None of these are the precepts of the fixed path;
they are of a distracted mind,
or are bound to other stages or realms.
How can the nature of the precepts be determined according to the preparatory application?
It should instead be established based on the volition associated with meditative concentration or the Path.
One who is a lay follower (*upāsaka*) is so named because they have desisted from evil conduct.
Misconduct refers to the first three branches as well as mental action;
among these, there is the abstention from drinking intoxicants,
which follows the course of desire.
Now, based on the majority view, we shall discuss the two causes for the one-day precept (upavāsa):
namely, maintaining the practice of abstaining from both desire and evil for a day and night serves as the cause for maintaining them for as long as life lasts.
Because their faculties and natures are inferior, they are called "near-dwellers" (*upavāsa*) because they dwell near the fruit due to being close to its cause. Regarding non-celibacy:
for householders, what is prohibited is the wrong [conduct], but not the right [conduct].
If one wishes to practice while maintaining one's current name,
it is not permitted; if one leaves the household life,
it is called "departing from evil conduct."
Abstaining from misconduct is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*);
thus, it is identical to the previous three in being a natural transgression.
Abstaining from misconduct—
They arise from greed,
because they are prohibited by its restraint;
this is just as the latter four offenses are all prohibited by the restraint against greed.
The four branches of a bhikṣu do not refer merely to the formal undertaking of the precepts; rather,
they refer to the four grave offenses (pārājika) and the four reliances (niśraya), and so forth, as explained in the first [chapter],
such as the accomplishment of śīla in the seventh fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
Second, he is well able to guard the prātimokṣa vows.
Third, his conduct and manner of behavior are entirely perfected.
Fourth, he perceives even the slightest fault with great dread.
And the accomplishment of ethical discipline (*śīla*),
which means not transgressing it,
and being able to emerge from it once a transgression has occurred.
Because one must manifest and train in each respective precept,
this first [category] becomes the sixth,
and the sixth becomes the first.
That is, "śrāvaka" consists of six elements:
*upa* means "near," *ka* means "matter," and *soka* means "male voice."
This is the feminine form.
By adding *sa* to the proximate base,
it becomes feminine because of this feminine suffix.
This distinguishes between male and female. Regarding the term "mother-color" (*mātṛ-varṇa*), a literal translation should be "mother-village" (*mātṛ-grāma*);
women of the household are the same as mothers.
Therefore, women are called "mothers" by those of the same village or community.

Regarding the discussion of what constitutes discipline (*vinaya*) and non-discipline (*avinaya*), it is said that— excluding the aforementioned discipline and non-discipline— all bodily, verbal, and mental actions that are wholesome or unwholesome are [included therein].
According to the preceding [explanation of] restraint, there is the attainment of one [non-restraint] even when not being maintained;
this refers to the superior grade,
which gives rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
If those of middling or inferior capacity do not currently engage in the ten paths of unwholesome action,
or even if they perform them only to a mild degree,
the non-informative [karma] arising therefrom all has this as its essential nature.
Furthermore, if one person maintains one part of the vows of restraint while not maintaining the others,
this is the intermediate state.
If one vows to perform only a portion of unwholesome actions,
this is not termed non-restraint; rather,
it is merely a state intermediate between the two.
Now, both restraint and non-restraint depend on only a portion [of the faculties],
and this is because they consist merely in a formal vow to abstain from the most intense [unwholesome states].
This is comprised within non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Within it, there are also three grades.
The treatise states: "complete abandonment, partial abandonment, and abandonment through injury."
As stated in the Abhidharma (Dharmapada),
there are five kinds [of weeds]:
namely, those that grow spontaneously, those that require half a month [to sprout], those that are jealous, those that require irrigation, and those that must be removed [by hand].
In this context, there is only the absence of sprinkling [water].
This is because envy is here divided into two types:
that which is directed toward oneself and that which is directed toward seeing others [prosper].
He causes them to be sprinkled together;
such beings belong to the class of the envious,
for they only gain power upon obtaining the vital essence and blood of others.
*Śaṇḍha* means "one without the power of sexual organs";
*pandaka* means "one who desires," so called because they take pleasure in others regarding themselves as objects of transgression.
If one were designated as "complete" merely by being born, there would be no basis [for such a designation],
because others take pleasure in seeing faults in oneself.
They are called *paṇḍaka* because they lack the functional capacity of sexual organs;
they are called *śaṇḍhaka* for the same reason.
Because the male faculty does not arise throughout one's entire life,
the second type, who takes pleasure in themselves,
is called a paṇḍaka.
There are those who possess and maintain a non-śaṇḍha body and possess the faculty;
because the power of the faculty arises at certain times.
Among those excluded [from the category], there are two types of persons.
This person differs from those born [as such];
it is impossible that they were ever without the male organ,
for they once possessed the male organ.
Although the absence of roots has been removed,
their nature remains uninterrupted;
this is because one does not take pleasure in others committing transgressions.
They are not *paṇḍakas*.
Because they lack the power of sexual organs, they are called *śaṇḍhakas*.
If one takes pleasure [in such acts], it is termed a transgression (*doṣa*), and thus they are called *paṇḍakas*.
Because they lack the [sexual] faculties.
Furthermore, as for those who dwell separately from the *śaṇḍha* (eunuchs),
their dwelling is clarified because their prior intention has been impaired.
Now, because the Dharma itself has been impaired,
although there may be differences in the sequence of their intentions regarding dwelling elsewhere,
this does not impair the distinct nature of the later time.
The treatise states: "Those obtained from others" refers to cases such as when one's parents pass away during childhood and one is taken in for adoption by another.
Although they are not one's own parents,
they are nonetheless others who have attained [the precepts];
such precepts may possess these obstacles and difficulties.
There are cases where one receives the precepts but does not obtain them;
however, this merely constitutes an offense and does not mean the precepts were not obtained.
"The monastery keeper" refers to the person who guards the temple gate. Among the five conditions for relinquishing the precepts for a bhikṣu:
The Dharma Master says:
According to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, regarding the forfeiture incurred by committing an offense,
one loses [the precepts] only if the offense was committed with an upper-grade (intense) state of mind.
This case is also like that;
it does not constitute a valid explanation,
because the Bodhisattva’s superior mind is devoid of shame and remorse.
Within these precepts of the śrāvakas,
one loses them immediately upon transgression,
regardless of whether the mind is superior, middling, or inferior.
Because they all transgress the teachings,
and because they all constitute natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
If one were not to commit a grave offense regarding the five precepts...
Because one is no longer designated as practicing non-celibacy,
remorse is likewise restored to purity;
furthermore, because the arising of both sexual organs does not prevent one from maintaining the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
The upavāsa precepts do not sever the roots of goodness,
because they last for both day and night; thus,
one does not incur the severance of the roots of goodness.
Because it must first be preceded by preparatory effort (*prayoga*),
there is likewise no grave offense (*pārājika*);
it is not a definitive abandonment.
Because it is not the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
In this context, only the rising of the sun constitutes relinquishment.
The Dharma Master says:
According to the *Śataśāstra*,
there is a period ranging from one day up to one year;
thus, we know that the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) precepts may also be observed for an extended duration.
Because the resolve is vast.
If that were so, it would be like the bhikṣu precepts,
where the resolve extends through many lifetimes.
Could this not be the limit of the continuity?
Because its force does not extend for a long duration;
if it were to last for a day or more, [the force would diminish].
However, this is merely a wholesome restraint that is neutral;
it is not [a formal] restraint.
What harm is there in its inclusion among the hundred practices?
It includes the goodness of the intermediate state.
Furthermore, how could a vow for the five precepts taken for only a single day constitute the discipline of restraint?
However, because it occupies a middle position,
the attainment of non-conception is as described in the second [chapter] of the Abhidharma.
In this context, there is no mention of retrogression.
Subsequently, when arising in the form realm, there is the fixed production of retributive maturation (vipāka),
whether previously attained or not yet attained.
As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*,
the faculty-nature (indriya-gotra) of one who has attained meditative concentration is not exclusively of the superior grade,
because there are three grades and so forth.
Therefore, in the preceding fascicle’s discussion on "concomitant transformation" (anuvartana),
it was stated only that this applies to the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru),
and not to the Non-percipient [Heaven] (asaṃjñin).
Because they end prematurely,
this stage consists of nine grades, just like the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
This meditative attainment (samāpatti) necessarily results in liberation from the retribution of the nine grades [of defilements].
It must arise based solely on the simultaneous exhaustion of all nine grades within the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva). Question: How does the seed of the mind guard the mind?
The essence of meditative concentration (samādhi) is not form;
it is the mind that, through the various types of form, guards against form.
The essence of ethical discipline (śīla) is neither mind nor form.
Answer: The element of form (rūpa-dhātu) prevents [the perception of] form;
the essence of this element is form, and thus it is not non-form.
The seeds of the mind guard the mind;
the substance of these seeds is not the mind, and is therefore termed "non-mental form" (acittaka-rūpa). Question: One guards form by means of form.
The category of form returns to being called form;
by means of the mind, one guards the mind.
The category of mind is neither non-mind nor form.
Answer: The substance of the category of matter (*rūpa-dhātu*) that is prevented by the category of matter is subsumed under matter itself.
If that is so, then the mind (*citta*) that is prevented by the category of mind (*citta-dhātu*) should likewise be subsumed under mind.
Answer: The wholesome form that arises from the prevention of wrongdoing through the seeds of form establishes precepts based on those seeds;
this is precisely the seed of the mind’s revulsion toward form.
It also guards the mind, because no other mind arises. This is neither mind nor matter.
Question: Regarding the categories of matter, it is said that they guard against non-material categories.
It is named "the arising of wholesome form.
The seeds of the mind guard the mental applications, and the seeds of those applications continue to give rise to the mind.
It is further explained that the mind arises [from them].
Answer: The substance of the mind fundamentally consists of the faculty of cogitation;
since it lacks an object of cognition, it is not "mind" or "thought.
It is designated as "form" (rūpa) by virtue of that which it prevents.
Because the seeds of thought are restrained, it is subsumed under form (*rūpa*).

The treatise states: "Furthermore, if, by reason of this cause and through this grasping, all produced minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that have arisen cease, this is called 'non-conception' (*asaṃjñin*)."
The Dharma Master said:
"At the moment of initial birth there is a mind;
this mind is common to both the wholesome and the indeterminate natures."
Because it arises spontaneously,
it is called "attained at birth.
Once this has ceased, [it exists] upon the ālayavijñāna.
This establishes the maturation of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*).
Master Jùn states:
"At the moment of birth, there is a resultant (*vipāka*) mental consciousness."
Because this consciousness ceases, the mind and mental factors obtained at birth cease.
The Grand Master said:
"As for taking birth in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva)..."
Furthermore, at the time of relinquishing life,
there is no mental consciousness.
To say that the mind and mental factors obtained at birth cease [at that point]— [End of excerpt]
That is to say, there is a final stage of the intermediate state;
because it arises spontaneously with a defiled mind,
it is called "attained at birth" (*upapatti-pratilambhika*).
When these mind and mental factors have ceased and one again undergoes rebirth in existence,
this is called the cessation of the mind and mental factors acquired at birth;
thus is the state of non-conception established.
However, the state of non-conception (asaṃjñi) is a distinct karmic retribution;
it possesses a functional capacity within the eighth consciousness that prevents the mind from arising.
This is the substance of individual retribution;
it is precisely the volition (*cetanā*) of the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
The substance of this volition brings about collective retribution.
Regarding the function of the mind that acts as a restraint above [the state of non-conception], it induces a distinct retribution. Question:
How can the eighth manifesting mind and its mental factors be called the "function of the mind of revulsion" and yet be termed the "distinct retribution of non-conception"?
Furthermore, since it is established that the mind and mental factors do not function in the state of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*),
for what reason does a single volition (*cetanā*) also bring about both collective and individual retributions?
Furthermore, how can an insentient karma induce the retribution of the eighth consciousness, which possesses sentience?
This current interpretation is incorrect.
If the volition preceding meditative concentration constitutes the karma for general retribution,
it brings about the eighth [consciousness] as the general retribution;
this is due to the functional capacity of the seeds of the mind of aversion.
This is karma of individual retribution (*prātibhāvikakarma*).
It brings about the arising of the sixth consciousness and the cessation of the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*),
as well as the individual retribution of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and so forth.
If, during the preceding preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the mind was not weary [of cyclic existence],
then the equanimity (*upekṣā*) that arises as the maturation (*vipāka*) of the rebirth-linking consciousness could have arisen; however,
because the mind was weary due to the preceding preparatory stage, [such equanimity does not arise].
The state in which the mind does not arise as a result in this life,

because within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they transform into the great elements (*mahābhūta*);
therefore, the great elements within concentration are omitted from discussion.
Although it is not said that they depend on the great elements for their creation,

Now, according to my reflection:
the previous fascicle states that one attains mastery over all forms.
It immediately transforms into the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

just as the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) induces the primary elements and so forth.
According to this text,

if it is not induced by preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Regarding the statement that "the primary elements only project derived matter," the subsequent text says it is not created by the primary elements,

Regarding the discussion on how it is known that this [intermediate state] must exist and cannot be like an echo or the like:
the Master of the Treatise now states,
"If there were no intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) to transmit consciousness within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)."
How is it that one can be born there?
An external opponent raises an objection:
"It is like the resonance of an echo."
How could it be that an object must be transmitted for its echo to be transmitted?
For instance, how could moon-reflections and the like require transmission to flow as shadows upon water?
It is just as when one perceives a distant object.
How could these three matters possibly require transmission through an intermediary? Since they do not depend on the transmission of material objects,

Now, because we are following that school’s tenet, it is said that [the primary elements] do not perish.

When the *Śāstra* states, "One should know that the great elements first occupy a location, and subsequently other derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) arises depending upon this location," this is based on the relationship between the supported (āśrita) and the support (āśraya).
When karma brings about its retribution,

Because luminosity possesses a square [or defined] substance.
The light is established by way of distinct characteristics.

This means, for example, when one takes away the spokes and the rim.

Regarding the two points of contention herein,
as reconciled in the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*,

the treatise states: "As in the section on the 'Compendium of Dharmas,' the superior matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) is comprised solely of visible form (*varṇa-rūpa*), and lacks odor, fragrance, and so forth."

Because there is no causal seed within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and other such realms;

"Attaining mastery over all things," and so forth—

Because it is also capable of manifesting reality.

They all attain mastery.

"The olfactory faculty of a bodhisattva..."
One perceives the fragrance of palaces in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).

what is manifested there is merely the fragrance and taste belonging to the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).

sounds, and so forth.
These are forms and sounds.

and because they lack utility.

This is because the seeds and the functions of odor and taste are absent there.
As for the absence of odor, taste, and so forth:
If that were so, then since there are no great elements (mahābhūta) or various seeds in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
they should not transform into the great elements and so forth.
Answer: In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is no karma or matter (rūpa);
however, because there is the matter of untainted primary elements (anāsrava-mahābhūta-rūpa), it possesses matter.
Since the realm of form (rūpadhātu) likewise lacks the retribution of fragrance and taste, [the same principle applies].
Furthermore, there are no untainted seeds of odor or taste.
As for the great elements of the formless realm that are non-retributive,
they do indeed possess untainted seeds.
Although the form realm lacks retributive odors and tastes, what prevents the existence of untainted seeds there?
The explanation says: because the great elements (mahābhūta) in the formless realm possess functional utility.
Although there is no great [result] that is retribution,
there is nonetheless the great [result] that is untainted (anāsrava).
This applies to the odors and tastes of the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Although there is no retribution,
because it is useless,
there is no untainted [phenomenon].
This is explained by means of two causes: the absence of seeds and the absence of utility.
If one examines this closely, it is as in the case of the Pure Land.
Is it not the case that there is no color, fragrance, or flavor resulting from superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*)?
Now, [these are absent] because they resemble the objects of a mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa*),
and because they lack the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*) which serve as the actual causes.
In reality, they do indeed exist.
Regarding the statement in the treatise that "there is no odor or fragrance in wind," one asks:
should there not likewise be no tactile sensation?
Since this object of touch fundamentally depends upon the wind element and others,
it is not analogous to fragrance or color, which are indeterminate;
its form is subtle and belongs to the desire realm.
According to this text,
visible form and tangibility are necessarily co-existent,
whereas odor and flavor are not so determined.

it maintains that all matter in the desire realm is necessarily not separated from odor and taste.
Because there is that which is separated [from the wheel],

as well as the remaining primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and fragrances (*gandha*), etc.
None of these can be established.

for they claim that things of equal measure do not undergo destruction.

However, the Grand Master (Taishi) stated that both explanations are found in the West.

such as the light of the solar disc.

how could it be that the sensation of heat is absent?
