it has the fire element as its substance.
How could there be a hot touch that arises apart from fire?
Thus, one knows that it also exists.
If one first explains the hot tactile sensation in the midst of the sun,
it is still the portion of fiery heat within the solar orb itself.
It is not the fire element that produces the color of light.
Sound should be understood by analogy with this. Question: Why are there no odors or tastes?
Because they are subtle, they are absent within light.
Because color and the sensation of heat are heavy,
they also exist within light.
If that which is touched is heavy, [it must be substantial].
Since light must exist within the fire element,
why do you say it does not?
When you now say there is no creator of light, [you contradict this].
It is not said that there is no heat from fire at midday;
likewise, one might as well say that fragrance has no lightness when it is gathered together with light.
There is also distant separation.
Does the fragrance from the hot portion at the site of the solar disc [reach here]?
He replied: "Because it is light."
As explained in the preceding text:
because there is the sensation of heat,
the other three great elements are absent.
It is said that there is no [matter] that is not the fire element, nor is there any other [matter].

The *Śāstra* states: "Furthermore, one should know that the superior matter which is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) depends solely upon superior concentration and does not depend upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)."
If this were contrary to what was stated above,
it has already been reconciled as previously explained.
Some claim that here [the term] refers exclusively to derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
The contemplation is called "contemplation of the indefinite" because it contemplates the great elements;
within meditative concentration, it does not transform into the great elements,
but is spoken of in terms of the essential nature of the image prior to concentration.
They likewise receive the name "great derivatives" (*mahābhūta-nirmāṇa*).
This is because the preceding discussion was based on the analysis of how the mind transforms the great elements (*mahābhūta*) during the preparatory stage;
thus, even the derivative matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced within meditative concentration is transformed into the great elements.
This is not the case here;

therefore, there is a distinction. Question: The directed intention (*āśaya*) does not constitute "greatness," and within the meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*), there are no great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The aspiring mind does not perform any conditioning.
Within this contemplation, there is no conditioned form;
is there only the primary elements?
Therefore, it is known that taking the preceding assembly as superior is correct.

The treatise states: "However, it is called 'constructed' because it arises from the concentration on the reflected image; it is not called 'constructed' because it depends upon that [image] for its arising.
Furthermore, it says: "This is based on the contemplation of all locations, such as blue and so forth."
The treatise states that the matter included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana-rūpa) is invisible and non-obstructive;
furthermore, it does not fully possess all the characteristics of the sphere of mental objects as defined in the Hīnayāna,
for therein only non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) could be so described.
In this Mahāyāna, it was previously stated that there is real matter within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
which is also received by others.
Why is this invisible and non-obstructive?
Because the matter transformed from the concentrated mind is,
in reality, extremely subtle.
It does not occupy a specific location and is not produced by karma; therefore,
it is non-obstructive.
The realms of form and so forth all rely upon specific locations;
therefore, they do not serve as a precedent for this case.
Herein, if it is for the enjoyment of others, [it is considered a gift].
If it is visual consciousness that sees, it should be subsumed under the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
Why, then, is it said to be the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?
The explanation is: from the time of its original arising.
Because this arises from a concentrated mind, it is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Although it may also be seen by the eye when used for another's sake, it is not intended here.
Is it called the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?
The treatise states: "The first outflow (*niṣyanda*) further has four kinds.
Among these, there are two at the beginning.
It is not separate from the two types previously mentioned—maturation and nourishment;
rather, it is a single entity whose intrinsic nature is that of outflow.
This is according to the subsequent text.
Excluding the matter of the sense organs (*indriya-rūpa*), the remaining three types of outflows (*āsrava*)—
namely, clarity (*vidyā*), the objects that support the sense organs (*viṣaya*), and the essential nature (*prakṛti*)—
have characteristics that are easily understood.
That is to say, it consists solely of the five external sense objects (viṣaya) within the five faculties (indriya),
comprising both the resultant (vipāka) and the nurtured (aupacayika) types.
All these are subject to transformation and decay;
they also constitute the second type of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
This category of "outflow" is broad in scope, encompassing results of maturation (*vipāka*) and other types as well.
The cessation of the preceding thought-moment and the arising of the succeeding thought-moment is called "equal outflow" (niṣyanda);
it flows forth as the internal faculties and so forth.
They receive the names "maturation" (*vipāka*) and "nourishment" (*aupacayika*).
Other external objects possess only two streams: the stream of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) and the stream of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
The stream of transformation is to be understood according to its meaning.
There are three types: those that are pervasive, those that are innate, and those that are nurtured by retribution.
The first, at the moment of its arising, is called the stream of maturation (*vipāka-srotas*);
from the second moment onward, it is as follows.
The stream of the maturation of the continuum.
This includes both nominal and substantial maturations.
As for substantial maturation:
From the very first moment of the ālayavijñāna until the end of life,
its essence is always that of maturation (vipāka).
It may also be called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*),
because it arises from the immediately preceding moment of maturation;
this is established by reconciling it with this very passage.
The term "vipāka" (maturation) refers to its initial excellence, being named from the first moment;
it is not as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other texts,
which say that the ālayavijñāna is the actual vipāka.
Because the others arise from maturation (vipāka),
they are metaphorically designated as "maturation.
Now, regarding the eighth consciousness:
It may also be termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*);
however, regarding its designation as a conventional maturation,
one should follow this text.
It may also be called "ripening" (*vipāka*),
because it is the very first moment of the ripening produced by karma; thus,
it is metaphorically designated as "ripening."
The second moment and those following it are also called "arising.
The rest is as explained in the third *Maulī Bhūmi*,
in the section on the "stream of nourishment" (*āhāraka-srotas*).
It occupies a vast and pervasive space;
because it possesses a continuous lineage [of such qualities], it is called "vast and pervasive," and its characteristics are intensely predominant.
This means that their substance increases.
As for the statement in the *Śāstra*: "One should know that other forms of nourishment and flow also arise from food," this refers to the fact that the aforementioned food serves as their basis.
"Sleeping the holy life" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because it involves cultivating superior mental attention (*manasikāra*).
The treatise states: "Furthermore, it should be understood that the various material faculties (rūpindriya) undergo transmigration by means of two flows.
This refers to the natural outflow (nisyanda), which causes those internal faculties to flow.
Why is it not a transformation or a result of uniform outflow?
Because when struck by contact,
there is disintegration.
This is not stated therein, yet it can be discussed.
Question: Why is maturation (*vipāka*) not a nourishment-stream (*aupacayika-srotas*)?
Answer: Because there exists a continuity of nourishment (*aupacayika*).
It is able to gather and sustain [the result],
because it flows as both maturation (*vipāka*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*).
As for the phrase "presently existing increase," etc.:
The stream of nourishment (*aupacayika-srotas*) sustains the stream of maturation (*vipāka-srotas*);
there is a distinct stream of nourishment,
for the stream of nourishment is not identical to the stream of maturation.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Just as an outer wall protects an inner city,
one should know that matter not included within the sense faculties possesses three kinds of flows."
This refers to the resultant (*vipāka*), the nurtured (*aupacayika*), and the outflowing (*naiṣyandika*).
"Outflow" (*niṣyanda*) here specifically denotes the outflow of transformation (*vikāra-naiṣyandika*);
there is also the outflow of essential nature (*prakṛti-naiṣyandika*).
To state it generally herein:
one should say that the internal [bases] support the sense faculties and their objects,
and possess both the retributive (*vipāka*) and the nurtured (*aupacayika*) types.
External objects possess only the flow of their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā-nisyanda*);
they lack the results of maturation (*vipāka*) or accumulation (*aupacayika*),
because they are not part of the internal body.
It is appropriate to speak thus.
Here, it is stated in general that all minds and mental factors [are momentary].
There is the flow produced by uniform outflow (*niṣyanda*) and maturation (*vipāka*),
as well as the second characteristic, the flow of augmentation and nourishment (*upacaya*).
In the preceding text, "matter" (*rūpa*) refers to a broad scope.
Because that which is nurtured is not mind.
The treatise states: "Furthermore, among the various elements of sound (*śabdadhātu*), there are also those that are maturation (*vipāka*) but are not sound.
The Great Master said:
Because the seeds of sound are constantly continuous,
the sound element (*śabdadhātu*) is a maturation (*vipāka*);
because its manifest activity is intermittent and subject to cessation, it is not.
It is not called "ripened result" (*vipāka*).
Master Jing says:
"The sound issues forth from seven locations."
The seven bases are called the sphere of sound (*śabdadhātu*);
this is a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
Now, this should not be so.
The seven bases are the seven types of maturation (vipāka).
This is because they consist of the seeds of all the faculties (indriya) among the twenty-two faculties.
All of these are maturations (*vipāka*).
Herein, sound should also be understood accordingly,
as was explained previously in the section on the analysis of the elements (*dhātu*).
That is to say, sound is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
These elements are produced as maturation (*vipākaja*),
but sound itself is not maturation.
This corresponds to the third transmission of sound,
as sound arises from maturation (*vipāka*).
This is explained within the treatise’s analysis of the five causes of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Regarding the fourth reason, which states that "it maintains that fundamental valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) so as not to let it diminish," this does not contradict the aforementioned sunlight;
this is as explained in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the third chapter on the "Local Grounds" (*maulī bhūmi*), the treatise states:

"Due to the distinctions among three types of volition (*cetanā*), form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*) become wholesome or unwholesome: first, preparatory volition (*prayoga-cetanā*); second, decisive volition (*niścaya-cetanā*); and third, consequential volition (*pṛṣṭha-cetanā*)."
In this Mahāyāna,
form and sound are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
On what basis, then, are they sometimes designated as informative action (*vijñapti-karman*)?
Is it the case that informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) is wholesome or unwholesome?
As for the volition of the preliminary stage (*prayoga-cetanā*),
it refers to the volition that arises from a distance with the desire to initiate this [action].
Second is the thought of the certainty that one will definitely perform this action;
third is the thought of origination,
which is the causal origination (hetu-samutthāna).
The arising of a mind in an adjacent moment that causes [an action] to become virtuous or non-virtuous must necessarily depend on the motivating volition (*samutthāpaka-cetanā*),
because it is a volition of superior grade.
This nature follows [the mind] and does not depend on volition through application (*prayoga*) or volition through determination (*niścaya*),
because it depends solely on the highest degree (*adhimātra*).
The first two are of inferior and middling grades.
Furthermore, these first two grades encompass both the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);
among these, the path of seeing is considered the most distant.
It is through preparatory effort (*prayoga*) that action is initiated; it is not initiated by the motivating cause (*hetu-samutthāna*).
This is explained at length in the thirteenth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* and elsewhere regarding the volition of action (*karma-cetanā*).
This is the third type of superior volition (*adhimātra-cetanā*).
This is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Furthermore, there is also volition (*cetanā*) arising at distinct moments;
for it is by depending on this that one obtains the precepts when entering the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*).
In this context, because they are initiated by the three types of volition,
visible form and sound constitute virtuous or non-virtuous informative action (*vijñapti*).
This is based on the classification of informative action as virtuous or non-virtuous.
It is not that their intrinsic nature is good or evil.
As for other things such as fragrances and tastes,
they are neither of these, nor are they produced by the three types of volition.
Therefore, the reason why they do not constitute the nature of good or evil is the intended meaning here.
This intended meaning responds solely to the question of why visible forms and sounds are good or evil.
It does not answer the reason why fragrance and so forth lack form;
this is explained in detail in the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa*.
That is to say, it consists of visible form, sound, and informative action (*vijñapti-karman*).
It brings about the accomplishment of the wholesome and so forth;
it is not that the karma itself is wholesome and so forth,
because it is a karma of activity (kāritra-karma).

The treatise asks: "Regarding the claim that there is motion based on the material aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*)," this refers to the Saṃmitīya school’s position that movement exists as a distinct entity,
and the Sarvāstivāda school’s position that karma exists as a nature of motion apart from the material aggregate.
Now this is asked:
because in the Mahāyāna, even the time of lifting the foot and shifting it is called "movement.
This question and answer constitute a general statement.
The second question provides a detailed explanation below.
Regarding the four meanings above— arising and non-arising,
cessation and non-cessation— all are lost.
If one says that there is movement at the very moment of arising,
this would transgress the characteristic of a single kṣaṇa;
for that which moves and acts—
To go from here to there is called "motion.
Motion occurs only after an aggregation of matter has arisen;
although motion may persist for many moments, it nonetheless transcends the [single] instant (*kṣaṇa*).
Regarding the meaning of momentary destruction:
although their school maintains that movement exists,
they also hold that matter (*rūpa*) is not momentarily destroyed.
However, that which arises in contradiction to reality or in contradiction to principle—
such as a lamp flame and the like—
if it does not arise, it possesses movement.
If it were like a rabbit's horn and so forth, it would not move.
If one says that it ceases, then it should be equal to other things;
for by moving and ceasing, motion is attained.
If the cessation of aggregated matter were itself movement,
then by analogy, movement should be equal to other aggregated matter.
Now, the formal argument is established as follows:
That which you call "motion" must actually be devoid of motion,
because it possesses cessation.
It would be like other [afflictions] such as greed.
Furthermore, one should say:
"Only through form does cessation give rise to movement."
Since the flame of a lamp has cessation, there must likewise be cessation [of the mind];
therefore, it says "the others, etc.
If one were to say that it does not cease, one would deviate from its characteristic mode of activity (*ākāra*).
Since all phenomena must perish moment by moment,
if they do not perish now,
they would transcend the characteristic of conditioned activity.
Furthermore, the causal conditions for arising in another location can be clearly perceived;
how then can you say that [the cause] does not perish?
The treatise states: "Furthermore, it should be said that the entire aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is of the nature of momentary cessation," and so forth.
Below there is further explanation.
First, the correct meaning is set forth.
The statement that [the mind] ceases spontaneously refers to the Sammitīya school's view;
these two positions are correct and not erroneous attachments.
The causes and conditions for arising and ceasing are as explained in the Sarvāstivāda:
fire serves as the condition for the cessation of fuel.

it is said that lethargy (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*) arise at the same time.
The wholesome and afflicted states that are their opposites are both comprised within the three dharmas beginning with lack of faith; thus,
it is said that they are both the objects obstructed and the manifest opposites.
For this reason, five dharmas are taught;
in reality, they do not necessarily arise simultaneously.
These six texts establish the definitive rule.
As for the remaining fifteen [assemblies],
each relies on a distinct meaning;
this assembly is the most excellent.
As for sleep, regret, and so forth, which are associated with all three natures— wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—
it is because these pertain to all three natures.
As for those that are part of delusion (*moha*), [they are unwholesome].
Because it is taught among the *paryavasthānas*,
it is exclusively of an unwholesome nature; thus,
it is said to be a portion of delusion (*moha*).
Regarding the other dissociated factors:
as with anger and resentment mentioned previously,
they arise based on matters concerning those with whom one dwells together.
Are they not dissociated?
The meaning is that although the objective sphere is the same,
they arise separately in the past and present.
This applies to all other cases as appropriate,
such as the fifty-eight instances where secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and so forth arise in two locations.
This passage is significantly different;
please examine it.
In the commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa* regarding the provisional and real nature of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), it states:
Regarding the claim that the four dharmas— lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), and laziness (*kausīdya*)— are substantially existent (*dravyasat*):
according to the Abhidharma,
anger (*krodha*) and the other [secondary afflictions] are all merely nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*).
As for why they are contradictory,
one explanation states that it is because that [text] relies on a general statement,
saying that anger and the rest are all metaphorically designated based upon this.
Because they are discussed according to their actual reality,
these four dharmas are real.
Furthermore, there are many forms of the conventional.
Some are designated as conventional designations despite lacking substantial reality,
such as anger and the like;
others possess substantial reality.
They do not arise from seeds;
rather, they are designated as "provisional" (prajñapti) based on their dependence upon factors such as greed and hatred.

therefore, it operates within the framework of the conventional (prajñapti).

namely, that lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) exist in all unwholesome states of mind.

It remains among the [five] object-specific mental factors (*viṣayaviniyata*) as being unwholesome in nature;
within this category of wholesome faith,
it follows along with erroneous faith.

it is known that those which arise as the opposites of the wholesome are [the secondary afflictions].

The treatise states that the two types—vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought)—constitute the preparatory stage (*prayoga-bhāga*) of the mind that gives rise to speech.

It is like the term used in the Abhidharma for the stages of "investigation" (*ūhana*) and "non-investigation."
In this context, as in the Abhidharma,
there should be a cross-examination of contradictions regarding those factors that share the same nature as greed (*lobha*).
Furthermore, there are others in the Western Regions who maintain that [the *ālayavijñāna*] exists as a substantial reality.

As recorded in a separate excerpt:
in the treatise’s explanation of the various types of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),

Once the resultant indeterminate state has arisen,
if one engages in walking or standing, it is deportment;
if one engages in sustaining life or crafts, it is craftsmanship.
Based on this, it is called the "sustaining life" (jīvitasaṃdhāraṇa) variety of the *samādhi* of sustaining life (*jīvitasaṃdhāraṇa-samādhi-viśeṣa*).
That is to say, the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) arises from maturation (*vipākaja*),
and the mind of transformation is associated with all three moral natures (*trividha-kuśalādi*).
It is not included herein;
rather, it is merely the initial gateway and is included within the category of neutral maturation (*vipāka-avyākṛta*).
According to the actual state of affairs, all four [types of phenomena] are common to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
If they are born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
this is discussed on the basis of the total retribution (*vipāka*).
It is said to be "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
Among the three types [of phenomena] categorized under the aggregates (*skandha*),
this is specified as distinct from the others by its characteristics.
If one were to simplify such statements as those in the *Zhongyōng* (Mādhyamaka-śāstra) and other texts,
it would say within the discussion of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):
"That is to say, [actions] of deportment (*iryāpatha*) or craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), which may at times be mutually associated."
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda* regarding the conventional and the real:
because the indeterminate mind is conventionally designated upon the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Regarding these three types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*),
why is it not said that they are associated with the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*)?
On this point, there is one interpretation.
If the mind of deportment or craftsmanship gives rise to two objects with single-mindedness,
or if it is a mind of maturation and so forth,
these are designated as the three types of neutral states.
It is not like that;
there is no contradiction.
This is explained in the treatise’s analysis of the conventional and the real.
As stated in the separate excerpt:
regarding "the various aggregates comprised within maturation," this refers to the simultaneous mind, mental factors, and so forth.
This is just as in the eighth [case],
where there is simultaneity, equality in number,
and the distinctions of mental application (*citta-prayoga*).
As for "provisional designation," it refers to those phenomena that arise spontaneously from the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*),
rather than through a separate application of effort.
If it is because the three types of neutral minds arise from preparatory effort (*prayoga*),

Because it is a conceptual designation (prajñapti), it is thus a provisional existence (prajñaptisat). Question: If that is so, then it is simply an indeterminate mind (avyākṛtacitta) and does not possess a separate substantial entity (svabhāva).
There is a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) that is spontaneous (*svarasavāhin*);

There is also [a mind] of application (*prāyogika*).
How is it that [the designation] is applied to the higher [realms]?
Because this is a category of seeds for names;

Apart from the seeds of names and phrases, the other three types of neutral minds do not arise from distinct seeds;
this applies to the four objects, such as those of deportment and so forth.
Because it is designated upon the five objects of the maturation [consciousness],

The treatise asks: "Since it is essential that one abides in the notion of non-self by means of the notion of impermanence, why is the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) explained first here? and so forth.
This question refers to the stage prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Prior to that, [one contemplates] that because it is impermanent, it is suffering;
and because it is suffering, it is non-self (*anātman*).
Since it is empty because of selflessness,
why is it now stated that emptiness comes first and impermanence follows?
The answer is: If it is as before the path of seeing,
then it is as previously stated,
beginning with impermanence.
If one enters true contemplation,
impermanence is not pervasive;
all [notions of] true contemplation are not performed.
One merely contemplates emptiness and so forth,
and subsequently enters the path of seeing through its characteristics;
this proceeds from the preceding emptiness in successive order.
This continues up to the contemplation of impermanence.
Prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), impermanence is the first;
once one has entered the path of seeing, [the sequence proceeds accordingly].
It begins with emptiness;
there is no contradiction.
As for other cases, they should be understood according to this principle.
The treatise says: Regarding the sequential order of the exposition of the Four Truths,
that which is the cause of suffering is designated as the first.

and it is suffering in the same manner as the Truth of Origination.

because one realizes cessation, it is blissful,
just as the path is so called because it leads to the bliss of cessation.

The treatise says: "Are these four truths conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) or ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)? Answer: Ultimate truth.
The intent of this answer is that the two truths of cessation (nirodha) and the path (mārga) [are ultimate].
This is indeed the ultimate truth;
it is the two truths of suffering and its origin by virtue of that characteristic of suffering.
The three types of sensation are all suffering due to conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*),
because they are of a single flavor of suffering;
this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If explained by way of distinction:
painful feeling is suffering;
the others, such as the origin and so forth, are not suffering by way of their intrinsic nature or specific distinction.
Therefore, it is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
This is the intended meaning of the answer herein.
[Regarding] conventional truth:
For example, there are four kinds of conventional [truth].
First is the conventional conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-saṃvṛti-satya*),
such as when one speaks of names for worldly things like beds, seats, armies, forests, and jars.
Second is the conventional truth of reasoning,
which refers to the conventional truth of reasoning regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Third is the conventional truth of realization.
This refers to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya and the four types of ultimate and conventional [truth], namely,
the teaching on the selflessness of persons, suchness, and so forth.
Now, within this context, that which pertains to the conventional based on reasoning is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
because of the distinction of intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
By this standard, one should know that in the West there are likewise four ultimate truths (*paramārtha-satya*):
first, the conventional ultimate; [and so forth].
That is to say, observing all things as having the characteristic of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Second is the ultimate truth of reasoning (*yukti-paramārtha-satya*),
which refers to the reasoning concerning the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.
It is not suchness itself.
Third is the realization of the ultimate truth,
namely, the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The fourth is the ultimate among ultimates,
which refers to entering true contemplation into the single flavor of suchness.
Herein, this is categorized according to the conventional ultimate.
The Dharma Master’s third point speaks only of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*),
namely that all things are suffering and so forth;
this is the ultimate among ultimates.
As previously stated, there is a passage below.
The treatise says: "Question: How many kinds of the clear realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya) are there? and so forth.
Regarding the statement, "Up to the point that those factors co-arising with it, such as the dharmas,
are called 'clear realization' (abhisamaya)," the Dharma Master says: "It is the definitive wisdom regarding the [Four] Truths."
This refers to the actualization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*) and its cause,
which is faith prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) that is still associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
That which is associated with it refers to untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*).
That which co-exists with it refers to...
That is to say, the clear realization of ethical discipline (*śīla-abhisamaya*).
If one provides this explanation, it does not fully explain "clear realization.
Furthermore, regarding the words in this passage and their underlying reasons:
This is precisely the cause for certainty regarding the Truths;
how could it be the cause of the untainted (anāsrava)?
If that were so, then it would be co-existent with them.
To whom does "that" belong? To explain it separately now:

definitive wisdom (*niścaya-jñāna*) consists of three types, namely, the realization of the truth of knowledge (*jñāna-satya*), the realization of the limit (*koṭi-abhisamaya*), and the ultimate realization (*paryanta-abhisamaya*).
Because they all arise conditioned by the truths, and as for their cause,
it is the contemplative realization (*cintā-abhisamaya*),
since this is the cause of the knowledge of the truths.
If it is as Vasumitra [states],
that this very [state] constitutes the direct cause for the *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti* and so forth,
one should understand the corresponding explanation according to the interpretation of Dharmapāla and others.
This refers to untainted faith and contemplation;
since these are all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*),
they are called "associated with themselves" (*sva-samprayukta*) because they depend upon the same [basis].
According to those who prioritize the untainted (anāsrava),
they conceal the tainted (sāsrava) faith and do not discuss the factors common to both.
Regarding the clear observation of the precepts (*śīla-abhisamaya*): this is merely designated as such because it is the common cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for that [clear observation of wisdom].
If so, why were wisdom, the truths, and so forth mentioned previously?
Regarding this, the first question was: "How many types of clear realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya) are there?
Now it is answered directly:
"The clear realization that takes the truths as its object."
This refers to the wisdom of the truths (*satya*), the limits (*koṭi*), the ultimate (*niṣṭhā*), and so forth;
other [types of wisdom] are not the actual clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
If they are called "clear realization" because they are causes for the clear realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*), then they are so designated.
Faith and so forth receive the name "clear realization" (abhisamaya) by virtue of being associated [with it];
ethical discipline receives the name "clear realization" because it is common [to all], and so on,
for it is not the actual clear realization itself.
Now, I shall answer out of sequence and skip ahead,
because this is the primary point for correctly manifesting the essence of contemplation;
as is stated in other passages.
Regarding "ignorance, volition, faith, and so forth":
these differ because they belong to different levels and stages within this state.
Herein, there are six types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
As will be extensively analyzed below,
this corresponds to the ten types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) in the tenth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*. Therefore,
the subsequent treatise states:
It refers to the three kinds of pure faith in the Triple Gem,
because they have reached certainty regarding the true meaning,
as well as the certain wisdom consisting of that which is heard and so forth.
If one were to speak according to reality,
this faith extends to both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*); however,
here it is spoken of solely in reference to the superior, outflow-free type.
How is this known? Because within the context of the outflow-tainted (sāsrava), the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) is mentioned;
prior to the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā), it first takes the teachings as its object.
This is because one must first possess the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Here, although it is not explicitly stated, the treatise refers to the wisdom derived from hearing. If that is so, why is the wisdom derived from hearing not established separately?
The commentary states: If one relies on the initial conditions of the Truths and the Jewels, faith must be the foremost of the path;
thus, it is through the increase of faith that progress is achieved.
The discernment of phenomena is supreme because reflection is supreme;

Regarding the statement that "it manifests at three times" within the context of the desire realm among the three realms of existence,
this refers to being born in this world.
First, that which has not yet attained the antidote;
this refers to all five aggregates universally.
Second, "or having attained" refers to those who have acquired it.
That is to say, while the body remains in the desire realm,
when one attains and enters the meditative absorption of the form realm,
the mental consciousness belongs to the form realm.
The remaining [fetters] bound to the desire realm are merely few;
these three have already been abandoned.
Having entered that meditative absorption, one emerges from it;
the remaining cases should be understood accordingly as threefold.
However, regarding the various sections above that accord with the Abhidharma (Dharma-paryāya),
there are significant differences in their extent and detail.
I have investigated this and know it;
however, as it would be cumbersome, I have not recorded it in full.
Furthermore, there are distinctions [to be made].
Regarding "samādhi accompanied by pliancy":
this distinguishes it from distracted samādhi;
the latter is not bound [to the object].
"Accompanied by pliancy and its retinue" refers to the mind and mental factors occurring simultaneously with it, as well as their resultant phenomena—
namely, the precepts associated with meditative concentration and the Path.
This establishes the objective realm of form (*rūpa*).
As explained in the preceding fascicles and elsewhere,
these are all bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth.
The remainder are bound to the desire realm.
Furthermore, regarding the distinctions:
these refer to the abandonment of faults and the cultivation of their remedies, and so forth.
In this regard, there are three parts:
first, the avoidance of faults;
second, the remedies for faults.
The third is conformity with the three merits;
this refers to the well-trained vision that abandons [the afflictions],
as explained in the fourth chapter of the Abhidharma.
Examine each of these one by one;
there ought to be distinctions [between them].
This is discussed in the refutation of the view that mental factors do not exist and that only mind is real.
This refutes the Sautrāntika masters who maintain that there is only the single dharma of mind-kings,
[whereas] feeling, perception, and formations are the mind.
It does not possess a separate substantial entity.
Now, we refute this by saying:
first of all, the five aggregates cannot be established.
Because there would be no distinct [moments of] perception, feeling, and mental formations,
this would contradict the sūtras and result in error.
One must therefore postulate that a single moment of mind possesses sequential stages.
There are separate [entities] such as feeling and perception;
it is not the case that feeling, perception, and so forth exist within a single moment.
Now, [the author] refutes [the opponent's view], showing that whether [the entity] exists or does not exist, both cases result in the loss of arising.
Because these mental characteristics are distinct,
there would consequently have to be actual teachings existing simultaneously.
For what reason, then, is only the first moment designated as "consciousness"?
The second moment of thought is called sensation (*vedanā*);
the third moment of thought is called perception (*saṃjñā*).
Thus, within a single mind, there can exist distinct perceptions.
Therefore, one should know that this is due to the mental factors (caitta) arising simultaneously [with the mind].
This is why it is so; it should be understood as being like the relationship between the object and the cognition of that object.
The first moment of thought and its subsequent moments should indeed be termed "feeling" (vedanā),
because the mind cognizes the object;
otherwise, there would be no such thing as a second moment of mind.
To distinguish separate stages during the state of conceptualization is to labor in vain;
it is merely calculating the measure of distinct positions.
As for your statement that the mind of the second moment should not be called "feeling" because its activity is no different [from the first], [this is incorrect].
Just as with the first moment of mind,
if one calculates that the six consciousnesses do not exist simultaneously but rather have six distinct states at different times,
that would not be the same as this case.
Because their bases and other factors differ,
these minds and mental factors arise simultaneously in a single location; therefore, they do not serve as a valid analogy.
Regarding the statement "if one speaks of transformation and so forth," it may be understood from the text itself.
Furthermore, concerning the phrase "there is no distinction between having mental conditions and lacking mental conditions," the previous calculation stated:
Regarding the establishment of feeling, perception, formations, and mind as distinct states of the mind:
no separate causes and conditions for these mental states can be found,
other than the very arising of the mind as its object-condition.
Regarding a single desirable object,
greed should arise at the very first moment,
and so on for all subsequent times.
This should be so as long as one has not yet departed from this object.
Why, then, is the first moment called "consciousness" (vijñāna) and the second called "feeling" (vedanā)?
Third is the notion of difference.
Since there are no distinct causes and conditions,

Regarding the statement that within a single moment of mind there are no distinct causes and conditions,
if you further argue:
Regarding the phrase "it is also unreasonable for consciousness to be primary," the opponent offers this defense:
"What is meant by the claim that craving arises simultaneously with the mind?"
For example, when one perceives a desirable object,
the first moment of awareness is called consciousness (*vijñāna*),
and the second is called craving (*rāga*).
One might ask: "What prevents greed from defiling the initial moment of mind?
Now, the refutation states:
"Because no distinct causal conditions can be found."
Regarding the metaphor of the lamp’s light:
the lamp’s light and its wick are metaphors for the mind and mental factors arising simultaneously, such as a mind defiled by greed and the like.
The *Ṣaḍdhātuvibhaṅga-sūtra* states:
"To manifest and explain that the most preeminent basis for matter (*rūpa*), motion (*iñjita*), and mental factors (*caitasika*) is [the mind],
among the six elements, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the basis for matter, and space (*ākāśa*) is [the basis for] motion."
This movement of coming and going is that which relies upon consciousness; this consciousness is a mental factor (caitta),
and its basis is the consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātra) basis.
If one says that among the six elements there are no mental factors (caitta),
then mental factors would have no distinct substance apart from the six elements.
It does not speak of derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
Regarding the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) in form, there are three analogies: milk, curd, and clarified butter (ghṛta).
The Dharma Master said:
"The sutra states that these three similes are taught within the scripture;
apart from these three, there is no other simile."
One might ask: "Are there not other mental factors outside of the six elements?
Master Bei said:
"This analogy refers to the kalala and other such stages."
The first three positions, the Grand Preceptors (Taishi), say:
"Milk is a metaphor for the four great elements of the desire realm being taken as self;
curd is a metaphor for that which should arise as having form in the form realm."
The simile of fresh butter represents the arising of the perception of emptiness in the formless realm;
it is used because this perception increases and becomes increasingly superior.
Thus, there are three similes.
However, is it not the case that apart from these three, there are no other form realms (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth,
nor any mindless states (*acitta*) and so forth?
Regarding the categories of the provisional and the real, why is it said that there are either seventeen or twelve [bases]?
Seventeenth: excluding the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
As stated in the subsequent text: "Because the six are unified as one, they constitute the six consciousnesses."
The immediately preceding cessation constitutes a single mind.
Regarding the twelve [bases],

Because one is divided into six;

This refers, first, to the conventional principles common to the Hīnayāna and other schools;
as for the Mahāyāna itself, it takes seven or eight [consciousnesses] to constitute the essence of the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
They are all substantially existent.
If that is so, since the element of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) is merely nominal, why was it not discussed?
Now, taking up the subject and object,
we do not mention nor exclude the element of tangibility (spraṣṭavyadhātu),
for this is a conventional existence (prajñaptisat).
The following text states:
"One becomes six," etc.,

Regarding the four propositions concerning the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*),
as explained in the second fascicle of the *Abhidharma* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*) in the section on the two disputes:
both seeds (*bīja*) and actual manifestations (*samudācāra*) are termed "elements" (*dhātu*).
This is the explanation.
This passage is taken by the master Jayasena as proof for the statement that "the seed and the arising of the manifest do not occur at the same time."
Now, taking the currently functioning eye as the sense-field (*dhātu*),

Second, [it would follow that] it should be among external objects.
There are four propositions regarding the attainment of the eye but not the attainment of visible forms,
and so forth. That is to say, when the eye does not transform into visible form,

Because those without eyes possess only the eighth characteristic of form,

both [the form and the eye] reach maturation together.
The two types of non-attainment (*aprāpti*) and so forth,

correctly take the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) as their objects.
In terms of its meaning, it can also be understood as referring to the six consciousnesses;

the seventh consciousness and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) should likewise be distinguished.
Just as with the five sense faculties, within the dharma-dhātu,

Jayasena, Candragupta, and Dharmapāla distinguish three meanings. Regarding the question:

Because it does not arise spontaneously at first;

Regarding the phrase "the skill in the elements (dhātu) serves as an illustration for the skill in the aggregates (skandha)," this refers to the final verse within the section on skill in the aggregates.

In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and related texts,

transcending the two wholesome [and unwholesome] states and the three natures,
is distinct from dharmas that possess substantial existence.
The absence of untainted wisdom and clarity is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
This would entail that all minds are defiled, and furthermore, that within a mental continuum devoid of clarity, clarity could never arise at any time.
Regarding the statement that all three natures,

this refers to not yet having attained untainted clarity (*anāsrava-vidyā*).
Within the continuity of the wisdom-mind,

The treatise states: Furthermore, if it is argued that the power of afflictions such as greed causes the associated wisdom to become deluded by nature,

Because of the power associated with views,
wisdom is rendered of a deluded nature. If that were so,
then greed would likewise render delusion [deluded].
It is not by having ignorance as its predominant factor or primary cause that all afflictions such as attachment arise;

all [factors] should likewise be established as having the nature of delusion (*moha*),
because they are defiled by the power of craving and so forth.
If it were as you say— that [ignorance] is seen—

The treatise states: "It should be known that herein, the winds of inhalation and exhalation are called bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*).

Just as in one who has been strangled to death,
the winds of inhalation and exhalation no longer circulate;

causing bodily actions and so forth to proceed;
herein lie two meanings.

"The winds of inhalation and exhalation are called the body.

It should be understood that whatever realms or stages one is born into, the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādāṅga*) therein are subsumed within these very [members].

"This is judged in relation to the place where one is to be reborn;

This refers only to a single member of the *aṅga* system;

Master Jing’s interpretation makes this point clear.
Regarding the inclusion of the cause by means of the fruit:
when one is born into this stage, birth,
aging, and death manifest before one.
These ten causes are capable of producing results that are bound to the same level as themselves. If this is so,
one should understand that ignorance belongs to the lower realms.
It does not produce karma belonging to the higher realms.
Regarding the inclusion of the three factors— karma, afflictions, and the objective basis—
within the members [of dependent origination], this contradicts the Abhidharma and the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*: "Craving and grasping are called the 'initiators.
The term 'arising' means 'to produce';
they are able to give rise to craving for existence and grasping."
It is also called "initiation.
It is not the affliction that initiates karma;
rather, it arises from ignorance regarding karma and the production of faith in what is improper.
It is said that Rudra-deva is named the Fierce and Evil Deva;
[and] Viṣṇu-deva.
These are called the "Delusive Deities" (mohanadeva),
for they are able to magically transform themselves into various forms such as geese and crows;
both are among the eight transformation bodies of the Lord of Sovereignty (Īśvara).
Some say that Viṣṇu is an emanation of Brahmā.
As for Maheśvara:
This refers to Brahmā.
The treatise states that ignorance acts as a productive cause in five respects in brief:
first, it can produce doubt.
First, because it can give rise to doubt regarding the three periods of time;
second, because it can give rise to craving,
being able to produce the three kinds of craving— internal, external, and so forth.
Third, it can produce faith in what is improper—
namely, the three types of false faith arising from cultivation, from difference, and from co-arising. Fourth,
it can produce views.
Because they do not correctly penetrate the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths,
sixty-two views, false views, and so forth arise.
Regarding the five causes and the fruit not yet attained—
namely, the attainment of the fruits of śrāmaṇya—
one gives rise to overweening pride (*abhimāna*) within the three types of persons.
Therefore, there are seventeen types of ignorance. Regarding the ignorance concerning the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśāyatana*):
this refers to the fact that when one attains the fruits of śrāmaṇya through the Path, one must realize that the emptiness of these six bases of contact is called "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*).
It is only through name-and-form that one attains ultimate realization;
yet now these non-Buddhists,
failing to understand, claim they have understood.
This refers to overweening pride (adhimāna),
which gives rise to the clinging to precepts and observances as a means (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
It constitutes the essence of skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible (sthānāsthānakauśalya) in the fifty-seventh fascicle.
This refers to subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which is the knowledge of the characteristics of the causes for attaining the fruit,
as well as the knowledge of what is possible (*sthāna*) and what is impossible (*asthāna*).
The treatise explains that the "explanation of the objects of knowledge" (jñeya-vyākhyāna) applies universally to all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).

Regarding the passage in the treatise which states, "namely, those other differentiated characteristics not subsumed under the first category of 'accomplishment' (*abhinirhāra-mukha*)," this means specifically those things not subsumed outside of the first category of accomplishment.
This now demonstrates that all varieties of distinctions are fully encompassed;
these are precisely the final three gates.
The treatise states: "There is no place and no occasion where coarse portions of water and fire could meet simultaneously; such a thing is impossible.
Here, "place" (*sthāna*) and "occasion" (*avasthā*) refer to temporal divisions.
This means there is no location and no temporal duration.
Regarding "coarse water and fire," this distinguishes [the former] from the subtle fire of the tactile sensation of heat within water.
Just as coarse ash cannot coexist with water,

so it is said in the treatise that it is impossible to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness while remaining bound by the afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and fetters (*paryavasthāna*) such as greed, without severing them.
This means that during the stage of being with outflows (*sāsrava*),
one first gives rise to the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth in order to suppress craving;
furthermore, one has already accomplished the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) which is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
The twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).
The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* says:
"The mind depends on these for its differentiation."
"This is abiding; this is affliction;
these are the provisions; this is purification.
Based on these measures, the faculties (indriya) are established. Because of this verse, they may not be increased or decreased.
Regarding the establishment of the five feeling faculties based on the predominance of experiencing the fruits of karma:
although sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is not itself a fruit,
it arises after one has obtained a fruit.
Furthermore, because they give rise to enjoyment within the state of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), they are called "fruition-enjoyment" (*bhoga-phala*). The treatise states:

"The six faculties are established to manifest the meaning of enjoying objects through the internal door; the two faculties are established to manifest the meaning of enjoying [objects] through the external door."
This refers to the six faculties, such as the eye and so forth;
because they do not depend on others as conditions but instead experience objects by themselves, they are called "internal doors."

The two sexual organs rely on others for their objects and are termed "gates" (*dvāra*) because they manifest the meaning of the virtues and faults of sentient beings. As for the establishment of the eight faculties:
among the three untainted faculties and the five beginning with faith, [the latter]...
These are the factors conducive to liberation; they are merits.
The five [faculties] beginning with faith are the factors conducive to merit.
Those that are with outflows are defects.
Furthermore, merit refers to the eight faculties;
faults refer to that which is abandoned by the eight faculties.
The treatise establishes the six faculties based on such names;
they are established among the eight bases of designation (*prajñapti-pada*).
Thus, the name is primary.
That is to say, the essence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is the first; the lineage is the second,
namely the lineage of one's parents.
Thus, experiencing pleasure and pain is the third;
thus, long life is the fourth;
thus, abiding is the fifth.
Thus, the limit of the lifespan is the sixth.
The above is established based on the Chapter on Householders.
In this manner, from faith up to wisdom, they are established.
The five faculties beginning with faith constitute the seventh.
Thus, the four fruits establish the final three untainted faculties as the eighth.
This is designated in the Chapter on Renunciation.
The treatise says: A single name is established for the accumulation of wholesome factors (kuśala-pakṣa), because the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) exists in dependence upon life.
One attains the cultivation of wholesome factors because the five feelings (pañca-vedanā) give rise to defilement (saṃkleśa).
One acts with clear comprehension,
so that the five types of defiled feeling do not arise.
As for the sixteen realities:
Excluding the male, female, and life faculties;
the latter three [faculties] are fully present in all [minds] of the subsequent seven consciousnesses;
the latter three are partially present in the five [minds of] perception, feeling, and so forth; and the fifty [faculties] are fully present, while the latter three are partially present.
Regarding the statement that this mind is dissociated from the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the answer is:
the latter three faculties are part of the nine faculties;
namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), faith (*śraddhā*), and the five [faculties] consisting of the three feelings (*vedanā*).
As in the tenth chapter of the Abhidharma,
the ten faculties constitute the faculty of "knowing what is not yet known" (ājñāsyāmīndriya); to those,
one adds the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya).
This treatise [states] that one sees the path with fifteen moments of mind,
because among these there is no sorrow (*daurmanasya*).
From that point onward, they have cultivated the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
This is precisely what is called the first faculty;
therefore, ten [faculties] are added with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*).
As for the statement in the treatise that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has no [corresponding] category, [it refers to its inclusion within the aggregate of formations].
The Dharma Master said:
"Thus we know that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not established solely upon the eighth mind-king (*citta-rāja*);
it is established upon all five mental concomitants (*caitasika*) occurring simultaneously."
Now, this interpretation is incorrect,
as it contradicts the text of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
Furthermore, there is the fundamental [force] and its remaining residual force.
Just as the three untainted [faculties] of male, female,
and so forth, all take their respective supporting faculties (indriya) as their basis,
with a single small portion constituting their essence.
It resembles the mind of its own original nature;
this is a designation established based upon that [mind],
as it is not a portion of the supporting sense faculty.
The statement that [the mind] has no affiliation does not mean that it is established as being common to all five mental factors (caitta) together,
as explained in the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra and its commentaries.
Question: How many are wholesome? [The answer is] either eight, or five, or a portion of six.
"Eight" refers to the five beginning with faith, as well as the three untainted [factors].
Regarding the general discussion of the five as both nominal and substantial:
the five beginning with faith are explained solely in terms of the five faculties.
As for these eight [faculties] and the five [faculties], they comprise the entirety of the five and a small portion of the six [faculties].
This refers to the five feelings and a portion of the mental faculty;
as well as a portion of the six unwholesome [faculties] and the five feelings,
and the eight indeterminate [faculties] consisting of the mental faculty.
That is to say, the seven material [faculties], the life-faculty, and five portions of the [five] feeling-faculties—
namely, the four feelings excluding sorrow, with the mind-faculty as the fifth.
How many among these possess maturation (vipāka)?
The answer is: "A portion of one and ten.
This means that the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is exclusively associated with maturation (*vipāka*).
A portion of ten refers to the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), the four feelings (*vedanā*), and the mind faculty (*manas*).
Because those that are neutral (*avyākṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) are excluded,
ten [of the eleven bases] and a portion of one [the mind base] are without maturation (*avipāka*).
That is to say, ten and a portion of the eleventh.
The eleventh refers to the seven material faculties, the life faculty,
and the three untainted faculties;
this is because the first eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because the latter three are untainted (*anāsrava*),
this is stated as the primary faculty in reference to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The "ten partials" refer to the five faculties beginning with faith, the four feelings, and the mental faculty,
excluding those that are wholesome or unwholesome.
"How many are results of maturation (*vipāka*)?
Answer: "One [aggregate] and a portion of one.
This refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) in its entirety.
Furthermore, there are seven types of material form and nine types of mental factors— namely, equanimity (upekṣā)—
along with a portion of others.
The remainder consists of the two natures of nourished matter (aupacayika-rūpa) and mind (citta), as well as equanimity and so forth.
Now, taking that which is produced by karma in an uninterrupted succession as the root,
there are three: joy, pleasure, and suffering.
Because they are interrupted,
not all seeds are such that their maturation (vipāka) is entirely [of that nature].
The Dharma Master says:
Because it maintains [seeds] within the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*),
everything is termed "maturation."
Furthermore, another interpretation is that "ripening" (vipāka) refers here to the continuum;
that is, all seeds are called ripening because they constitute a continuous succession.
All are termed "ripened" (*vipāka*).
This text does not follow the initial [explanation], because [the beings there] lack the seeds of male and female, as they do not exist in the lower hells,
and because [their existence] is not a continuous stream (*saṃtati*).
As explained in the second chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*,
among the non-maturation [dharmas], twelve are not included in their entirety:
namely, the five beginning with faith and the three untainted [dharmas].
And because of the interruption of sorrow, joy, pleasure, and pain;
as for the "nine partials":
The seven material faculties and the mental faculty, along with a portion of equanimity— these nine,
as previously specified, are the remainder;
the life-faculty is exclusively a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
The four [mental factors] bound to the desire realm are complete;
that is, male-faculty, female-faculty, grief, and suffering.
Fifteen [factors] are partial.
That is to say: the five material sense-faculties, the three feelings, the mental faculty, the life-faculty,
and the five faculties beginning with faith,
excluding those that are untainted (anāsrava).
This is the same as the preceding text.
Regarding "a portion of fifteen [factors] of the form realm":
the first fifteen are those of the formless realm.
Because the five material faculties are excluded,
and because joy and pleasure are excluded,
eight [factors] are entirely non-bound, and nine are partially non-bound.
This differs from what was stated previously.
The reason why there are eleven factors in the stage of *anāgamya* (the threshold) is that the eight beginning with faith (*śraddhā*),
plus mental equanimity (*upekṣā*) and joy (*prīti*), are added.
If that is so, why is the factor of joy (*prīti*) not established?
Because it is close to the agitation of the desire realm,
the first fundamental dhyāna is not established [as having joy].
The first gate was established because it has already been explained at length.
As for the explanation of the stage of "not-yet-attained" (anāgamya),
it refers to the body being moistened by the joy and bliss born of seclusion.
The section beginning with "pervading" constitutes the subsequent gate;
for while the former merely moistens the mind,
the latter gladdens the body and so forth.
The latter is superior and the former is inferior.
Why, then, did the previous statement speak of "pleasure"?
It was to clarify that pleasure does indeed exist.
Now, "manifest" (khyab) is established to indicate joy;
by mentioning both the hidden and the manifest,
only the manifest is taken here.
To explain this by means of reasoning:
there is indeed pleasure in this stage as well,
because it is called "pleasure" (sukha) due to its capacity to gladden the sense faculties.
Because they have no location and do not follow the stages,
and because the five faculties are concealed, they are not mentioned; however,
it would not be contradictory to say that they exist.
The dharmas of the stage serve as a basis, for they are both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*).
In the first [dhyāna], eighteen [mental factors] are excluded: male-faculty (*puruṣendriya*), female-faculty (*strīndriya*), grief (*daurmanasya*), and suffering (*duḥkha*).
The preceding discussion concerns the factors associated with the outflows (*āsrava*). It is not at all erroneous that they differ according to whether they pertain to the higher or lower realms.
In the third and fourth [dhyānas], joy and bliss are respectively eliminated.
In the sphere of infinite space, because the five [sensory] colors are eliminated, there are eleven.
In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, because it is the path for severing delusions, there are eight.
If one practices the contemplations and so forth, they all pertain to the eleven [factors];
however, by means of the eleven factors of the sphere of infinite space, one attains realization in accordance with the Abhidharma,
through the roots of goodness conducive to liberation.
All are termed the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
Therefore, eleven [faculties] differ from the previous [classification].
This is based on the remote preparatory stage (*dūre-prayoga*).
Regarding the previous passage which cites fifteen moments of mind in the path of vision (*darśanamārga*):
among these faculties, one type is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*),
while another type pertains to both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted states.
One passage states that they are associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and dissociated from it;
another passage states that they are exclusively dissociated from it.
One passage states that their nature consists of nine faculties (*indriya*).
The nature [of this] consists of ten roots for each single [unit].

There is a textual passage stating that the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla) extend even to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
The eleven faculties mentioned previously in the section on the sphere of infinite space are identical [to those here];
they shall be reconciled when we reach the subsequent text.
Regarding "the outflow-free state of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-saṃskāra-anāsrava*):
this refers to its general category.
That is to say, it is called "outflow-free" because, within the category of the path that abandons afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa-mārga-jāti*), it is devoid of [outflows].
If considered in terms of the continuum (*saṃtāna*), it encompasses both types;
or, it may refer to the "category" (*jāti*),
meaning the untainted state of the category that is free from the afflictions of that particular stage.
Furthermore, it is called "untainted" (anāsrava) because of liberation from afflictions;
this refers to subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna).
Some say that in that stage, as within the body of an Arhat,
there are various faculties (indriya) that are dissociated from outflows (āsrava);
it is not the severing of outflows that is called "outflow-free" (anāsrava).
The text below states:
"In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is the outflow-free [state].
It cannot be said that this is due to liberation from afflictions."
The tainted faculties constitute the six faculties;
when they exist within an untainted body,
they are termed "untainted," because otherwise they would contradict what follows below.
In the desire realm, with respect to many individuals abiding in the dharmas,
all eight faculties of the hells are both manifest and possessed as seeds.
Excluding two of the three types from among the three [categories],
the three, one, and three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*)—
this one, in terms of actual manifestation (*samudācāra*), does not constitute a seed.
Whether it is established or not,
the second and third feelings are extremely erroneous in this context.
Consulting the sixth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:

regarding the statement that "the two disputes [concerning] the eight faculties are established both through actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) and as seeds," this refers to the five [faculties], such as the eye.
As well as the mind and life-faculty,
which are exclusively continuous;
this differs from the Lesser Vehicle.
Because life is characterized by suffering, it is endowed with the five sense faculties.
The male and female faculties are not fixed;
they may be absent, or even their seeds may be indeterminate.
Just as with the seeds of the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) mentioned in the text,
because they too have been impaired,
they do not manifest in active operation (*samudācāra*).
The non-arising of seeds is invariably included within the category of "existence"; the same applies to the five faculties beginning with faith.
Just as one who holds wrong views suppresses and damages the seeds of the wholesome, this is also termed the "non-arising of seeds."
This is because it refers to the seeds within the context of the three types of accomplishment;
it does not mean that if they are not manifesting, the seeds do not exist.
They definitely exist.
Regarding the second point—that the three [mental factors] manifesting as actualities do not constitute a fixed seed—this refers to joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
This is established according to the system of the six consciousnesses. Question: Why is equanimity simultaneous with the eighth [consciousness]?
It is not said that [the other feelings] invariably manifest as suffering.
As for the statement that sorrow is invariably suffering, the answer is:
it is because the neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is overwhelmed by [the presence of] suffering.
As stated in the fifty-first passage,
it is therefore said to be "only suffering.
Furthermore, because it is established in relation to the six consciousnesses, it does not exist [as a separate entity].
The eighth is simultaneous abandonment.
Among the six types of intermediate equanimity,
wholesome karma is not included because it does not induce the interruption [of the meditative state].
Regarding "not grasping at the faculty of sorrow":
in the Mahāyāna, the faculty of sorrow exists in the state of ultimate suffering;
it is like how extreme joy is designated as "pleasure."
Because this sorrow is designated as "suffering," they possess only suffering;
it is not said that sorrow does not exist.
They are not mentioned because they arise only adventitiously as afflictions.
If that is so, why are they not included in the second or third triads?
Because their manifestation does not constitute the formation of seeds.
Because it is one and the same entity as suffering,
it is not mentioned separately since it receives the alternative name "suffering";
there are only the five faculties beginning with faith, plus the two types, male and female.
The present [mental states] are both indeterminate;
the remaining [states of] grief are as explained according to their meaning.
By this principle, the second [category] is to be understood accordingly.
Regarding the statement "there are those who understand the eight, meaning both the manifest and the seeds are established":
this refers to the taking up, abandoning, and excluding of suffering;
it concerns the middle period following the performance of the eighth [meditative] operation.
Manifest activity does not constitute a seed;
it invariably constitutes the grasping of suffering within the middle [state].
Why was it not previously stated that it is suffering?
Because there is withering and exhaustion,
why are the latter three not said to involve sorrow?
It is because they are mutually present or absent.
Since they exist or do not exist [accordingly],
and since pleasure and joy exist without being mutually absent,
why is it that sorrow and suffering are so?
The answer is: Because it is also extremely painful.
When the flow of sorrow enters the mind, it is termed "suffering" (*duḥkha*);
one does not say "sorrow-suffering."
Regarding the statement that "grief removes suffering," the former interpretation is superior.
In this context, Jayasena and Ratnakīrti [hold this view].
Regarding the two disputes concerning "original existence" (*mūla-bhava*), Candragupta cites this as proof.
The treatise asks: "How many faculties are established when one is deficient in faculties?"
Answer: With the exception of the five, there may be others.
That is to say, excluding male and female faculties and the three untainted faculties, one cannot lack the eye and other sense organs.
It is not definitely suffering,
because it lacks the certainty of male and female and is further deficient in the latter three [faculties].
How does this differ from the five causes for being a paṇḍaka?
Answer: The former case is based on being born without a physical form, whereas the paṇḍaka is based on having a physical form;
they are distinguished because the latter has already eliminated suffering.
There is no further textual passage on this matter;
therefore, it is known that those lacking the male or female faculties cannot enter the state of a noble one (ārya).
Furthermore, if one follows the perspective of the Hīnayāna, there is no contradiction;
for they state that one enters the noble state only after reaching the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*),
and thus it does not hinder entry into the noble state prior to that point.
It may be that what was previously deficient is now rectified; yet, based on what was not previously deficient,
the sages of later times have not erred.
Men and women do not possess two sexual organs simultaneously;
there are no beings with three organs, nor those who have severed the roots of goodness through the outflows-free [attainments].
Excluding the last eight types of beings born in other realms, there are nineteen types of persons.
From the moment one has entered the Path of Seeing for the first time,
it is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), as previously explained.
Because all those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are designated as "those who have seen the truth" (dṛṣṭasatya),
[the category] includes all those in training, with the exception of those who possess complete knowledge (ājñātāvī).
Twenty-one for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
excluding the first two untainted [faculties] as well as the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*).
Nineteen for the first candidate (*prathamapratipannaka*).
This is because the latter two untainted [factors] are excluded.
Twenty [factors] constitute the first fruit,
because the first and last untainted [factors] are excluded.
Twenty are non-returners (*anāgāmin*),
because they exclude sorrow and the initial and final untainted states (*anāsrava*).
Nineteen are arhats (*arhat*).
As with those beyond training (aśaikṣa),
in the form realm (rūpadhātu) one excludes male and female faculties, as well as grief and suffering;
in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), one further excludes the five beginning with the eye faculty.
The first root of the formless outflow-free [attainment] is as previously analyzed;
by relying on it, one accomplishes the path of vision.
If it exists only in the five stages of the formless realm (*ārūpya*),
then since there is no body after death,
how can it be said that the five [mental states]— such as acquisition (*prāpti*), relinquishment (*tyāga*), faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth— arise?
The skillful means of relinquishing the superior and attaining the inferior constitutes the relinquishment of birth-and-death.
This is called the twenty-first [category] by way of the meaning of its objective sphere.
There is an interpretation that one [of these] is not [the case].
That is to say, regarding the relationship between life-force (*jīvitendriya*) and the principle (*nyāya*):
the teaching (*śāsana*) is able to express the principle.
"Principle" (li) is termed "object" (yi).
When the sense faculties encounter their objects,
those objects are termed "objects."
The seven types of form cannot function with respect to their objects by themselves;
only when accompanied by non-form [factors] can they apprehend an object.
The remaining fourteen faculties have both material and non-material factors as their companions.
As for the meaning of the faculty of sensation (*vedanendriya*), it accords with the five types of feeling-dharmas.
This includes the meaning of the six sense faculties together with the mind.
It refers to the meaning of "that which is yet to be known" regarding wholesome dharmas,
once the desire for such dharmas has already arisen.
This refers to the meaning of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
According to their substantial nature (*dravya*),
they pertain to those bound to the three realms as well as those that are unbound.
The subsequent passage explains the preceding one.
Some say it is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*);
others say it is exclusively bound to the realms (*dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) or unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
This is based on the untainted [state];
therefore, it takes only the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing.
However, if one were to include the roots of goodness of the stage of penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), then...
It penetrates both that which is bound to the realm of form and that which is unbound;
likewise, it also penetrates both that which is bound to the three realms and that which is unbound,
and there is no contradiction therein.
In this assembly of texts,
it no longer appears;
that which possesses form is taken as the meaning.
That is to say, with the exception of the seven material faculties and the life-faculty,
fourteen faculties have both material and non-material things as their referents. How, then,
does the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) apply to this?
The commentary states: "The objective aspect (viṣayabhāga) of the faculty of suffering takes form (rūpa) as its object;
its self-verifying aspect (svasaṃvittibhāga) takes non-form as its object.
Furthermore, it is said generally that the objective aspect of the faculty of suffering does not exist."
The twenty-two faculties are not visible;
that which is seen is the object-field of form (rūpāyatana).
The eye-faculty is, in one respect, material,
because its defining characteristic is the seeing of visible objects;
and it is also, in part, non-material.
Whether simultaneous with the eye,
or not simultaneous with it,
that which takes the object-field of form (rūpārambaṇa).
The term "one who has vision" (sadarśana) is the correct Sanskrit original;
the term "visible" (dṛśya) is [the meaning].
The Sanskrit original does not contain this;
it may also be called "having manifest form.
Because the characteristics of the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) are coarse and manifest, it is called "having manifestation."
The seventeen elements are not like this;
for that which is manifest can be pointed out as being here or there,
just as one can display a reflected image.
It is like a reflection in water or a mirror;
here, only the name "form" (rūpa) is said to appear.
In the Sanskrit original, there are two interpretations: "to be seen" (dṛśya) and "to appear" (pratibhāsa).
However, the current character uses "zi" (字).
In secular texts, there is no "yu" (玉);
therefore, it is now rendered as the character "jian" (見).
A portion of the formless [realms] is designated as having resistance as its object,
yet its essence is not resistant.
Or it may be associated with its counterpart and take both as objects.
Regarding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), when it is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) and takes the contaminated as its object,
this means its substance is contaminated.
In the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
