it is called "outflow-free" (anāsrava) because it is not an outflow; however, its substance is a dharma bound to the realms (dhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
There is no contradiction with the preceding or following context.
Furthermore, as for the untainted faculty of suffering (*anāsrava-duḥkhendriya*),
it is called "untainted" because it serves as a guide toward the untainted.
The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not like that;
its objects are eight conditioned phenomena:
the seven material factors and suffering.
In this context, within the upper and lower [realms],
there are no life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*) among the faculties of meaning.
Regarding the discussion on the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the seven material faculties (*rūpīndriya*), their meaning is that they exist in the past and do not exist in the non-past.
The Dharma Master said:
"These eight faculties, whether in the future or the past,
all belong to the present world."
There is a sense that although objects exist, they are said to be non-existent;
for instance, consider the eight faculties when they perceive objects in the present.
This faculty exists in the present,
while its object has entered the past;
this eye occurs in the second moment, subsequent to its object.
Furthermore, that which enters into the past time is designated as "past";
its meaning is not that it is non-past.
However, those [factors] that share the same object in the present—
They enter together into the past;
the past also takes the past as its object.
For instance, consider the case of the formless faculties (arūpīndriya) as they are understood now.
In the present, they universally take the three periods of time as their object;
in the past and future periods, according to the conventional explanation,
each takes the objects of the three periods of time as its object.
The eight faculties, such as the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya), exist only in the present;
because they take only the present as their object, they are designated as such.
When they flow into the past, [they are no longer so designated].
Because their power is weak and because they exist in the future and so forth,
it is not said that they take the present world as an object-condition.
As explained previously:
why is it that the sense faculty (*indriya*) and its object (*viṣaya*) both exist in the present and can function as a condition (*ālambana*),
whereas the faculty abides in the present while the object has already entered the past?
The commentary states: First, the present object-field (*rūpāyatana*) enters the past;
subsequently, the future eye-base (*cakṣurāyatana*) enters the present.
Once the present eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) has entered the past...
It cannot take the past as its object.
Furthermore, the sense faculties that lack consciousness perish together with their forms into the past.
It cannot take past objects as its cognitive object.
The *Śāstra* states: "Furthermore, this portion [of the faculties] exists in the future, taking the past, future, and present as its objects.
This means that the aforementioned formless faculties exist in the future.
Is it conditioned by the three periods of time?
The eight material faculties exist in the future;
they do not have the future as their referent.
It is also attained because both the faculty (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) exist together in the future time;
however, when the object enters the present or past,
the faculty remains in the future.
This is because it is said that one enters the realm of the past and present;
thus, it is stated that the future does not take the future as its object.
This is the latter interpretation.
The explanation is the same as before.
Regarding the fourth, the bond of desire (*kāmayoga*):
its meaning is defined by being a bond of desire.
That is to say, the sorrow of men and women is suffering;
this is defined as pertaining solely to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
which is stated here according to the majority of cases.
Furthermore, because the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) arises from the seeing-aspect (darśana-bhāga),
and since the seeing-aspect belongs to the desire realm (kāmadhātu),
the remaining statements regarding its universal objectification of that which is unconditioned by the three realms (traidhātuka-viprayukta) are thus established.
This is discussed according to the essential nature;
there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, it is based on that which takes the five sense-faculties as its gate and conditions.
The first takes only the desire realm as its object;
the second is bound to both the desire and form realms,
taking that which is bound to the desire realm as its referent.
This means that although the nose and tongue desire form,
they lack the conditions for consciousness;
thus, they are defined solely by their connection to the realm of desire.
The same applies to the meaning of being bound to the three realms of desire,
form, and the unbound: namely, the two faculties of eye, ear,
and body are bound to both the desire and form realms, as well as being unbound.
Regarding the meaning of being "bound to the three realms" and "unbound":
this refers to the fact that joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as well as being untainted (*anāsrava*);
whereas faith (*śraddhā*) and the other four faculties, along with equanimity (*upekṣā*), are of seven types.
The meaning of being bound to the three realms and being unbound is likewise.
The category of "the knowledge of what is not yet known" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) has as its referent that which is bound to the form realm and that which is unbound.
That which pertains to both the three fetters and the unfettered refers to the stages of penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) and untainted wisdom (anāsravajñāna).
The essential nature of this faculty has already been reconciled as previously explained;
the latter two may be understood accordingly.
The five faculties beginning with faith, when discussed in combination as both provisional and real, along with the three untainted faculties, constitute eight wholesome faculties.
These take the three natures as their meaning.
The four feelings, excluding sorrow and taking the mental faculty as the fifth, [constitute the faculties of sensation].
It pervades the three natures;
its meaning consists of the three natures.
Sorrow pertains to one [nature], while its meaning consists of the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
The five indeterminate faculties— the nose, tongue, body, male, and female—
have only the indeterminate as their nature.
The two indeterminate faculties of the eye and ear have all three natures as their nature.
According to this, regarding those that are designated as manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*),

the nine factors consisting of the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), joy (*prīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the mental faculty (*manas*) pertain to all three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).
The three trainings constitute its meaning.
The seven material [aggregates] are neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
they likewise take these as their meaning.
The faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) pertains to all three trainings;
its meaning is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa),
which refers to the fact that the essence of suffering is contaminated (sāsrava).
Because it arises within the bodies of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
it is said to pervade three kinds of objects; however,
it is exclusively neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
In reality, it is emptiness.
The statement that "it is induced by untainted contemplation" is made because [the feeling of] sorrow is not induced by the contemplation of emptiness.
It is not classified as suffering or mental grief because it frequently coexists with the afflictions;
regarding mental grief, it is as explained in the Abhidharma.
It has the two initial untainted faculties as its essence,
because it comprises ten faculties;
thus it is called "the learner" (*śaikṣa*) and "neither-learner-nor-non-learner" (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
It takes the three types as its meaning.
Regarding the "nine faculties for those who wish to know what was previously unknown" mentioned in the preceding text,
this refers to the attainment of the nine untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Since this [path] extends to the wholesome desire for the Dharma and beyond,
it is said to extend to the "learner" (śaikṣa).
The first two untainted [paths] are the learner's path.
It has three meanings as its referent.
Full knowledge is the state of one beyond training;
it has three meanings as its referent.
Answer: Fourteen [factors] are such that one part is abandoned by insight and one part is abandoned by cultivation.
The seven types of form, vitality, the five feelings,
and the mind are the bases for the discernment of the unwholesome;
as well as the fruit of this karma.
These are abandoned by insight;
the remainder are abandoned by cultivation.
Twelve are partially abandoned by cultivation.
One part is not severed;
that is to say, among the aforementioned fourteen, there are six and the other six.
Regarding the six within the former: [text continues].
This refers to the five feelings and the mind-faculty (*manas*).

The remaining six refer to the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), because they encompass both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
Question: For what reason are the two faculties of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*) said not to be abandoned?
The essence of the faculty of suffering consists of dharmas subject to abandonment;
because it arises within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
it is as previously explained.
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is taught as being conducive to detachment from desire;
it constitutes the essence of the first two untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*),
while the essence of those two untainted faculties is never severed.
The masters maintain that [the acquisition] is not severed;
although it does not exist within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
it exists because its essence is a wholesome dharma.
It is only the severing of the bonds of conditions,
not the severing of the substance itself,
because one aspires to and seeks nirvana.
It is also called "non-interruption," because from the third fruit onward,
non-analytical cessation does not arise.
Regarding the statement that they are abandoned through cultivation or not abandoned at all:
furthermore, the explanation of the first six [faculties] refers to the four types of feeling— excluding sorrow— as well as the mental faculty and the life-faculty.
The life-faculty exists in the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
just as the faculty of suffering does;
or alternatively, because the Tathāgata is untainted (anāsrava).
If that is so, how can the five faculties of the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) be understood as being comprised within the other two [categories] that are not to be abandoned?
They have the latter two untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) as their essence.

If it were not so, the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) would also be included among the ten [faculties] that, according to the Abhidharma, are subsumed under the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
This passage serves as proof that wholesome dharmas exist within the three evil destinies.
They are not abandoned by the path of seeing;
the latter six are abandoned only by cultivation,
as they are also not abandoned [at all].
As noted in a separate excerpt:
regarding the fact that the various faculties of the formless realm are of three types— those abandoned by seeing, those abandoned by cultivation, and those not abandoned—
how is it that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) can have as its object that which is not abandoned?
One explanation says this is stated according to the majority.

Among the formless faculties (*arūpīndriya*), the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is also excluded; for the faculty of suffering has as its object only what is to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*).
This is stated here according to the majority view.
Furthermore, regarding the exclusion of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*),
this is because its self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvedanabhāga*) is abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*).

The name "object-condition without interruption" refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). The previous [classification] as "taking the desire realm and so forth as objects" was based on that same seeing-part.
Nor is there any contradiction.
How many faculties are manifested through the relinquishment of defilement?
With the exception of the various wholesome faculties and so forth.
This means that defilement (*saṃkleśa*) is itself what is to be abandoned, while purity (*vyavadāna*) is that which abandons.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "abandoning" refers to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Excluding the faculties that are wholesome by nature,
the remaining faculties can produce defilement;
the faculty of equanimity excludes the eight wholesome faculties.
The first five external objects of sensation include a portion that is wholesome and so forth,
while one portion is exclusively wholesome;
this refers to that which is manifested by pure equanimity (*śuddha-upekṣā*).
This refers to the sense of being an object-condition (*ālambana*).
It means that the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) give rise to afflictions (*saṃkleśa*), such as equanimity (*upekṣā*) and so forth,
and they constitute the sense of perversion (*viparyāsa*).
This refers to the five feelings and the mind being inverted;
why then is it not said that "a portion" [is inverted]?
Furthermore, regarding the statement about the six faculties:
This refers to the six faculties, beginning with the eye;
it is so designated because they encompass all instances of the arising of inversion regarding their respective objects.
Such is the intrinsic nature of inversion.
Regarding the phrase "a portion of six":
this refers to the five sensations and the mind-faculty (*manas*).
Within this context, it is a partial portion.
Therefore, one should know that the grasping of the six faculties, such as the eye faculty and so forth,
constitutes the meaning of perversion;
the eight [faculties] beginning with supreme faith are their antidotes.
Among the faults of desire,
there are eight, namely the eight beginning with faith;
this is a combined discussion of both the provisional and the real.
Alternatively, there are five [faculties] consisting solely of the real [faculties]:
faith and the other four, plus the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) as the first.
Furthermore, there are five [faculties] consisting of the five feelings (*vedanā*).
Just as the perception of food as a mere lump is cultivated,
the faculty of suffering also has the sense of being an antidote;
alternatively, "one" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is able to serve as the direct antidote.
As for the four virtues mentioned below,
they are permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The third virtue is that of the "attractor," which refers to initial attainment.
Once attained, there is the cultivation;
once cultivated, there is the utilization; and once utilized, there is the relinquishment—this constitutes its function.
Because it exercises sovereign transformation,
it is the self;
it is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
Regarding the bases for realizing the second and third fruits and so forth:
this refers to those who attain them by leaping over stages.
The treatise states that the first phrase describes their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
This refers to the single phrase, "this body has form.
Second, as for its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*):
it is composed of coarse, solid waste.

To exclude the matter of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is said that there are three types of causes: the cause of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya-hetu*), the cause of origination (*utpatti-hetu*), and the cause of growth (*puṣṭi-hetu*).
These refer to: first, that which is derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);
second, [the cause of origination]; and third, that which is nurtured by food and so forth.
That which is caused by cold is covering oneself;
that which is caused by heat is bathing;
weariness refers to massage.
Regarding the two initial stages of existence:
this refers to the moments when there is cutting, tearing, and destruction;
it is because these [actions] exist that [the term "existence" applies].
At the time of death, there are thus two states:
namely, that which is subject to dispersal and extinction,
and that which is dispersed and extinguished by another.
Second, they naturally disperse and cease.
Furthermore, dispersion is one,
and cessation is one.
There are eight ways by which a man is bound by a woman:
first, dancing; second, singing; third, laughing; and fourth, gazing.
These are her charms during times of play.
First, exquisite touch;
second, respectful service;
third, the perfection of etiquette.
Regarding the fourth point,
"that which is comprised by the experience of evenness at the time of enjoyment," the Dharma Master says:
The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) refers to the specific characteristic of joy and pleasure;
the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) refers to the capacity for reception.
Regarding the characteristic of the basis:
it means that this feeling is able to provide benefit to its basis.
This is the characteristic of the basis.
The basis is the body itself.
Now, regarding the explanation of its specific characteristic:
it is because the feeling of joy alone resides in the mind.
The common characteristic is pleasant feeling,
because it pervades all six consciousnesses.
As for the characteristic of the basis:
This is because it is the body that serves as the basis for this capacity to provide benefit;
[it possesses] both specific and general characteristics.
This refers to the emergence of the experience of equanimity.
"That which serves as the basis" indicates that it is comprised within feeling (*vedanā*).

The treatise states: "This reveals that for one whose resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding hearing, reflection, and cultivation is firm, it is said that this belongs to the establishment of the arising of the preceding faculties;
that is, pure faith (*śraddhā*) can serve as the faculty for hearing."
He gives rise to that thought and establishes the wisdom of cultivation;
furthermore, this is steadfast.
It is displayed through skillful means according to one's faith and understanding;
that is to say, the "Lord of the Arising of Wisdom" and the "Pure and Most Excellent One" refer to the aforementioned śramaṇa as wisdom.
Because he is a wise śramaṇa,
he is called a brāhmaṇa;
among those born into the four castes, he is the most excellent.
"Lord" refers to the celestial Māra,
the ruler of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Pure" refers to Brahmā, that is, the King Brahmā (*brahmarāja*).
"Supreme" is the general term that applies to all the preceding phrases;
it refers to the firm application of faith.
It reveals all supreme virtues;
even the arising of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and so forth cannot shake it.
This means that one has attained untainted faith and understanding;
therefore, it is called "indestructible.
This is the second explanation.
That is to say, mundane faith and resolve serve as the foundation for supramundane goodness; that is,
untainted (anāsrava) wholesome faith.
The establishment of pure resolute conviction is firm;
both the preceding and subsequent convictions are equally untainted (*anāsrava*).
However, their establishment differs slightly:
the former is established as the arising of the faculties,
while the latter pertains to hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Next is the establishment of the arising of the faculties (*indriya*).
This refers to the arising of untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) from tainted faith (*sāsrava-śraddhā*), and so forth.
Furthermore, it explains that pure faith (*śraddhā*) is profound and firm.
This is the faculty of faith arising in association with the wisdom derived from hearing;
this is the establishment of faith in association with reflection;
this is faith in association with cultivation.
The [terms] "by means of hearing, reflection,
and cultivation" belong to the preceding phrases;
it should be understood that the first [phrase] is the heading.
Regarding the latter two as explanations of the phrases:
"Profound and firm" and so forth is the first declarative phrase.
From "The root arises and is established for all the world" onwards [is the second].
To unify these two passages,
in the second interpretation of the latter two [verses],
it is said: "That faith is firm and stable."
This firm pure faith is the root of supramundane goodness;
it is the superior faculty that gives rise to the pure and sublime resolve for supramundane wholesome dharmas.
This is the supreme establishment;
it should be understood as appropriate.
The five types of diligence are to be correlated with the verses as follows.
The first method of verification:
The treatise states that "the remaining wholesome dharmas are subsumed under the faculties of faith and so forth," which refers to the latter three untainted (anāsrava) faculties.
Because the provisional does not depart from the real, it is not explained separately.
However, what has been discussed above concludes with the explanation of only the sixteen faculties,
and does not include the three faculties of suffering, pleasure, and equanimity.
However, since the final three [foundations of mindfulness] have not yet been discussed within the sequence,
we now specifically designate the mindfulness foundation of the body as consisting of the seven types of physical form.
The five feeling faculties and the mind faculty;
the latter nine factors should be understood as explained in the treatise.
Regarding the "nine as the preeminent bases for the truth of suffering":
This refers to the seven [bases] consisting of the five material faculties, the life faculty, and the equanimity faculty,
plus the five [mental factors] consisting of the five feelings; these are the fruits,
because they are the basis of affliction.
The Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) should be understood as follows:
for all those who are defiled, it is the attainment of abandonment; for those who are purified, it is the attainment of realization. The Path (mārga) consists of the eight [limbs].
Furthermore, because the truth of suffering involves the grasping and abandoning of the faculties (*indriya*),
one excludes the intention of grasping and abandoning within the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
If, within the truth of suffering, one does not grasp or abandon feeling (*vedanā*), [then that same principle applies].
Regarding the faculty of mental apprehension (*manas*),
it is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) within the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).
As for the statement "nine wholesome thoughts," [it refers to the following:]
This refers to the five faculties beginning with faith, the three untainted faculties,
and the mental faculty (*manas*), as they are explained by way of the gate of attachment and defilement. Regarding the "ten wholesome" [faculties],
it is the nine [faculties] with the addition of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Sixteenth, because of speaking what is wholesome,
one removes the sorrow, suffering, life, and mental afflictions arising from evil thoughts;
"six" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandha).
This is because it takes up only the defiled portion;
alternatively, it is explained as five by excluding equanimity.
Furthermore, it likewise takes up six.
Because it reverses "welcome" (svāgata), there are thirteen types of misconduct (*duṣkṛta*).
This excludes the last eight wholesome [factors] as well as life.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that there are nine types of "well-considered" (*sukṛta*) [actions].
Taking faith and the other four [roots], along with joy, pleasure, and equanimity, there are nine mental factors;
excluding suffering and grief.
Suffering exists among the five sense-faculties and is not a mental factor (*cetanā*).
Sorrow is not taken up because it is not pleasant;
the ten [factors] within the middle [dhyāna] are mentioned because sorrow is added.
Because they arise from the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya*),
there are sixteen wholesome [faculties]:
namely, the five beginning with the eye-faculty, as well as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Adding the previous ten,
there are sixteen;
these constitute bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
They are based collectively on the male and female faculties;
they are not the roots of goodness, nor are they untainted (anāsrava),
because they are not ultimate and do not pertain to the mental states of ordinary beings.
Alternatively, those who possess evil volition [possess] only three [faculties]: sorrow, suffering, and equanimity;
for these are of an evil nature.
"Bad speech" (*dur-vyāhṛta*) refers to the addition of the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the defiled portion of form (*rūpa-sāsrava-bhāga*);
thus, there are four.
"Bad conduct" (*dur-ācāra*) adds the five [faculties] beginning with the eye (*cakṣus*) as well as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); thus, there are ten.
Or it may include both male and female;
as the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* states:
"The most excellent [basis] consists of nine [factors], namely, karma and its locus."
That is to say, the seven types of form, as well as suffering and mental distress;
based on the five feelings, afflictions and karma arise.
As for the eighth, it is the experiencing of the abandonment of afflictions and karma.
Excluding two—
namely, grief and suffering—
the eleven [faculties] that experience auspiciousness and its ruin are as follows:
That is to say: the seven material [faculties], the faculty of grief,
the faculty of suffering, the mental faculty, the life faculty, and the eight [faculties] that are capable of projecting [rebirth].
This refers to the eight sufferings.
Regarding the five kinds of performing auspicious acts:
it means observing people and then relinquishing them.
This constitutes the third [category].
The remainder may be understood accordingly.
As for the ten kinds of patience:
The first three take the three periods of time as their objects.
The next two refer to those who harm me because they love my enemies,
and those who benefit me because they favor my friends.
The aforementioned five supernormal powers are designated as the sixth:
the endurance of all enmity and harm.
Even when an enemy, having devised skillful means, comes to inflict injury;
Furthermore, one should endure those skillful means,
for they are the cause of enmity and harm.
Another interpretation is as follows:
Patience toward all enmity and harm means that one practices patience as soon as one encounters an enemy.
Patience toward all causes means...
This means that patience consists in enduring when enmity arises from a desire to harm.
Receiving instruction is the eighth [factor],
because one endures based on the instructions received from others.
The ninth is the patience of reflective discernment;
the tenth is the patience of enduring natural hostility.
When someone comes to take one's life because they have received instructions [to do so],
this is called "endurance of harm inflicted by those following instructions. Or,
when another person, having reflected well, intends to harm me.
This is called "patience through the power of discernment.
As for its essential nature (*svabhāva*), it is the innate capacity to overcome harm.
Furthermore, it is the patience that endures all causes of enmity and injury.
That is to say, taking hostility as the cause;
furthermore, one is able to endure all matters involving desires and patience,
and receives instruction through the following three [stages].
These correspond, respectively, to the patiences associated with the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra*, "In this context, that which possesses the characteristic of relinquishment and the equipment for relinquishment is called 'relinquishment' (*upekṣā*)," the Dharma Master says:
The "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) is the essence (svabhāva).
That which is associated with non-attachment and possesses volition (cetanā),
as listed above, is it.
Furthermore, the characteristic of relinquishing and the essence of that characteristic constitute the fifth, supreme relinquishment;
for it is the relinquishing of one's own body.
"Endowed with" refers to the four aforementioned [factors] and material wealth.
"Without inversion or breach of obligation" means not fraudulently seizing the property of others.
To grasp at things as having a self-nature is the inversion of existence; now,
this does not exist within heedfulness.

Regarding the phrase "cultivating all wholesome dharmas and guarding against unwholesome minds," this means that the cultivation of wholesome dharmas likewise possesses the characteristics of both cause and fruit.
Since the protection against unwholesome states is likewise so,
it is said that both constitute its characteristics;
that is, both constitute the characteristics of cause and effect.
The five powers may be assigned individually,
and they may also be assigned collectively.
Regarding the statement that "first, the acquisition of the afflictions consists of eight":
this refers to the seven material [faculties], life, mind, and name-and-form as conditions;
because the sixth [sense-base] is the six sense-bases.
With contact as condition, there are five: feeling, faith, and so forth, up to eight.
The wholesome is conditioned by diligence.
The seven material factors and vitality should be guarded.
The mind alone should be disciplined and stilled;
the five feelings should be brought to cessation;
and the eight wholesome natures, such as faith, should be made compliant.
As for the Bodhisattva Karuṇāpāśa,
his "lasso" does not cause one to leave saṃsāra;
it is like a horse caught in a lasso.
When one attains the third fruit based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya),
why does the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) of the first dhyāna not arise?
Answer: There is one who can enter and one who cannot.
That is to say, one with sharp faculties whose body is supported by a multitude of wholesome qualities is able to manifest it.
This consists of two factors:
first, sharp faculties;
second, the support of numerous roots of goodness.
Just as one of dull faculties cannot enter [the path] despite receiving abundant assistance,
because their faculties are dull.
Just as one with sharp faculties cannot enter [the path] if lacking the aid of wholesome roots,
it is only when sharp faculties are assisted by the wholesome that joy arises;
this is like the case of one who is unable.
Only after attaining the fruit does one separately give rise to the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
The Dharma Master asks:
"Why is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) not mentioned?"
Since pleasure (*sukha*) is identical to the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*),
it is not mentioned as having a separate entity;
this is as in the case of the third dhyāna.
Only then does one experience true pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*).
According to this principle, it is established that pleasure is also attained;
thus, the previously cited proofs for the existence of the feeling of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*) are validated.
There is also the expression "pleasure," which signifies the gratification of the five sense faculties;
however, there is no other distinct means [to achieve this].
The five faculties are established in their fixed locations;
there is no harm in their existence being implicit rather than explicitly stated, as this is the same [as other cases].
The treatise states: "Regarding the eight faculties that enter the first dhyāna, three parts can enter and one part cannot enter.
The "eight" refers to the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the faculties of joy, equanimity, and the mental faculty.
This is the combined explanation of the fundamental skillful means.

As for the statement that they "cannot," it means that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cannot [attain it], because the substance of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is subtle; therefore, it is not mentioned.
In the third dhyāna there are eight [factors],
distinguished by the same joy and bliss;
from the fourth dhyāna upward, bliss is excluded.
There are seven other cases.
The final three may be understood [from the context].
The treatise states: "Either by means of one faculty, or by means of eight faculties, one attains the first fruit."
The first refers to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
This is attained during the stage of progress toward the fruit,
not simultaneously with the attainment of the fruit itself.
Eighth, this refers to the five faculties beginning with faith, the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*);
these are stated both collectively and individually.

As for the statement that one who attains the fruit of a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) does not take [the faculty of] pleasure (*sukhendriya*), it is because pleasure exists only in the third dhyāna. Thus, there are either two or nine [faculties].
Regarding the "two nines" of the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of 'having known' (*ājñendriya*):
these consist of the aforementioned eight [faculties] plus the faculty of 'having known' for those who progress gradually (*ānupūrvika*),
and for those who leap over (*vyutkrāntaka*).

It constitutes the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), because it functions in conjunction with the factors of the path. Alternatively, there are two cases where the nine faculties of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) are not firmly established:
namely, the faculty of joy belonging to the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-dhyāna*).
If one excludes either nine or ten of the fruits of non-returning, or eleven or two, there are eleven in total when combining the general and the specific.
These eleven are: the five faculties beginning with faith;
the faculties of joy, pleasure, equanimity, and mind; and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
This is because both [the leap-over and the gradual] are discussed in terms of both the leap-over (*vyutkrāntaka*) and the gradual (*anupūrva*) sequences.

(11) Second, there are two provisional faculties (*prajñapti-indriya*): the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*).
These are the distinctions between the leap-over and the gradual sequences.
Combining these two treatises, one attains the fourth fruit either as one or as ten.
"One" refers to the provisional root;
this is based on the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The former is also the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*).
The tenth consists of the five faculties beginning with faith, plus the faculties of joy, pleasure, equanimity, and mind, along with one conventional faculty.
In the Mahāyāna, it may also be said that there is both gradual and transcendent [attainment].
The essence of the fourth fruit is attained by two [faculties] together with ten faculties.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, this includes the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The faculty (*indriya*) is also added as this one.
The treatise states: "Relying on the relinquishment of the single nature, one relinquishes the various relinquishments.
This means that together with the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), one relinquishes the relinquishment of the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*).
It takes the equanimity of the sphere of non-perception as its basis;
this is the equanimity of a single nature.
Furthermore, it is explained as the equanimity of the formless realm.
That which takes only mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) as its object is called "equanimity of one nature" (*ekavidhā upekṣā*).

That which takes the manifold objects of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as its object is called "equanimity of variety" (*nānāvidhā upekṣā*). That which takes the mindless state as its object is called "equanimity of non-mind."
The name "equanimity without basis" refers to equanimity toward the nature of existence when taking it as an object;
now, it refers to equanimity that relinquishes even the emptiness of the mind when taking it as an object.
This is because there is the mental state of equanimity.

Regarding the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) by persons of the five spiritual lineages, as in the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (Dharmapada) Fascicle 13: Question: If one is a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*),...
When practicing the refinement of the faculties,
once the refinement of the faculties has been attained,
one also realizes the fruit of the Once-returner.
Answer: Regarding "realization and so forth," when one who has attained the first fruit transforms their faculties,
they apply mental attention in pursuit of sharp faculties.
Furthermore, when one attains the second fruit and abandons the six grades of afflictions, the fruit is again transformed through the refinement of the faculties (*indriya*).
The two obstacles of the roots and the fruits are abandoned by the six paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
This is stated in terms of their simultaneous abandonment through the shared attainment of the resolve for liberation.
If one forms a distinct intention for a specific time,
one will likewise attain the fruit and so forth at that distinct time;
it is not the case that one cannot avoid returning.
The *Śāstra* states: "Two causes are difficult to counteract.
This refers to the first of the three difficulties encountered when one becomes free from desire in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) is also counted as one.
That which is said to have "vastly great attained meaning" refers to the vastness of the merit of the fruits of dhyāna;
it also manifests the multiplicity of unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) fruits.
It is not said that one who has attained the stage of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) attains the stage of Non-returner (anāgāmin), as this is not the same as the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna);
although [the latter] is attained, it is merely through a distinct aspirational mind.
There is no sense of simultaneous acquisition;
it does not contradict the state of being free from desire,
as it is also based on a formal resolve.
Now, when you of the Mahāyāna transform your faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) itself severs [the obstacles];
this is the meaning of not yet having attained the fruit. Question: How is it that the path of refining the faculties (*uttapana-mārga*) is itself the path of severance?
The Dharma Master said:
"Just as in the Hīnayāna, when those in training (śaikṣa) refine their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti),
it is reckoned as a single category according to the Path of Vision (darśana-mārga)."
The refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) for one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) consists solely of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). As for its being of nine grades:
if that is so, then in this case, it is like the case of taking a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
Regarding the path of abandonment for the six categories [of afflictions],
how is there the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃskāra)?
It is accomplished precisely through these six categories.
Therefore, one knows that it is also impossible to attain even a single grade,
because [the path] consists of six grades;
nor can one refine the faculties through nine grades.
Although there are six grades, one attains the stage of Once-returner;
this is the Mahāyāna.
Either one cultivates a single grade as when attaining the refinement of faculties (indriya-saṃskāra),
or six grades as when entering the path of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin-mārga),
because in both cases one applies the mind toward refining the faculties.
The treatise states: "Regarding the establishment of the first faculty (*indriya*) and so forth on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), there are two explanations.
One says: 'This refers to the Mahāyāna.'"
The stage prior to the grounds of the Hīnayāna is called the Stage of Practice through Resolute Belief (adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi) and is termed "desiring to know what is not yet known.
Upon entering the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), one enters the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga).
Up to the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi),
it is called the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya),
because one has already fully realized the meaning of suchness (tathatā).
The *tathatā* that has not yet been fully realized is called "that which one desires to know through what is not yet known.
This is not like the Lesser Vehicle’s notion of "knowing again what was not yet known" after having already known it.
Because it is called "the faculty of that which is yet to be known" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Thus, this current text is correct:
from the moment one has entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) onwards, all are termed the "faculty of what is already known" (*ājñendriya*).
Because the stage of the Tathāgata is luminous and full, it is called "possessing complete knowledge.
Because the vajropama-samādhi of the path of immediate succession is not yet luminous and full, it is not so called.
It is not called "fully knowing.
A second interpretation states:
in reality, it is the first faculty.

The uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) refers to the period prior to the fifteenth moment of mind, as long as one has not yet emerged from meditative absorption;
this is stated here in terms of the majority of cases.
Because it is spoken in terms of a stage that is manifest and easy to understand,
there is no contradiction in referring to it as the "stage of practice through resolute belief" (adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi).
These are all explanations from the Treasury of the True Dharma (Abhidharmakośa).
Among the three fulfillments, they are all treatises concerning the trainings; this is because the questions are formulated in relation to the trainings.
These three each possess their own distinct essential nature.
Just as when the faculties are perfected, one attains the first two fruits;
likewise, one may also attain the perfection of meditative concentration.
Because one must exhaustively sever the seeds of afflictions from the third dhyāna downward,
only upon attaining the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) does one achieve the fullness of the fruit; that is,
one severs only the nine grades of afflictions belonging to the desire realm.
When even a single grade of the higher stages has not yet been abandoned,
one immediately attains the state of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa);
this also possesses three distinct entities.
First, the fulfillment of the faculties;
second, the fulfillment of meditative concentration;
third, the fulfillment of the fruits—these constitute "all."
In this context, the fulfillment of the fruit cannot be generalized by claiming it must necessarily involve both states of mind and states without mind.
Only after attaining the mindless state does one attain the fulfillment of concentration.
The fulfillment of the fruit pertains to both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Having attained the state beyond training, one achieves the fulfillment of the fruit.
Because within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the absence of mind (*acittaka*) is considered weighty;
and because among the fruits of the path, the obstruction to non-returning (*anāgāmin*) is considered weighty.
The treatise states: "The faculties are termed 'undisciplined' (*adānta*) due to four conditions."
That is to say, up to the point of ensuring one does not become heedless constitutes the first;

if there is that which should be abandoned, down to the point of ensuring it does not manifest constitutes the second. The power of the antidote of abandonment extends down to having a nature free from attachment.
Third, they are of the nature of afflictions and do not manifest again.
Fourth, these four are all [characterized by] views; those with loose faculties are untamed.
Conversely, those with firm faculties are untied and tamed.
Fourteen faculties subsume sentient beings into three groups;
that is to say, excluding the eight [faculties] beginning with faith,
because these are exclusively wholesome.

The "partial portion of the external bases" refers to the five sense objects that support the sense organs, as well as the mental factors and so forth within the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*); thus it is said to be a "small portion. It is "appropriated by the five sense organs."
This means that because the five feelings and the three feelings mutually subsume one another, they are not included within the category of "mental factors" (*bodhipakṣa*).
As for why there are either four or six,
it is because speech-activity and livelihood are combined into one.
The four are expanded into six.
Based on this text, [it corresponds to] right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*);
although it involves the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of uttering speech.
This is not the same as the *vitarka* (applied thought) of the Hīnayāna;
here, we take the wisdom (*prajñā*) that serves as its basis, considering it in terms of its essential nature.
Within the inclusion of the five faculties—faith and the others—and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) by the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), [this is how they are subsumed].
The three untainted [faculties] are broad;
the five beginning with faith are narrow.
As for "thorough knowledge" (parijñā):
It is wisdom (*jñāna*).
It is designated as "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) because it arises from causes;
it refers to universal knowledge (*parijñā*). Within this, there are two types.
This refers to those who have entered the stream (srotāpanna) and leap over to attain the fourth fruit;
or it refers to three types,
namely those who leap over to become non-returners (anāgāmin).
Subsequently, because of being free from desire for the realms of form and formlessness,
there are four [types of persons],
namely those who attain the fruit of stream-entry through gradual succession.
Because one subsequently becomes free from desire for the three realms,
in this Mahāyāna, the path of seeing consists of only a single stage.
Such is the reason why it is so.
Alternatively, there are five: namely,
the four truths of the Stream-enterer constitute four,
and now in the Mahāyāna as well, one cannot distinguish between realms, stages, or time periods.
However, because a single truth constitutes a single moment,
there are four [moments] for the transcendence and attainment of the fruit of Arhatship;
as for the "five or six," this refers to the three minds common to both vehicles during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This means that because there are three types of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
there are six or seven [moments];
now, because there are four truths for the path of seeing and three for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Seven or nine are as stated in the text,
following the gateway of principle;
or ten, as in the obstacles of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*).
In this context, there is not even one [of these] that is established by means of two conditions. As for the eighth,
it is established by means of two conditions.
"Thorough knowledge" refers to the six [moments] of the path of seeing,
which involve penetrating the principles of the truths.

The path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) eternally transcends the realms. As for the establishment of two types of full knowledge (parijñā)—namely, those based on the homogeneous realm (sabhāgadhātu) and the heterogeneous realm (visabhāgadhātu), as well as the homogeneous [aspect]—it is because suffering and its origin are a single entity.
Because it shares the same sphere (*sabhāga*),
it is not the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
because it is of a different sphere (*tatsabhāga*), it is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The thorough knowledge of the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya-parijñā*). The origin of suffering is a single entity,
because it is established by combining the two realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because they are established by way of their names, characteristics, and homogeneous classes (sabhāgatā), as well as their respective realms,
the full knowledges (parijñā) of suffering and its origin are established for the form and formless realms; however,
the path and cessation differ in their characteristics.
Because the desire realm is distinct from the form and formless realms,
the two universal knowledges (*parijñā*) of cessation and the path are established above the desire realm;
this is because the characteristics of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are distinct.
Because the homogeneous nature (*sabhāgatā*) of the levels of the form and formless realms ceases,
the two universal [factors]— the cessation and the path— are established for the form and formless realms respectively.
Combined with the preceding, there are six.
Regarding the three stages below the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), the Treatise states:
"Those comprised by the primary marks (lakṣaṇa) and secondary signs (anuvyañjana), the tongue faculty (jihvendriya), and the bases (adhiṣṭhāna) of the four faculties."
This refers to the mark of obtaining the supreme flavor,
which is the mark of excellence (lakṣaṇa) of the tongue faculty;
the others are merely the bases for four faculties.
That is to say, the body hairs point upward, with a single hair growing from each pore;
the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel is the locus of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).
He possesses the physical characteristics of a horse-king;
the base of his male organ is concealed,
and his eyes are a deep blue-black color.
The locus of the eye faculty is the tongue,
which covers the mouth and is broad and long.
Regarding the locus of the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*), the Ten Powers (*daśabala*) take the two faculties as their essence, being fully known through wisdom (*prajñā*).
Herein, by analogy with the Fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), all five faculties may be taken as their essence;
this is discussed according to what is predominant.
As it is said, "Because of the Tathāgata’s ten powers of knowledge, his wisdom is powerful.
This specifically cites the four fearlessnesses;
as for the five faculties, there is no question of their being strong or weak.
All are considered to constitute the essence. There are three types of foundations of mindfulness;
that is, they consist of the three wholesome roots.
Specifically, non-attachment arises toward those who are objects of veneration.
Non-hatred arises toward those who revile;
non-delusion arises either universally or specifically,
as it arises only toward those who remain neutral.
The treatise states that great compassion is not subsumed under the [six] faculties, but is subsumed under non-hatred and non-delusion;
thus we know that non-delusion possesses a distinct ontological nature.
As for the six faculties realizing the permanent severance of habitual tendencies:
This refers to the five faculties beginning with faith,

together with the faculty of one who has perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*). Regarding the statement in the treatise that "the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of the category of maturation (*vipāka*) have not yet been severed by Arhats and others," one interpretation states:
The various seeds are called "ripening" (vipāka);
because this category of coarse and stubborn nature has not yet been severed,
there are such things as high pedestals and pitfalls.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that by the power of the afflictions acting as conditions,
the arising of the resultant indeterminate (*vipāka-avyākṛta*) characteristics is induced; thus,
even though the afflictions have been severed, [the result persists].
However, due to the power of the habitual tendencies of afflictions,
the substance of the maturation (vipāka) possesses a state of unfitness for function.
That which follows along is called the "coarse heaviness" (*dausthulya*) category of maturation (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, the seeds of the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) are subsumed under the category of maturation among the four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*).
The term "category" (*pakṣa*) here refers to a class or type.
This is because it is a seed of maturation (*vipāka*);
this is the explanation in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
Now, due to the presence of these coarse burdens (*dausthulya*) of suffering, [it is so called].
It is called the "coarse heaviness" (*dausthulya*) of the maturation (*vipāka*).
The Tathāgata has eternally severed this.
As the treatise says: "Contact is able to grasp and sustain [it]."
Regarding "a portion of joy, pleasure, or equanimity":
it is now explained that contact (sparśa) takes the six consciousnesses as its essence.
This associated contact is capable of fully encompassing both feelings of joy and pleasure.
Furthermore, the relinquishing of a portion of what has been undertaken constitutes "beneficial inclusion" (*anugraha*),
which carries the sense of growth and nourishment.
Sorrow, suffering, and adverse harm are not beneficial inclusion.
The "abandonment" (prahāṇa) applies to both wholesome and unwholesome fruits;
since we now take up the abandonment of the wholesome fruit,
it is called "one part."
Alternatively, having abandoned both the pervasive [states] and longing for joy or sorrow,
one has not yet attained the arising of joy and bliss;
therefore, it is called "one part."
Some say that from this it is known that the number of "contact" (sparśa) taken as the substance of the nutriment of contact (sparśāhāra) is established; however,
this does not constitute a valid interpretation.
Because it contradicts the Abhidharma.
Furthermore, regarding this approach that accords with reason,
the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
The nutriment of contact belongs to the six consciousnesses.
As for "mental volition, aspiration, and the faculty of joy," these comprise that which benefits wholesome consciousness.
This mental consciousness is accompanied by feeling,
which also extends through the three feelings of joy, pleasure,
and equanimity; however, because the characteristic of joy is coarse, it is specifically mentioned here.
Alternatively, this may refer exclusively to the majority of cases in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
however, since the higher realms also possess pleasure (*sukha*),
even though [pleasure] exists in the lower [realms], it is set aside.
This is not discussed in detail here because it is intended to be associated with the three types of feeling (*vedanā*).
The nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) and the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsañcetanāhāra*) are designated as "beneficial" (*anugrāhaka*).
One does not wish to include the two mental factors of *vedanā* (feeling) and *sparśa* (contact),
because the former two [feeling and contact] benefit the eighth [consciousness],
whereas the category of contact (*sparśa*) depends upon the present.
Because consciousness takes future objects as its intentional condition,
it subsequently becomes clear, sharp, and nourished.
Because it subsequently becomes clear, sharp, and nourished, it is called the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).
This also generally includes those [consciousnesses] among the six consciousnesses that are nurtured,
because the first three of the four nutriments— namely, edible food and so forth— sustain and maintain the consciousnesses.
It causes the faculty of mind to become more brilliant and vigorous, producing benefit;
because it is nourished by these two,
sleep and so forth are not nutriment.
First, nourishment (*puṣṭi*):
this refers to the capacity to cause the distinct faculties to be nourished, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) to increase, and each respective function to flourish.
Second, non-injury (*anupaghāta*).
The nourishing factors such as sleep have a subsequent [existence] but no initial [existence].

Because the four nutriments have both an initial and a subsequent [existence], they are "nutriments. If that is so, is it not the case that the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is also something nurtured by meditative concentration (*samādhi*)?
The commentary states: Although these arise from meditative concentration, they are precisely produced by the nutriment of contact and volition within that concentration;
they cause the sense faculties and the primary elements to be nourished and to increase.
Concentration merely prevents harm;
it cannot bring about benefit.
As the treatise states: "By means of three gates, the two kinds of defilement increase," and so forth.
The three gates refer to the aforementioned three nutriments;
the two defilements of affliction and karma depend upon the nutriment of consciousness.
The [mental] factors are predominant over consciousness;
the remainder are present before one.
As for the treatise stating, "Because they are numerous and because they are easily perceived":
That is to say, for the most part, these four nutriments arise from karma; if that is so,
would it not be the case that they arise for the most part [from karma]?
That which is easy to perceive and know is distinguished from the Awakened One;
for although the prior karma and the ordinary person’s freedom from obstructions are easy to know, [they differ].
It is easy to enter into the foundations of mindfulness;
for this reason, these four lines are taught, namely:
edible food enters the body.
The nutriment of contact enters into feeling;
the nutriment of consciousness enters into the mind;
the nutriment of volition enters into mental phenomena.
The four types of nutriment provide sustenance easily on a daily basis;
for this reason, others do not.
Among these, there are various hells.
There are certain increasingly subtle winds called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
Regarding this, the *Mūlabhūmi* and other sections on the stage of investigation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra*) state:
"It does not exist. This is based on the heavy hells.
Furthermore, because it is difficult to know,
it is not mentioned;
this [present] location is correct.

The treatise states: "Alternatively, there is that which relies on one [element], namely the sense-faculties of the same class (*sabhāga*)," meaning that the sense-faculties of the same class rely solely upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
"The second" refers to the material sense-faculties of the same class.
That is to say, it relies upon two bases: the four great elements and its own consciousness.
Third, "relying on form" means that the mind dwells depending on form;
second, relying on the mind.
Third, because they abide in dependence upon the mind,
the mutual dependence of the three faculties and the mental factors is likewise so.
In the formless realm, there is no form.
There are only two bases;
this remains the case up to the eighth [consciousness].
Here, the reference is to those that function as simultaneous dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
This is designated as the "roots. The verse says: "By means of the various phrases—object, basis, locus, realization, inclusion, and sustenance—there are six [categories] herein.
From the preceding verse:
How many faculties [function] by way of their objects?
How many are based on both name and form?
How many faculties are first acquired through the influence of prior afflictions? Below.
Reaching the point where the various faculties are called "undisciplined" due to the four conditions,
this clarifies the realization [of the truth].
Below, it explains how the fourteen types [of faculties] subsume the three groups of sentient beings.
Up to the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*),
it clarifies their inclusion as stated in the Sūtra,
following the section on the four nutriments (*āhāra*).
In the hells there is a subtle wind;
because it is difficult to perceive, it is not described here.
This clarifies the fifth type of nutriment.
The following clarifies the various phrases.

The *Śāstra* states: "Because they fully encompass and maintain all meanings (*artha*) and fully encompass and maintain the meaning of all formations (*saṃskāra*), they are called aggregates (*skandha*).
The *Vyākhyā* explains: "In order to clarify the sense of repeated inclusion, there is this redundant expression."
Furthermore, another interpretation is that the former term refers to the essence (svabhāva),
while the latter term refers to the designator (vācaka).
It is because the essence is such that [the latter applies].
This is why such names are established;
the others should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the establishment of the six causes within the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth:
These are sequentially assigned to the three types of skillfulness.
That which takes the conventional person as its body refers to the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
This is that upon which the person (pudgala) relies.
Among the six types of erroneous attachments to be eliminated,
it is called "reliance on erroneous attachment."
This means that taking what is relied upon as the cessation is called the "breaking of the aggregates" (skandha-bheda).
The cause is the elements (dhātu).
To be refuted: regarding the third [type of] false attachment to a self as that which possesses the basis for support,
namely, the externalist view that matter (rūpa) possesses the basis for support—
that is what I shall now refute.
These are the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
They are so called because they serve as the gateways for the arising and growth of consciousness.
The rest is understandable.
Regarding the ten benefits of skillful observation,
there are two interpretations.
The first is that one attains the perception of unity.
First, it refutes the self as permanent.
Second, up to "one does not slander," it refutes the false view that slanders [existence] by asserting non-existence.
Third, having already attained faith, it causes that faith to increase, eliminates doubt, and gives rise to further conviction.
Fourth, it serves as the condition for the long endurance of the holy teaching so that the True Dharma does not perish.
Fifth, having realized the principle of dependent origination up to the point that there is no agent,
one refutes the self as an agent and so forth by means of its lack of substantial reality.
Sixth, the faculty of wisdom is vast.
One should dwell well in mindfulness, even unto the various distinctions of dependent origination;
seven times, even unto the various distinctions of dependent origination,
one should dwell well in mindfulness.
Eighth, up to the nature of one-pointedness of mind;
ninth, up to causing the faculty of noble wisdom to arise.
Tenth, it leads to the realization of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Furthermore, it is explained that [the first] removes the notion of a unified self (*ātman*) and so forth,
while the second exists because phenomena (*dharma*) abide.
1. One does not engage in slander;
2. one is free from doubt; 3. one is personally without uncertainty;
4. one provides skillful answers to the questions of others.
Fifth, causing others to have faith;
sixth, causing the teaching to endure for a long time—
the latter four are the four "also" (yòu) characters.
Thus it is ten.
Regarding the mention of King Yama in this section of the fifty-eighth fascicle,
the *Maulī Bhūmi* refers to him as King Śānta (the King of Quiescence).
All errors are stilled.
According to the meaning of this passage,
the messengers of Yama—
The wardens, the youths, and so forth,
all arise through the power of their own karma;
they do not belong to the category of those born by transformation.
Among those who act as messengers, it naturally corresponds to the numerical categories of sentient beings.
As the treatise states: "Because of the saltiness of the water, a portion of land-dwelling sentient beings find it difficult to obtain [this].
This refers to all except for the Wheel-Turning King appearing in the world and the Treasure of the Minister of the Treasury.
If one were to place a hand within the great ocean,
all the jewels and gems within the sea would emerge along with it;
thus, there would likewise be those who obtain the jewels.
Therefore, it is excluded here.
Regarding those who discuss various philosophical views (*dṛṣṭigata*),
it is like the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
This is the place where sentient beings find refuge;
it is the place where the sixty-two views find their ultimate resort.
Therefore, it is said that these are "tendencies toward views.

When the treatise states, "To claim that there are no such things as virtuous or non-virtuous actions is called 'denial' (apavāda)," this contradicts the first chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* and other such texts.
Examine that text. In the discussion on the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it says:
"That which is undertaken and maintained, which conforms to and is associated with the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and which is concomitant with the clinging to views."
This means that because of the adherence to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa),
one undertakes ascetic observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa);
these ascetic observances follow from that adherence to views.
The view-grasping is its retinue;
it follows from that dharma.
From this grasping, the grasping at precepts and observances arises.
The four types of hatred are:
views that harm oneself or others,
and sentient beings who harm oneself or others.
This constitutes twenty-two [factors].
These can be understood according to the text.
Among the types of pride (*māna*):
Regarding "conceit with respect to future existence," this refers to those who calculate that they will exist or not exist in the future, and so forth.
As the subsequent text states:
That which moves is said to exist;
that which does not move does not exist.
"There will not be one who creates through conceptual proliferation.
This explains the extensive exposition mentioned above.
"Up to 'I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient'";
this is the intended meaning here.
Now, consult the following [passage], number eighty-six.
There is also this text, which distinguishes three types of pride:
namely, [pride] regarding what is inferior, equal, or superior.
This [classification] subsumes four [types].
As stated previously in the fifty-sixth [fascicle]:
"Among the desires, two are subsumed under pride (māna):
namely, the pride of self (asmimāna) and overweening pride (abhimāna)."
Regarding the second [category], the arising in a future existence, there is one:
namely, false pride (*mithyāmāna*) in the form "I shall become non-percipient" and so forth.
This refers to the locus of the seven matters.
The treatise [discusses] whether there is confusion or non-confusion regarding pride toward those inferior to oneself;
this is explained through two inversions.
This should be correlated with the seven types of pride (*saptavidha-māna*).
Regarding the doubt concerning the distinctions among the five marks that should correspond to those in the heavens:
this refers to doubting the existence of future lives.
Doubt has no functional efficacy;
doubt has no cause or fruit;
doubt has no truth.
The fifth [point] is that doubt lacks reality.
The *Śāstra* states: "That is to say, the ten afflictions all mutually serve as objects for one another and for all other afflictions, both self-referential and other-referential.
This passage serves as proof for the two types of grasping: grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) and grasping at precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
It is not only conditioned by the objects of views and precepts that it arises;
rather, it arises in conjunction with the various cravings and so forth that rely on views and precepts,
because these serve as its objects, and thus there is no contradiction.
That afflictions of a higher stage cannot take all afflictions of a lower stage as their objects accords with reason;
as it is stated in the fifty-ninth passage below:
Higher stages give rise to pride by taking lower stages as their object.
As the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
"The formless realm takes as its objects those things bound to the three realms as well as those that are unbound."
Since all [defilements] function as a portion of the conditions for pride,
how could they take a lower realm as their object?
This [objection] is also raised here.
Nevertheless, it is not the same as wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth.

As for the statement in the *Śāstra* that "the innate view of a self-identity (*sahaja-satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) because it manifests frequently," this is as stated below in [section] ninety-four.
The world does not submit to this;
it can only be severed by the vajra.
As stated in the subsequent text of this fascicle:
In the world, cultivation may be subdued while views are not;
within cultivation, there may be the subduing of either attachment or aversion,
as well as the subduing of their immediate counterparts, such as hypocrisy and pride.
And because of the ignorance associated with this,
as well as the pride and craving that coexist with it— regardless of whether they involve the view of self or the view of extremes.
This treatise states:
"There is the expression 'proximate conceit,' which excludes conceit that is proximate to greed and hatred."
As stated in the ninety-fourth [verse] below,
however, since this one is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta) in nature,
how can it be established as being of nine grades?
"Under which categories of the desire realm are these subsumed?
The Dharma Master said,
"These belong to the latter three categories."
When the mundane path suppresses the nine grades,
it suppresses only the first six grades,
because these latter three cannot be suppressed by it.

However, since the first six categories also consist of nine grades each, it is said that "the mundane path subdues the nine grades. Question: How are the first six categories divided into nine grades?
If one grade were divided into nine grades,
there would be the error of fifty-four grades;
if one grade were divided into three grades, [the same error would follow].
This would entail eighteen categories of faults.
Furthermore, if an Anāgāmin does not abandon the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth pertaining to the desire realm,
then he would have failed to exhaust the nine grades [of afflictions] of the desire realm.
Because the latter three [fetters] have not yet been abandoned,
this *anāgāmin* has not abandoned them;
he merely suppresses the afflictions to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
It is not the case that one does not sever the afflictions of the fifth grade and below, because they do not obstruct the fruit.
Answer: This is not so.
This is precisely the Anāgāmin.
According to the stage of detachment from desire, only the seventh [affliction] associated with the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) remains.
Although the Anāgāmin has abandoned all nine grades [of afflictions], [the seventh remains].
That is to say, ordinary beings merely suppress the six grades of the desire realm.
The present commentary explains:
these likewise consist of nine grades.
This is because it is taught as that which arises as a predominant factor in conjunction with whichever affliction is present; or else,
it refers specifically to the ninth category.
Ordinary beings also suppress and exhaust all nine grades;
however, within the ninth grade,
there remains a certain category that has not yet been exhausted.
This is precisely the view of a self (ātmadṛṣṭi).
Therefore, the mundane path is not [sufficient];
for within the ninth category, [the afflictions] are subtle.
The treatise states: "Excluding those previously performed karmas conducive to rebirth in the evil destinies that are to be experienced in subsequent lives.
The three causes mentioned above clarify that it is present karma that leads one to the evil destinies.
Excluding those karmas previously performed that are to be experienced in subsequent lives and which result in rebirth in the miserable realms,
for they are not the causes for results in this present life; thus,
having been experienced, they are excluded next.
Regarding the four views in the desire realm that are associated with pride, joy, sorrow, and equanimity,
this is as explained in the seventh fascicle of the Abhidharma (Abhidharmakośa), as well as in subsequent fascicles.
One should deeply understand this.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The ten afflictions abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) are called 'without a basis' (*avastuka*); the remainder have both a basis and no basis."
This is as stated in the fifth fascicle of the Abhidharma (Dharmapada), which describes the contradictory passages.
The treatise says: "If there are categories of afflictions that conform to and coexist with such afflictions," and so forth.
"Conforming" is the general term. Alternatively,
vitarka, vicāra, middha, and so forth,
are not in their essential nature afflictions (*kleśa*).
They are called "afflictions" (kleśa) because they are conformable [to them].
Alternatively, it is said that among the mental factors of the "object-specific" category, those that function in conjunction with the afflictions are secondary afflictions (upakleśa),
because they function in conjunction with the primary afflictions by way of four characteristics.
Regarding the "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*) as categories of affliction (*kleśapakṣya*):
these are precisely those such as anger (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), and so forth, as detailed below;
that is to say, they constitute the various categories [of afflictions].
Regarding the establishment of distinctions:
this is to be understood through the assemblies as explained in the preceding fifty-five fascicles.
Furthermore, regarding the various secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and so forth that the Blessed One taught in the *Vinayakṣudraka-vastu*:
This refers to the present *Dharmaskandha-pāda* and the extensive explanations of its meaning in the following eighty-nine sections,
according to the Mahāsāṃghika school.
Apart from the Tripiṭaka,
some establish a separate *Kṣudraka-piṭaka* (Miscellaneous Piṭaka) for the Mahāyāna;
however, the Sarvāstivādins do not have a separate *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*.
Because there is a "Miscellaneous Chapter" (*saṃkīrṇavarga*) within the *Vinaya*,
that [topic] is explained there in detail:
how the various afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth arise in dependence upon the twelve bases (*āyatana*) according to their secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
This refers to arising as a collective aggregate,
such as the fifty-five [mental factors] mentioned previously;
it does not contradict their arising in separate locations within association with non-dissonant afflictions.
As stated previously in the fifty-fifth [section].
Regarding the treatise’s statement that “deceit (*māyā*) and guile (*śāṭhya*) are the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of the category of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*”),
the fifty-fifth [section] says:
Regarding the phrase "this is the outflow of delusion":
because delusion is predominant in those with wrong views,
this refers to wrong view in terms of its specific activity.
It is a factor of delusion because it is discussed in the general treatises;
furthermore, it is a factor of delusion because its essential nature is so described.
This is because [delusion] increases at the time when these [mental factors] arise in their specific modes of activity (*ākāra*).
Regarding the statement that [wrong view] is the outflow of [wrong view],
this is a detailed examination of various treatises. It was previously stated that the intrinsic nature of wisdom (prajñā) is among the dissociated factors (viprayukta-saṃskāra).
How can speech and discursive thought (vitarka-vicāra) arise in conjunction with wrong view,
and how can they coexist with that view?
The commentary states: At this time, [the mind] relies upon vitarka and vicāra, not upon prajñā;
therefore, there is no contradiction or difficulty.

The treatise states: "If individuals who are bound by all fetters are born in the desire realm, they mature the latent tendencies of the afflictions of the three realms; if they are born in the form realm as ordinary beings, they mature the latent tendencies of the afflictions of the desire realm that have been suppressed and subdued by śamatha."
This contradicts what was previously stated regarding the attainment of maturation, which is consistent with the Abhidharma;
this passage should be reconciled as before.
The treatise states: "It is only with respect to the present that these types of afflictive latent tendencies (anuśaya) are called 'fetters' (saṃyojana)."
The Dharma Master says:

Regarding the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, it is called "binding" (*bandhana*) because the seeds that have been perfumed and activated exist in the present. Question: The treatise states, "One should know that all other afflictions are likewise of this same nature. What does this mean?
The Dharma Master says it is like one category;
the remaining afflictions are likewise. The Great Master said:
"Just as that which is bound exists in the present, not in the past or future."
One should know that regarding the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*),
latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and so forth— the same applies to the other categories of afflictions (*kleśa*)—
these are included here solely by way of the present, not the past or future.

Question: The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states that regarding delusion concerning suffering (*duḥkha*) in the desire realm, there are ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), while for the origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*), there are eight, excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Since these [treatises] such as the *Abhidharmakośa* maintain that there are ten [underlying tendencies] for each of the four truths, why is there this contradiction?
The commentary states: Regarding the principle of reality as it is, there are two gates.
The first is the gate of afflictions deluding the truths.
The gate of the practice of the two truths as an antidote:
if one is confused regarding the gate of the truths,
it is as explained in the Abhidharma.
Each Truth has ten [factors]. If one considers the antidotes to the practice of the Truths,
then according to this treatise, each of the three Truths has eight [factors].
