Only the aspects of suffering, emptiness, and non-self serve as the antidotes;
therefore, the view of a self-identity is established [as its counter-position].
Because extreme views arise based on the view of a self-identity,
it is said that the practice of emptiness and so forth sever them;
furthermore, because [emptiness] is capable of counteracting [the notion of] a self and [the notion of] a person.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is that which is to be countered,
because there is the practice of impermanence (*anitya*).
The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is that which is to be countered.
Because the remaining truths do not exist [in that context],
they are omitted and not discussed.
This is based on specific conditions.
Regarding the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
the phrase "prior to the path of seeing" and so forth refers to the state as it truly is.
All afflictions are empty and are abandoned through the practice of non-self;
they are said to be "abandoned by insight" because they are taught according to the points where delusion arises.

In fact, one does not sever the afflictions by taking the principle of the truths as a distinct object. Question: According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) exists across all the truths.
How are these similar?
Answer: In both cases, the afflictions beneath those respective truths take [the aggregates] as "self."

These are precisely what are called the views of self and extremes (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the clinging to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa) underlying these truths; the same applies to the others. If that is so, and one collectively reckons the afflictions underlying the four truths as constituting a "self," by which truth are these abandoned?
Answer: There is no such thing, for it cannot take [the object] as a whole;

it arises from specific conditions. Question: If that is so, then the views of self and what belongs to self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within the realms of suffering and origination would likewise be unable to take all five sense-gates as their object.
For this reason, it is explained that those [afflictions] associated with the five gates possess power and preeminence,
and because their delusion regarding the meaning of suffering is increased,
they are abandoned only by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Under each of the three truths, the power of the views of self and extremes is weak;
they cannot universally take the five objects as their cognitive domain,
because they consist only of specific delusions.
Regarding the view that these are what are abandoned: Question: Why is it not the same for the views of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) under the Truth of Origination?
Answer: Because the power of the views of self and extremes is weak.
If one is specifically deluded regarding origination,
then it takes only the name of the truth of origination as its object,
because it is abandoned by the vision of the truth of origination.
The twenty phrases concerning the various types of suffering show that since the view of self arises from delusion regarding suffering,
it is understood that [this view] is abandoned through clear insight alone.
The path of cultivation is thus non-existent.
The *Śāstra* states that those who deny parents and so forth are "partially deluded regarding suffering" and the like;
this is because there is a distinction between the fruit and the cause in terms of their delusions.
Regarding the distinction between those abandoned through the vision of suffering and those abandoned through the vision of origination, the *Śāstra* states:

"Furthermore, there are various views that falsely conceptualize Maheśvara, Prajāpati, Śakra, Brahmā, and other such categories as being permanent, eternal, and unchanging; such wrong views are likewise deluded regarding the Truth of Suffering."
This means that reckoning Brahmā as eternal does not arise subsequent to the view of self;
therefore, it is a false view. Question: At the beginning of this fascicle, it says:
Theories of universal permanence (*sarvatraga-śāśvata-vāda*) and theories of partial permanence (*ekadeśa-śāśvata-vāda*), among others,
are all forms of extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*). Since these specifically reckon Brahmā to be eternal,
why is it stated here that they constitute wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)?
The answer is: there are two explanations.
If one gives rise to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and conceives of Brahmā as the self, one subsequently conceives of him as eternal.
This view of permanence is subsumed under the "view of extremes" (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) because it conceives of a self as being reborn,
as stated in the preceding text.
Here, however, the focus is on that which is not the view of a self as being reborn.
This is not the view of permanence, and thus it is subsumed under false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*);
there is no contradiction here either. Question: Ordinary persons suppress cultivation but do not suppress views.
What kind of view is this?
Does the view of self belonging to the form realm arise from a lower realm?
If it were the view of self belonging to the desire realm and so forth,
how could it take the form realm as its object and arise?
Answer: This view of self belongs to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Because it takes names as its object (*ālambana*), it arises by taking those [names] as its objective support.
"Name" refers to names and words;
one conditions them by hearing those names.
Furthermore, "name" also refers to the four aggregates.
This is precisely the characteristic of this mind;
apart from the mind, there is no separate entity.
Therefore, it is said that [the mind] takes names as its object. Question: If this is so, what is the difference between this and desire?
Answer: This shall be further understood in the section on the objects of lower-level conditions,
where the distinctions between the two theories will be explained in detail.
All these theories of universal permanence are termed wrong views;
they do not arise subsequent to the view of self.
Therefore, the preceding text states that this is an extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, and other treatises state that it is subsumed under the category of extreme views.
It resembles the view of permanence,
yet its essence is actually false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Now,
as for what is called the "view of extremes" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*):
This is because it must be the view of self that arises subsequently.
Therefore, the preceding passage in this same text states:
"One takes precisely this view of self as the basis."
Regarding the five aggregates, one perceives them as a self characterized by annihilationism or eternalism;
these two views of annihilationism and eternalism arise solely subsequent to the perception of a self.
This doctrine of universal permanence does not take [the self] as its object;
therefore, it is not an extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, there is no view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) regarding this stage.
It is not like the Sautrāntika school, which holds that [phenomena] arise based on the destruction of conditions;
nor is it like the Sarvāstivāda school, which holds that they originate based on the existence of conditions.
Herein, one relies upon the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) as the basis for such conceptualization.
Because there is that which is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*),
it is said among the "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that one conforms to this view.
That is to say, it takes the faculties and objects as its basis;
this view conforms to those dharmas,
namely the mental states and so forth that arise simultaneously with it.
Furthermore, the former serves as the cause for the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), while the latter serves as its fruit. Regarding doubt (*vicikitsā*), it says:
"This and the remainder."
This means that these non-Buddhists and other sentient beings are wavering regarding suffering;
they are all deluded about suffering. Among the [afflictions of] hatred, there is only mention of that which takes views as its object;
therefore, one knows that this refers to the hatred of the Mahāyāna path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Arising solely by taking views as its object;
that which takes sentient beings and their affairs as its object is the anger of the path of cultivation.
Furthermore, this [view] arises merely by taking [the aggregates] as its object;
it does not exist within the phenomena themselves. Question: Why are the views of finitude and infinitude placed below the two truths of origination and the path?
If the treatise states: "Furthermore, there are all false views of erroneously calculating various false liberations;
these are false views that are deluded regarding cessation," in the Lesser Vehicle this is called "false views deluded regarding suffering."
The destruction of the lower false views necessarily takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object;
however, this present passage also separately takes other tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena as its objects.
This occurs within the path that destroys those false views.
The same applies to reckoning what is not the path as the path;
for one is deluded regarding the middle way,
and consequently reckons that there is a distinct alternative path.
The name [of this view] is that it is abandoned by the Truth of the Path;
for, according to this principle, it correctly overturns delusion,
yet there is a separate grasping [at it].
If one takes all four truths as a collective object and views them as superior,
this constitutes the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
The Great Master said:
This applies to all four truths;
the abandonment of the clinging to precepts and rituals is likewise.
If that is so, then the view of a self should also be the same.
There are other two truths,
both of which possess pervasive results and causes,
because they arise by universally taking the five sense-gates as their objects.
Now, to explain that taking views which take the four truths as their general object constitutes "view-grasping" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa):
this refers specifically to the view-grasping within the category of the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya),
while the other truths can all be taken as its specific objects.
As I have said previously: [The opponent] asks, "Is it not so?
This wrong view, which separately conceives of a false liberation, is likewise deluded regarding contaminated suffering."
How is cessation abandoned through vision?
The answer is: one is deluded regarding cessation and clings to the notion that there is a separate, distinct cessation;
this applies even to the path.
Because their objects increase [in number], they are abandoned only by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
This is because, among the preceding truths such as the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), there is no separate teaching of these [afflictions].

The treatise states: "Excluding only anger—that is, the arising of a mind of fear toward the Truth of Cessation, up to the arising of a mind of resentment and affliction—such anger deludes one regarding the Truths of Cessation and the Path."
The commentary states: According to this text, this refers to hatred (*dveṣa*) which takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object;
for it arises by taking the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) as its immediate object.
This differs from the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
This will be explained in detail later in the section on the objects of cognition, such as names and so forth. Furthermore, it does not state that [the object] is a delusion.
Having already desired to see [the object], anger arises.
Under which truth is this anger subsumed?
The answer is stated below:
The rest is as previously explained.
This is based on the preceding discussion of anger (*dveṣa*);
it also arises conditioned by views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the phrase "if it is based on greed and so forth," since this has already been addressed previously,
one should consult the preceding section as before.
This is called anger in the desire realm.
In the three realms, there are three types:
greed, pride, and ignorance.
This is called the wisdom of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-prajñā*).
Regarding the path of cultivation, it is as with the [five] desires:
there are only four [fetters], while in the three realms there are ten, excluding the fetters of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
What are the four?
The answer is that there is no textual passage because this follows the Hīnayāna.
Within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga):
There is no distinct counteractive practice,
as in the path of seeing; rather,
it is so described because there is a distinct practice regarding emptiness and selflessness.
As previously explained among the ten types of delusion regarding the truths (*satya*), this accords with the understanding of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The treatise states: "It is merely long-lasting, spontaneous, and firm."
This statement was made because these [afflictions] are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); however,
among those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
there are those that arise with conceptualization regarding their objects.
The treatise states: "It should be known that there are briefly five kinds [of objects] to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.

...up to: "In this context, regarding those objects such as the entities of suffering and its origin, the delusions produced by the outflowing afflictions of suffering and its origin take these as their objects."
Because it is a mind of affliction whose essential nature is similar [to that of the object],
it is called "initial discrimination.
The objective realm transformed by this is called "erroneous discrimination."
The objective realm consists of the afflictions (*kleśa*) under the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*).
This is likewise the case for those [afflictions] that take other realms as their objects.
Under the two truths of the path (*mārga-satya*) and cessation (*nirodha-satya*), there are ten afflictions.
The single dharma for removing doubt,
along with the precept against taking [what is not given], is explained separately below; therefore,
it is not mentioned here as "removing."
The remaining eight take views as their objects.
Among them, the one [type of] doubt arises only by taking the truths as its object;
it does not arise by taking views as its object.
Wrong view and ignorance have both objects that are untainted (*anāsrava*) and objects that are tainted (*sāsrava*).
The previously mentioned "theory of five kinds of nirvana" is a false view that is deluded regarding cessation;
it separately calculates that there exists a path [to liberation].
This is the wrong view that is deluded regarding the Truth of the Path;
it has outflowing objects as its condition,
not outflow-free objects.
Because wrong view and ignorance arise conditioned by views,
the single factor of doubt does not arise conditioned by views.
Now, it is stated in general that these take views as their objects.
The grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arises mostly in dependence upon precepts and observances;
thus, it takes precepts and observances as its object.
Only this grasping at views does not arise by taking views as its object; likewise,
grasping at precepts and observances does not arise by taking precepts as its object.
Therefore, one should know that this passage and others like it constitute a formal treatise (*śāstra*).
Thus, one should understand what was stated previously:
"The ten afflictions (*kleśa*) mutually serve as objects for one another."
That which has the untainted as its object,
as well as that which belongs to the lower realms of the suffering and origin truths within a different sphere—
these are called objects of cognition.
It is because afflictions arise merely upon hearing their names;
if one were to see their actual substance,
one would be unable to give rise to delusion.
Because it is not an object of delusion,
it is not similar to that [delusion];
unlike [the truths of] suffering and its origin, which take delusion as their object.
"Name takes name as its object. Question: As in the two lower realms, there are names that can be taken as objects;
how is it so in the formless realm?
The answer is: The two lower realms take names as their object;
those born subsequently in the formless realm do so because they previously cultivated the preparatory means that take names as their object.
Those [cognitions] that arise taking the untainted as their object and so forth are also called "naming the name," due to the power of habitual practice.
It is not necessarily the case that [this] arises solely on account of a name;
furthermore, "name" refers to the four aggregates.
If it were merely the objective aspect (nimittabhāga),...
These are one's own four aggregates.
Delusion arises conditioned by these four aggregates,
for they do not resemble the original substance.
It is said that they take names as their object; however,
the treatise states that these afflictions do not have them as objects,
because [factors] such as the untainted (anāsrava) possess objects of cognition.
Therefore, it is called an "object" (*viṣaya*).
This is one explanation.
Regarding the second [explanation], the object perceived by the seeing [consciousness]:
However, regarding the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
all [subsequent] paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) arise with that very seeing as their object;
thus, doubt is eliminated.
This section is titled "General Analysis of the Delusions of View According to One Gate," because the other gates provide specific analyses.
Within this, it says:
If one distinguishes [them] by stating that the various afflictions are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*),
then where would the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) belonging to the levels below the cessation and path truths be included? Which door would they fall under?
This is also subsumed under the gateway of seeing conditions;
however, because it is a general gateway,
it is as previously explained.
Why is it said "abandoned by seeing" (*darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth?
This is to distinguish it from the greed abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
If one were to simply say "greed" (*rāga*) and so forth, [it would be ambiguous].
Fearing that this might indiscriminately include the afflictions such as craving that pertain to the path of cultivation,
[the author] has already provided the names of the objects of focus for the truths of suffering and its origin;
these [afflictions], however, are those that take the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) aspects of cessation and the path as their objects.
By stating only that they are "abandoned through vision," one knows that those abandoned through cultivation are excluded;
this refers to the greed and other afflictions of the lower stages of the paths of cessation and the path.
The treatise states: "At that time, although noble wisdom takes suffering as its object, it does not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding the phenomena of suffering," and so forth.
This passage comprehensively clarifies the preparatory practices prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) for all three vehicles.

The preliminary expedient means of the Mahāyāna consist either in the contemplation of established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*) or in the contemplation of non-established truths (*avyavasthāpita-satya*).
This differs from the Hīnayāna, as was already explained previously in the fifty-fifth [section]. The treatise states:

"Based on the superior power established by the first [moment], it is said that within the category of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna-pakṣa) there are four types of mind, and within the category of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna-pakṣa) there are likewise four minds. For as long as these eight types of mind proceed, for that same duration they are collectively termed 'the single mind entered immediately after [the path of preparation],' which is a mind manifested by pure śamatha. Thus, collectively speaking, there are nine types of mind at the culmination of the path of vision (darśanamārga)."
This clarifies the path of insight (*darśanamārga*) of the clear light.
Briefly, there are three explanations.
One says that the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and so forth—
"Category" (*varga*) refers to types;
the term "types" includes patience (*kṣānti*) as well.
That is to say, the four types of dharma-patience and the four types of dharma-knowledge;
when these categories are combined, they are called the four minds.
The same applies to the subsequent knowledges (anvaya-jñāna).
These are the eight types belonging to the category of wisdom (*jñāna-varga*),
which possess the power to sever delusions.
This explains the timing for subsequently entering the category of the wisdom that realizes suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*).
Because the eight stages of meditative concentration (aṣṭa-samāpatti) are capable of bringing about tranquility,
because they involve the abiding of the mind,
and because they are collectively termed the single mind of śamatha.
Regarding the nine minds, they belong to the category of wisdom (jñāna);
regarding the eight minds, they belong to the category of meditative concentration (samādhi), with one mind belonging to both.
This is because the category of meditative concentration lacks the power to sever afflictions (kleśa).
It is not for the sake of wisdom;
rather, it is collectively termed "one mind.
Although there is concentration at the time of wisdom, [it is still one mind].
When in a state of meditative concentration (samādhi), there is wisdom (jñāna);
because their functional capacities differ,
when in a state of wisdom, concentration is latent.

The timing and the concealment of knowledge are not discussed here. Question: If the four dharmas—dharmakṣānti and dharmajñāna—constitute four moments of mind, and if the subsequent knowledges (anvayajñāna) are likewise so, then this should accord with the interpretation of the Hīnayāna.
This is because it distinguishes between the afflictions of the upper and lower realms.
Furthermore, regarding the distinction of the Mahāyāna,
it is as explained in the Abhidharma.
Because there is a distinction between the first immediate [attainment] and the subsequent immediate [attainments],
it is said that each constitutes a separate category; thus,
there are two explanations.
Now, as for the term "category" (*varga*), it carries the meaning of "classification.
As the treatise states: "The category of dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna-varga*).
One does not take up the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna),
but rather takes up the receptivity to phenomena (dharmanirvedhabhāgīya),
because it belongs to the same category as the knowledge of phenomena.
These consist of four dharmakṣāntis and four anvayakṣāntis; thus,
eight moments of mind are able to sever the afflictions.
Because these are paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), they receive the name "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
There are four knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and four subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*);
taken together, they constitute a single moment of mind.
This is called the path of pure śamatha;
because it cannot sever the afflictions,
it is not the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga).
Taken collectively, these are called the nine minds.

According to one explanation, the four consisting of the patience and knowledge of the dharma (*dharmakṣānti-jñāna*) and the four consisting of the subsequent patience and knowledge (*anvayakṣānti-jñāna*) constitute the nine minds.
These are called the eight minds.
Because they are conjoined with the path of seeing,
these eight possess the category of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) simultaneously.
These are also eight types of mind, but they merely cause the mind to abide in tranquility through their functional capacity;
they are not like wisdom, which is capable of severing afflictions.
Therefore, it is said that attaining the unified mind in its entirety is termed "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
Because there are eight minds, there are nine [states] in total;
this is because the first [state] distinguishes between the preceding and succeeding moments.
Because the thirty-two minds are combined and treated as one,
they are collectively referred to as nine minds;
however, according to this interpretation, there are only sixteen minds.
Because concentration and wisdom are distinct,
it is called "nine times nine" (eighty-one) minds.
Among these three explanations:
Regarding the latter interpretation as superior to the initial one concerning the thirty-two moments of mind, the treatise states:
"It is precisely during that duration.
Thus, we know that concentration and wisdom are simultaneous, and there are only sixteen [moments].
How can it be said that there are thirty-two?
According to the second interpretation of the treatise,
it is because they belong to the category of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
It can be said that taking patience (*kṣānti*) as the fourth [member] constitutes four;
the third interpretation is superior.
In the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*), there is both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Either sequentially, or simultaneously;
the three explanations are as above.
Alternatively, it is due to the distinction between the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Alternatively, it is because the abandonment of wisdom and thought are distinct,
or because they share a common meaning.
This concludes the presentation of the various schools' views as previously described.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "the first is abandoned by insight (*vipaśyanā*) and the second is abandoned by tranquility (*śamatha*)," this follows the Sautrāntika explanation concerning pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) and among the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Because there are seeds.
Regarding the first form (*rūpa*) among those that contain various seeds,
this is abandoned through insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Regarding the seeds within the second [category] of mind and mental factors,
these are abandoned by *śamatha*;
these seeds are subsumed within this form and mind.

As stated in the fifty-first fascicle: Question: Why is it that in this context, the seeds within form are severed by insight (*vipaśyanā*) rather than by tranquility (*śamatha*), whereas the seeds within the mind are severed by tranquility rather than by insight?
Answer: Because within pure form...
The aspects of the afflictions within the mind are differentiated part by part;
because they are difficult to discern and subtle,
it is said that they are abandoned through observation.
The seeds within the mind correspond to the seeing-division (darśana-bhāga) of the mind;
this category is easily understood.
Therefore, it is said that they are abandoned through cessation;
in reality, however, both are abandoned through observation,
and both are abandoned in accordance with cessation.
However, because the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are easy to recognize according to their specific occurrences,
they are taught as being abandoned individually.
Furthermore, one understands that form (*rūpa*) has many distinct varieties and contemplates the emptiness of these manifold forms.
Only then can one sever the afflictions.
Because their function is predominant,
it is said that form is abandoned through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Those who cultivate meditative concentration mostly take the mind as their object,
in order to cause the mind to abide within its focal object.
Samādhi is named "one-pointed mind" because it is defined by its predominant function;
it is so called because it is capable of contemplating the emptiness of both the mind and mental factors.
It is said that observing and severing the delusions within the mind are actually simultaneous;
both are termed "that which severs."

If it is said that those knowledges subsumed under the category of "contemplation" (vipaśyanā-pakṣya) give rise to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) as they follow along, and so forth...
This refutes the position of the Sautrāntika masters.
Since they do not admit the *ālaya-vijñāna*,
when the seeds subsumed under mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) arise as the wisdom of the category of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), [the following occurs].
The seeds of those afflictions must still be observed as they arise;
only then can one observe that which is capable of severing them.
If one does not observe them as they arise, [they cannot be severed].
If the seeds follow the tainted mind into the past,
and since the past has no substantial reality,
following what would the seeds arise?
Therefore, it is said that the observation follows [the object] in the present.
Thus, we now refute this by saying:
if it follows [the object] as it arises, [then...]
It should not be called the essential nature of the antidote,
because awakening and delusion are mutually contradictory,
and because the natures and characteristics of the antidote and the object to be remedied are distinct.
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:

The category of contemplation belonging to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and so forth cannot be the essence of an antidote (*pratipakṣa*), because the seeds of afflictions (*kleśabīja*) continue to follow along with it; this is the reason (*hetu*).
Just as with the analogies for the tainted mind and mental factors,
because this contradicts the principles of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
the Blessed One said:
The followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and others take this as an analogy; that is,
they proceed from simultaneous liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*),
because of the enumeration previously stated.
These followers by faith and followers by dharma constitute the sixth [category],
distinguished by their dull and sharp faculties respectively,
because each follows the stage of practice through faith and dharma.
However, it is called the sixth because it is a vision;
herein, this sixth kind is signless (*animitta*),
unlike that in the ninth chapter of the Abhidharma (Abhidharmakośa).
As explained extensively in that [work],
in the commentary on the six kinds of signless abidings (*animitta-vihāra*),
it is like the sixteen moments of mind in the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) according to the Abhidharma.
All are practitioners who follow by faith or follow by dharma;
upon reaching the stage of fruition, they are termed "those resolved through faith" (śraddhādhimukta) and so forth.
Specifically, the sixteenth moment of mind is "resolved through faith."
It is also within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Why, then, is it said to be "signless" (*animitta*)?
To say that entering the path of seeing immediately eliminates "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*)—does this mean that the sixteenth moment of mind within the path of seeing is eliminated?
Regarding the abiding in the signlessness of the Abhidharma,
it occurs within the sixteen moments of mind.
The answer states three explanations.
First is the gate of conformity to principle;
because the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the Hīnayāna consists of fifteen moments of mind,
these [stages] such as faith-understanding (*śraddhādhimukta*) are so designated.
That is to say, it occurs during the path of cultivation;
therefore, it is excluded here.
The two explanations are as in the *Abhidharma* regarding the sixteen moments of mind.
All abide in the signless (animitta).
However, among these, the first fifteen moments of mind are the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), characterized by the predominant sense of completely severing the afflictions.
In this context, we take [the fifteenth moment] for now;
we do not say that the sixteenth moment is taken,
because it is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Therefore, excluding the three [stages] such as faith-understanding (adhimukti),
that treatise discusses the Dharma by taking all sixteen moments of mind to be signless (animitta).
This is called the sixth.
This is discussed in terms of persons;
if one takes up those who possess faith and understanding, and so forth.
Because the six types [of minds] do not exist [therein],
they are now excluded, and fifteen minds are taken.
Furthermore, the states of faith-understanding (śraddhādhimukta) and so forth are not fixed positions.
Because these exist within all other fruits,
we now take those that are definitively signless; thus,
the faith-understanding and others are excluded.

The treatise states: "If ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are free from the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) solely by means of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
it is because the afflictions of the path of cultivation obstruct the spontaneous arising of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and its activities."
One merely suppresses the afflictions of the path of cultivation;
however, the afflictions of the path of seeing arise from conceptual discrimination and obstruct the realization of reality, and thus they are not suppressed.
Among the meditative concentrations that subdue through cultivation,
one was previously only able to comply with greed, anger, and pride;
now, one is able to subdue them.
If one conforms to pride through views such as the view of self,
one will be unable to subdue it;
as stated in [the *Śālistamba-sūtra*], chapter sixty-nine:
The view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth do not submit [to this], because both the scripture (*vyañjana*) and the meaning (*artha*) are equally arrogant.
Question: If that is so, then greed (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) are likewise [not subject to it].
If one wishes to see both [extremes] together,
one does not submit;
this mind is one of arrogance.
Because they arise for the most part following me,
the treatise specifically excludes those that are fixed, emergent, or born;
this refers to the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
These three meanings arise at times:
if one who is concentrated enters into or emerges from a concentrated mind,
that is a defiled concentration.
This is the discrimination of afflictions,
such as when non-Buddhists calculate back eighty thousand kalpas and so forth,
resolving their minds to enter meditative concentration to observe them.
One enters from the concentrated mind;
this is the mind of conceptual clinging,
namely, wrong views and so forth.
This refers to the conceptualization of afflictions;
it is either a designation for the entering and exiting of clarity and meditative concentration.
If one speaks of "arising," it refers to the arising of a distinct, scattered mind;
"birth" refers to the production of that [mind].
The treatise states: "Briefly, there are two kinds of *dausthulya*:
first, the *dausthulya* of the outflows (*āsrava*);
second, the *dausthulya* of that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), and so forth."
As stated previously in the third *mūla-sthāna*:
"Wholesome dharmas are not termed *dausthulya*,
nor are they *anuśaya*."
How is it that within this context there is mention of "outflowing heaviness" (*sāsrava-dausthulya*),
as well as the twenty-four kinds of heaviness and the heaviness of karma (*karma-dausthulya*) and so forth found in the Abhidharma?
Daiyi said:
"The single nature of coarse heaviness refers to the seeds of afflictions and so forth."
Regarding the term "leakage-dysfunction" (*āsrava-dausthulya*) used herein:
it refers to the lack of pliancy in these two types of mind, which is called dysfunction;
this includes all contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome dharmas and so forth.
Regarding the term "defiled heaviness" (*sāsrava-dausthulya*) mentioned here,
it refers to the aforementioned third category of heaviness according to its nature (*svabhāva*),
as the treatise states: "because of [the presence of] wholesome dharmas and so forth."

Is it not the case that, according to this context, the same applies to tainted wholesome dharmas (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) with respect to their lack of pliancy (*akarmaṇyatā*) and their coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*),
such that there would be no contradiction?
The treatise states: If one possesses afflictions, the wholesome and indeterminate dharmas within one's continuum become outflows (*āsrava*);
they become mixed with them and lack pliancy.
Therefore, it is called "habitual tendency" (vāsanā).
Arhats possess these wholesome states and so forth;
although they have become attenuated, they still exist.
The essence of the dharma still persists;
that is to say, the non-cessation of the outflows is called "habitual tendencies" (vāsanā).
These coarse and heavy (dauṣṭhulya) portions of the outflows reside within the body.
It is neither identical to nor different from its admixture with wholesome dharmas,
just as when poison is within the body,
there is a constituent part that is neither identical to nor different [from the body].
When the latent dispositions (anuśaya) are abandoned,
these [dispositions] become attenuated,
because the Buddha’s mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) has arisen.
Regarding the statement on the "permanent severance of habitual tendencies," the treatise says: "Furthermore, there are two types of grasping,
namely, the grasping of the faculties and objects as 'I' and 'mine.'"
Second is the grasping at sentient beings;
that is, the clinging of the conceit "I am" and so forth,
which has no separate entity apart from this clinging itself.
This is the conceptual understanding of "I" and "mine.
The aforementioned various distinct expressions of attachment can be understood by investigating them.
As for the reason it is called "tortoise," it is because its appearance resembles the meaning of "covering";
this excludes the single part that is the tail.
Because it is useless.
Alternatively, the tortoise shell has five uses;
thus it is called "resembling the five limbs. Anger is like a she-ass.
Because the nature of a mother donkey is wicked, she makes much noise while chewing grass;
anger is likewise. Stinginess and jealousy resemble congealed blood, due to their similarity in being thin, insubstantial, and flavorless.
Benefit is likewise so. Ignorance is like a wave;
some say it resembles a jackal, for its nature is one of lack of knowledge.
Furthermore, it resembles a mongoose;
when a snake is about to hiss,
its tail has many hairs.
Just as a snake is prevented from hissing by an obstruction, so too is ignorance;
for it obstructs the wisdom of hearing.
Furthermore, it is said in the Western Regions that the "Ear-Hair People" have hair in their ear canals which obstructs sound,
such that they cannot hear human speech.

The fifty-ninth fascicle discusses how all ten afflictions, such as greed and the rest, are capable of initiating karma; however, it is only when they manifest with intense force that they initiate karma leading to the miserable destinies (*apāya*). Furthermore, it is karma initiated through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) that gives rise to this [rebirth], not that which arises spontaneously (*svarasa*).
This is the method for cultivating universal vision;
because in the path of seeing, [the afflictions] of the desire realm are exclusively unwholesome.
All are capable of initiating karma.
Regarding this within the context of cultivating the path,
as stated in the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (Dharmapada), fascicle 4:
That which spontaneously gives rise to unwholesome conduct is the unwholesome; namely,
the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth.
Because there are those who are incapable [of abandoning them],
the afflictions are designated as "to-be-abandoned-by-insight" (*darśana-prahātavya*).
This is as stated in the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmapada*.
Only this [ignorance] gives rise to karma leading to the three evil destinies;
it does not pertain to the path of cultivation.
However, in this context, the discussion concerns the projecting and completing causes of karmic results.
Within the process of cultivating the path,
what prevents there also being karma that produces distinct retributions in the evil destinies? Therefore,
we know that the present [discussion] refers to the drawing forth of the fruit.
It does not rely on the full fruit.
The remainder is as explained in the first commentary on the *Maulī Bhūmi* of the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharma-kośa*.
The treatise states: "As it is said that the essential nature of *dausthulya* (coarseness) is called *anuśaya* (latent disposition), and so forth."
This refers to the explanation in terms of the coarseness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-dauṣṭhulya*).
This coarseness is also called a latent tendency (*anuśaya*),
because it is of the nature of affliction (*kleśa*).
The term *anuśaya* refers to its essential nature (*svabhāva*),
not to its designation as "coarseness" (*dausthulya*) based on its lack of peace;
for that [lack of peace] is not itself called *anuśaya*.
As explained in the previous fascicle,
among the eighteen types of *dausthulya* (coarseness),
there are three types of *dausthulya*: intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), maturation (*vipāka*), and so forth.
Candragomin said:
"Because seeds have existed from beginningless time,
they are called the 'intrinsic heaviness' (svabhāva-dauṣṭhulya)."
Jinagupta said:
"This refers to the maturation of new conditioning;
their essential natures are distinct, yet they exercise a predominant influence."
This is precisely what is called "coarseness" (*dausthulya*).
It is termed the coarseness of intrinsic nature, maturation, and so forth;
however, regarding the "obstructions of karma" and the like, this discussion is based on heavy obstructions.
Regarding the turning of power and lack of power:
in the preceding *Maulī Bhūmi*, there was no separate category for "power" and "lack of power.
[This refers to] those whose afflictions are collectively intense and of the highest degree.
That which is called "possessing power" is not so;
that which is called "lacking power" is likewise not so.
The treatise states: "It should be known that a portion of the unwholesome afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) possess maturation (*vipāka*).
These refer to the unwholesome afflictions of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) pertaining to both the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
However, if one has entered the state of a noble one (*ārya*),"
Alternatively, that which is unwholesome within the body of a noble one is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and lacks a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*);
furthermore, those afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm that are neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Because it does not attract a fruit,
there is no division within the middle;
this interpretation is found in the subsequent text.
Regarding the transformation of deluded conduct, as the seven types have already been enumerated with their distinct meanings in the *Maulī Bhūmi*, what are they?
As stated in the eighth fascicle of the *Maulī Bhūmi*:

there are those who possess the names [of views] but lack understanding; namely, the three—view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—which give rise to wrong conduct toward the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
These are exclusively afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and not of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
because the [afflictions of] self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and views regarding extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) do not arise through delusion regarding the [Four] Truths.
As this treatise states:
Because one turns toward deluded conduct regarding the Four Noble Truths,
other afflictions such as greed arise solely by taking the Four Truths as their object;
based on this view, the [notion of] "truth" arises.
This can be understood through reading.
The first four gates specifically identify the afflictions (*kleśa*),
concluding with the discussion of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) conditioned phenomena as their objects.
In the fifth and sixth sections,
the afflictions associated with each of the Four Noble Truths are explained separately;
those pertaining to Suffering and its Origin are increased within the context of the "Correspondence with the Conditions of Affliction."
Therefore, they are called "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Because the cessation and the path eliminate afflictions, they are called "fears.
In the seventh category, there is only one door, which is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Since this arises spontaneously and does not arise through delusion regarding the truths,
it is known that the preceding six categories are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
Regarding the section on "The Presence or Absence of Affairs," the fifth and sixth [sections] of the *Abhidharmakośa* (Dàfǎ) concerning the upper and lower [realms] contradict one another,
as detailed in the respective commentaries (*chāo*).
Regarding the association of afflictions with feeling (*vedanā*),
consult the preceding seventh fascicle of the *Abhidharma* (Jñānaprasthāna) according to the corresponding passage.
The explanation of coarse characteristics (*audārikalakṣaṇa*) and so forth is easily understood;
the distinction between coarse and subtle will appear naturally in the subsequent text,
which reconciles any apparent contradictions.
The maturation of the continuum refers to the seeds of the liberation-body and enjoyment-body.
As for the fetters of signs and the fetters of coarse heaviness:
That is to say, the six sense objects are called "sentient beings.
Attachment to these is bondage;
by taking them as objective conditions, one gives rise to acquisition.
These are called the bond of signs and the bond of coarse heaviness;
that is to say, the seeds of the afflictions.
Regarding this statement that the three minds constitute the culmination of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*):
it is as previously explained in the fifty-fifth assembly.
As for those whose bodies and speech are heavy with the coarseness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of non-restraint, they delight in seclusion.
This refers to the nature of physical fatigue experienced by one practicing seated meditation.

The *Śāstra* states: "Next, one should further abandon suffering and mental distress," and so on, up to "all hindrances belonging to the category of obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*)."
This refers to the obstacles such as the unconditioned state of immovability (*āniñjya-asaṃskṛta*) within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
which should be applied accordingly.
The first four are obstacles common to the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
The obstacles of ordinary beings prior to the path of seeing;
the obstacles of noble ones subsequent to the abandonment [of defilements] through seeing;
and furthermore, the obstacles to meditative concentration common to both vehicles.
The cognitive obscurations pertain only to bodhisattvas;
this nature of the meditative obscurations pertains only to śrāvakas.
This belongs to the category of maturation (vipāka) and is subsumed under the category of the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa),
as in the *Buddhabhūmi*.
Regarding the two vehicles within this context, for the first five [categories],
one interpretation follows the explanation of the śrāvaka’s obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*);
the remaining [categories] for the pratyekabuddhas can be understood accordingly.
Because the Pratyekabuddhas have attained superior supernormal powers,
only they eliminate the hindrances to meditative concentration;
otherwise, this applies generally to both vehicles.

Furthermore, regarding "having seen forms with the eye, one is neither elated nor dejected," this refers to the six modes of constant abiding (*ṣaḍ-ābhoga-vihāra*). Furthermore, regarding "by nature having few desires" and so forth,
this refers to the eight thoughts of a great person (*aṣṭau mahāpuruṣavitarkāḥ*).
The Treatise says: "There are fourteen objects that serve as conditions for others.
That is to say, those in the form realm [take] the afflictions of the desire realm as their object; those in the formless realm [take] the afflictions of the form realm as their object;
and so on, up to those who, regarding the sentient beings of the lower stages, because they themselves possess constant, eternal bliss, purity, and superior virtues, consider themselves superior."
That is to say, within the Mahāyāna, those in higher stages may give rise to afflictions by taking lower stages as their objects. Question: What kind of delusion is this?
Answer: There is an interpretation.
This is the pride of views (*dṛṣṭi-māna*).
As in other places, there are further [types], but here it simply says: "I am superior to this."
He is not equal to them;
even if he gives rise to the conceit of "I am," it is not the case that all afflictions arise.
Furthermore, it is explained that all afflictions, such as greed and the rest, are likewise so;
for they constantly and perpetually perceive things as permanent and pure,
which constitutes the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Although such conditions exist,
they do not resemble the essential nature [of the object].
A condition is called an "object" (viṣaya).
As stated at the beginning of the previous fascicle and in the sixth chapter of the Abhidharma,
it is said elsewhere that "the higher [levels] do not take the lower as an object."
This is a passage that accords with reason. Question: Greed and pride of a lower stage cannot take a higher stage as their object;
what about pride belonging to a higher realm?
How does one take the lower [stages] as an object?
The answer is: because the lower stages are inferior, pride does not arise toward them.
Because it is superior, it can arise;
this refers to the second section of the *Abhidharma* (the *Jñānaprasthāna*),
concerning the passage stating that the formless realm does not take lower stages as its objects, and so forth.
As it is reconciled therein, the treatise asks:

"Should it be said that all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the entire realm (*dhātu*) bind one to rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), or not all? The answer is: It should be said that they are all [the causes], not that they are not all."
This question concerns the defilement that moistens rebirth, not the arousal of karma.
Although ten afflictions may arouse karma,
they are neutral (avyākṛta) and belong to the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
The afflictions such as craving in the higher realms do not incite karma; therefore,
the present [discussion] is based on the "self" that moistens rebirth.
Craving is the primary moisture;
the others are auxiliary moistures,
as will be explained below.
This is to refute the Lesser Vehicle’s [claim] that craving alone moistens rebirth;
for the Abhidharma, based on the primary moisture,
states that it is "self-love" alone.
This is not contradictory. The treatise states:

"Briefly, there are seven types of rebirth-linking (pratisandhi): first, those with both active outbursts (paryavasthāna) and latent dispositions (anuśaya), namely ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana); second, those with only latent dispositions, namely those who have seen the traces of the noble ones (ārya-mārga-darśin)."
This is based on the fact that ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) employ both the manifest and the seeds of the latent dispositions (anuśaya),
because they are subsumed within the nine types [of afflictions] in the Abhidharma and because they necessarily arise.
It is said that because greed and anger arise,
it is not the case that there is no seed;
for one who has attained the fruit of the Path of Seeing is born within a specific realm and stage.
If they are born in the same stage,
they are also moistened by their active manifestation;
for example, as when one is born in the first heaven of the first dhyāna.
Regarding "the second [intercalary month] arises next":
this refers to the manifestation of an intercalary month as well,
because the power of the path is inferior.
Although born in different stages,
by means of the eight kinds of intercalary [attainments],
the third fruit is excluded.
Regarding the external [factors] that serve as "intercalary" conditions for the seeds alone,
this is as explained in the first fascicle of the *Maulī Bhūmi* and the fifth fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

Regarding the statement here that "a bodhisattva takes birth through the power of knowledge," this refers to taking birth through the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), as explained in the Abhidharma.
Although this fruit is contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is also summoned by contaminated wholesome karma.
Nevertheless, because it follows the place of its arising,
one should know that within the exposition of the paths of action (*karmapatha*), this karma is also established with five characteristics (*pañcalakṣaṇa*).
It then states that there are three fundamental paths of action—
those of body, speech, and mind—
as well as four preparatory stages.
There are five subsequent [mental factors].
These are explained in detail as before in the eighth chapter of the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
As for greed, anger, and so forth:
In the Hīnayāna, there is no preparatory application;
it consists solely of the fundamental [path].
Now, in the Mahāyāna, there is also a preparatory application.
In brief, it is through the actions of body and speech that the fundamental [karmic path] is actually generated,
as explained in other excerpts.
The section on "skillful means" (*upāya*) and so forth differs from that in the seventh chapter of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*;
please consult it.
Regarding the three types of killing discussed in the treatise:
the first is dominated by the volition of karma;
the second arises from the volition of wrong action.
Third, regarding the case where a bodhisattva kills for the sake of benefiting others:
within the treatise on killing,
it says "a corpse or half a corpse."
That is to say, among the various perverse practices such as cursing someone to death,
causing corpses or half-dead bodies to rise up and kill others, and so forth,
there are those performed at improper times and so on.
This differs from the preceding text,
as well as from the eighth chapter of the *Maulī Bhūmi* and the *Abhidharma*.
This may be understood.
Regarding Rudra and Viṣṇu,
they are as recorded in other excerpts.
The sixtieth fascicle of the treatise states: "Or there may be a person, or one who possesses the characteristics of a person.
The commentary explains that this refers to the stages such as the *kalala* and so forth, which correspond to the development within the womb.
It is called the gravity of taking life.
In this Mahāyāna, this also constitutes a pārājika offense;
in the various schools of the Hīnayāna, it is likewise so.
Except for the Sarvāstivādins,
all others maintain that it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense,
because the characteristics of a human being have not yet been fully established.
Furthermore, regarding the perception of a person:
it refers to killing a non-human being who has transformed into a human form,
with the intention of killing a human.
This is called the *Saṃghāṭa*.
"Saṃgha" means "assembly.
Here, it is referred to as "Saṃghī."
This is what is meant by "the various things.
Such is the transformation of sounds.
Regarding the five fruits of the paths of action:
As in the ninth *yogasthāna*.
Consult the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* (or *Abhidharma-samuccaya-bhāṣya*). Regarding the "implements for sacrifice":
The factors of the basis,
such as the requisites for ritual offerings;
and the factors of wisdom.
Alternatively, whatever requisites are necessary are used for such purposes as ritual implements.
The treatise states: "Or because they increase those [virtues]."
By causing his wife or concubines to be humiliated by others,
if they follow those instructions and engage in sexual misconduct,
he will consequently encounter the arising of anger and resentment.
Regarding the offense of similar sexual misconduct,
it is simply termed "sexual misconduct" and is not designated as being "completed by means of the body."
It is also because they give rise to the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). Question: The ten paths of action (*karmapatha*) have volition (*cetanā*) as their essence.
Since volition is itself karma, how can it be called a "path"?
Master Bei said:
"Because wholesome and unwholesome [actions] can bring about the fruits of the path, such as the desirable and the undesirable,
that karma is itself the path."
The meanings of body and speech are explained as follows in the subsequent text;
that which is collectively termed greed and hatred as mental karma is likewise so.
These are the paths of action.
This is not karma;
it is not like this,
as explained in the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa*.
This is the same as the eighth *maula-bhūmi* mentioned previously;
there is no need to elaborate further.
Greed, hatred, and false views are the path of volition (*cetanā*).
Because it is that which the mind traverses, it is called the "path" (*mārga*).
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that it arises in relation to the objects of greed for wealth through taking what is not given:
this refers to even when one commits theft against other sentient beings.
It is also called "wealth" and is the object of frivolous speech;
although it is directed toward sentient beings.
To speak in terms of what is proximate:
the mental faculty arises conditioned by names,
because volition (*cetanā*) gives rise to phrases, names, and so forth.
Although phrases are also conditioned by names,
they are collectively designated as "names.
Regarding those that arise in relation to the sphere of false views and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*):
That is to say, one interpretation states:
those that take only the truths of suffering and its origin as their objects do so because they pervade all five doors.
The "predominant" refers to the sphere of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
It does not take up the path of cessation,
yet in reality, it is also that.
Therefore, the Abhidharma states:
"That which has the sense of being substantially existent refers to all four truths."
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it exists only in three truths,
excluding the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*),
because this is the case for the majority of instances.
Alternatively,
it may be that the Four Truths are all termed "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*),
because they are transformations of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the mind.
The same applies to the Abhidharma-śāstra.

The treatise states: "If an action is heavy by reason of its motivation—such as when it is instigated by the fetters of intense greed, hatred, and so forth—it must necessarily have been preceded by greed and other such [afflictions] within the paths of karma."
The conditions for initiating karma are weighty;
if they are not intense,
they are not subsumed under the category of karma.
The unwholesome roots give rise to volition (*cetanā*), which is [the agent] that is light.
The *Śāstra* states: "It should be known that this is merely a transformation of this very volition, transformed by the power of those [roots]," and so forth.
This means that it is precisely karma that gives rise to karma.
The seeds of volitional effort (*prayoga-cetanā*) undergo transformation because they give rise to suffering for others.
In every moment, non-informative matter (avijñapti) of mixed unwholesome discipline arises;
this is due to its power.
Because it arises through the nature of things (*dharmatā*),
just as one receives the precepts while in a state of mindlessness;
this text serves as the proof.
The same applies to the karma of killing:
it arises from both the manifest action (*vijñapti*) and that which is not manifest (*avijñapti*),
as explained in other excerpts.
It should be understood that the brahmin Śāriyaka is a brahmin by birth and lineage.
The *Śāstra* states, "Furthermore, there are four types of karma," etc., clarifying that the Mahāyāna speaks of only four types of karma. The *Śāstra* further states:

"Whatever unwholesome karma of fixed retribution possessed by Arhats—whether committed in a previous life or during this very life while still in the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*)—is called 'ripened fruition' because it was performed as a minor suffering intended to afflict [them]."
Regarding the phrase "up to establishing determinate karma":
one interpretation states that this refers to first producing this birth,
wherein one performs unwholesome karma while in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Because this is determinate karma,
one experiences only slight suffering at the time of attaining arhatship.
It is called "fruition" because it has already matured and attained the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*),
being the nirvāṇa with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*).
All unwholesome determinate karma that would otherwise result in the maturation of fruit is entirely not experienced.
One experiences only a slight degree of suffering and immediately repays this;
this is the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) that is the residual force (*vāsanā*) of previous unwholesome karma.
It causes retribution and experience to arise;
it is not unwholesome karma because it is present. Question: This is definitive.
For what reason does an Arhat experience [karmic results] much more lightly?
The answer is: The Buddha established determinate karma (niyata-karma) based on ordinary persons whose bodies have not yet attained liberation.
For one who has not yet attained liberation,
the karma that establishes meditative concentration in the body can be transformed into a light experience.
Second, regarding the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*):
it refers to the fact that upon entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, because the seeds no longer exist,
one does not undergo any further [rebirth].
Based on not having entered nirvana without remainder,
one establishes determinate karma;
[this refers to] entering nirvana without remainder.
This is called the continuity of liberation.
Even when an Arhat enters nirvana with remainder,
they are still said to be "not yet liberated."
Therefore, one experiences light karma.
Furthermore, it is explained that after attaining *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, there remains a residual force (*śakti*).
Thus, [the karma] now possesses its functional efficacy.
Now one experiences only slight and light suffering;
because the seeds of its retribution have been permanently severed,
one will not experience any of it in the future.
This is the meaning. Furthermore,
another interpretation holds that the superior karma exists solely in ordinary beings,
or perhaps during states of conscious awareness.
Because it is slightly oppressed by suffering,
it is called "already ripened";
this is named after its fruit.
Therefore, it is said that an Arhat has already attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) in this present body.
Were it otherwise, they would still be a learner (*śaikṣa*) in a future body and would undergo further minor suffering.
If one attains the vajra path,
thereafter one will not receive any karmic retribution,
because the seeds no longer exist.
Regarding the statement that there are snakes and other such creatures within the body of an Arhat,
this is a result of karmic retribution.
It is a result of uniform outflow (niṣyanda-phala),
not a ripening result (vipāka-phala) of the present;
it occurs after one has already attained the third fruit.
Because [the afflictions] have been exhausted and because the state of perfection has been attained,
it is said that one achieves the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*).
As explained in a separate commentary,
the treatise states: "The Buddha as the head of the great bhikṣu-saṃgha" means that the Buddha is the head.
The term "bhikṣu" distinguishes [the Buddhist] from non-Buddhists.
The disciples of non-Buddhists also call themselves bhikṣus,
claiming, "I am a bhikṣu who has Maheśvara as my preceptor."
The present statement says "the Buddha is the foremost," thereby distinguishing him from others. The treatise states:

"For a bodhisattva who has already entered the stage of pure intention (*śuddhāśayabhūmi*), all unwholesome karma is ultimately severed; through this power of non-delusion, they are liberated from fetters and free from afflictions."
That is to say, because the afflictions of a bodhisattva still exist,
they should cause karma to arise; however,
it is only because they do not forget their mindfulness [that this does not occur].
There is no cultivation of the path regarding unwholesome karmic seeds that have not yet been severed through the cultivation of the path.
Because one does not forgetful of mindfulness,
non-arising is called "permanent abandonment.
There is no distinction between this and the absence of seeds.
At the stage of the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*), because all [defilements] are forever severed, the treatise states:

"Volition (*cetanā*) is karma but not a path of action; the seven [actions] such as killing are both karma and paths of action; and the three paths such as wrong view are paths of action but not karma."
The preceding section discussed manifest action (vijñapti-karma),
which is in essence volition (cetanā).
How, then, could volition not be the path within this context?
Wandering along the named path is not the Way;
it is only through contemplation that one attains the fruit. Therefore, it is contemplation that is the Way.
It is called the path of fruition.
Volition is also the path of fruition;
the same applies to mental action.
As in the fifty-third [fascicle] of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa*,
and the eighth fascicle of the aforementioned *Yogācārabhūmi*.
In the commentary on the eleven births,
what is the distinction between the seventh and the ninth?
The explanation states that the first seven refer to the substance of birth itself.
The latter nine are spoken of in terms of their bases.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the first seven are called "pure" because they are free from defilement,
while those of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are called "impure."
Because it serves as the basis for the newly born Bodhisattvas and others, the ninth [ground] is called "Pure" (*śuddhā*), as its essence is free from defilement;
yet, at this stage, one cannot yet perceive the Truths (*satya*).
It is called "born in an impure place" because it is formulated in contrast to the states of leisure (*kṣaṇa*).
Fifth, regarding those who are not insane and so forth, [the text] analyzes the joints and members.
This refers to the practice in the West where, when one wishes to cremate a corpse,
they hire someone to dismember the limbs before burning them,
because it is easier to burn [the body] once it has been dismantled.
The person mentioned below as the *pugdalas* is precisely this individual.
The treatise states that ignorance is able to act as an obstacle in five locations.
This refers to the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning;
these constitute the contaminated path,
which is mundane in nature.

The Treatise states: "Feeling conditions craving; craving conditions grasping; grasping conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions aging and death. This is the sequence of the suffering of experience.
Craving, grasping, and becoming are the causes of suffering.
Birth and so forth are the fruits of suffering;
that which is able to produce these fruits is called "attainment" (*prāpti*), as was previously stated in the tenth *Maulī Bhūmi*.
The suffering of the fivefold embryonic development is the cause of suffering; therefore,
it is called "craving."
Abridged Commentary on the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Fifteen;
Abridged Commentary on the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Sixteen.
Main Treatise, Chapters 61, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
Ji (基) states that the one called "King Udayana" is what was previously referred to as King Udrāyaṇa.
According to the original phonetics, it is pronounced *Udāyana*, which here means "Emergence"; *Vatsa* means "Love"; and *Rāja* means "King. "Udrāyaṇa" is a corruption [of the original term].
The Treatise states: "A dissimilar son" refers to one born of lowly status,
because his birth is not similar to that of a king.
One who resembles the son is the king’s true son;
he is similar to the king.
Because his physical appearance and demeanor resembled those of his father,
everyone loved him;
he never had a scolding expression or harsh words.

The treatise says: "What is meant by 'suffering because it is accompanied by manifold sufferings'? This refers to birth in the hells (*naraka*) and the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), which is exclusively suffering.
... up to what is called 'suffering because it is accompanied by manifold sufferings'."
That is to say, it should be stated here that a portion of animals also experience suffering;
furthermore, this passage appears frequently in the preceding texts.
In this context, the statement is made based on those who experience suffering for the most part;
since animals experience less suffering than hungry ghosts, [the former are mentioned first].
This suffering of birth, old age, sickness,
and death has been extensively analyzed previously in the tenth chapter of the *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya* and in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.

The treatise asks: How is it that the five aggregates of clinging are suffering? One should know that this suffering is also characterized by five aspects. Regarding the phrase "because they are the basis for the arising of suffering" and "because they depend on the basis for the arising of suffering":
this means that depending upon these [aggregates], the arising of suffering occurs.
Because birth is the vessel for suffering,
it is called the "vessel of the suffering of birth.
Thus, based on birth, the other six types of suffering arise.
This refers to the suffering of old age and so forth;
they are collectively termed the "vessel" (āśraya-bhājana) because they serve as the basis for the arising of suffering.
It is in dependence upon this vessel that suffering arises.
It is said that they are the basis for the arising of the vessel of suffering;
alternatively, this [basis] is the vessel from which suffering arises,
while the other six bases of suffering arise from this vessel of suffering.
It is called the vessel that gives rise to suffering;
the other six [aggregates] exist in dependence upon the arising of this suffering,
and thus birth itself serves as the vessel for suffering.
Taken together, they are called "the instruments of the suffering of birth";
alternatively, the first [of these] is the suffering of birth itself.
The second is that which gives rise to all instruments of suffering (*duḥkha-āyudha*).
Taken together, they are collectively termed "relying on the instruments of suffering.

The treatise states: "Receiving the factors of full ordination (*upasaṃpadāṅga*) refers to the factor of natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīlāṅga*); receiving the various branches of training according to the Dharma refers to the factor of receiving the precepts at the final stage when the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*) and so forth are taught; and protecting the minds of others refers to the factor of the prohibitive precepts of dignified conduct (*airyāpathika-vinaya-śikṣāpada*)—these three constitute the factor of protecting the various branches of training as previously received at the time of ordination."
This refers to the two types of precepts: those that are followed (*anuvartana*) and those that are received (*samādāna*).
Master Bei states:
"As explained previously in the fifty-third [section]."
Within the exposition of the vows (vinaya-saṃvara),
there are these four branches,
namely, the fourfold precepts of a bhikṣu.
The six branches constitute four branches;
this is distinct from that [previous case].
Therefore, the former interpretation must be incorrect.
Regarding the ten classes of sentient beings who take delight in and rejoice in these ten kinds of dharmas,
they may be understood by correlating them in sequence;
the meaning is clear and easy to comprehend.
There are three ways in which karma is initiated:
first, initiation through association,
which refers to momentary origination (*kṣaṇasamutthāna*).
Second is production by the two parents;
this is the proximate cause (*upaniṣad-hetu*).
Third is production by the predominant influence (*adhipati*).
This refers to the remote causal motivation (*dūre-samutthāna*),
which further draws forth other afflictions to initiate karmic action.
Alternatively, what was previously [discussed] has already been fully subsumed;
it is only when the fourth, the predominance [of ignorance], further gives rise to afflictions that they manifest.
This concludes the four fascicles above.
From the fifty-eighth [fascicle] onwards, these are the three stages beginning with vitarka and vicāra.
Fascicle sixty-two: the stage of samāhita and so forth. Among these, those termed secondary afflictions (upakleśa) are as follows.
Those that afflict the mind in accordance [with the primary afflictions] are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Furthermore, those that arise in accordance with the primary afflictions are also called secondary afflictions.
Regarding this, there are two interpretations.
If it refers to defiled mental factors,
they arise in accordance with other afflictions.
As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*, Chapter on the Latent Dispositions (*Anuśaya-nirdeśa*),
regarding the mental factors (*caitta*) within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), they are all to be understood here according to the preceding [explanation].
As in the *Kṣudrakavastu*,
all [of these] are included;
however, this is stated according to what is predominant.
This treatise speaks only of twenty-two [factors] and so forth;
among these, whatever exists outside of the twenty-two does not exceed the substance of those twenty-two.
They may be understood by seeking them out through their mutual inclusion.
For example, as stated below: "Pride has flattery and deception as its essence."
It is said that here, by the predominant power of guile (*śāṭhya*) and deceit (*māyā*),
one proceeds forward with a body characterized by that predominant influence; this refers, for instance,
to the time when receiving offerings, accepting invitations from others, and so forth.

If one proceeds while standing in front, what is meant by "being detached from the yoke of the wholesome"? It refers to being far removed from extreme bedding and seating, and being detached from the various evils one has practiced; it means abandoning them as if they were a secluded chamber, casting them away from oneself, and not giving rise to desire or pleasure for them.
This refers to the "extreme bedding," which is the very limit of the most wretched bedding;
by relying upon this, one is able to remain detached.
This is called "the bedding that is remote from the extremes.
Furthermore, it is explained that "bedding remote from the extremes" refers to the foremost and most excellent bedding.
To be able to remain far removed from such pleasant and unpleasant bedding is called "staying far removed from the extremes of bedding."
"Far removed from what resembles a quiet chamber" means being fully endowed with a secluded and tranquil place that resembles a quiet chamber,
such as a place for ascetic training and the like.
It refers to secluded places within a chamber;
it is called "abandoning" because one leaves them,
and it is also understood as a place for engaging in sexual desire.
That which is frequented by all manner of evils is called a semblance of a quiet chamber;
one should distance oneself from it and not give rise to desire or pleasure therein.
The intention of relinquishing is called "distant from the yoke of the wholesome.
Regarding the statement in the treatise that "cultivating the ten universal bases (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*) can accomplish five matters," Master Bei said:
Regarding the five matters: by means of the aforementioned eight universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana), one is able to bring forth three matters;
namely, first, the matter of transformation (nirmāṇa).
There are two types of transformative matters;
the supernormal powers of the various noble ones constitute the third.
This [subject] possesses such supernormal powers.
Fourth, because of the sphere of infinite space, one brings forth the unimpeded noble superknowledges (*abhijñā*) for traveling to and fro;
because of the sphere of infinite consciousness, one brings forth supreme qualities such as the absence of conflict (*araṇā*).
This constitutes the fifth [section].
The following text explains the functional capacity of the fifth consciousness in all locations.
If one follows this principle according to the flow of the text,
the phrase "the supernormal powers of all noble ones" occurs within the discussion of the eight types of production.
Regarding the point that it is categorized separately as one [of the powers]:
within the exposition on the induction of emptiness,
it is stated that the supernormal powers of the noble ones involve unimpeded movement to and fro.
The statement that "the supernormal powers (abhijñā) of the various noble ones (ārya) should each have a distinct substance as one" is now explained as follows:
The first eight [kinds of supernormal power] induce a single matter;
whether it be a transformative act or a modification of matter,
they differ only in that the object is either originally non-existent or originally existent.
The second is the unimpeded supernormal power of proceeding and returning, induced by the sphere of infinite space;
this is because there are three types of intermediate existence induced by the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The fifth refers to the single quality of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and so forth.
The accomplishment of the liberation of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vimokṣa*), the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokṣa*), and the cessation liberation (*nirodha-vimokṣa*) constitutes the second.
The three modes of practice—boundless, immeasurable, and pervasive—are established as three. Question:

Why is there a separate particle "and" (*ca*) for the liberation of cessation (*nirodha-vimokṣa*), while "and" is omitted for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanya-āyatana*) and others, which are combined into one?
Answer: Because the force of the text is such, there are three instances of the term "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*);
it is stated at both the beginning and the end.
Because this [state] is the sphere of infinite consciousness,
it is said that it does not exist within this liberation of cessation; however,
it is merely stated because of its being the cause for its fulfillment.
It is precisely because of this that the causes for the fulfillment of non-existence and so forth are established; therefore,
one should know that they are combined into one.
Because it belongs to the category of this liberation,
