the Great Meaning (Mahārtha) says:
"There are three types of the sphere of consciousness."
First, the elicitation of knowledge such as the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā-jñāna*);
second, the liberation of the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
and third, the liberation of cessation (*nirodha-vimokṣa*). Regarding the statement "proceeding by way of infinite, immeasurable, and all-pervading activity":
This summarizes the preceding [section] because the sphere of consciousness (vijñānāyatana) has been accomplished.
From "one attains all merits" onwards constitutes the great meaning.

These various merits are explained in the twentieth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*. Question: Why is it that, by accomplishing the first eight universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), one brings forth transformative activities and the transformation of objects?
Answer: Because one has attained mastery over objective forms through the previously mentioned universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
one is thus able to bring forth transformative and metamorphic feats.
In this state, there is an obstruction to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*),
because it has not yet attained the concentration associated with the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*),
which is acquired based on the fourth dhyāna.
Is it not that one can attain the transformation of phenomena and the alteration of phenomena?
This is stated according to the terminology of the superior [attainments].
Ordinary persons cannot attain the first eight universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*). Question: Why is it that they do attain the universal base of space (*ākāśakṛtsnāyatana*)?
It induces the unimpeded supernatural power of going and returning;
the answer is that because it is empty and formless,
it is therefore able to induce the unimpeded [power] of going and returning.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmapitaka* (Treatise on the Higher Dharma), chapter thirteen, states:
"By attaining the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one suppresses and eliminates the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*);
it is not that there is no capacity to eliminate form."
If one has attained unimpeded coming and going,
one may also attain the sphere of empty space;
however, the obstructions have not yet been exhausted.
Now, speaking in terms of the point where all obstacles are exhausted:

one must attain the sphere of emptiness (*ākāśa-kṛtsnāyatana*) in order to sever these obstacles. Question: For what reason does the cultivation of the sphere of totality of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana*) bring about such superior qualities as the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*), and so forth?
Answer: All dharmas of merit are merits of the mind-consciousness,
for they are all mental factors.
Because one has attained mastery over the sphere of consciousness,
one attains mastery over the object as consciousness itself;
subsequently, one relies upon the fourth dhyāna.
The arousal of this knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā-jñāna*) and so forth,
as well as the supernormal power of unimpeded coming and going,
also rely upon the four dhyānas.
One must rely on the sphere of infinite space in order to eliminate the obstruction of impeding matter;
thereafter, one enters the four dhyānas.
He travels back and forth without obstruction;
although he may not yet have attained the spheres of totality such as emptiness,
he nonetheless attains unimpeded coming and going.
This is not the speech of one who has attained preeminence,
because their obstructive impediments regarding form have not yet been exhausted; thus,
there remains spatial limitation and resistance.
Now, according to the Victorious One, it is unimpeded in all places; furthermore, regarding the transformation of immeasurable and pervasive conduct:
one practices this sphere of consciousness by performing the contemplation of the immeasurable and boundless.

Because the boundless applications (*apramāṇa*) reach their ultimate consummation in this [sphere], no further *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality) or *abhibhvāyatana* (sphere of mastery) is established. The *kṛtsnāyatanas* constitute the path capable of purifying the various liberations (*vimokṣa*), meaning that liberation is taken as the fruit.
The superior spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) serve as the preliminary practice (*pūrvaprayoga*).
The end of the thirteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmapitaka* states:
"Based upon the liberations (*vimokṣa*), one cultivates the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)."
Therefore, one initiates the preparatory application;
through pervasive cultivation, it reaches fulfillment;
and through fulfillment, one attains ultimate perfection within liberation.
The Sarvāstivādins hold that liberation arises solely from initial cultivation;
one must first rely on a portion of liberation to effect the abandonment of hindrances.
The spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are exclusively results,
because they are cultivated last.
The spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) pertain to both cause and result.
Because they are cultivated prior to the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) after liberation,
it is just as stated in the Abhidharma texts.
In this context, liberation is taken as the fruit,
while the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are taken as the causes;
this is consistent with the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
It is said that those universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) serve as the cause and liberation (vimokṣa) serves as the fruit;
the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) encompass both cause and fruit and are cultivated subsequently.
If it is already thus according to this sequence, it is the same as this treatise.
Furthermore, the Abhidharma states:
"The path of ultimate liberation."
The Sarvāstivādins define it in terms of the initial stage;
that is, the first cultivation and initial practice.
At the time of such cultivation, liberation is taken as the primary focus.
Therefore, the Abhidharma states that one undertakes cultivation based on liberation,
because one abandons hindrances based on liberation;
the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, however, refers to the latter.
This means that at the time of final consummation, because one must achieve the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
liberation (*vimokṣa*) is only then fulfilled;
for liberation is taken as the fruit.
This statement identifies the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) as the path of purification for liberation.
The Abhidharma also states:
"If the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are fully accomplished..."
Liberation is itself the ultimate.
This statement is made from the perspective of the time of finality.
It is in this way that they are harmonized herein.
This is the great principle;
even a literal reading of the text confirms it.

The *Śāstra* states: "Furthermore, all liberations are manifested by liberation from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); for this reason, it is said that the minds of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others are liberated from the cognitive obstructions."
This is the transformational and non-transformational [feeling] born of maturation;
it is the pure, indeterminate dharma.
Because it obstructs the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*),
it is of the nature of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, it is associated with both defiled and non-defiled feelings.
However, because it merely obstructs the knowable,
it receives the name "obstruction to the knowable.
The followers of the Two Vehicles eliminate this.
This is called the abandonment of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

As the treatise states: "Briefly, by means of the cultivation of characteristics and so forth, one attains the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)," referring here to the attainment of craving (*tṛṣṇā-samāpatti*).
First, having emerged from meditative concentration, one then craves past attainments (*samāpatti*).
Second, or perhaps not yet having realized [the future], one craves the flavor of the future,
craving the future concentration.
Either one has already attained the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) and relishes the future fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*),
or one has already attained the lower grade.
Regarding those of superior attachment to the flavor of pleasure:
by the predominant power of that attachment to the flavor,
they pursue future meditative concentrations and so forth.
And one gives rise to a relish for it.
Third, having attained either the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) or the fundamental stage (*maula*) and so forth,
one enters into and emerges from the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*).
The mind resembling meditative concentration does not abide in a state of distraction,
yet it gives rise to attachment and relish;
the following explains away this objection.
Upon emerging from meditative concentration, one may give rise to attachment to its flavor;
while actually in concentration, there is no such attachment to flavor.
Attachment to flavor is defilement.
Because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is wholesome, the treatise states:

"If one is born in a lower stage and gives rise to craving for a higher stage, yet has not attained detachment from desire and lacks a mind of non-concentration (*aniyata-citta*), it should be known that this craving is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)."
Regarding the three aforementioned aspects of attachment to gratification (*āsvāda*),
the first— the attachment to gratification not yet attained—
is precisely the craving of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-rāga*).
One gives rise to craving for the higher realms by taking them as an object-condition;
thus, they serve as an object-condition for another realm.
Alternatively, this differs from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which takes the seeking of higher meditative concentrations as its object-condition.
All these are termed "desire for wholesome dharmas," because within their minds there is both defilement and non-defilement,
as indicated by the characteristics of the text.
This is identical to the fifty-ninth [case] above:
the higher stage and the lower stage, as well as the upper and lower objects, mutually serve as conditions for one another.
This is also described as "I shall attain it at that time."
Such attachment to flavor is precisely that which takes the higher [realms] as its object;
it is called the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of one's own mind. This refers to those who have not yet attained [the state beyond] regression.
One is called "receding" because one is unable to give rise to the attainment of dharmas not yet attained;
"receding from what has already been attained" refers to the arising of afflictions after having already attained those dharmas; and "receding from practice" refers to...
The non-arising of dharmas already attained is called "retrogression. Question: What is the distinction between the latter two types of retrogression?
Answer: It is explained that although a noble one (*ārya*) has severed the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*), they may retrogress such that the afflictions arise and manifest before them.
One loses all merits;
this is called "regression from what has already been attained.
This refers to whatever merits belong to the noble ones (*ārya*).
They cannot arise simultaneously.
This is called "retrogression from practice," because one merely refrains from giving rise to afflictions.
This is not the same as the "regression from what has already been attained.

The *Śāstra* states: "If it is the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*), one should know that its objects of focus (*ālambana*) are pervasive (*vyāpyālambana*) or untainted (*anāsrava*), and so forth.
This refers to the three paths—the preparatory (*prayoga*), the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and the liberation (*vimukti*)—based on the access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) of the four dhyānas.
One contemplates the six lower stages as defects and the higher stages as tranquility;
this occurs only during the fourth path of superior progress.
Alternatively, taking as an object the pervasiveness of selflessness in all phenomena is with outflows;
alternatively, taking it as the clear realization of the truths is without outflows.
Regarding those that take the higher stages as their object:
this contemplation is untainted (anāsrava),
whether one intends to abandon [the defilements] or to observe them.
Whichever stage this may be,
all uncontaminated [states] are included therein.
Regarding the inclusion of the seven mental attentions within the four paths, one should cross-reference them with the characteristics cited in the ninth chapter of the Abhidharma.

The treatise states: "If one knows that the meditative concentration manifested by the doors of liberation—emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness—which are subsumed under the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), is the fourth [dhyāna], it should be understood as supramundane concentration."
The stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The doors of liberation such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth are without outflows (*anāsrava*) on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
because it is by means of the stage of penetration that one attains emptiness and the others.
Regarding what is subsumed by the term "speech," although there is emptiness and so forth within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, [it is not the case that it is not subsumed].
It is not called a gate of liberation.
How is this known?
As stated in the second fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*:
This is because it is said that the gates of liberation consist exclusively of untainted cultivation;
just as the presentation of the "levels of discernment" (nirvedhabhāgīya) is able to induce that which is comprised by the acquisition of the untainted.
This refers to the cultivation of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) because they are obtained by depending on those [levels].
"Depending" means having the aspiration to rely upon them.
This means that one seeks those [objects],
taking what is sought as the basis.
This continues up to the point where one cultivates [the meditations] and so forth in order to attain the preliminary stages (*sāmantaka*) of the first [dhyāna].
Furthermore, because the emptiness and so forth within the stage of "decisive distinction" (nirvedhabhāgīya) constitute the supramundane practice of liberation,
it is called the fourth supramundane meditative absorption (dhyāna).
Because they are named according to their fruition, practice, and understanding,
they are called "gateways to liberation.
Among these, the first is the primary meaning.
The following is a general explanation.
Regarding the statement that Bodhisattvas of the distant stages (*dūrabhūmi*) are able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
one interpretation of its great significance states:
The seventh stage is "Far-Reaching" (Dūramgamā),
for it is only by practicing the signless (animitta) that one is able to enter it.
Prior to the sixth stage,
one still gives rise to afflictions and does not subdue the hindrances to meditative concentration.
The Bodhisattva who has entered the seventh stage has suppressed all afflictions of the three realms and attains that meditative concentration.
This is spoken from the perspective of the most eminent cases;
in reality, as stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*,
one may also enter directly into the first bhūmi.
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle Eight:
Although the stages are seven,
one is able to enter them moment by moment.
He understands "great discernment" (*mahā-vicaya*).
Furthermore, he understands this term "distant stage" (*dūra-bhūmi*) as referring to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).
It is called the "Distant Ground" because it is practiced through preparatory application (*prayoga*),
not because it is the ground of "Far-reaching Travel" (*dūramgamā*).
The treatise states that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are unable to enter it.
This refers to the Bodhisattva’s ability to enter;
because one who enters the stages is precisely a Bodhisattva,
it is like the distant ground.
This is the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Although the bodhisattva gives rise to supramundane wholesome dharmas,
he causes this concentration to manifest before him.
By virtue of skillful means for benefiting sentient beings,
one does not abandon afflictions,
but gives rise to the mind [of awakening] without interruption.
The old explanation states that it is because they retain their afflictions;
this is a hollow claim.
Here, the discussion is based on those who proceed directly.
This is because those who take circuitous routes may also attain it prior to that stage.
Furthermore, the *Great Meaning* (*Da yi*) states:
"The distant stage" refers to—
Those who have entered the stage of the ten levels of understanding (*daśa-vyavakīrṇabhūmi*) also attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
This absorption of cessation is a semblance of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Its nature is that of being with outflows (*sāsrava*).
When it is now said that it is neither an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) nor something with outflows,
this does not refer to all ordinary persons.
And there are also those who possess mundane outflows (*sāsrava*) in a general sense;
these may be ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) at the stage of entering [the path],
who attain [this state] by conceiving the notion that it is *nirvāṇa*.
If a bodhisattva attains the concentration that subdues hindrances,
they may attain it as either contaminated (sāsrava) or uncontaminated (anāsrava).
The two vehicles are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*);
this is because they cannot suppress the acquisition of meditative hindrances (*samādhy-āvaraṇa-prāpti*).
However, there is no contradiction if they were to sever the acquisition of meditative hindrances from the fourth dhyāna upward.
Because this is not within their sphere of activity,
it is conventionally designated as "neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
This is because they abide in the fulfillment of the path of training.
Because it is attained through the fulfillment of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*),
it should also be called both "with-learning" (*śaikṣa*) and "without-learning.
As for the six kinds of mental attention (*manasikāra*):
Among the four types of mental application, such as right knowledge (*samyak-parijñā*) and so forth,
the second consists of three mental applications as described in the text;
these are those that have been abandoned as mentioned above.
This can be understood by seeking it out.
As for "relying on the three bases," this refers to the higher mind (*adhicitta*).
First, the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection;
second, the stage of cultivating and purifying karma;
third, the wisdom that does not share the three conditions with non-Buddhists.
This refers to the dharmas of the three lower stages.
Regarding the purity of the four fruits:
this refers to the non-arising of afflictions in the four subsequent stages.
These are the five fruits of purity.
Through the tranquility and liberation of the four dhyānas,
one attains the formless attainments and enters the attainment of cessation.
The attainment of cessation is the liberation of tranquility. Regarding the nine fruits:
these consist of the first three among the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, as well as the six supernormal powers (abhijñā).
"Not attaining the fourth fruit" refers to the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).
In the concluding passage below, there are five instances of the word "because" (*hi*). Regarding "purity in the non-concentrated states" (*asamāhitabhūmi-viśuddhi*):
This immediately severs the four preceding types of impurity in the non-concentrated stages,
namely, the impurity of violating the precepts and so forth.
Regarding "purity of the stage":
One should attend to it in this way:
that there is a lower realization of joy and bliss,
up to the point of fully comprehending impermanence and so forth.
Regarding "comprehension through purification," this refers to the fact that,
by relying on the three bases such as the *adhicitta* (higher mind),
one comprehends all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
The latter two [cases] may be understood.
As for Mahākauṣṭhila,
he is what was formerly called Mahākauṣṭhila.
*Mahā* means "great.
*Kuṣmāṇḍa* is translated here as "belly" (*tu*);
*ra* is translated here as "to hold" (*chi*).
He is none other than Mahākauṣṭhila;
he is the maternal uncle of Śāriputra,
the brahmin Dīrghanakha.
The interior of the belly signifies the meaning of the Three Piṭakas.
Because he upholds the meaning of the Three Piṭakas, he is named Mahodara-dhara (Holder of the Great Belly).
[He possesses] liberation through wisdom and liberation of mind.
Each [of these] is either with-outflow (sāsrava) or without-outflow (anāsrava). This is the text of this single sūtra;
herein, it is termed "the mundane" and "wisdom."
First, the liberation of the mind through contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) is clarified;
next, the liberation of the mind through uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is clarified.
From this point on, it proceeds based on liberation through wisdom.
...up to: "Precisely by the predominant power of liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*),
as explained above regarding the liberation of mind through impure wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*),
from that which proceeds by means of supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-prajñā*)..."
This clarifies the liberation of the mind through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā-vimukti*).
First, it clarifies that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*);
herein, from "based on liberation through wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukti*) onwards, [it clarifies the latter].
Furthermore, based on the liberation of the mind, one clarifies wisdom through higher insight;
furthermore, based on the liberation of the mind, one clarifies the mind through lower insight.
Within the context of clarifying wisdom:
first, the object of wisdom is clarified;
below that is its essential nature.
The essence of clear wisdom can be understood;
it is likewise so within the liberation of the luminous mind.
First, the defiled and purified mind is elucidated; next,
the fruit of the liberation of the mind is elucidated,
namely, that which follows the passage beginning with "Furthermore, based on the liberation of the mind."
The capacity to apprehend and discern,
which clarifies the mind as it is defiled or purified,
is precisely the objective sphere of form and so forth.
The mind that grasps;
that worldly wisdom;
and the fruit of liberation of the mind—these are the lower [categories].
Upon arrival, because of the predominant power of wisdom-liberation (*prajñā-vimukti*),
the fruit of liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*) is clarified;
that is to say, by virtue of the power of mundane wisdom (*laukika-prajñā*) from previous lives.
That mind emerges from both the bondage of association and the bondage of objects;
as for what is meant by "association":
"Correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*) is bondage;
"intermingling" (*saṃsarga*) is the bondage of conditions (*pratyaya*).
Furthermore, as for "correspondence":
Defilements arise simultaneously;
they arise in mutual admixture and in successive succession.
This is the fruit of mundane liberation of mind.
It can be associated with non-defilement and arise intermittently;
it is not something separated from conditions, bonds, and so forth.
If it were separated [from them],...
This is precisely the fruit of the untainted liberation of mind.
The untainted liberation of wisdom and the liberation of mind also both take the two types of objects as their domain.

Regarding the characteristics of the fruit (*phala-lakṣaṇa*), the treatise states: "Furthermore, it should be known that the characteristics of the fruit of supramundane right view (*lokottara-samyag-dṛṣṭi*) are precisely the permanence of the preceding and succeeding [moments], and so forth.
Below this, it clarifies that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the fruit of right view.
Therefore, it is said to be permanent.
If one says "the phenomena that are the objects of antidotes," this excludes conditioned phenomena, which are not permanent.
One interpretation states:
"If it is a dharma" refers to all things collectively designated by the name "dharma."
If that which is to be abandoned were to arise and not subsequently cease— that is,
if the afflictions to be abandoned were to persist—
then there would be no path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga).
Once it has arisen, it does not perish while coexisting with the afflictions.
If that which is to be remedied were non-existent at the time of its cessation, yet there were still something arising,
this would mean that the affliction to be remedied was already absent.
Once the path of uninterrupted transition and the afflictions have both ceased together,
the path of liberation arises;
this constitutes the relationship between the object to be abandoned and its antidote.
Because there is cessation and arising,
one should know that because there is a counterpart, it is not permanent.
Furthermore, as for the interpretation of "if a phenomenon":
This is the dharma of the Truth of the Path.
As for that which is to be remedied, if it exists,
it refers to the period prior to the diamond-like mind (*vajra-citta*).
Up until the attainment of the path of seeing,
because the afflictions still persist,
they are termed "the existence of that which is to be remedied."
The path prior to the vajra-like mind and so forth are called "non-extinguished once arisen," because they arise repeatedly.
Because it is currently capable of arising;
at the time of the subsequent vajra-mind,
all afflictions no longer exist as objects to be remedied.
Because, after the cessation of the previously attained path,
the path of the perfected fruit arises,
it is said that "having ceased, there is arising."
This Truth of the Path is called impermanent because it possesses arising and ceasing;
since the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is not this [truth], it is permanent.
Here, "this" specifically excludes only the Truth of the Path.
If one does not generate the vajra-mind prior to [generating] the equal resolve,
one may fail to attain the Mahāyāna.
How could that which is to be remedied exist once it has arisen, yet not be extinguished, while being accompanied by the afflictions of the path?
Regarding "among all feelings and among causes and conditions": [this refers to the fact that] within the various feelings and within the causal conditions, [the afflictions persist].
Contact is the causal condition for craving;
conditioned by it, craving, grasping, and so forth arise.
Therefore, there is future birth.

The treatise says: "Furthermore, because those [factors] are intermingled and associated, one should know that the mental factors which depend upon them become pure; thus, they are not defiled by present conditions, for they experience those [objects]."
This explains right view;
there is no distinct meaning for its fruit.
As for the treatise stating, "because of the six kinds of tranquility":
This refers to the three occasions of the mind emerging through distancing, and the three occasions of the mind emerging through proximity and tranquility.
It is because the purified consciousness dissolves into equality, and not because its basis [the ālayavijñāna] is equal. Thus it is said.
This explains the superior function within the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
That is to say, together with the attainment of cessation,
the untainted and pure consciousness subsides into equanimity.
Because it does not arise from preparatory effort (*pūrvaprayoga*) and because it is equal to the body that serves as the basis for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
it is called the "attainment of cessation. Regarding the three modes of activity and non-activity:
When emerging from meditative absorption,
one first initiates mental activity,
followed by physical activity.
Subsequently arising verbal formations do not exist now in meditative concentration;
you cannot maintain that there are bodily formations and other such factors within mental concentration.
In the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*,
"understanding that which is to be remedied" refers to understanding [and overcoming] passionate attachment.
Thereafter, there is no further delight;
because one understands and perceives defilement, one is unable to realize [the truth].
The three aggregates are established in order to counteract the three kinds of defilement.
The first is the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha);
the next is the aggregate of meditative concentration (samādhiskandha);
and the last is the aggregate of wisdom (prajñāskandha).
These three aggregates themselves encompass the Eightfold Noble Path.
Furthermore, there are four aspects for understanding their basis.
The first is easily understood.
As for the second characteristic, it is the essential characteristic of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to their intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
The "three objects of focus" (ālambana) refer to the meditative objects (samādhi-viṣaya).
Regarding the "causes and conditions for accomplishment": this refers to the causes and conditions for attaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

It is also said that concentration is the cause and condition for accomplishing all meritorious qualities (*guṇa*); "understanding these qualities" refers to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and so forth. Furthermore, there are five types of this.
This refers to the cessation of phenomena;
that is, it is the functional essence of meditative concentration (samādhi), which is not associated [with the object],
and constitutes the capacity of the seeds of the mind of revulsion (nirveda).

Regarding the phrase "because it is a similar image of the tranquility of the extinguished entity," this means that one knows concentration is conventionally existent and does not possess a substantial reality.
However, because it is a similar image,
and furthermore because one understands that this meditative concentration intends to enter into and take nirvāṇa as its object—
nirvāṇa being the truly quiescent dharma.
Concentration resembles nirvāṇa;
it is the image of tranquility.
This is the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
Although it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
it is called a "reflection" because it resembles *nirvāṇa*. The eightfold contemplation of the signs is as described at the end of the eighth chapter of the *Mūlabhūmi*.
This is also as explained at the end of the fifty-third [fascicle].
Here, "relative" refers to designating pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) in contrast to painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*).
It is neither pleasant sensation nor painful sensation;
this consists of three pairs of opposites,
as explained in the fifty-sixth [sūtra].
Comparing these relative to one another:
regarding the "entanglement of sleep" (*middha-paryavasthāna*), it is called the entanglement of sleep because one enters meditative absorption due to the cause of sleep.
As for the characteristics of the five kinds of antidotes:
1. Being far removed from the signs of darkness;
2. Reaching the principle of application;
3. Destroying all views.
The fourth is the function of all views;
the fifth is the function of the basis upon which all views rely.
The first is the cultivation of radiance characterized by the departure from darkness.
The second is to eliminate lethargy by taking pure objects as one's focus;
the third is to diminish various views so that one does not give rise to dogmatic attachment to views or other such views;
the fourth is to perceive the efficacy of spiritual practice.
This refers to that which can give rise to unwholesome conduct and the sixty-two views;
it is now being treated.
The fifth is the vision based on effort,
which is the merit of that vision.
Regarding the five kinds of dharmas that sustain meditative concentration:
First is seclusion;
this concentration is the seclusion from afflictions.
Second is the place of seclusion.
That is to say: the place for practicing meditative concentration;
the teachings conducive to concentration;
and the third, the requisites conducive to an undefiled mind.
That is, the bedding at the edge.
Fourth, from "by one possessing wisdom" downwards;
fifth, from "in all the worlds" downwards. Furthermore, another interpretation takes "seclusion" and "the place of seclusion" as the first [point].
1. Following the undefiled mind, there are two below; 2.
from "possessing suffering" onwards, there are three below; 3.
regarding all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), there are four below.
The preceding fifth [section] is divided into two parts,
because untainted conduct (*anāsrava-caryā*) constitutes the fifth.
Below follows the section on "Departure from the World" (*niḥsaraṇa-dhātu*).
This means that three persons each cultivate one mode of appearance (*ākāra*).
As in the case of the three characters below, person and phenomenon are explained in combination;
therefore, there are six.
This realm of renunciation is itself nirvāṇa;
it consists of the six factors conducive to nirvāṇa.
This is called the sixfold cultivation. Furthermore, it is explained that three types of persons practice six modes of conduct.
These six modes of conduct constitute the sixfold renunciation;
specifically, the first type of person cultivates four modes of conduct.
The remaining two each constitute one practice:
namely, cultivating loving-kindness toward those who act as enemies,
and giving rise to compassion toward those who commit evil deeds.
To give rise to joy toward those who practice pure conduct and to give rise to equanimity toward those who practice acts of kindness—
both are termed the concentration with sentient beings as its object.
This constitutes the fourth [type].
Taken together as one,
it is because the meditative concentrations focused on sentient beings are identical.
The second is the concentration on the dharma as object;
this refers to those possessing the roots of goodness conducive to liberation.
The third is the cultivation of the contemplation of the truths.
These are the persons possessing the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
Because they take the Dharma as being in accord with the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, there are six types.
Although three types of persons are mentioned, [the sixfold classification is established].
Because of the three modes of the Dharma and because there are six distinctions in the objects of focus,
there are six conforming dharmas.
In the sixty-third fascicle, within the section on the three characteristics of impurity:
as for "concordant outflow" (*niṣyanda*),
it has the characteristic of being a concordant outflow of excrement and filth.
The first is the substance itself, which is excrement and filth;
the second is that which is a derivative flow (nisyanda) of excrement and filth;
the third consists merely of the four great elements and the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa), including both the support and that which is supported.
There are eight causes and conditions for abandoning a disciple who observes the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling precepts):

1. Because of hatred toward the disciple; 2. Because one desires to receive honor for oneself; 3. Because of gain and offerings; 4. Because of the transgression of precepts; 5. Because of following [the path of] abandonment; 6. Because there is someone who benefits the teacher; 7. Because it is necessary; 8. Because of the teacher’s own [afflictions].

One who diminishes [the Teacher] does not require these four: [1] precepts, [2] five [faculties], [3] concentration, [4] six [perfections], [5] wisdom, [6] the affairs of disciples, [7] the affairs of the great assembly, and [8] the affairs of the Saṃgha;
such a person is unable to endure them.
Although he is well-versed among the great assembly,
for the sake of his disciples, he cannot endure [their faults]. Furthermore, another interpretation is that "hating and despising disciples" constitutes one [offense],
while "abandoning them" and "gain and honor" combined constitute the second.
The remaining six are the same as before.
Regarding the obstacles to the first dhyāna herein,
they differ from the text of the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (Śrāvakabhūmi) as follows:
As stated in the ninth chapter of the Abhidharma,
among the objects to be abandoned by the four dhyānas,
the first dhyāna eliminates suffering.
The phrase "the two concentrations also exclude suffering" means that the first excludes the active manifestation [of suffering],
while the second severs the forceful tendencies of the latent predispositions (*dausthulya*).
The third object of abandonment:
as for the "three kinds of exultation," this refers to superior joy (*prāmodya*).
The former is the essence;

the latter is the predominant function. Furthermore, it is explained that this is the attention (*manasikāra*) which takes joy as its object, giving rise to an extreme state of mental application and exultation.
This joy has a nature of inferiority because it follows unskillful wisdom;
since [this wisdom] is absent in the second dhyāna, [the joy] does not exist there.
It is said that this excludes a state of inferiority;
within the first and second dhyānas,
this joy exists and cannot be described as inferior.
However, it can also be attained part by part.
Excluding those of inferior nature, for one who has awakened to the bliss of the fourth dhyāna,
this refers to the mental attention directed toward that bliss.
Because pleasure reaches its ultimate limit,
the designation "attention as a condition" is called "arousing realization.
As the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
It refers to awakening through conditions.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states it refers to the mental application (*manasikāra*) of joy.
The treatise says that the factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*) are established as an antidote to the practice of self-inflicted suffering.
First, it is the antidote to deficiency.
As for "antidote," it refers to the afflictions of asceticism.
Because it can counteract the noble path and cause the noble path to become deficient,
this affliction is termed the "counteractive factor of deficiency."
Vitarka and vicāra are able to counteract these;
this is called "antidote" (pratipakṣa).
The terms "deficient," "diminished," and so forth are easily understood.

The treatise asks: For what reason is it known that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) has not yet been abandoned in the first dhyāna? It answers: Because the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of that category has not yet been removed. If the faculty of suffering were abandoned, there would be no distinction between one dwelling in the first dhyāna and one dwelling in the second dhyāna.
Daiyi said: "In the first dhyāna, the coarse and heavy faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) is also present;
it is only upon attaining the second dhyāna that it is completely exhausted."
Regarding the phrase "the heaviness (dausthulya) of that category" and "not yet free from heaviness":
this refers to the unserviceability (akarmanyatā) of the basis [of consciousness] as it corresponds to that [category].
However, because the three consciousnesses still remain in the first dhyāna,
joy is not yet perfected and the coarse and heavy afflictions are not yet exhausted.
Because the three consciousnesses are concordant with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*),
whereas joy (*prīti*) is directly opposed to the faculty of suffering;
and because the three consciousnesses do not exist in the stage of the second dhyāna.
Because joy is completely fulfilled,
and because the coarse and heavy (dausthulya) elements are eliminated; thus,
in the first dhyāna, if one is free from the coarse and heavy nature of suffering.
This would mean that joy is fully present;
because joy is fully satisfied, the three consciousnesses would not exist,
and thus it would be no different from the second dhyāna.
This refers to the severance of the heavy residues (dausthulya),
outflows (āsrava), and the nature of dependence (āśrayatva) that exist above the faculty of suffering;
it does not mean the severance of seeds or their association with consciousness.
Because it has already been severed previously.
If it were an unwholesome seed,
one could say that it was severed in the first dhyāna because it coexisted with the afflictions.
If it concerns wholesome or indeterminate [states],
even an Arhat may still give rise to them;
as for what is now called "abandoned," [it refers to those that have been severed].
It merely severs the nature of gross heaviness (dauṣṭhulya) of the higher realms;
it is like when black iron enters fire,
its black color immediately vanishes.
Because it arises as red,
once the fire has emerged, it becomes black again;
this is because the red color has ceased.
This is also like that:
having attained entry into the second dhyāna,
the coarse and heavy faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) is extinguished.
The three consciousnesses do not arise because the joy of the fulfillment of the untainted (anāsrava) arises;
this occurs when emerging from the second dhyāna and descending into the first dhyāna, and so forth.
Because there is no further arising of satisfaction from the black [state],
the corresponding dharma is thus:
the second dhyāna with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Because one lies prostrate upon the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the outflows (*sāsrava*),
the two dhyānas free from outflows (*anāsrava*) eliminate this coarse heaviness of suffering,
due to the presence of untainted joy (*anāsrava-prīti*).
Therefore, this is not possessed by those such as the non-regressing ones (avaivartika).
This entry into the first dhyāna involves coarse and heavy birth.
The treatise states: "Furthermore, there are four kinds of cultivation of samādhi," and so forth.
Daiyi said:
"The first refers to those in training who have seen the truths and abide in the future dhyāna."
Seeking the fundamental dhyānas:
the second [case] refers to an ordinary person who has already attained meditative concentration but has not yet attained the five supernormal powers.
This refers to those seeking the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) of the wisdom regarding birth and death, and so forth.
The third [category] consists of those with dull faculties who have realized the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*),
who dwell in the fundamental dhyānas while seeking sharp faculties.
The fourth [category] consists of those who have already seen the truths and seek the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Why,
in this context, are there no dull-witted individuals among those who have seen the truths?
Dwelling in the preparatory dhyāna (anāgamya),
one seeks the fundamental stage and those of sharp faculties.
For what reason do ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) not seek the vision of the truths?
One who has seen the Truth does not seek the five supernormal powers;
such a person as this is, for the time being,
fully encompassed by those aforementioned unrighteous practices.
Furthermore, those of dull faculties who have realized the truths (dṛṣṭiprāpta) and abide in the future [attainment] are unable to seek entry into the fundamental [dhyāna].
Regarding those who turn toward benefit:
initially, their faculties are dull and their progress is slow;
therefore, they are treated briefly and not discussed in detail.
It does not mention ordinary beings or those who have seen the truths,
because they take the attainment of the five supernormal powers as sufficient;
herein, for the time being, the supernormal power of knowledge regarding birth and death is cited as preeminent.
Because he knows the causes, effects, and events of the future,
he never speaks of others who lack the five supernormal powers, such as the vision of the truths.
There are also those who possess the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Because they both seek the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*),
their objects of focus (*ālambana*) consist of immeasurable sentient beings.
This refers to having already attained the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) that take sentient beings as their object.
The *Śāstra* states: "If one proceeds by way of the path of sluggish progress characterized by ease, even though one has already seen the truths and so forth...
[and] furthermore, regarding the sensations, perceptions, and discursive thoughts of the desire realm, one should abide in right mindfulness and arouse right clear comprehension."
That is to say, because of this dull faculty,
one dwells upon the wholesome dharmas of the desire realm through feeling,
perception, and applied thought.
Right mindfulness is the wisdom that discriminates through right knowledge;
it seeks after sharp faculties.
"Feared" refers to the dharma of falling back (*parihāṇadharma*).
"Reception" (*vedanā*) refers to the frequency of receiving;
its meaning is that of experiencing (*anubhava*).
It increases the experience of the pleasure of the dharma of desire.
"Perception" (saṃjñā) refers to the grasping of images within the objective spheres of all phenomena.
"Volition" refers to the simultaneous investigation through sensation and perception;
herein, one gives rise to right mindfulness and perception,
as well as the loss of mindfulness.
One should give rise to correct awareness and develop discerning wisdom.
There are six kinds of detachment from desire,
as explained in the sixth chapter of the Abhidharma.
There are ten types,
which differ according to their expansion and contraction. As for Aśvajit:
The old *Abhidharmakośa* refers to him as Aśva;
in fact, it should be called Aśvajit, which translates as "Horse-conqueror," referring to the bhikṣu who debated with the Brahmā King.

The treatise says: "Furthermore, there is a person who has already attained freedom from desire; having emerged from meditative concentration, at one time his attention proceeds by alternating with the signs of that samādhi," and so forth.
This refers to both ordinary persons and noble ones who,
having attained the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the nine paths of liberation,
abide within the path of excellence.
At times, his mind of superior progress may arise intermingled with a distracted mind.
This distracted mind is either associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*),
because it is comprised within the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and so forth.
Otherwise, it refers to the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection within the desire realm;
or, at certain times,
the purely concentrated mind serves as the path of superior progress.
This is not the path of uninterrupted liberation;
rather, while abiding in the path of superior progress,
if one encounters external conditions such as powerful sounds.
Upon emerging from meditative absorption, the ear-consciousness takes it as its object;
this occurs simultaneously with the sixth consciousness of the mind in a state of concentration.
This is exclusively the ear-consciousness taking it as its object.
Because there is no sixth consciousness that shares the same object of perception as the auditory consciousness.
The treatise states: "It is not the case that the mental consciousness associated with that very meditative absorption can apprehend this sound."
The meaning of this statement is as follows:
for a śrāvaka who has emerged from meditative concentration,
the ear-consciousness and the mental consciousness arise and function simultaneously.
However, because the mental consciousness does not share the same object as the auditory consciousness,
it is said that this mental consciousness is not necessarily associated with meditative concentration.
Regarding the ability to apprehend this sound, it is asked: As stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*,
when any one of the consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, arises,
it necessarily functions simultaneously with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
"How is it that the ear-consciousness arises alone while the mental consciousness does not share the same object?
The commentary explains: "That sūtra refers to the occasion when the five consciousnesses arise together within a state of distracted mind."
They always function together, because there must necessarily be mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Question:

If that is so, how can the seventh [chapter] of the *Abhidharma* state that, because the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) are absent during meditative absorption, [the manas does not arise]?
The commentary states: That treatise relies on the statement that the five consciousnesses are necessarily absent;

furthermore, it relies on the fact that if one is in a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) regarding objects that arise spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*), the five consciousnesses do not arise at all.
If a new object arises and manifests before one, then according to this textual determination,
there exists auditory consciousness within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The Great Master (Dàyì) provides this same interpretation for both cases.
Furthermore, the claim that the five consciousnesses are entirely absent during meditative concentration is incorrect.
Question: If the distracted mind is to be judged by the standard of the concentrated mind, how can this be?
"Furthermore, as for those who possess the five consciousnesses:
do they share the same objects of perception as the mental consciousness? He replied, "No."
Because that which apprehends a clearly manifest object must necessarily be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If there were another condition, [it would not be so].
This would contradict the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* and other texts;
for it would entail the error that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) simultaneous with the five sensory consciousnesses is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
whereas in states of distracted mind, the mental consciousness does not arise concurrently [with the five].
The five consciousnesses do not arise.
If they were to arise, they would necessarily do so simultaneously,
because [the ear-consciousness] hears a powerful object even while in a state of meditative concentration.
The ear-consciousness is able to take the mental consciousness as its object;
because it remains firmly fixed on a single object,
it does not share the same object [as the mental consciousness].
The treatise states: "If it were not so, because one would not perceive this sound, one should not emerge from meditative absorption," and so forth.
This refers to the Sarvāstivādins, who maintain that the five consciousnesses do not exist within meditative absorption.
Now, to refute this, it is said:
If the ear-consciousness arises from within the indeterminate [state] and takes sound as its object,
then regarding this very sound—
Since one does not experience [the object] during meditative concentration,
one should not subsequently emerge from that concentration and abide in a state of distracted mind.
If auditory consciousness exists within meditative concentration,
it is not at that time grasping sound; therefore,
the mental consciousness must have already emerged from concentration.
It is because the ear first receives the sound,
and subsequently, due to the presence of expectation within the mental consciousness,
[the cognition] emerges at a later time.
Furthermore, when the auditory consciousness apprehends sound while one is in meditative concentration,
it does not follow that one immediately emerges from concentration;
rather, it apprehends the sound while remaining within concentration.
It must be auditory consciousness alone;
for even while in meditative absorption, having already perceived a sound,
there remains a desire for further experience.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) subsequently emerges.
These points are all explained according to the school that maintains there are definitely five sensory consciousnesses;
this explanation is as found in a separate transcription.
Furthermore, in the seventh chapter of the Abhidharma,
within the section on the "Mind-Basis" (cittabhūmi),
it says: "It is, for example, like waves depending upon a turbulent current, or like a reflection depending upon a bright mirror."
As stated in the fifty-first [chapter], regarding the two types of liberation and so forth,
from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*),
the eight consciousnesses are of one essence.
Just as waves do not depart from water,
according to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
the eight consciousnesses are each distinct.
Because their applications differ,
as in the interpretations of the two masters in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
This text serves as the proof for this point.
Regarding the meaning of "Great Master":
the sensation associated with the ālayavijñāna is called "maturation" (vipāka).
This is in direct contradiction with the Abhidharma, as explained therein.
The treatise states: "The ālayavijñāna is devoid of afflictions."
This exclusion has no basis;
it can be understood by reflecting upon it.
However, it possesses full constructive conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
The grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) can be established.

It does not exist in the eighth and the fifth [consciousnesses] because they lack this discrimination. Question: Both the fifth and the eighth [consciousnesses] lack both types of discursive calculation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).
Furthermore, there would be no attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha). Since the absence of an object for the attachment to phenomena is the same [for both],
the five consciousnesses should likewise be devoid of afflictions (kleśa).
Answer: The five consciousnesses are likewise led by the mind;
therefore, they possess afflictions. Question: It should also follow that they are led by the mind, and thus could be designated as having the grasping of dharmas.
Attachment to phenomena arises from discursive calculation;
because it is induced by a mind of calculation,
afflictions cannot arise [from it].
Because those of dull faculties are led by it, [the manas] arises.
The treatise states: "The manas is spontaneously associated with the four afflictions, up to and including the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*)."
The *Saddharmapiṭaka* states:
"If one sees that the afflictions of the path of vision are ignorance,
it is called 'unshared' (*āveṇika*)."
That which does not correspond with the afflictions is called "unshared" (āveṇika);
this refers to the ignorance of the manas within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
It arises throughout the stages of all three natures;
for this reason, it is called "unshared" (āveṇika).
It is not that it does not associate with afflictions.
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*:
"Just as with the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*),
so too up to the functioning of the six consciousnesses."
It does not associate with the manas;
thus it should be called "unshared" (*āveṇika*) and so forth.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it is associated with a single category [of mental factors].
It is called "unshared" because it differs from the various consciousnesses.
Guhagupta says:
Just as among the six consciousnesses,
when afflictions take external objects as their conditions,
they are clear and distinct.
When craving and other afflictions are predominant,
the ignorance that arises simultaneously is designated merely as "associated."
The manas takes the internal as its object and is deluded and attached;
it takes an indistinct object as its domain,
and the power of ignorance is strong.
Because the power of views, pride, and so forth is weak,
while ignorance is predominant in its function, it is called "unshared" (āveṇika).
Although it is associated with views, pride, and so forth, [ignorance alone is designated as such].
It is not called "associated" (*saṃprayukta*);
rather, this is established as "unshared" (*āveṇika*) in contrast to the Hīnayāna.
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* establishes in detail: [text follows].
Regarding the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) and so forth: Question:
Why are the unique [afflictions] of view, pride, and craving not included within the *manas*?
Answer: This is only in contrast to the Hīnayāna.
For this reason, ignorance alone receives the designation "unshared" (asādhāraṇa).
It does not take the perceived characteristics as its object like views or pride;
rather, it takes the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) as the self.
According to the interpretation of Master Candragomin,
[the self] is merely the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and not the objective support (ārambaṇa).
This is the general statement.
It is the meaning of the treasury of the True Dharma.
It is the sense of being the "self" for my household;
it is the meaning of protecting the Dharma.
The treatise states: "If all these types [of afflictions] do not manifest in those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa), there are two interpretations regarding this:
grasping at persons and grasping at phenomena.
Thus, Rāma said:
Because the manas-consciousness consists solely of the grasping at a self,
it does not appear in the untainted contemplation of the two vehicles; [in that state],
there is only the eighth consciousness.
The seventh [consciousness] is entirely non-existent.
Master Śīlabhadra stated that there is also grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha).
This is stated in reference to the phenomena obstructed;
since it refers specifically to the grasping at a self (pudgala-grāha), it says that [the path] does not function,
but this does not mean that the grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha) is also extinguished.
As stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*,
because this category [of afflictions] lacks the distinction between coarse and subtle,
they are severed all at once and simultaneously.
Because it does not obstruct the path of cultivation that serves as the remedy for the trainee (*śaikṣa*), the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) effects its severance.

As the sixty-fourth fascicle of the *Śāstra* asks: "What is meant by 'recollection' (*anusmṛti*)? Therefore, one should distinguish the Three Jewels and recollect them according to their respective characteristics, such as the Buddha Jewel and so forth."
Regarding the phrase "up to and including the Buddha, the World-Honored One," this means that the Buddha contemplates them through their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
namely the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and so forth.
The marks of the qualities of omniscience are the jewel of the Buddha;
they consist of other characteristics such as cessation, freedom from desire, the unconditioned, and nirvana.
One recollects the Jewel of the Dharma.
One recollects the Jewel of the Sangha by means of the characteristics of its qualities, such as non-contention (*araṇā*).
The "remainder" refers to the Three Jewels viewed in relation to one another as the remainder;
that is, the characteristics other than those of the Dharma and the Saṅgha constitute the Buddha Jewel.
Regarding such distinctions as these,
the names "recollection of the Buddha" and so forth are further explained as referring to the Blessed One and others.
This concludes the other characteristics, such as the Jewel of the Buddha and so forth.
The *Mahārtha* states:
The treatise says, "Furthermore, for those who seek..."
Seeking the objects of the five desires consists of five types:
first, seeking through appropriation, and so forth.
This extends even to those who seek through skillful means:
such as seeking a wife and children for the sake of support,
or seeking wealth and grain for the sake of enjoyment.
Just as one seeks the requisites for pleasure for the sake of play and enjoyment,
these three [types of seeking] are easy to understand.
Fourth is the seeking of those who lack understanding.
Because one has understood, one seeks understanding.
"Seeking fame and reputation" means seeking renown.
Those who have seeking seek the body of the three realms of existence;
this is not the same as the Lesser Vehicle. Regarding the middle five:
"Those who seek by the nature of things" refers to sentient beings at the end of a kalpa;
it is the nature of things that they are reborn in the higher realms.
Daiyi said: "That is,
it is the natural law that all sentient beings seek a body for future existence."
Second is seeking through aspiration,
which refers to aspiring to be born in such-and-such a place or to attain such-and-such things.
Third is seeking through delusion.
This refers to non-Buddhists and others who seek it because they conceive of the higher realms as nirvana;
this is due to their ignorance.
Daiyi says:
Because of ignorance, one seeks birth in the realms.
This is the fourth: seeking through weariness and aversion.
This is because of the weariness with and aversion toward the lower realms.
The Great Meaning (Dai-i) states:
"It is the weariness with this body and the seeking of a future body."
The seeker who investigates with discernment is one who possesses wisdom and seeks rebirth in the higher realms.
One does not regard this as nirvana.
The Great Meaning (*Mahārtha*) states:
"It is the seeking of birth by deliberating upon a suitable place of rebirth. Regarding the five types of seeking the holy life (*brahmacarya*):
"Only for those who seek" means for those who wish to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The *Mahārtha* says:
This refers to seeking the holy life through the mind of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, there is only the mind that seeks,
but it has not yet been able to give rise [to practice].
Because the holy life (brahmacarya) is difficult to seek,
they have not yet been able to practice it;
those who merely seek it [attain] what is easily obtained.
This means that the cause for initiating practice is called "attainment through cultivation.
The *Dàyì* (Great Meaning) states:
"To separately seek a single matter."
It is called "seeking for attainment through inclination.
One seeks for the sake of attaining through inclination.
As for "seeking for what is presently attained":
Practicing the holy life results in the attainment of fruit in the present;
seeking after [the fruit] results in the attainment of fruit in the future.
Investigative seeking:
this refers to a wise person who, seeking to attain nirvāṇa,
practices the holy life.
Because one seeks the holy life (*brahmacarya*) as the cause for the Path, there is further differentiation within this [seeking].
Regarding the seeking of the conventional designation (*prajñapti*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
the *Mahārthavibhāṣā* states:
To seek oneness through conventional designations refers to the non-Buddhists and others;
to seek oneness through the ultimate truth and so forth refers to [the Buddhist view].
Furthermore, regarding the designation of the conventional and the ultimate as one:
this refers to false brahmacarya,
which is the pursuit of the ultimate through conventional designations.
Because it is not the true holy life (*brahmacarya*),
one investigates and seeks that which is called the true holy life.
Seeking by observing phenomena that are to be abandoned or rejoiced in;
seeking without skillful means,
which refers to seeking liberation through wrong methods.
There is seeking through skillful means;
this is manifest seeking for true liberation.
The *Mahārthaviniścaya* states that there are either three layers of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) or four layers of conventional truth.
This is the gateway of the two truths;
that is to say, there are four conventional truths,
and the ultimate truths are likewise four.
Within the mundane world, there are two types of truth:
first, the truth of conventional designations which lacks substantial reality;
second, the truth of differentiation according to phenomena.
Third is the truth of established realization;
fourth is the truth of the unconditioned as a conventional designation,
which refers to the truth of the ultimate meaning as conventionally established.
Yet there is no essence of dharmas,
because the essence of dharmas is ineffable.
This passage contains only the fourfold conventional truth.
There is no ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
As for the threefold classification established previously,
it was proposed because there are phenomena (*dharmas*) that are suitable for such categorization.
The subsequent establishment of four [truths] is due to their being provisionally designated and established; likewise,
there are those in the West who establish four levels of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) in the same manner.
Relative [truth] is as previously explained.
The conventional and ultimate truths are,
in essence, the aforementioned conventional truth of principle.
It is called "ultimate" (paramārtha) because it is the supreme conventional truth;
it is called "conventional" (saṃvṛti) because it establishes the distinctions of phenomena, such as cause, effect, and dependent origination (paratantra-svabhāva).
Second is the ultimate truth of reasoning (*yukti-paramārtha-satya*).
Its essence is the aforementioned conventional truth of realization;
it is called "reasoning" because it possesses the meaning of attaining the fruit and abandoning the afflictions.
Because it transcends the conventional reality described by the aforementioned principles, it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This refers to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth.
The third is the ultimate truth as realization (*adhigama-paramārtha*).
That very essence is the conventional and ultimate as they are established;
it is called "ultimate" because there exists the sense of "realization," which is designated as "realization."
Because it transcends what was previously realized as conventional, it is called "ultimate" (*paramārtha*).
This fourth [truth] is the ultimate of the ultimate;
that is, the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).
The essence of suchness (tathatā) cannot be established as a conceptual construct;
therefore, it is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha). Among the nine types of knowledge realized through the wisdom attained by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, [it is included therein].
Because it is superior to the previous conventional [truth] and is itself supreme,
it is called "ultimate" (paramārtha).
Within the aforementioned conventional [truth],...
The first conventional truth is exclusively this.
The treatise states that among the three types of pratyekabuddhas,
one has previously already attained the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
"Attaining what has not yet been attained;
attaining what has already been attained.
Regarding these two types of attainment, the former two constitute the emergence from the assembly.
Because they have previously attained the stages of "warmth" and so forth as śrāvakas,
the time for entering the fruit is brief,
and they are unable to practice for a long duration.
Thus, they become those who emerge from the multitude.
If, within the stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), birth is not yet fixed,
one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) after a long period of time.
Those who have turned their minds toward becoming pratyekabuddhas while in the stage of the *nirvedhabhāgīya*,
as well as those persons who have not yet attained the wholesome roots of the *nirvedhabhāgīya*.
The transformation of the mind is likewise so;
because one has practiced for a longer period of time,
the faculties have been refined and sharpened.
In this context, both are termed "not yet attained" and "attained," as explained in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*. Here,
the term "attained" (prāpti) refers to...
The wholesome states of the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (stages leading to penetration) are termed "attainment" (*pratilambha*),
because one has already been able to realize the truth and has acquired the untainted (*anāsrava*) state.
Thus, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth are themselves the attainment of attainment.
Just as one who has not yet attained the fruit is said to be "one who has not yet realized what is to be realized," it is further stated that they have not yet attained the fruit.
Or it may be the third stage;
because it exists within the state of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*),
it differs from the preceding two.
The treatise states: "That which is subsumed under the *mātṛkā* consists of the seventeen grounds and the four kinds of subsumption.
This is the *mātṛkā*."
The term "mātṛkā" (matrix) refers to its meaning.
For example, the *Saptadaśabhūmi* (Seventeen Stages) constitutes the four sections of the *Maulī Bhūmi* (Basic Section),
while the "compendium" (*saṃgraha*) refers to the latter four sections.
The commentary states that because the Buddha’s original sūtras speak of the seventeen stages and the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*),
Maitreya taught them to Asaṅga.
Thus, it is said that the Buddha himself spoke this, which is why it is called the *Mūlamātṛkā* (Root Mother).
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that Maitreya is himself a Buddha,
who taught the seventeen stages (*bhūmi*) and the four types of compendiums (*saṃgraha*) to Asaṅga.
This is precisely the *mātṛkā*, which is called the *mātṛkā*. Regarding "that which is subsumed by both":
this refers to the synthesis of the preceding two.
There are these ten kinds;
namely, the Pitakas and the Mātṛkās. As for the ten kinds:
first, the teaching on the characteristics of the Truths (satya-lakṣaṇa-śāsana).
This refers to the characteristics of the Four Truths and the Two Truths:
knowing suffering, severing the origin, realizing cessation, and cultivating the path.
These four, combined with the aforementioned five, constitute [the ten].
The sixth [chapter] is the differentiation of the categories of the Four Truths.
The seventh is the relationship between the basis and that which is based upon it.
As for the basis:
The first interpretation refers to the cause,
namely the truths of origin and the path;
the basis upon which it relies refers to the fruit.
This refers to the two truths of suffering and cessation.
There is an understanding that the principle of the Four Truths is the basis;
it is spoken in reliance upon this principle.
The teaching is that which relies [upon wisdom];
it is the teaching in which the expressive words correspond to the expressed meaning. The eighth is the teaching on the factors that obstruct thorough knowledge and so forth;
this refers to the teachings on the truths of suffering and its origin. The ninth is the teaching that accords with the Dharma.

This refers to the teaching on the two truths of suffering and cessation. Regarding the tenth [section], the teaching on the faults of not fully knowing and so forth, and the merits of full knowledge:
as for "not fully knowing and so forth,"...
This refers to the teaching on faults;
it is the aforementioned obstacle to the thorough knowledge of the Truth of Suffering and so forth,
because it is not the thorough knowledge of what is wholesome.
This is called "non-pervasive knowledge.
The teaching on the merit of pervasive knowledge is termed the "teaching of pervasive knowledge," which is precisely the aforementioned "teaching in accordance with the Dharma."
The teaching on conventional truth refers to signs,
names, and conceptualization;
the teaching on ultimate truth refers to...
This refers to the Four Noble Truths and suchness; herein,
correct knowledge is not discussed.
Because it is conditioned,
it can be conventional;
because it is untainted wisdom, it is [ultimate].
It may be termed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);
therefore, it is not discussed exclusively here.
This shall be reconciled when we reach the section on the five dharmas.
Śrīparvata is the name of a tree;
it is a corruption of the former term "Śiṃśapāvana."
The Buddha then told Ānanda that the area where the leaves of the forest trees were large or small was where this Hu-tree stood;
the Buddha sat beneath this tree.
If Ānanda were not in the forest,
the sixteen intentions would have as their essence the two factors of desire and resolute conviction.
This is precisely the mental disposition (*āśaya*).
The second, "separation," refers to wearying of and detaching from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);
it is the separation from birth-and-death.
The third is the stage of generating the resolve through exhortation and so forth;
the fourth is the stage of the aids to liberation;
and the fifth is the stage of the aids to penetration.
The sixth causes one to enter the path of seeing;
the seventh is the actual entry into the path of seeing;
and the eighth is the attainment of the fruit and its maturation.
The ninth [topic] concerns the cultivation of meditative concentration after having attained the fruit.

The tenth causes one to attain the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). The eleventh is the Buddha’s specific intention to lead the assembly gradually into [the path], as explained in the twelfth [chapter] of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
This causes one to realize the previous specific meaning and gives rise to joy;
the following may be understood accordingly.
The four types of knowledge regarding concentration are the four aspects of the truth of suffering: suffering,
impermanence, emptiness, and non-self.
This refers to the cognition associated with the four inverted views.
Regarding "because it arises":
it means that there is a dharma of birth that exists separately from the aggregates.
Because of the characteristics of its arising,
the essential nature, the formal marks,
and the functional activities of the self can be known.

The treatise asks: What is the truth of the path? It refers to the path of provisions (*sambhāra-mārga*), the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*), and the path of purification (*viśuddhi-mārga*); these are called the truth of the path.
This is the same as in the eighth chapter of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*, just as it is in the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharma*.
Among those [afflictions] abandoned through seeing and cultivation,
it is said that they are abandoned because the eightfold path, such as the Truth of the Path,
and the preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*) are contaminated (*sāsrava*).
The abandonment through the path of cultivation is as detailed in that commentary.
The treatise states: "Furthermore, these very truths serve as the basis, the support, and the foundation for establishment."
The explanation of the thirteen types of *pudgalas* and so forth is established because the six truths of suffering serve as the basis for their results,
and the truth of origination serves as the basis for their causes.
The Truth of the Path serves as the basis for establishment,
because it brings about the attainment of the stages of those in training (śaikṣa) and so forth;
the Truth of Cessation is not included herein.
Because these are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, these general terms are explained according to their basis and establishment.
It is simply a single entity;
it cannot be separately assigned.
It is precisely the dharma of the three truths.
Alternatively, the four truths are established through distinctions such as the realization of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) by means of skillful methods (*upāya*).
In this regard, the bodhisattva...
They are not born in the formless realm and so forth,
as explained in detail in the *Dharmapada-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Abhidharma), Fascicle 13.
The body of the Tathāgata is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because it transcends the three realms, it is called "inconceivable.
The *Śāstra* states: "The six obstacles" refers to any one of the eleven kinds of obstacles manifesting; these are precisely the twelve obstacles.
Excluding this sixth [obstacle],
taking the five preceding and the six following makes eleven;
these constitute the obstacles to this sixth.
There is no separate entity [between them].

The *Śāstra* states: "The distinction here is that the faculties (*indriya*) are of the nature of the fruit (*phala*), while the elements (*dhātu*) are of the nature of the cause (*hetu*); resolute belief and understanding (*adhimukti-adhigama*) are of the nature of the cause, while the mental disposition (*āśaya*) is of the nature of the fruit."
Regarding the two types— the faculties and the elements—
whether defiled or purified,
they universally employ the five faculties beginning with faith as appropriate.
Furthermore, it has the five feeling faculties (*pañca-vedanendriya*) and the mind faculty (*manendriya*) as its substance. However,
only those in actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) are termed "faculties" (*indriya*),
while their seeds (*bīja*) are termed "elements" (*dhātu*).
Daiyi said: "Alternatively, when initial cultivation has not yet reached fulfillment, it is called a 'realm' (dhātu);
this carries the meaning of increase."
That which has already reached fulfillment is called the "root" (*mūla*).
Because it carries the sense of being predominant (*ādhipatya*), it is called the "fruit" (*phala*);
thus, it is referred to as the "causal fruit."
Yet their essence is not distinct; their nature as faith, understanding, and intentionality is as described in the various treatises.
Whether defiled or purified, they both take the two factors of desire (*chanda*) and resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) as their essence.
All are identical and without distinction;
it is simply that faith and understanding are the cause,
while intentionality is the result.
That which is called "seed" is termed "resolute belief" (adhimukti),
while that which is the "fruit" is termed "intention" (āśaya).
This is the scriptural proof found in various treatises.
Daiyi said: "The very moment one first gives rise to faith and so forth is called 'faith-understanding' (śraddhādhimukti);
therefore, it is the cause."
The subsequent arising of faith and so forth is called "intention" (*āśaya*);
it is thus a result,
and is not to be understood as referring to seeds and the like.
The meaning is as follows.
The treatise states: "Furthermore, there are two kinds of the category of those fixed in wrongness (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*):
first, those who are fixed in wrongness by nature (*prakṛti-mithyātva-niyata*)."
The two types of fixedness in wrongness regarding skillful means are:
first, those who lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*);
second, those who have severed their roots of goodness (*samucchinnakuśalamūla*).
This applies to both those with a nature [for liberation] and those without it.
The *Dàyì* states:
"It is not necessarily the case that those who have severed the roots of goodness and continue in succession are all those who, due to wrong views, have committed the five heinous crimes."
Regarding "because they are fixed in either the right or the wrong":
Da Yi states that there are two kinds of fixedness in the right nature (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
First is the certainty of the fundamental and correct nature;
second is the certainty of the correct nature through skillful means.
The former refers to those individuals who possess the distinct, inherent, and determinate natures of the three vehicles.
Next, this person has already entered the Noble Path;
this is the "Great Meaning.
Furthermore, there are two types of "Indeterminate" [persons].
First, indeterminate by nature;
