second, indeterminate by means.
The former refers to those individuals who possess the lineage of the three vehicles by nature.
First, because within a single person's continuum there exist the seed-natures of the three vehicles;
second, because their skillful means are indeterminate.
The previous explanation has already established that the Noble Path has been attained;
since one now begins to turn the mind toward the Great Vehicle and so forth, entering the preparatory stages (*upāya*),
it is termed "indeterminate" because the preparatory stage itself is indeterminate.
When these predecessors were ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
they possessed the seeds of the three vehicles;
some immediately turned their minds [toward enlightenment].
Alternatively, for those who are either collectively determined or undetermined,
their status is not fixed;
the same applies to those whose nature is subsequently fixed.
This person of indeterminate nature may possess the seeds of all three vehicles,
or possess only two seeds, and so forth.
The Treatise states: "Furthermore, if one correctly understands the gateway to that true meaning, it should be known that one is able to enter the five kinds of 'departure from birth' (*niyāma*).
In the Western regions, the term 'birth' (*jāti*) refers to food that has been stored overnight."
It is like a person who has undigested food remaining in the body;
this can then become a source of affliction.
The afflictions of the path of seeing are likewise;
they act as a source of suffering for birth and death within the body and for sentient beings.
Because the affliction of death has now been severed,
this is "leaving birth" (*niḥsaraṇa*).
This corresponds to the older expression "transcending and leaving birth."
These five all enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The first three are Śrāvakas;
the first is the gradualist (*anupūrvika*).
The next two are the leap-over [attainments],
which can be understood by Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas;
both are termed "leaving birth" (*vairāgya*).
The treatise states: Furthermore, there are five kinds of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*).
First is craving for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatārāga*), which refers to the period before the kalpa [begins].
This is because, as a natural law (*dharmatā*), craving arises for the higher realms,
just like other natural laws.
Second is the craving of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-tṛṣṇā*).
It is not that at this time other vows arise externally to produce that state;
rather, it is through the three types of delusion and craving that outsiders falsely conceive of that state as nirvana.
Fourth is the craving for renunciation,
which refers to the ordinary worldling’s general distaste for lower realms and craving for higher ones.
Fifth is the craving for deliberation.
This refers to noble ones born there,
such as those who progress upward through concentration and wisdom (*samāpatti-vidyottara-gāmin*).
The *Da yi* states:
Now, when it is said that there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*),
it does not necessarily take the two upper realms as its object;
it is sufficient for it to take the internal body as its object.
Regarding those who love the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they love it spontaneously;
this is like the seventh consciousness, which possesses only afflicted attachment (kliṣṭa-sneha).
The love of the vow (*praṇidhāna-preman*): as when one makes a vow,
thinking, "I shall certainly obtain such and such a body and so forth."
The foolish person increases craving through ignorance;
their cycle of birth and death is like that of the non-Buddhists who seek rebirth in the heavens and so forth.
Regarding "one who is weary of and detached from craving," the treatise states:
"one who lacks shame regarding the craving for the dharma of equanimity."
This is to abandon the dharma of receiving [offerings] without shame;
it is to abandon people right now;
this is to feel weary of these matters.
Regarding the object of craving:
as for the analysis of the craver,
it is like the analysis of speech.
Humans and devas are superior;
my Dharma gives rise to them.
Furthermore, they are the seeds of power and craving.
In the commentary on the three types of outflows (*āsrava*), their seeds, forms, and so forth are all categorized as "intermediate.
Regarding the five characteristics of the outflows with taints (*sāsrava*):
the first three correspond to the three realms.
The latter two exist within the five destinies.
The miserable destinies are termed "having no desire-joy and having afflictions.
The fortunate destinies are termed "having joy and having afflictions."

Because the afflictions that arise there have pleasure as their object; herein, regarding the "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*) which has the five sensory objects of the desire realm as its objective support:
if one gives rise to afflictions by taking internal bodies within the desire realm as an object, it is called the "outflow of existence" (*bhava-āsrava*).
The designation "impure body" and so forth applies exclusively to the internal [self],
whereas the objects of desire (kāmaguṇa) mostly exist externally.
Regarding the great meaning:
the two upper realms are called "afflictions with the desire for pleasure," while the desire realm is called "afflictions with desire for pleasure."
Among these, the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) refers exclusively to the ignorance associated with the sixty-two views;
it exists solely within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
These sixty-two views are called "obstructions" because they hinder liberation and so forth,
as explained in the Eighty-ninth [Fascicle].
Ignorance is the primary factor.
This statement that ignorance is in fact [a form of] view is also as explained in the Eighty-ninth [Treatise].
However, in this context, only the views regarding the future limit (*aparānta*) are mentioned, while those regarding the past limit (*pūrvānta*) are not;
for the treatise states: "If one wishes [to know] the outflows of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*..."
"Desire" (chanda) has the meaning of longing.
It arises with a preponderance of longing directed toward the future limit,
not toward the past limit.
Seeing is not termed the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).

This is as stated in the [Abhidharma] treatise in eighty-nine [sections], which says regarding "characteristics": "It is by virtue of the basis (*āśraya*) and by virtue of the mode of activity (*vṛtti*)."
As with consciousness,
here [the two statements] do not contradict one another based on a single meaning.
Taking the faculties as their basis and the objects as their sphere of activity,
they observe consciousness and the other [aggregates] through their own discernment.
The rest may be followed accordingly.
Furthermore,
it is explained that "the ultimate hearing" refers to the evil incantations of the Brahmins.
He said, "If one merely hears this mantra of mine,
one immediately attains merit and the task is brought to completion."
It cannot be explained.
As the Treatise says: "That which penetrates through a single syllable and is realized as eternal is, for example, the syllable 'Aṃ' (or 'A')."
To know [the nature of] letters as permanent is such that they can never be altered or changed,
for this is the very root of letters. To thoroughly penetrate the meaning of letters and realize them as impermanent— this is true understanding.
That is to say, the meaning realized through words can be transformed according to different regions;
because the meaning is established [differently], it is called "impermanent."
Just as the eye is called "eye," it is also called "that which illuminates" or "the path of discernment," and so forth;
these are the meanings based on the etymological derivation of the term.
This is impermanent; therefore,
one should know that names, phrases,
and so forth are likewise impermanent.
Because they are subject to transformation;
furthermore, because these syllables and so forth signify the meaning that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent.
Names and meanings are impermanent.
In the sixty-fifth fascicle, concerning the stage of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*),
two fascicles are exhausted therein.
From the latter fascicle onward,
twenty-nine [stages] are clarified;
at the end of the latter fascicle, the position of the twenty-ninth stage of cessation is established.
Seeking the following passage for clarification,

the *Treatise* states: "Regarding 'the cognition of existence and non-existence as explained in the *Maulī Bhūmi*,' conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena constitute 'existence'."
The absence of self and what belongs to self is called "non-existence.
The treatise states: "If [it were] a substantial entity (*dravya*), a thing (*artha*), or a referent (*artha*)," and so forth.
There is an interpretation that the first reason among these proves the existence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
This second reason proves that the perfected nature exists;
such names as these are alternative designations for *tathatā* (suchness).
There is no other designation for them.
Furthermore, the interpretation of these three "nature" (svabhāva) characters also serves as proof for the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
"Substantial entity" (dravya) excludes that which merely resembles a phenomenon;
"phenomenon" (dharma) refers to its ontological essence (svabhāva);
